en: Now begins the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa:
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Jaya.
Homage to that Varāha who playfully uplifted the earth!
For him, Mount Meru, situated between his hooves, makes a clinking sound.

By Him, who possesses an infinite form and a vast, ancient, and immense body, the earth— surrounded by the oceans and together with its mountains and rivers— was lifted up like a lump of clay upon the tip of His tusk;
He is this very enemy of the demon Kaṃsa, the destroyer of Mura, Naraka, and Rāvaṇa, who dwells within all things.
May Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the gods, and the primordial deity Varāha, drive away my enemies.

He who, like a boat in the ocean of saṃsāra—terrible with the crocodiles and waves of death, old age, and disease—is the remover of fear for his devotees; he who, in the form of a boar, brought an end to Mura, Naraka, and the ten-faced Rāvaṇa;
this Viṣṇu, the Lord of all, whom those of perfected intellect attain here with ease.
May those whose souls are liberated not fall into sin, and may the lord of the earth have the faction of his enemies destroyed.
Sūta said: At that time, when the earth had previously been lifted by Viṣṇu in the form of a boar, she questioned the Supreme Lord with devotion.
The Earth said:
"O All-pervading Lord, in age after age you alone lift me up;
yet, O Keśava, I do not know your true form, nor your primordial creation."
And when the Vedas had been lost, you became a fish, entered the netherworld (rasātala),
retrieved them, and gave them back to Brahmā.
Furthermore, O Madhusūdana, during the churning of the ocean, you supported Mount Mandara with your tortoise form against the onslaught of the gods and asuras.
Furthermore, assuming the form of a boar, the Blessed One indeed lifted me up from the great ocean with a single tusk as I was descending into the netherworld (rasātala).
Hiraṇyakaśipu, arrogant because of the granting of boons,
was struck down by you while he was oppressing the earth;
and Bali, O Blessed One, was bound by you in the form of a dwarf.
Furthermore, O Lord, the earth was previously rendered devoid of Kṣatriyas by you as well,
O Master, having become Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, on numerous occasions.
Furthermore, the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa has been destroyed by the splendor of your kṣatriya power;
yet, O Lord, I do not know anything of your specific deeds.
Having withdrawn me, how do you create the world? And by whom was it created by you?
Once it has been made, by whom is it sustained and protected? (1.12)
"By what means, O Lord, are you easily accessible at all times?
And how, O All-pervading One, could there be a beginning of creation, and how could there be an end? (1.13)
How is the calculation of the Yugas performed, and what is the number of these Anucaturyugas?
What are their specific characteristics, O Maheśvara, and what is their state?
Which kings were performers of sacrifice, and which attained supreme perfection? Be gracious to me and tell me all this in brief.
Thus addressed by him in the form of a boar, the Supreme Lord laughed;
and as he was laughing, the Sustainer of the World beheld [the universe] within his belly.
The Rudras, the gods, the Vasus, and the hosts of Siddhas, together with the great seers.

She beheld all this in its entirety— down to the seven worlds together with the moon, sun, and planets, and all the dharmas contained therein— as long as the earth remained with all its limbs trembling.
When the Great-Souled One was seen by the Earth, whose every limb was stainless, with his mouth opened,
she then beheld him sleeping upon the great ocean in his true form as four-armed.
Seeing Lord Janārdana sleeping on his serpent-couch,
and seeing the four-faced Brahmā situated within his navel-lotus,
the Goddess Dhātrī, with her palms joined in reverence, uttered this hymn of praise.
The Earth said:
Salutations to you, O lotus-petal-eyed one; salutations to you who are clothed in yellow garments;
salutations to the Supreme Self, the destroyer of the enemies of the gods.
Salutations to you, whose chest bears the beauty of the Śeṣa-couch;
salutations to you, Lord of all gods; salutations to you, the bestower of liberation.
Salutations to him who bears the Śārṅga bow, the sword, and the discus, who is devoid of birth and death;
salutations to him whose birth is from the great lotus-seat arisen from his own navel.
Homage to you, who are beautified by hands like sprouts and a face as red as coral!
I have come to you for refuge; I am gracious, so protect me, a woman who is innocent.
O Janārdana, having seen you as a boar with the appearance of a full mass of dark collyrium, I am once again terrified that the entire world has come within the range of your body.
Now, O Lord, show me mercy; save me from this great fear! 1.24
May Keśava protect my feet; may Nārāyaṇa protect my shanks;
may Mādhava protect my hips; and may Govinda protect my private parts.
May Viṣṇu protect my navel, and Madhusūdana protect my belly;
may Trivikrama protect my thighs, and Vāmana protect my heart.
May Śrīdhara protect my throat; may Hṛṣīkeśa protect my face; may Padmanābha protect my eyes; and may Dāmodara protect my head.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Hari and the names of the worlds, he then ceased, having said: "Salutations to you, O Blessed Viṣṇu."
Thus ends the first chapter in the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. || 1 ||
Sūta said: Then Hari, pleased by her devotion, revealed his illusory power (*māyā*) as it entered the body of Dharaṇī and remained there in that very form of a boar.
He said: "O lady of beautiful hips, what is this most difficult question of yours?
I shall explain the subject of the Purāṇas according to all the scriptures. (2.2)
For this is known to be common to all the Purāṇas;
O Earth, having ascertained this verse, listen again to it in its entirety. (2.3)
The venerable Varāha said: "Cosmogony, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manvantaras, and the history of the dynasties— this is the Purāṇa characterized by five marks."
O fair-faced one, I shall first relate the primordial creation,
from which the conduct of the gods and kings is known,
as well as the fourfold eternal Supreme Self.
In the beginning, I was the great void; from that, the single atom arose, and from me, the intellect (buddhi) came into being.
It became threefold through the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, each endowed with its own distinct essential nature.
In that very moment, he became the great darkness;
he is ever called the foremost among all knowers of the truth. Even more than him, the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) became powerful.
Then there arose the thought, "I have come into being. || 2.7 ||

Therefore, O auspicious lady, from those [elements] arose the causes for hearing and the other [sensory functions]; from that, the rosary was established for the world. And by means of the elements and their movements alone, this physical form was fashioned by me out of my own self.
It was void there, but from that [void] arose sound and space; from that, wind, and after that, fire;
from that, water, and after that, O Goddess, you were created by me as the sustainer of beings.
In the yoga of the earth, like water, there arose from that [earth] the embryo (kalala) with bubbles, and indeed the egg;
when that had proceeded and was moving in two directions, I existed as the self consisting of water, at first [creating] the self by means of the self.
Having created those Nārās there, I then [established] myself therein,
so that my name might be "Nārāyaṇa";
in kalpa after kalpa, I enter into that state again and again.
May there be one born from my navel, just like the first [Brahmā], while I am asleep. || 2.11 ||
O Goddess, while I was in such a state, the four-faced one arose from the lotus of my navel; he was addressed by me thus: "O high-minded one, create living beings."
Having spoken thus, I vanished; and he too remained reflecting, O Mother of the World, until he perceived nothing at all.
At that moment, a great wrath arose within Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest;
from that wrath, a boy was born from his own body and stood upon his lap.
He who was crying and restrained by that Brahmā of unmanifest form said, "Give me a name"; he (Brahmā) gave him the name Rudra.
O auspicious lady, having been told by him, "Create this world," he,
being unable to do so, then plunged into the water, resolved upon ascetic penance.
When he had submerged himself in the water, Brahmā again created another Prajāpati, the most excellent among beings, from his right thumb;
and likewise, from his left thumb, he created his wife.
In her, that lord begot Manu Svāyambhuva;
from him, the creation of living beings was formerly brought forth by Brahmā.
Dharaṇī said: O Lord of the Gods, tell me in detail about the primary creation,
and how this one called Nārāyaṇa became Brahmā at the beginning of the Kalpa.
The Blessed Lord said: O Goddess, listen as I describe in its entirety how he, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, created all beings; O Earth, hear this from me. 2.20.
At the end of the past kalpa, having arisen from sleep during an auspicious night,
Brahmā, overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva), beheld the world as empty.
Nārāyaṇa is supreme and inconceivable, the first-born even of the highest beings;
the Lord is of the nature of Brahman, without beginning, and the source of all existence.
And in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa, the divine one whose nature is Brahman, the source and the dissolution of the world: 2.23. [The verse follows.]
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara;
since they were his first abode (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa. (2.24)
As he was contemplating creation just as at the beginning of previous kalpas,
there appeared before him, without his conscious intention, that which consists of darkness (tamas).
Darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, and utter darkness—
this fivefold ignorance has manifested from the Great Self.

The creation that exists in fivefold states, which is devoid of consciousness for one who meditates, lacking external or internal light, with its nature obscured and consisting of immobile beings— this is to be known as the *mukhya-sarga* (primary creation) by the wise who understand the process of creation. || 2.27 ||
Furthermore, as he was meditating upon the supreme creation, another [being] came into being;
because it flowed crosswise, it is indeed known as Tiryakstrotas.
Those such as cattle are well known as those who follow the wrong path;
considering even that to be ineffective, the Four-faced One [Brahmā] directed the stream toward the animals.
The upward-streaming [type] is threefold, being characterized by sattva and proceeding according to dharma; from that arise the gods who move upwards and are born from all types of wombs.
Abounding in happiness and joy, unobstructed both within and without,
there was delight in that creation, and then the progeny were brought forth.
Then, having created another creation, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) reflected,
considering those born from the primary creation and the others to be ineffective.
Then that Lord reflected: "Those who flow downwards are indeed the downward-streaming ones; those born in the downward stream are considered to be human beings, the practitioners. (2.32)
And they abound in illumination, yet are intensified by darkness and dominated by passion; therefore, they are full of suffering and act repeatedly again and again. (2.33)
Thus, O fortunate one, these six creations of yours have been described:
the first is the creation of the Great Principle (mahat), and the second is that of the subtle elements (tanmātras). || 2.34 ||
The third creation, however, is known as the Vaikārika, which pertains to the senses.
Thus, this Prākṛta creation has arisen preceded by intelligence. (2.35)
The fourth is the primary creation (mukhyasarga), for the immobile beings are indeed known as primary;
that which is called the transverse-stream (tiryaksrotas) is described as the transverse-stream creation.

Likewise, the seventh is that of those who flow upwards (ūrdhva-strotas), which is the best; that human creation is the eighth, the creation of grace (anugraha-sarga), and it is characterized by both goodness (sāttvika) and darkness (tāmasa).
These five are known as the modified (vaikṛta) creations, while three are remembered as the primary (prākṛta) ones;
the ninth is remembered as the Kaumāra creation, which is both primary and modified.
Thus, these nine creations of Prajāpati have been fully described;
they are both primary (prākṛta) and secondary (vaikṛta), and are the fundamental causes of the world.
These creations have been told; what else do you wish to hear?
Dharaṇī said:
The ninefold creation was produced from Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest. O Lord, how did it increase? Tell me this, O Acyuta.
The illustrious Varāha said: First, the Rudras and others rich in asceticism were created by Brahmā;
thereafter, Sanaka and his brothers, as well as Marīci and the rest, were created.
Marīci, Atri, as well as Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu,
the highly resplendent Pulastya, Pracetas, Bhṛgu,
Nārada as the tenth, and Vasiṣṭha of great austerity.
By him, Sanaka and the others were employed in the dharma known as *nivṛtti* (withdrawal),
while Marīci and the others were employed in the dharma known as *pravṛtti* (engagement), with the single exception of the sage Nārada.
That Prajāpati who was first born from the thumb of Dakṣiṇa—
by his lineage, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings [was produced] at the beginning.
The gods, the dānavas, the gandharvas, the serpents, and the birds—
all were born from the daughters of Dakṣa, and they were all supremely righteous.
He who was known as Rudra, born from the wrath of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), emerged from his forehead which was furrowed with a frown.
Having a body that was half-woman and half-man, Pracaṇḍa, who was exceedingly terrifying,
vanished once more after being told by Brahmā, "Divide yourself."
Thus addressed, he divided himself into two: womanhood and manhood. He then split that manhood into eleven parts—both tenfold and onefold.
Thus the eleven Rudras, born from Brahmā, became renowned.
O sinless one, this creation of Rudra has been declared by me in brief;
now I shall describe the majesty of the Yugas in summary.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four ages (caturyuga).
Hear now that dharma and action which the great-souled kings who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees, as well as the gods and asuras, performed during this [cycle].
In the past, during the first kalpa, there was Svāyambhuva Manu.
To him were born two sons of superhuman deeds,
named Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, both devoted to righteousness.

There, King Priyavrata, a great sacrificer whose strength lay in austerity, having performed various extensive sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), [attained his goal]. (2.52)
Having established his own sons, Bharata and the others, throughout the seven islands,
he himself went to Viśālā, the bestower of boons, and performed great austerity.
While that king, a universal monarch, was thus established in asceticism,
Nārada approached him there, desiring to see the practitioner of dharma.
O king of kings, seeing Nārada in the sky with a splendor like that of the blazing sun, he then rose up joyfully to greet him.

Having properly offered him a seat and water for his feet, they addressed one another with greetings such as "welcome. At the conclusion of their conversation, the king questioned Nārada, the teacher of Brahman.
Priyavrata said:
O Blessed One, Nārada, tell me of anything wonderful that has been seen or even heard of in this age known as Kṛta.
Nārada said:
O Priyavrata, listen to a single marvel that I have seen.
O Indra among kings, on the day before yesterday, I went to the place called Śveta.
There, on that island, he saw a lake garlanded with blooming lotuses.
On the bank of that lake, having seen a wide-eyed maiden, a girl with long, beautiful eyes, I was struck with wonder. (2.59)
Then, O Indra among kings, I questioned that sweet-spoken lady:
"Who are you, auspicious one? How are you here, and what is your purpose in this place? Tell me, O beautiful one with lovely limbs, what must be done by you, O radiant one. (2.60)
When she had been addressed thus by me, that large-eyed woman, seeing me, remained silent for a moment after reflecting; at that very time, my supreme knowledge [arose].
Indeed, all the Vedas and all the Śāstras have been forgotten,
as well as the Yoga-śāstras, the phonetics (Śikṣā), and the Smṛtis of the Vedas.
"O King, as soon as I saw everything, it was stolen from me by the maiden in an instant.
Thereupon, I was overcome with amazement, filled with anxiety and grief. (2.63)
O King, while I was still seeking refuge in her alone,
I beheld a divine man appearing within her body.
In the heart of that man as well was another, and on his chest yet another,
glorious one with blood-red eyes, resembling the twelve suns.
Having seen it thus, O observer of noble vows, three men there entered the bodies of the maidens; yet in an instant, I no longer saw even one of those maidens there.
Then I asked that princess,
"O blessed lady, tell me how my Vedas were lost and what was the cause of their destruction."
The maiden said:
"I am the mother of all the Vedas, known by the name Sāvitrī.
Because you did not recognize me, the Vedas have been taken away from you."
When she had spoken thus, O King, the ascetic, filled with wonder, asked:
"O beautiful one, tell me who these men are. (69)
The maiden said:
"O beautiful-eyed one, he who resides within my body with all his limbs is indeed the god Nārāyaṇa himself, known by the name of the Ṛgveda."
Having become like fire, it quickly burns away sins immediately after its recitation.
The son who was seen by you in his heart is the mighty Brahmā, existing in the form of the Yajurveda.
Resting upon his chest as well is this one who is pure and radiant;
he exists in the form of Rudra, bearing the name Sāmaveda.
When remembered, he swiftly destroys sins, just like the sun.
O Brahmin, these three great Vedas are remembered as the three gods;
O twice-born one, the vowels beginning with 'a' are indeed the *savana*s here.
All this has been told to you in brief, O best of the twice-born;
accept the Vedas, the Śāstras, and omniscience, O Nārada.
"O observer of great vows, perform your bath in this lake of the Vedas;
by bathing there, O best of beings, you will remember [the events] of another birth."
Having spoken thus, O lord of men, the maiden vanished from sight;
I, having performed my ablutions there, have come here desiring to see you.
Thus ends the second chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. || 2 ||
Priyavrata said: O Blessed One, O Divine Sage, tell me everything regarding that which was his conduct in another birth; for my curiosity is indeed great. (3.1)
Nāradarada said:
O king of kings, after I had bathed in that Veda-lake and heard the words of Sāvitrī, [I beheld] my existence for a thousand births therein.
Recollection arose for me at that very moment; listen to my account of another birth.
"O King, there is a city called Avanti; formerly, I was an excellent brahmin there, known by the name Sārasvata, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. (3.3)
O King, he will have a large retinue of servants and abundant grain;
indeed, he will be possessed of supreme intelligence during that other age known as Kṛta.
Then, reflecting in solitude, I thought: "What shall I do with this?
Having entrusted all these dualities to my sons, I shall go quickly to Lake Sārasvata, having resolved to practice asceticism. (3.5)

Thinking thus, I worshipped Keśava through the ritual section of the Veda (karmakāṇḍa); likewise, I honored the ancestors with funeral rites (śrāddha), the gods with sacrifices, and other beings as well.
Then, O King, having set my mind upon asceticism, I departed from there for that lake named Sārasvata, which is known as Puṣkara.
Having gone there, I worshipped with devotion the ancient Viṣṇu, the Puruṣa, the Auspicious One, performing the recitation (*japa*) dedicated to Nārāyaṇa.
O King, by reciting this supreme hymn consisting of the *Brahmapāra*,
the Blessed One became pleased with me and appeared before my very eyes.
Priyavrata said:
O best of beings, what indeed is the further shore of Brahman? I wish to hear it; please explain it out of grace, O divine sage of tranquil intellect. (3.10)
Nārada said: [I bow to] Viṣṇu, the highest of the high, the immortal, the ancient, the ultimate shore, the supreme, and possessed of infinite valor.
I perpetually bow to the Ancient Being, the ultimate refuge, who has gone beyond all beings.
Ancient, peerless, primordial, both transcendent and immanent, the one who has reached the further shore, possessed of fierce splendor,
and the foremost among those of profound and deep intellect.
I am born [to worship] the divine Hari, the Lord.
The one higher than the highest, the supreme Pradhāna, the abode of the Supreme, the pure state, the vast expanse;
the Lord higher than the highest, the ancient Puruṣa.
With a pure disposition, I praise Nārāyaṇa. || 3.13 ||
In ancient times, that preeminent Puruṣa created this city which was then empty; because he remained there,
he became renowned among people— may he be my refuge.
Nārāyaṇa, free from stain, the ancient one. || 3.14 ||
To Viṣṇu, the further shore, the supreme, whose form is boundless, the ancient one, the foremost among those possessed of statesmanship,
the lord of the earth who maintains forbearance and upholds peace—
I always praise that auspicious one of great majesty. || 3.15 ||

I praise Nārāyaṇa, the immortal Supreme Lord, who has a thousand heads, infinite feet, and many arms; whose eyes are the moon and the sun; who is both the perishable and the imperishable; and who sleeps upon the ocean of milk. 3.16
Accessible through the three Vedas, possessing the single form of the three and nine,
abiding in the three pure states, distinguished by the three sacrificial fires,
characterized by the three principles, manifesting in the three ages, and having three eyes—
I bow to the immeasurable Nārāyaṇa.
In the Kṛta age, he is white; likewise, in the Tretā Yuga, he is the ancient one with a red body;
and similarly, from the Dvāpara onwards, in the Kali age, he is Hari.
And then I bow to him who has made his own self black.
He who created the Brahmins from his very mouth,
the Kṣatriyas from the space between his arms, the Vaiśyas from the pair of his thighs, and likewise the Śūdras from the tips of his feet.
I bow to that ancient one whose body is the universe.
Kṛṣṇa, the supreme beyond the supreme, the object of knowledge who has gone to the further shore, the lord of battles,
who by his very nature wields the mace, sword, and shield in his uplifted hands— him [I salute].
I bow to the immeasurable Nārāyaṇa.
Thus praised, the best of gods, pleased, spoke to me with a voice like the rumbling of clouds:
"Choose a boon," he said repeatedly; then I—
And he desired dissolution into the body of that very [deity]. || 3.21 ||
Having heard these words of mine, O Brahmin, the eternal God of gods spoke to Prakṛti: "Enter this inexhaustible cycle of worldly existence."
A thousand yugas constitute a day of Brahmā; from him you shall originate. Furthermore, he will bestow upon you a name that shall serve a specific purpose.
"Water for men" (nāraṃ pānīyam) is what you have always given to the ancestors;
therefore, your name shall be Nārada.
Having spoken thus, the god immediately vanished from sight on high;
then, by means of asceticism over time, I abandoned my body.
O King, having attained dissolution into the body of Brahmā, he was then born again at daybreak along with ten sons. (3.26)
For that which is the beginning of the day for the god Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, is undoubtedly the beginning of the creation of all beings, including the gods and others. (3.27)
This very creation of the entire world proceeds from the nature of the Lord;
this, O King, is my primordial birth about which you ask me.
Therefore, O King, having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa, I have arrived from the beyond;
therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should be devoted to Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the third chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. || 3 ||
Dharaṇī said:
"O Blessed One, is that Lord Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Supreme Self, [identical] with all beings in every respect, or is he not? Please tell me."
The illustrious Varāha said:
"The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-Lion, and Vāmana;
Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki—these are the ten."
O Upholder of Beings, these forms of his have been described;
they shine like stairways for those who desire to obtain a vision of him. 4.3.
The deities do not behold that which is his supreme form; therefore, they sustain their resolve by beholding him in a form such as our own. (4.4)
Brahmā, by means of his form, [arises] from rajas and likewise from tamas;
by these two, the universe is established and set in motion for its maintenance.
O supporter of the earth, you alone are that god’s first form;
the second form is water, and the third is known as the fiery one.
The fourth form is Vāyu, while the fifth is named Ākāśa.
These indeed are his forms; for those of pure intellect, he is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Likewise, there are three other forms of his; thus, these are the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti).
"O Goddess, this entire world has indeed been pervaded by Nārāyaṇa; thus has it been told. What else do you wish to hear?"
Dharaṇī said:
O Supreme Lord, by your grace, please tell me what King Priyavrata did after he had been addressed in this manner by Nārada.
Śrī Varāha said:
Having divided you into seven parts and bestowed them upon his sons,
Priyavrata performed austerities, his wonder having been aroused by what he heard from Nārada.
Having himself recited the supreme Brahman whose essence is Nārāyaṇa,
he then, with a satisfied mind, attained the ultimate state of supreme Nirvāṇa.
Listen further, O lady of excellent hips, to another account concerning the Supreme Lord,
regarding what occurred in former times while he was striving for the propitiation of a king.
There was a king named Aśvaśiras, supremely righteous;
having performed the horse sacrifice with very abundant sacrificial fees. (4.13)
Then, having performed the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) and surrounded by brahmins,
while that royal sage was still seated,
the illustrious Kapila, the best of yogis, and Jaigīṣavya, the king of yogins, arrived.
Then, rising quickly, that king,
the best of monarchs, filled with supreme joy, performed the rites of hospitality.
Seeing those two of sharp intellect and knowledge of yoga seated upon the honored throne, the mighty king questioned them as they had arrived there of their own accord.
"O two Brahmins, O best of men, I ask you about my doubt:
how may one propitiate the supreme god Hari Nārāyaṇa? (4.17)
The two brahmins said:
"O King, who is this teacher Nārāyaṇa of whom you speak?
O monarch, here we two are both Nārāyaṇas, present before your very eyes."
Aśvaśiras said:
"You two are perfected Brahmins whose sins have been burnt away by asceticism;
how then was this statement uttered: 'We two are Nārāyaṇas'? (4.19)
Janārdana, the great god, holds the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, wears yellow garments, and is seated upon Garuḍa; who on earth is his equal?
Having heard the words of that king, those two brahmins of rigid vows laughed and said, "Look at Viṣṇu, O King! (4.21)
Having spoken thus, that Kapila himself became Viṣṇu,
and Jaigīṣavya was instantly born as Garuḍa.
Then, upon seeing the eternal god Nārāyaṇa mounted upon Garuḍa, that circle of kings instantly broke out into cries of "Alas! Alas! (4.23).
Then, with his palms joined in reverence, the highly illustrious king said:
"Be appeased, O brahmins; this Viṣṇu is not such as this."
From whose navel-lotus Brahmā was born,
and from that Brahmā Rudra arose— he is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord.
Having heard these words of the king, those two bulls among sages then performed a supreme illusion, specifically the power of yoga-illusion.
Kapila, Padmanābha, Jaigīṣavya, and Prajāpati shone there; seated upon a lotus, he was short in stature, and a young boy rested upon his lap.
The king beheld the red-eyed one, whose splendor was like the fire of cosmic destruction.
"The Lord of the Universe does not appear in this manner; this is always a mere illusion for yogis," the king declared, "for the glorious Hari is all-pervading."
Then, at the conclusion of those words in the assembly of that king,
mosquitoes, bedbugs, lice, bees, birds, and serpents [appeared].
Horses, cows, elephants, lions, tigers, jackals, and deer—
indeed, all other animals, both domestic and wild, as well as insects—
are seen by the millions in the royal palace, O Sustainer of Beings. (4.30)
Seeing that assembly of beings, the king was struck with wonder in his mind; and as he reflected, "What could this be?",
he came to understand the greatness of Jaigīṣavya and of the wise Kapila.
Then King Aśvaśiras, with his palms joined in reverence, asked those two sages with devotion: "O best of the twice-born, what is this? (4.32)
The two twice-born ones said:
"O King, we were asked by you how Viṣṇu is worshipped here, or how He is attained, O Great King; therefore, this has been shown to you. (4.33)
O King, these qualities which have been shown to you belong indeed to the Omniscient One;
and that god Nārāyaṇa is omniscient and able to assume any form at will.
It is said that the gentle one, though established somewhere, may indeed be reached by men;
and through his propitiation, his word shall become meaningful.
But the Supreme Self, the Lord of the universe, who dwells within all bodies, is seen within one's own body through devotion; He does not reside in a single location.
For this reason, O King of kings, the form of the Lord, the Supreme Self, has been shown to you so that you may have conviction in both of us. In this way,
O Lord of men, Viṣṇu is omnipresent within your own body.
O King, those who were shown as the ministers, the assembly of servants, the gods and others, as well as the animals and the swarms of insects— they too are pervaded by Viṣṇu.
One should make one's meditation firm, thinking: "Hari is all-pervading; there is no other being equal to Him," and thus serve Him with such a conviction. (4.39)
O King, this true nature of knowledge has been proclaimed to you;
by remembering Nārāyaṇa Hari with a completely devoted heart.
With a mind full of devotion, remember Nārāyaṇa as your guru;
through offerings of flowers, incense, and the gratification of Brahmins, and through well-established meditation, the Supreme Lord is swiftly attained. (4.41)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 4.
Aśvaśiras said:
"You two ought to sever this one doubt of mine here, by the severing of which my liberation from saṃsāra may come to pass. (5.1)
When the king had spoken thus, the sage Kapila, the best of yogis and a soul of dharma, then replied to the king, the most excellent of sacrificers.
Kapila said:
"O King, most righteous one, what doubt is in your mind?
Tell me what you desire, so that having heard it, I may dispel it. (5.3)
The King said:
"O Sage, is liberation attained through action or rather by the man of knowledge?
Cut asunder this doubt of mine, if you have shown me favor. (5.4)
Kapila said:
O great king, in former times this very question was asked by Raibhya, the son of Brahmā, as well as by King Vasu, to Bṛhaspati.
In former times, there was an excellent king named Vasu, who was learned and a lord of liberality.
In the time of Cākṣuṣa Manu, Vasu, who increased the lineage of Brahmā,
went to the abode of Brahmā out of a desire to see him.
O King, having seen the excellent Vidyadhara Caitraratha on the path, Vasu affectionately asked him, "O Lord, when will there be an opportunity for Brahmā? (5.7)
He said, "The assembly of the gods is taking place in the house of Brahmā.
Having heard this, Vasu then stood at the door of Brahmā’s abode;
at that very moment, Raibhya, a man of great asceticism, arrived there.
With a joyful mind and a heart full of contentment, King Vasu honored him and said: "O Sage, where have you come from?"
Raibhya said:
"O great king, I have come from the presence of Bṛhaspati in order to ask the preceptor of the gods about a certain other matter."
While Raibhya was speaking thus, O Lord, that great assembly of Brahmā rose up,
and the hosts of gods departed to their own abodes.
Then Bṛhaspati, having reached an agreement there with Raibhya,
departed for his own abode, well-honored by Vasu.
Raibhya Āṅgirasa and King Vasu sat down together;
O Indra among kings, when they had all taken their seats, he spoke.
Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, spoke these words in the presence of Raibhya:
"What shall I do, O illustrious one, you who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences?"
Raibhya said:
"O Bṛhaspati, is liberation attained through action or by the man of knowledge? O Lord, explain this to me who asks you about my doubt. (5.15)
Bṛhaspati said: Whatever action a person performs, whether good or evil, by dedicating it all to Nārāyaṇa, he is not tainted while acting. || 5.16 ||
O best of the twice-born, it is heard that there was a conversation between two deceivers:
a certain Brahmin sage of the Atri lineage who was devoted to the study of the Vedas.
Constantly residing there, bathing at dawn and devoted to the three daily ablutions,
he was formerly known by the name Saṃyamana; one day he went to the river Bhāgīrathī in Dharmāraṇya to bathe— she who is blessed and auspicious.
There, a skilled hunter named Niṣṭhuraka, bow in hand and resembling the God of Death, arrived with the intent to kill that great herd of deer as they sat there;
he fixed an arrow to his bow.
Then the brahmin Saṃyamana, seeing him intent on hunting, restrained him, saying: "O gentle sir, do not commit this slaughter of living beings."
Having heard these words, the hunter spoke this speech preceded by a smile:
"O best of the twice-born, I do not indeed kill a living being that is separate from me."
The Supreme Lord himself plays with these elements;
it is just as when clay is fashioned into oxen—of this there is no doubt. (5.22)
O Brahmin, this state of being is always ignorance for those seeking liberation;
this entire world is characterized by activity devoted solely to the journey of life.
In that regard, the word "I" does not attain correctness. (5.23)
Having heard this, that best of brahmins, the twice-born Saṃyamana,
then spoke these words with amazement to the cruel hunter Niṣṭhuraka.
“O good man, why do you speak such words that are so clearly supported by reason?
Having heard this from the sage, the hunter, who was knowledgeable in dharma, spoke to the brahmin:
“Having fashioned a net of iron, he placed a blazing fire beneath it. (5.25)
Having offered the fire, he said to the brahmin, "Let this heap of wood be ignited.
Then the brahmin, having kindled the fire with his mouth, ceased.
Furthermore, O twice-born one, when the fire was blazing, he led that net made of iron away by the thousands through various internal networks,
even though the fire remained in a single place, by means of those iron lattices.
Then the hunter said to the brahmin, "O great sage, take a single flame so that I may bring about the destruction of the rest here."
Having spoken thus, he quickly threw a water-filled jar into the fire;
the fire was suddenly extinguished instantly, as before.
Then the hunter said to that brahmin whose wealth was asceticism:
"O Blessed One, give me back the flame that you took from the fire,
so that I may bring meat and eat it on the roads."
When the brahmin had spoken thus, he looked at the iron net; yet there was no fire there, for it had been consumed and brought to destruction.
Then, out of a sense of embarrassment, the brahmin of celebrated vows remained silent; at that moment, the hunter spoke these words: || 5.32 ||
O best of men, O twice-born one, just as this blazing fire with its many branches would be destroyed upon the destruction of its root, so too is this [the case].
That Self, abiding in primordial nature (prakṛti), becomes the refuge of all beings; from that very source, this creation of the world and the existence of the world occur again. 5.34.
By applying to himself whatever vow has been prescribed for him according to the rule of receiving alms-food, he who performs it does not come to grief. (5.35)
When the hunter had spoken thus to the brahmin, O best of kings,
a rain of flowers then fell from the sky upon him.
And that best of brahmins beheld great, divine celestial chariots, moving at will, magnificent, and filled with many jewels.
Among them, the brahmin beheld there Niṣṭhuraka, who was greedy, present among all of them, and capable of assuming any form at will.
Having seen his many bodies accomplished through yoga by means of the latent impression of non-duality, the brahmin, filled with joy, departed for his own hermitage.
O best of the twice-born, O King Raibhya, for one who possesses such knowledge and performs his duties according to his own nature, liberation will certainly come, even while living, O Vasa.
Thus, O King, having attained the destruction of their doubts from Bṛhaspati, Raibhya and Vasu departed from his abode for their own hermitage.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should worship the Lord Nārāyaṇa, perceiving that sovereign as non-different from the one residing within your own body. 5.42
Having heard the words of Kapila, the powerful King Aśvaśiras summoned his eldest son, the fortunate one named Sthūlaśiras,
and having consecrated him in his own kingdom, that king departed for the forest.
O lady of beautiful hips, there in the place called Naimiṣa, he propitiated the Guru, whose body is sacrifice and whose form is the sacrifice itself, through austerity and with hymns of praise.
Dharaṇī said:
"O highly fortunate one, how was the hymn of praise for Nārāyaṇa, whose body is sacrifice, performed by the king? Tell this to me once again. (5.45)

The illustrious Varāha said: I bow to the one who is to be sacrificed for the lord of the thirty gods, for Bhava, for Sūrya, and for Hutāśana; I pay homage to Hari, the Lord of Sacrifice, who possesses manifold forms and is the sacrifice personified, as well as to King Soma and the Maruts. 5.46
He has most formidable tusks and eyes like the moon and the sun;
his belly is the year, the two solstices, and the pair of ages (yugas);
the blades of darbha grass are the hairs on his body, and he holds sacrificial fuel as his spear.
I bow to the eternal Sacrificial Man.
For this space between heaven and earth, as well as all the directions, is pervaded by his body; [worship] him,
the praiseworthy Lord, the source of the worlds.
To that Janārdana, I am perpetually bowed in reverence.

I bow to that Lord, the primordial form of sacrifice, who, being himself without beginning, creates his own first body in age after age for the sake of the victory or defeat of the gods and the asuras. 5.49.
Possessing fierce splendor, he held for the sake of victory a discus composed of māyā, shining with stainless rays;
this one has four arms, equipped with a mace, a sword, the Śārṅga bow, and other weapons.
To that embodiment of sacrifice, I am perpetually bowed in reverence.
In one place he bore a thousand heads; in another, his body was like a great mountain;
and in yet another, he was as small as a mote of dust.
I bow to that Man of Sacrifice who is ever thus. || 5.51 ||

I bow eternally to him who, as the four-faced one, creates the entire universe; who, as the discus-handed one, protects it; and who, resembling the fire of time at the end of an aeon, brings about its destruction—to him whose form is sacrifice.
He who is worshipped for the sake of performing the movement through the wheel of saṃsāra, he who is omnipresent and ancient,
and who is meditated upon by yogis as immeasurable.
To that embodiment of sacrifice, I am perpetually bowed in reverence.
When I have fixed my mind rightly upon that Reality which is truly visible within my own body,
my conviction becomes firm that there is nothing else.
May he protect me from this and that, with a pure disposition.
Thus addressed, a splendor resembling the flame of a sacrificial fire appeared before him;
having fixed his mind upon that, the king entered into it and attained dissolution within the embodiment of the sacrifice.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 5.
Dharaṇī said:
O Lord, having heard the words of Aṅgiras, what did that Vasu and the most excellent Raibhya do after obtaining the resolution of their doubt? 6.1
Śrī Varāha said:
That Vasu, the knower of all dharmas, while protecting his own kingdom, performed many great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees. 6.2.
Through the ritual section of the Veda, that king of kings propitiated the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, the master of the gods, contemplating Him as non-different from himself.
Then, after a long time, the mind of that king—who had desisted from the enjoyment of sovereignty and had reached the end of his suffering—indeed [awakened]. (6.4)
Then, having consecrated his son Vivasvat— the best among his hundred brothers—
in his own kingdom, he departed for the forest of asceticism.
Puṣkara is the most excellent among sacred fords (tīrthas), where Keśava,
known by the name Puṇḍarīkākṣa, is worshipped by those devoted to him.
Having gone there, that royal seer Vasu, the sovereign of Kaśmīra,
withered his own body through extremely intense asceticism.
Chanting with devotion this hymn to Puṇḍarīkākṣa, the wise king,
desiring to propitiate the stainless god Nārāyaṇa,
attained absorption into Him at the conclusion of the praise, O best of kings.
Dharaṇī said:
"O Lord, how was this hymn to the Lotus-Eyed One remembered?
O Supreme Lord, tell me truly what it is like."
The illustrious Varāha said:
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O slayer of Madhu.
Salutations to you, Lord of all worlds; salutations to you, wielder of the sharp discus.
I bow to the lotus-eyed Lord, the universal form, the mighty-armed, the giver of boons, the embodiment of all splendor, who is both knowledge and ignorance. 6.11
I bow to Madhusūdana, the primordial god, the great deity, who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and who is profound among all the gods. 6.12
I bow to the lotus-eyed one, the universal form, the great form, the form of knowledge, the triple-formed one, the armor of all the gods.
I bow to the Supreme Lord, the god with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and mighty arms, who stands pervading the entire universe.
I bow to the eternal Lord Viṣṇu, the victorious one, the refuge and the worthy protector,
who resembles a dark blue cloud and holds the discus in his hand.
I meditate upon Hari, who is pure, omnipresent, eternal, of the nature of space, everlasting, and liberated from both existence and non-existence, pervading all things.
I see nothing else whatsoever distinct from you, O Acyuta;
I behold all this, both the moving and the unmoving, as consisting of you alone.
While he was speaking thus, a person of dark-blue hue, dense, fierce, and terrifying, indeed emerged from his body in embodied form.
Red-eyed and short of stature, with a luster like that of a charred pillar, he spoke with palms joined in reverence: "What shall I do, O lord of men? (6.19)
The king said:
"Who are you? What is your business here? From where have you come?
Tell me this, O hunter; I wish to know this."
The hunter said:
"O King, formerly in the Kali age, you were a king in the southern region,
born of perfect righteousness, illustrious and wise in Janasthāna."
Once, O hero, you came to the forest surrounded by horses, specifically to hunt wild beasts. (6.22)
There, out of desire for another, you cast the sage who was wearing the guise of a deer onto the surface of the earth at a distance with a pair of staffs.
O best of Brahmins, you died instantly, while the king was filled with joy; O monarch,
as soon as he saw, "This deer has been killed," the Brahmin in the form of a deer died on Mount Prasravaṇa.
Having seen him, O Great King, with your senses and mind agitated,
you went home and then spoke of it to someone else.
Then, O Lord of Men, after a few days had passed, you, with a mind terrified by the fear of killing a Brahmin, thought this during the night:
"I shall perform an act for the sake of pacification, by which he may be released from his sin. (6.26)
Therefore, O great king, having meditated upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa even once, this pure twelfth day was observed as a fast by you, O King.
Having said, "Nārāyaṇa is well-pleased with me," on an auspicious day, a cow was given according to the prescribed rite; immediately, he died from a sharp pain in his belly.
Regarding the reason why one should not eat on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), I shall explain it: your wife, auspicious by name as Nārāyaṇī, [is the cause]. 6.29.
Because it was uttered by you with your life-breath reaching your throat,
O Great King, your destination for one kalpa has been established in the city of Viṣṇu.
And I, residing within your body, know everything exhaustively;
it is my intention that this most terrible Brahma-graha shall afflict you.
At that time, O King of kings, I was struck by the servants of Viṣṇu with clubs and brought to destruction; yet from my pores I remained,
even while staying in heaven, established in my own splendor.
Then, O best of beings, when the day had ended and the night had begun,
at this time of the primordial creation, O most excellent of kings.
"O Great King, you were born in the house of King Sumanas, the sovereign of the land of Kaśmīra; and I am born from your own body."
"You have performed many sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees;
yet I was not overcome by them, for they were devoid of the remembrance of Viṣṇu. (6.35)
Now, O best of kings, by the power of that hymn to the lotus-eyed one which you have recited, I have cast off my body hairs; having become unified once more, I am born again in the form of a hunter.
"O Lord, having heard this hymn of praise from the Blessed One, I—formerly a personification of evil—have been liberated; now, O All-pervading One, my mind is fixed upon righteousness."
Having heard these words, the king was filled with great wonder;
that best of kings invited the hunter to choose a boon.
The king said:
"O hunter, I have been reminded of my previous birth by you;
likewise, through my grace, you shall become Dharmavyādha."
And whoever should hear this supreme [work] concerning Puṇḍarīkākṣa,
for him there shall be the fruit of performing the ritual bath during the pilgrimage to Puṣkara.
Śrī Varāha said:
Having spoken thus, O bearer of all things, the king then ascended an excellent celestial chariot and attained union with the Supreme through supreme splendor.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 6.
Dharaṇī said: "O Lord, having heard that Vasu had attained perfection, what did that tiger among sages, Raibhya, do himself? This is a great doubt of mine. (7.1)
Śrī Varāha said: Having heard that Vasu had attained perfection, that tiger among sages, Raibhya,
whose wealth was his austerity, then came to the meritorious Gayā, the sacred site of the ancestors.
Having gone there, satisfy the ancestors with devotion by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Then, while that wise Raibhya was performing that most intense and exceedingly difficult penance,
a great yogi of supreme brilliance arrived, seated upon a celestial chariot.
In a pure celestial palace, radiant like the sun and as fine as a mote of dust,
there dwells a man of brilliant splendor, minute as an atom.
He said, "O Raibhya, O you of noble vows, what is the purpose for which you perform penance?
Having spoken thus, that man indeed measured the earth from heaven.
There too, he beheld a celestial chariot, shining like five suns and resembling the sun itself, pervading the realm of Brahmā all at once.
Then Raibhya, overcome with wonder, bowed down and asked him:
"Who are you, O great yogi? Please tell me."
The Puruṣa said:
"I am the younger brother of Rudra, the mind-born son of Brahmā;
by name Sanatkumāra, I dwell in Janaloka."
"O ascetic, you have come to my side out of affection;
you are blessed in every way, dear child, the enhancer of Brahmā’s lineage. (7.9)
Raibhya said:
"Salutations be unto you, O best of yogis! Be gracious, O Viśvarūpa, and show me compassion."
Tell me, O lion among yogis, what is to be done here; for how indeed have I been called blessed by you? (7.10)

Sanatkumāra said: Blessed indeed are you, O foremost of the best of the twice-born, since you delight in the teachings of the Vedas and gratify the ancestors with mantras, vows, recitations, and burnt offerings, as well as by reaching Gayā and offering balls of rice.
Listen further: there was a king named Viśāla who dwelt in the city of Viśālā.
Blessed, steadfast, and childless, that sovereign of Viśālā himself [honored] the foremost of the twice-born.
He questioned them for the sake of a son; those brahmins, of undaunted spirit, spoke to Amitrasāha.
"O Lord of Men, by going to Gayā and making numerous offerings of water,
it is certain that you will have a son who is a great benefactor and a sovereign ruler of the entire earth."
Thus addressed by the brahmins, the king, the lord of Viśālā, was greatly delighted;
he came with great effort to that preeminent sacred ford.
Furthermore, that which is performed for the ancestors with devotion during the Maghā asterism [is most meritorious]. || 7.14 ||

Seeing those beings of supreme form in the sky, who were diligently offering funeral cakes according to the prescribed rites, the king spoke to the white, yellow, and black men: "What is this that is being neglected by you?
Tell me everything; a great curiosity has arisen in my mind. (7.15)
Sita said: "O dear one, I am Sita, your father; I am so by name, by conduct, and by my deeds."
And this father of mine is red-colored, a doer of cruelty, a slayer of a Brahmin, and an evildoer.
His supreme father is named Adhīśvara;
Kṛṣṇa is so called by his very nature and by his deeds as well.
By this Kṛṣṇa, they were indeed slain in the past.
In this birth, there were many ancient seers.
"O son, both of these have died and have fallen into the Raudra hell known as Avīci.
My father was the sovereign lord, and Kṛṣṇa is his supreme father; both have remained there for a long time.
And I, by my own pure deeds, have attained from that place the throne of Śakra, which is so difficult to obtain."

Moreover, by you, a knower of mantras, these two were summoned at Gayā through the offering of funeral cakes; by the power of that offering of *piṇḍas* at the sacred ford, even though they were dwelling in hell, they have been brought together with me.
"O subduer of enemies, that water which was given by you with the thought, 'I shall gratify my fathers, grandfathers, and likewise my great-grandfathers'— "
Therefore, O best of men, our simultaneous union has been brought about by this speech;
through the power of the sacred ford, we shall go to the world of the ancestors, without a doubt. (7.21)
"By this offering of funeral cakes, these two grandfathers of yours, though they had fallen into a miserable state and were transformed by their evil deeds, have now attained perfection. (7.22)
This is the power of the sacred ford: even for the son of a slayer of a Brahmin, that son may effect his father’s liberation again by the offering of funeral cakes.
"For this reason, my son, having indeed quarreled with these two, I have come to see you; I shall now depart.
For this reason, O Raibhya, you are called blessed by me. (7.24)
To visit Gayā even once, and to offer the funeral cakes even once, is difficult to achieve; yet you remain here perpetually.
O Lord Raibhya, what more can be said? This merit of yours is such that you have seen Nārāyaṇa himself, mace in hand, in person.
Therefore, Gadādhara himself is established in this sacred ford;
for this reason, O best of the twice-born, this ford is most renowned.
Śrī Varāha said:
Having spoken thus, the great yogi vanished right there;
and Raibhya then performed a hymn of praise to Hari, the mace-wielder.
Raibhya said:
[I bow to] Gadādhara, who is praised by the hosts of gods,
who possesses forbearance, and who destroys the suffering of hungry people.
I bow to Śiva, the crusher of the vast armies of asuras, who destroys all inauspiciousness at the mere thought of him.
To the ancient primordial Person,
worshipped by many, the one from of old, stainless and free from blemish, the refuge of men; to Trivikrama, who upheld the earth and slew Bali.
I bow in secret to Keśava, the wielder of the mace.
Of perfectly pure nature, surrounded by riches, encompassed by glory, free from stain, and discerning;
he who is praised by lords of the earth whose sins have been removed.
He who bows down to Gadādhara shall dwell in happiness.
To him whose lotus-feet are worshipped by gods and asuras,
who wears armlets, necklaces, bracelets, and a crown,
and who reclines upon the ocean with the discus in his hand.
He who bows down to Gadādhara shall dwell in happiness.
In the Kṛta age, the omnipresent Lord was white; likewise, in the Tretā age, the infallible one was reddish-brown; and in the third [age], he was yellow-hued;
in the Kali age, Maheśvara is like a dark cloud.
He who bows down to Gadādhara shall dwell in happiness.

May he who, as the seed-born, creates the four-faced Brahmā, and likewise sustains the world in the form of Nārāyaṇa, and likewise brings about its end in the body of Rudra—the wielder of the mace, possessing sixfold aspects—be victorious! (7.34)
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are the three qualities; indeed, there is no arising of anything else within them.
May that one Gadādhara, who is himself threefold, grant me steadfastness in both dharma and liberation.

May Gadādhara rescue me, who am sinking deeply and helplessly in the great flood of the ocean of saṃsāra— its waters being the sufferings of existence, its terrifying crocodiles the torments of separation— by means of his boat-like great vessel.
The Lord himself, the triple-formed (Trimūrti), by his own power, created this cosmic egg from within himself as if from himself;
within it was a seat arisen from water, possessing noble splendor.
I bow down to that mountain whom he created.

May the All-pervading Lord, who bears the mace, whose names such as Matsya and others in the worlds arise solely from his protection of the gods and others, and who is Vṛṣākapi in his primary form, grant me the supreme goal. 7.38.
Śrī Varāha said: Thus praised then with devotion by the wise Raibhya, Janārdana Viṣṇu, clad in yellow garments, suddenly manifested himself.
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, seated upon Garuḍa and traversing the sky,
Puruṣottama spoke with a voice as deep and steady as a thundercloud.
"I am pleased with your devotion and your hymn of praise, O best of the twice-born, as well as by your bathing at this sacred ford, O lord; tell me, what is it that you desire?"
Raibhya said:
"O Lord of Gods, grant me a place where Sanaka and the others dwell;
by your grace, O Gadādhara, may I reside there."
The god said:
"So be it," O Brahmin; having spoken thus, he vanished.
And the venerable Raibhya was likewise endowed with divine knowledge.
In an instant, by the Lord who was fully satisfied,
the wielder of the discus went to where those perfected ones, the great seers headed by Sanaka, were located.
And whoever recites this hymn to Viṣṇu, the wielder of the mace, as proclaimed by Raibhya, is superior to one who has gone to Gayā and performed the offering of funeral cakes.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. || 7 ||
Śrī Varāha said:
He who, having become a hunter, dwelt within the body of King Vasu,
remained established in his own occupation for a period of four thousand years.
Having killed a wild deer for the sake of each individual member of his family,
he always provides gratification for his servants, guests, and the sacrificial fire.
In Mithilā, O lady of beautiful hips, that wise man always performs the śrāddha for his ancestors on every auspicious occasion, following proper conduct.
Constantly attending upon the sacred fire, speaking truthful and well-spoken words,
and intent only on sustaining his life, he shall not cause the destruction of living beings.
While he was living in this manner, a son named Arjunaka was born to that great ascetic Dharmabuddhi; like a sage, he was self-controlled.
In the course of time, through the virtuous conduct of that wise man,
there was born a daughter of excellent complexion named Arjunakī.
When she reached the bloom of youth, the knower of dharma reflected:
"To whom shall this daughter be given, and which man indeed is worthy? (8.7)
While Mataṅga was thus reflecting upon his son,
the son of Dharmavyādha spoke very clearly to him, addressing him by the name Prasanna.
Having reflected thus,
Mātaṅga was intent upon Prasenajit and said to his father:
"O best of those who shine, please accept for the sake of Prasannā this Arjunī cow, which I myself have given to that great-souled one."
Mataṅga said:
"This son of mine is well-pleased; he is an expert in all the scriptures.
O best of hunters, I shall accept your daughter, the maiden Arjunakī."
When this had been said, the great ascetic Dharmavyādha then gave his daughter to the wise and gracious son of Mataṅga.
Then the Dharma-fowler, having given away his daughter, went to his own home;
she too became intent on serving her parents-in-law and her husband.
Then, after a long time, that auspicious maiden Arjunakī was addressed by her mother-in-law: "O daughter, O child, you are such a killer of your husband;
you do not know how to perform penance, nor how to propitiate your husband."
That slender-waisted young woman, having been rebuked for even a slight offense,
went to her father's house, weeping again and again.
Questioned by her father, "Daughter, what is this cause for your weeping?
that beautiful woman, thus addressed, then spoke.
O father, I was addressed by my mother-in-law with intense and great anger, crying out repeatedly and loudly, "O hunter! You are the son who would kill his own mother! (8.16)
Having heard this, that righteous hunter, filled with anger,
then went to Matanga’s house, which was surrounded by the people of the district.

When he had arrived, Mataṅga, the best among victors and his kinsman, honored him with a seat, water for the hands, and water for the feet, and spoke these words: "What is the purpose of your visit? What service may I perform for you as a guest?"
The hunter said:
"I wish to eat some food devoid of consciousness,
for it was out of curiosity that I came to your house."
Mataṅga said:
"Wheat and rice have been prepared in my house;
O best of those who know dharma, O rich in asceticism, eat as you desire. (8.20)
The hunter said:
"I see what these wheat, rice, and barley are like; they exist in their own true form, by which I may know you, O best of beings. (8.21)
Śrī Varāha said: When Mataṅga had spoken thus, another earthen vessel filled with wheat and another with rice was shown there to Dharmavyādha.
Having seen the rice together with the wheat, the Dharma-fowler rose from his excellent seat and began to depart, but was restrained by Mataṅga. (8.23)
"O high-minded one, tell me why you have begun to depart?
The most excellent food has been fully prepared in my house even before you ate;
having cooked it yourself, why do you not eat today? (8.24)
The hunter said:
"Day after day you kill living beings by the thousands and by the millions;
what virtuous man would eat the food of such a sinner?"
"If there were insentience in the house, there would be well-prepared food;
but now, these aquatic creatures are seen here. (8.26)
(When sown, O Sage, they reach a thousandfold every year. || 8.26 (1) ||
"Every day in the forest, I kill a single animal for the sake of my family;
if I prepare it for the ancestors and give it to them, I may then eat it along with my followers. (8.27)
But you, having slain many living beings together with your family and followers, constantly enjoy this which is, in my opinion, unfit to be eaten. (8.28)
In ancient times, the herbs and all the creepers were created by Brahmā for the sake of sacrifice; indeed, the sacred revelation (śruti) declares that they are the food of living beings.
The divine, the elemental, the ancestral, the human, and the Vedic—
these five great sacrifices were created by Brahmā in ancient times.
For the benefit of the Brahmins and others as well, that [dharma] is their primary source;
indeed, for the other castes, auspicious [deeds] are performed under the direction of the Brahmins.
Thus, if there were a separation [of the food], that choice food would be pure;
otherwise, even these grains should be considered as individual beasts and birds for the giver and the eater, for that is traditionally known as "great meat" (mahāmāṃsa).
I have given my daughter, who possesses the form of a goddess, to you for the sake of a son;
yet she was told by your wife that she is the daughter of a slayer of living beings.
For this purpose I have come to your house to observe your conduct,
your worship of the gods, and your hospitality toward guests.
Not even one of these is seen here;
therefore, I wish to go to that house with the desire to perform the śrāddha for my ancestors.
"I do not eat at my own home because of the duty toward my ancestors;
I am a hunter who kills living beings, whereas you are not a hater of the world."
O ascetic, since my daughter and your son have both committed the slaughter of a living being, its gravity has increased; therefore, a penance must be performed.
Having spoken thus, he then rose up and cursed the woman on earth:
"May there never be any trust between daughters-in-law and mothers-in-law. (8.38)
"And may no daughter-in-law ever desire her mother-in-law while she is still living.
Having spoken thus, O beautiful lady, the hunter departed for his own home.
Then, having worshipped the gods and the ancestors with devotion, that wise man of great asceticism established his son Arjunaka in his own lineage.

The Dharmavyādha went quickly to that supreme sacred ford renowned throughout the three worlds called Puruṣottama; having gone there, O Earth, he performed austerities with self-restraint and concentration, reciting this hymn.
I bow to Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the enemies of the gods,
whose broad chest is the abode of Śrī,
the excellent teacher, and the supreme goal of those possessed of wisdom.
Trivikrama, the eternal upholder of Mount Mandara.
Dāmodara, who delights the surface of the earth, whose fame is bright with rays of light, who possesses the luster of a bumblebee’s body,
the upholder of the earth, the enemy of Naraka, praised by the many.
I bow to Viṣṇu, Janārdana, the refuge.
[Seek refuge in] Nara, Narasiṃha, Hari, the Lord, the Sovereign, the one named Tridhāman, possessed of infinite splendor, whose mouth is well-refined, the Supreme among Men.
I go constantly to that god Acyuta,
who exists in three ways, who holds the sharp discus in his hand,
who abides in righteousness, and who is satisfied with unsurpassed qualities.
I bow to Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, the Guru who is known as the ultimate beatitude and who has destroyed all else. 8.44.
In ancient times he slew both Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
and indeed, he always supports the earth upon his head;
thus has the Eternal One been praised by me with force.
May Viṣṇu bestow upon me abundant strength and happiness.
May Mahāvarāha, Janārdana, who feeds on oblations and water, the benefactor of mankind whose mouth is the sacrificial fire, [grant me well-being].
May that great Viṣṇu, the supporter of the earth who is like the ocean at its ebb, protect me as I seek refuge.
By whom the three worlds have been fashioned as a web of illusion, just as the single fire pervades all that is moving and unmoving;
he himself is everywhere within the moving and the unmoving.
May that Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, be my refuge.
He who in birth after birth created Kaṃ, from whom this entire world with its moving and unmoving beings was produced,
and into whom it subsequently dissolves— that being who possesses the nature of Rudra is likewise called Hari, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
May that eternal Lord Viṣṇu, who assumes inconceivable forms, grant me perpetual well-being— he whose manifestations arise as ether, the moon, earth, wind, fire, the sun, and water. 8.48.
When this had been said, Sanātana himself appeared before him, his form being a sight of wonder.
Dharaṇī said:
O Lord, what was performed by Nārāyaṇa, who possesses a universal form, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga? I wish to hear all that in accordance with reality.
Śrī Varāha said:
Formerly, Nārāyaṇa alone existed; there was nothing whatsoever beyond Hari.
He, acting according to his own will, found no pleasure in being all alone. (9.2)
Desiring a second [son] for him, there appeared a thought consisting of the intellect, which for a moment shone like the sun under the designation "Asau" (This One). (9.3)
Even she, the speaker of Brahman, had a twofold thought; for that which exists eternally in the mortal world under the name of Umā [was also present]. (9.4)
Then, having become the single-syllabled "Om," he created this earth;
he [as "Bhūḥ"] created "Bhuvaḥ," and he also created "Svaḥ" and then "Mahaḥ."
And then, the person, as well as austerity and the self, dissolve away;
this [world] is woven across and lengthwise like clusters of gems upon a thread. (9.6)
The world arose from the Praṇava; at that time, this remained as emptiness.
This very form of the Blessed One is Śaṅkara himself, who is Hari.
Having seen these worlds as empty and desiring to create them, he agitated the abode of his mind; there, from his own essence alone, he assumed a supreme form.
When he remained within that agitated state, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) came into being;
and when it was split asunder, the earthly realm (bhūrloka) became established therein.
He went to another world in the midst [of the universe], which was like the sun;
the Ancient Person, having pervaded it, remained within the calyx of a lotus.
For that god Nārāyaṇa, by means of the splendor belonging to Prajāpati, emitted from his navel the vowel beginning with 'a' and the consonants. 9.11.
Then, after creating the formless [beings], the scriptures sang forth from the quarters;
having created them, the immeasurable Self then reflected upon their sustenance.
As he was thus reflecting, a great radiance issued forth from his eyes:
that on the right resembled fire, and that on the left was like snow.
Having seen that, the Moon and the Sun were fashioned by the Supreme Lord;
then Prāṇa arose from the Supreme Lord, as did Vāyu.
That very wind is the Lord, the all-pervading one who even today resides within the heart;
from him fire arose, and from that fire came the great waters.
That which is Agni is indeed the splendor of Brahman, the supreme cause;
with his two arms, he also created the splendor of the Kṣatriya.
From his thighs the Lord likewise created the Vaiśyas, and from his feet the Śūdras;
thereafter, the omnipresent Lord created the Yakṣas and the Rākṣasas as well.
With four kinds of beings— those moving through the atmosphere filling the Bhūrloka and Bhuvarloka,
and others moving through the celestial path filling the Svarloka— he completely filled the worlds.
Likewise, he filled Maharloka with those various beings such as Sanaka and others, and then he filled Janaloka with the Vairājas.
Then the god filled the world of heat (tapoloka) with those devoted to austerity;
he filled the world of truth (satyaloka) with gods who do not return to death.
Having thus created the creation, the divine Lord, the creator of beings,
the Supreme Ruler, remains awake throughout his own day known as a kalpa.
Within that universe, the world of the earth (bhūrloka) and the atmospheric world (bhuvarloka) are born;
the celestial world (svarloka) also arises—these three are all produced, of this there is no doubt.
When the God is asleep at the end of a kalpa, a night of equal duration is likewise intended; during that time, these three worlds remain asleep, having fallen into a state of dissolution.
Then, when the night had passed, the lotus-eyed one arose;
he thought of those Vedas and his mother in all four directions.
While reflecting, that Lord of Gods did not find those Vedas.
Deluded by the sleep of ignorance, the Lord of Gods reflected on how to establish the way of the world: "The Vedas are not established here. (9.25)
Then, seeing them dissolved within his own form called Water, the Lord of the Gods,
desiring to seize them, reflected and entered the water having become a fish.
Having meditated thus, the Great Fish was born at that very moment;
and the god entered the water, as if agitating it on all sides.
When that best of gods had suddenly entered the great ocean, assuming the form of a massive mountain and taking on the body of a fish, the water became visible.
They praised Hari, who had lifted up the earth, with hymns of praise.
Salutations to you who dwell within the Vedas and are beyond the reach of logic;
salutations, O Nārāyaṇa in the form of the Fish!
Salutations to you, O one of beautiful voice and universal form!
Homage be to you, who bear the form of non-dual knowledge! 9.29
Salutations to you who possess the nature of the moon, the sun, and the winds; O beautiful-eyed one, you who abide within the waters and the universe!
Salutations to you; we go for refuge to Viṣṇu.
Protect us, having abandoned this form of a fish.
O God of infinite form, this universe is pervaded by you; when it is perceived as separate, is there anything here that exists apart from you?
You have no form distinct from yourself; we have come to you for refuge.
O Lotus-eyed One, the ether, the self, the moon, fire, and the mind are the form of your ancient body;
O Śambhu, forgive me if I have been devoid of devotion.
By you, O God of gods, the world is illuminated.
This divine form of yours, so terrifying yet melodious, resembling a mountain— O Ancient One, Lord of Gods, Abode of the World— is incongruous with [your former appearance].
O Acyuta, O one of intense splendor, attain tranquility.
For we have all come to you for refuge, having beheld this form of yours out of fear; indeed,
the entire world would be lost without you.
There exists nothing pertaining to the body that is ancient.
Thus praised, the God then assumed an internal form and took up from within the waters the Vedas,
along with the Upaniṣads and the Śāstras.
As far as the form of the Blessed One extends, so far indeed does this world extend;
when he remains in his unchanging state (kūṭastha), the world dissolves into him, and when he remains in his transformed state (vikṛtistha), it increases.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. || 9 ||
The illustrious Varāha said:
Having thus created the entire universe, the Blessed One, the creator of the worlds, then desisted;
O Earth, the creation then began to flourish.
Then, when creation had become old, all the gods, worshipping the ancient Person known as Nārāyaṇa with various sacrifices, [proceeded].
In all the continents and in all the regions, the gods, endowed with faith, performed great sacrificial sessions (satras) for Hari;
desiring to make him their object of worship, they gratified him exceedingly. || 3 ||
While they were thus propitiating him for many thousands of years,
the god, being pleased at that time, manifested himself before their very eyes.
Then, with many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes, scraping the peak of the great mountain like a mountain-peak itself,
the Lord of the Gods said: "What is to be done?"
"O best of gods, speak the boon; what boon do you desire? || 5 ||
The gods said:
"Be victorious, O Govinda of great majesty! By you, our protector, we gods have been favored."
Even in the world of men, there is no one other than you, the Primordial One, who belongs to us.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and those who are Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, the Maruts, and the Uṣmapās—
all of us have come to you for refuge.
Perform these acts of worship here, O you whose form is the universe!
Thus addressed by them at that time, Hari, the great Lord of Yoga, said,
"I shall make you all worthy of worship," and vanished.
The gods also went to their own eternal abodes while offering praise; the Supreme Lord likewise assumed a threefold state.
Thus, O King, having become the sustainer of the three worlds, Maheśvara propitiated the gods who exist in three ways— as sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasa.

One should study the Vedas with the *sāttvika* mode and worship the deities with sacrifice through the *rājasa* mode; for Keśava, having become a limb of one's own self, is present even in that [rājasa] state.
He worshipped with devotion his own *rājasa* form, which was terrible, embodied as Time (*kāla*), and naturally holding a trident;
yet he remained among the asuras even through a *tāmasa* disposition.
Thus, having become the sustainer of the three worlds, Maheśvara propitiated the gods; consequently, the world also became threefold.
Assuming the names Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna, he remains established [in those forms];
and that Lord Nārāyaṇa is the sovereign in the excellent Kṛta Yuga.
In the Tretā age he appeared in the form of Rudra, in the Dvāpara age he possessed the form of sacrifice, and in the Kali age the Lord Nārāyaṇa was born in many forms.
O lady of beautiful hips, O beautiful woman, listen now as I relate to you in its entirety the deeds of that Viṣṇu, the first creator, who possesses immense splendor. (16)
In the Kṛta age, there was a king named Supratīka, possessed of great strength;
he had two wives who were indistinguishable from one another and both were charming.
Vidyutprabhā and Kāntimatī were their two names;
however, although the king exerted himself, he did not obtain a son equal to those two.
At that time, he gratified Mātreya, the best of sages who was free from all taint, according to the prescribed rites on Citrakūṭa, the most excellent of mountains.
For a long time, that sage was propitiated by him who sought a boon;
then, desiring to grant a boon, the son of Atri, the sage, spoke.
Meanwhile, the exceedingly powerful Indra also approached his side on an elephant,
surrounded by the divine armies, yet remaining silent.
Seeing that internal joy and lack of joy, the sage was pleased;
yet he became enraged at the king of the gods and cast a fierce curse upon him.
"O fool, Lord of Heaven, because you have shown me contempt, you shall therefore be displaced from your kingdom and dwell in another world. (23)
Having spoken thus in anger to that lord of the gods and to the king, he said: "O King, a son of firm prowess shall be born to you."
"Resembling Indra in form, glorious, with uplifted weapons, and full of majesty;
skilled in the power of knowledge and in action, yet a performer of cruel deeds—he shall be an invincible and exceedingly powerful king. Having spoken thus, the sage departed. (25)
That king Supratīka, who was conversant with dharma, also conceived a child in his wife Vidyutprabhā; and she, in due time, gave birth.
To her was born a son of great strength named Durjaya;
the sage himself performed for him the birth rites and other sacraments.
(The sinless sage, named Durvāsas, [performed these] for that body of asceticism.)
By the power of that sage’s spiritual practice, he indeed became gentle;
he became one who had reached the further shore of the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, righteous, and pure. (28)
The second wife of that high-souled king was the blessed Kīrtimatī by name; she had a son named Sudyumna, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. (29)
Then, after a long time, that king, the best of monarchs,
Supratīka, seeing his son Durjaya nearby fit for the task, [acted].
And the powerful lord of Vārāṇasī, O beautiful lady, reflected upon his own old age and the matter of the kingdom concerning Durjaya.
Having reflected thus, the righteous king gave him the kingdom,
and he himself went to the mountain named Citrakūṭa.
Although Durjaya was already a great king, the lord, having equipped himself with elephants, horses, chariots, and cavalry, reflected upon the further expansion of his kingdom.
Having reflected thus, the wise one assembled an army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, and took his stand facing the northern direction;
all the regions to the north of that high-souled one became his domain.
Having conquered this region known as Bhārata,
that invincible one then also subdued the region named Kiṃpuruṣa.
Beyond that, he conquered another region, Harivarṣa;
and he also conquered Ramya, Hiraṇmaya, Kuru, and Bhadrāśva.
He conquered all of this, including Ilāvṛta in the center of Meru.
Having conquered this island named Jambū,
that king proceeded to conquer the King of the Gods (Indra), who was accompanied by all the deities.

Having ascended Mount Meru, the sage Nārada, son of Brahmā, then proclaimed the victory over Durjaya to the king of the gods, [asking]: "Have the gods, gandharvas, dānavas, guhyakas, humans, or daityas been conquered? (38)
Then Indra, accompanied by the world-protectors, being filled with haste,
went to slay Durjaya— who had been conquered by his weapons— in a short time;
leaving Mount Meru, he arrived here in the mortal world.
And in the eastern region, the lord Indra, together with the world-protectors, will reside;
his very great deeds shall come to pass.
After Durjaya had conquered the gods and was returning,
he established his camp on the slopes of Mount Gandhamādana;
having thus settled his forces, he encountered those two ascetics.
Having understood this, O King, they both said: "O Durjaya, the world-protectors have been restrained by you;
without all the world-protectors, the universe does not function. Therefore, grant us that supreme station. (42)
When this had been said, Durjaya, the knower of dharma, then spoke: "Who are you two? Thereupon those two subduers of enemies replied, "O giver of honor, we are two asuras named Vidyut and Suvidyut."
If you now desire that we both, well-prepared among the virtuous, should perform all the duties of the world-protectors according to dharma, O invincible one! (44)
When this was said by Durjaya, those two were immediately established in heaven and made guardians of the world (lokapālas); thereafter, they vanished from sight.
On that mountain, those two shall also perform great deeds;
and on Mount Mandara, there will be a great king who is invincible.
Having beheld the divine forest of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), which resembled the Nandana grove,
that best of kings wandered joyfully through this delightful place for as long as he desired.
