There, beneath a golden tree, he saw two maidens who were endowed with supreme beauty and possessed a most wonderful appearance. (48)
Upon seeing them, he was filled with wonder and thought, "Who are these two, O fair-eyed one? While he remained thus reflecting for a single moment,
he beheld two ascetics in that forest.
Seeing them, the king suddenly attained supreme joy out of affection;
quickly descending from his elephant, he himself bowed down before the two of them. (50)
Seated upon an excellent seat made of kuśa grass offered by the two of them, he was asked:
"Who are you? From where have you come? To whom do you belong? And why are you staying here? (51)
Laughing, the king known as Supratīka said:
"A son has been born to him, named Durjaya by name. (52)
"O best of beings, all the kings on earth desire victory here;
I have come, and I must certainly be remembered by you, O you whose wealth is asceticism. Tell me who you two are, out of a desire to show me favor. (53)
The two ascetics said:
"We are the two sons of Svāyambhuva Manu, known as Hetu and Prahetu.
We went to Mount Meru for the purpose of destroying the gods."
There, our great army, teeming with elephants, horses, and chariots,
conquered all the gods by the hundreds and thousands.
And those gods, seeing that entire great army struck down and deprived of life by the asuras, then went to him for refuge. (56)
There, in the Ocean of Milk where the Lord of Gods, Hari, the Sovereign himself, lies asleep,
they all made their petition preceded by prostrations.
"O God of gods, O Hari, this entire army has been defeated by the foremost of the asuras;
protect us who are terrified and whose eyes are distraught. (58)
O Keśava, in the past, during the war between the gods and the asuras, we were protected by you from the cruel Kālanemi, who possessed a thousand arms, in that battle. (59)
Even now, O Lord of Gods, there are two Asuras who are thorns to the gods, named Hetu and Prahetu, accompanied by a vast retinue of troops;
having slain them, protect us all, O God of Gods, O Lord of the World! (60)
Thus addressed, the Lord Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the Sovereign and Master of the World, replied:
"I myself shall go to slay them. (61)
Having been addressed thus, the gods then set out from the vicinity of Mount Meru, reflecting in their minds upon Janārdana.
But as soon as they had merely thought of him, the god who bears the discus and mace, alone and possessed of great strength, entered our army.
Having made himself one-fold, ten-fold, a hundred-fold, a thousand-fold, a hundred-thousand-fold, and ten-million-fold by his own power, the Lord of the World [manifested]. (64)
While that best of gods stood thus, O King, whichever asura among our army relied upon the strength of the two of us was seen slain, fallen to the ground, and deprived of consciousness. (65)
Thus, that army, crowded with horses and filled with foot soldiers and elephants, was suddenly struck down by Viśvamūrti through his illusory power.
Having destroyed the entire fourfold army, the Lord who bears the discus,
seeing us two emaciated, then vanished from sight.
Having witnessed such deeds of the divine wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
we have indeed sought refuge in him alone for the sake of his propitiation.
And you, O King, are the son of our friend and the offspring of Supratīka;
and these two daughters of ours, Hetū and Sukeśī, as well as Miśrakeśī, the daughter of Prahetu—accept them, O lord of men! (69)
Thus addressed by the two auspicious daughters of Heti, Durjaya,
the lord of men, took them as his wives according to the sacred law.
Having obtained them, the king, suddenly filled with supreme joy, returned to his own kingdom surrounded by his own army. || 71 ||
Then, after a long time, two sons were born to him:
Suprabha was the son of Sukeśī, and Sudarśana was the son of Miśrakeśī.
Having obtained those two auspicious sons, the illustrious King Durjaya himself,
in the course of time, went to a nearby forest.
While staying there, indeed terrifying the various forest-dwelling creatures,
he beheld a sinless sage standing in the forest, having taken refuge in the wilderness.
To the illustrious and auspicious one named Gauramukha, who was performing austerities, the protector of the host of sages and the savior of sinners himself; (75)
In that twice-born man’s hermitage— filled with pure waters and excellent, fragrant trees wafted by the breeze—
his house shone like a great cloud descended from the sky to the earth, resembling a magnificent celestial chariot.
The sky was illuminated by the fires of the blazing sacrificial altars; his garments were perfectly cleansed and perfumed;
and the sound of the *sāman* chants was raised together with his disciples.
Surrounded by beautiful women and daughters of ṛṣis—
such was his dwelling in that excellent hermitage,
where all the trees were in full bloom with flowers. (77)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 10.
Śrī Varāha said: Then, having seen that hermitage of Gauramukha to be such as this, Durjaya reflected upon that beautiful circle of hermitages.
"I shall enter here and see the most righteous sages.
Having thought thus, the king then entered that hermitage.
Then, once the king had entered, the righteous sage Gauramukha, filled with supreme joy, performed a worship for him.
Having performed the rites of welcome and so forth, at the conclusion of their conversation, that great sage said to him,
"O best of kings, I shall provide food for you and your followers according to my capacity."
"I shall do so; let the draft animals be released," said the twice-born man.
Having spoken thus, that sage of rigid vows remained silent.
The king also remained there, accompanied by his own attendants, out of devotion to him;
at that time, about five akṣauhiṇīs of his army were stationed there.
[He thought: "And what food will this ascetic give to me here?"
Having then invited King Durjaya, the brahmin Gauramukha reflected: "What kind of food should be given by me to him?"
As that great seer of purified soul was reflecting in this way,
the Lord of Gods, the sovereign Hari Nārāyaṇa, stood within his mind.
Then, having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa with his mind,
that best of sages entered the Gaṅgā and propitiated him.
Dharaṇī said: O supporter of the earth, how did Gauramukha please Viṣṇu?
My curiosity to hear this has arisen with a desire for a complete account.
Salutations eternally to Viṣṇu; salutations to you who are clothed in yellow;
salutations to you whose form is primordial; salutations to you whose form is water.
Salutations to you who abide in all things; salutations to you who recline upon the waters;
salutations to you whose form is the earth; salutations to you whose essence is light.
Salutations to you who have the form of wind; salutations to you whose form is space.
You are the god of all beings; you are the Lord, residing within the heart. 13.
You are the syllable *oṃ* and the exclamation *vaṣaṭ*, and you are established everywhere;
you are the beginning of all the gods, yet no beginning of you is found.
O God, you are Bhūḥ, you are Bhuvaḥ, you are remembered as Janaḥ and Mahas;
you are Tapas and you are Satya; O God, all that is moving and unmoving resides within you.
This entire universe has arisen from you; the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas have originated from you;
the scriptures were born from you, and the sacrifices are established in you. || 16 ||
From you come the trees and the creepers; from you, all the forest herbs;
from you alone, O Janārdana, come the cattle, the birds, and the serpents.
O Lord of the gods of gods, King Durjaya has also arrived; I am eager to offer hospitality to this guest.
O God of gods, Lord of the world, O Lord of deities, for me who am now destitute and bowed down in devotion, please provide a store of food today.
Whatever I touch with my hand, whatever I see with my eye—whether it be a tree or grass and tubers—that becomes for me the fourfold food. (20)
Likewise, whatever else has been meditated upon by me with my mind, may all that be accomplished for me; salutations to you, O Supreme Lord. (21)
Thus praised, Keśava, the Lord of gods and Master of the worlds,
was pleased and revealed his own true form to that sage.
With a highly gratified soul, he said, "O Brahmin, choose a supreme boon.
Having heard this, as soon as the sage opened his eyes—
Then Janārdana, holding a conch and a mace in his hands and clad in yellow garments,
appeared radiant, seated upon Garuḍa and possessing the splendor of twelve suns.
If the light of a thousand suns were to rise simultaneously in the sky,
it might perhaps resemble the radiance of that Great-Souled One.
There, O Goddess, that sage beheld the entire universe situated in one place, yet divided into many parts, his eyes wide with wonder.
He approached the God with his head bowed and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke: "O Keśava, if the God will be a granter of boons to me, his devotee... (27)
Now, this king, together with his army and vehicles,
having taken his meal in my hermitage, shall depart for his own home tomorrow.
Thus addressed, the Lord of Gods became the granter of boons to him;
he bestowed upon him the perfection of his heart's desire and a jewel of great luster.
Having given that, the god vanished, and the sage Gauramukha went to his holy hermitage,
frequented by various sages.
Having gone there, that best of Brahmins, the sage, reflected upon a house with a hundred stories,
which was as high as a great cloud and shaped like a peak of the Himalayas,
resembling the rays of the moon.
Then the brahmin, having obtained the boon from Viṣṇu, constructed thousands, lakhs, and crores of such houses everywhere.
Then, near the walls were gardens attached to them,
resounding with the cries of flocks of cuckoos and filled with various excellent birds,
and abounding in *campaka*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, and *nāgakeśara* trees.
Likewise, there were trees of various species everywhere in the house gardens,
as well as elephant stables for the elephants and horse pens for the horses.
The brahmin made collections of various kinds of food in every way—
various sorts of things to be chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked— and likewise prepared a great store of cooked rice and other foods, along with golden vessels on all sides.
Having done this, that brahmin said to the king of great splendor,
"Let all the troops enter the houses."
Having been addressed thus, the king then entered that mountain-like mansion;
meanwhile, his other servants quickly entered within.
Then, after they had entered, the sage Gauramukha took that divine jewel and spoke thus to the king: || 38 ||
"O King, for the purpose of bathing and eating, as well as to relieve the fatigue of the journey, I shall send you courtesans and female slaves. (39)
Having spoken thus, that best of Brahmins placed that auspicious Vaiṣṇava jewel in a secluded spot while the king looked on.
As soon as that jewel, which possessed a pure and even luster, was placed there,
thousands of women of divine form emerged from it.

Some excellent women, with delicate limbs, unguents, and the like; with beautiful cheeks, lovely features, fine hair-ends, and beautiful eyes—some of them set forth, taking golden vessels in their hands. (42)
In this manner, the groups of women there, as well as the men and laborers—all the servants of that king—departed; they took only their food first and all their clothing. (43)
Those women, acting with haste, provided a bath on the royal highway for all the servants, as well as for the men, horses, and elephants.

Various kinds of musical instruments were played there on all sides; other women danced during the king’s immersion, while others sang there as he bathed, just as they did for Śakra when he was bathing.

Having thus bathed with divine offerings, the high-minded king, that lord of kings, reflected with a mind filled with wonder: "Is this the power of the sage, or rather the result of his asceticism, or perhaps the jewel? (46)
Having bathed in this manner and likewise donned two excellent, auspicious garments,
that best of kings partook of various kinds of food according to the prescribed rite.
And just as the worship was performed by that great seer for the king, in the same manner the best of sages performed it for his servants as well. (48)
While that king was eating together with his servants, troops, and mounts,
the sun, glowing with a crimson radiance, went to the mountain of setting.
Then night arrived, now adorned with the autumnal moon and the circle of stars;
and that lord of Rohiṇī brings forth passion.
And she was also well-endowed with the quality of gentleness. || 50 ||
The preceptor of the Daityas, the lord of the gods, who was formerly uplifted together with the descendant of Bhṛgu by the rays of Kṛṣṇa’s dark splendor,
no longer shines now that he has fallen into the midst of the [hostile] faction.
The cognition of embodied beings arises through the connection with intrinsic nature. || 51 ||
The son of the Earth (Mars) releases his deep redness, and Rāhu is freed from the white rays of the moon;
the world’s inherent nature is released by gods and asuras, yet the powerful king remains well-disposed toward that very nature.

In the stainless orb of rays proclaimed by the Lord of the Site (Siteśvara), which is like the sun and perfected by the Siddhānta, Ketu does not cause great darkness; likewise, the state of those with evil conduct becomes stainless.
The son of the king shone through his own deeds, manifesting to the world the exalted wisdom of Mercury;
for a long time, he was one who cherished his dependents and was wedded to the forest.
This agreement among the virtuous would certainly be established. || 54 ||
The comet makes the sky appear intensely tawny for a long time as it stands upon the path of the gods;
yet a wicked man never [causes such distress] in the assembly of the virtuous.
He performs his own pure skillful action. || 55 ||
Even though illuminated by the rays of the moon,
the noble-born women, devoted to their duty, shone forth at every step as they proceeded toward the place where the Dharma was being proclaimed.
Through the conjunction with great splendor, there is the exaltation of the great.
The son of the Sun, having been completely defeated by the son of King Varuṇa— who was intent upon the three humors—
shines forth, established by Kauśika.
The ritual action of the knower would never be otherwise. || 57 ||
That child of mine who, in former times, subdued the dualities of those assembled together and propitiated the throne of Hari,
now shines forth for a very long time with both Fortune and Wisdom.
Through constant remembrance of Viṣṇu, that which is difficult to attain [is achieved]. || 58 ||
Thus did that auspicious night pass for the sage in the excellent hermitage of King Durjaya,
who was accompanied by his servants, vassals, noble horses, and elephants.
By means of worship with excellent garments, ornaments, and so forth. || 59 ||
Thus, in such houses, there were then excellent couches adorned with choice jewels, covered with fine cloths, and provided with the finest spreads.
Resplendent with the graceful gestures performed by beautiful women.
There, the king dismissed the lords of the earth along with their servants to their respective homes from all sides;
when they had departed, he slept, attended by an excellent woman.
Like the Lord of the Gods, the powerful one went to heaven. || 61 ||
Thus, by the power of that high-souled sage Sumanas, the servants and their master all slept peacefully and joyfully at that time.
Then, when the night had passed, the king saw that those women had again vanished from there, as had those houses.
Seeing those invisible, highly precious, and excellent seats and waters, the king was overcome with wonder and reflected in distress: (64)
Thinking again and again, "How can this jewel become mine?", King Durjaya then eventually attained it.
Thinking, "I shall take this wish-fulfilling gem from him," that king set out from the outskirts of the hermitage;
having gone not very far outside the hermitage, he remained there with his mount. (66)
Then he indeed dispatched a minister named Virocana to the task of requesting the jewel from the sage Gauramukha.
Approaching that sage, the king prepared to request the jewel, saying:
"O vessel of gems, let the jewel be given to him. (68)
Thus addressed by the minister, Gauramukha, filled with anger, said:
"The Brahmin receives and the king indeed gives;
yet you, being a king yourself, how is it that you beg like a wretched man? (69)
"Speak thus to the ill-behaved King Durjaya himself:
'Go quickly, O Durācāra; let not the world pass you by! (70)
Having spoken thus, the sage departed to gather kusha grass and fuel, while reflecting in his mind upon that jewel which destroys enemies. || 71 ||
Having been addressed thus, the messenger then went into the presence of the king and related everything that had been said by the brahmin.
Then, his soul overcome with anger upon hearing the Brahmin's speech, Durjaya said to the vassal named Nīla: "Go without delay;
having seized the jewel from the Brahmin, return quickly as you please."
Thus addressed, Nīla, accompanied by a vast retinue of troops, then went to that forest hermitage belonging to the brahmin.
Having seen that jewel placed there in the fire-chamber,
Nīla descended from his chariot and alighted upon the ground.
Then, as that most terrible Nīla had descended,
beings with cruel intentions emerged from that jewel, weapons in their hands.
Accompanied by charioteers, banners, horses, arrows, swords,
and shields, and equipped with bows and quivers— these warriors, exceedingly difficult to conquer and possessed of great strength, emerged in countless numbers after piercing that jewel.
There, fifteen great heroes were ready;
O illustrious lady, I shall tell you their names—listen to them. (78)
Suprabha, Dīptatejas, Suraśmi, Śubhadarśana, Sukānti, Sundara, Sunda, Pradyumna, Sumanas, and Śubha. (79)
Suśīla, Sukhada, Śambhu, Sudānta, and Soma—these fifteen are declared to be the leaders arising from the Maṇi. || 80 ||
Then, seeing Virocana surrounded by a vast army,
they, with various weapons in hand, undauntedly engaged him in battle.
Their bows, radiant as gold, their arrows bound with well-fashioned shafts of Jāmbūnada gold,
and their terrifying swords fell [upon the enemy].
The *bhuśuṇḍī* and the *śūla* are the most excellent [weapons]. || 82 ||
Chariot stood encircling chariot, elephant against elephant, horse against the steed of Hara,
and foot-soldier of most fierce prowess [against his counterpart].
He advanced on foot alone toward the foremost [of the enemy].
Likewise,
many duels took place in the battle as the heroes fled while hurling insults at Vibhīṣaṇa, whose path was marked by his drawn bow.
A most terrible conflict arose, born of their arms.
Then, as that tumultuous battle proceeded,
the king’s minister was slain, rendered unconscious, along with his followers and all his forces.
He went to the abode of Vaivasvata. || 85 ||
When that minister of King Durjaya had been slain, King Durjaya himself approached with his own army,
accompanied by horses and chariots, and exceedingly fierce.
The valiant one fought with those jewel-like weapons.
Then, at that time, a great slaughter appeared among the king's troops;
thereafter, having heard from both the cause and the agent that his son-in-law was in battle—
Then, as the mighty-armed one was fighting, two armies advanced against him;
hear now, O Dhara, who those Daityas in that force were, as they were described by Hari.
Praghasa, Vighasa, Saṅghasa, Aśanisaprabha, Vidyutprabha, Sughoṣa, Unmattākṣa, and Bhayaṃkara. (89)
Agnidanta, Agnitejas, Bāhuśakra, Pratardana, Virādha, Bhīmakarman, and likewise Vipracitti. (90)
These fifteen excellent Asuras possessed supreme weapons; each one here was individually accompanied by an Akṣauhiṇī of followers.
In that battle, the followers of Mahāmāyā, accompanied by a vast retinue of troops, fought against the great-souled Durjaya and his sons born of Maṇi.
Suprabha, however, struck Praghasa in battle with five arrows that resembled venomous serpents, like blazing birds of prey. || 93 ||
Taptatejas pierced Vighasa with three arrows;
Surashmi pierced Sanghasam in return with ten arrows.
The one of auspicious appearance pierced Aśaniprabha with five arrows in battle; Sukānti pierced Vidyutprabha, and likewise Sundara pierced Sughoṣa. (95)
Then Sunda pierced Unmattākṣa with five swift arrows and cut his bow with a sharp, straight-knotted shaft.
Sumanas [conquered] Agnidamṣṭra, Suśubha [conquered] Agnitejas, Suśīla [conquered] Vāyuśakra, and Sumukha [conquered] Pratardana. (97)
(Śambhu was thus [fought] by Virādha of terrible deeds, and Vipracitti likewise [fought] Soma; this battle was great. || 98 ||
Having caused them to fight one another with great skill in weaponry,
those Daityas were then slain in their respective order by means of weapons produced from the jewel.
While that truly terrible and great battle between them was increasing, the sage Gauramukha, having gathered sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, and other materials, [prepared for his ritual]. (100)
He has arrived at this great wonder, a battle of terrifying appearance,
accompanied by a vast retinue of troops and standing there as invincible.
Seeing him at the gate, that sage sat down, deeply absorbed in thought, and then sought to understand the very cause of the jewel.
Having thus brought about that fierce and intense battle involving the jewel,
the sage Gauramukha meditated upon Hari, the Lord of Gods.
That god, clad in yellow garments and seated upon his bird-vehicle, appeared before him and uttered these words: "What service can I perform for you here? (104)
That sage, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Puruṣottama:
"Slay this wicked one, who is difficult to conquer, along with his army and his followers. (105)
Thus addressed by him, he then released the Sudarśana discus, which resembled a blazing fire—the Kālacakra—against Durjaya’s army. || 106 ||
By that discus, that Asura army, difficult to conquer, was reduced to ashes in many ways in an instant, in the mere blink of an eye. || 107 ||
Having done this, the god then spoke these words to the sage Gauramukha in an instant: "The Dānava force has been destroyed."
Then, in this very forest known as Naimiṣa-araṇya, it shall indeed become true to its name, especially for the Brāhmaṇas. || 109 ||

And I, O Sage, am the Sacrificial Person (Yajñapuruṣa) in this forest-dwelling; and these fifteen leaders shall always be my officiating priests (yājyās). In the Kṛta Age, they will become kings born of jewels, O Sage.
Having spoken thus, the Lord, the Sovereign, then vanished;
the twice-born man also remained in his own hermitage, filled with supreme joy.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 11.
Śrī Varāha said:
Then, having heard that his son had been consumed by the fire of the wheel, the best of kings,
Supratīka, with a clear mind, reflected, O monarch.
As he was reflecting in this way, there then arose an idea in his mind.
On Mount Citrakūṭa, Viṣṇu is always celebrated as Rāma;
therefore, I praise the Lord of the Universe by the name known as Rāma. || 2 ||
Supratīka said:
I bow to Rāma, the lord of men, the infallible,
the ancient sage, the destroyer of the enemies of the gods.
To Maheśvara, whose nature is Śiva, the source of all, who eternally removes the distress of those who take refuge in him, and who upholds prosperity; || 3 ||
O Lord, you who assume all forms always produce the splendors of all luminous bodies;
likewise, you exist as the five qualities in the earth and in the water.
O Hari, you are established as fourfold in earth, threefold in fire, twofold in air, and as the person whose body is sound in the ether.
You are the moon, the sun, and the sacrificial fire;
it is said that this entire world is dissolved within you,
for the world finds its delight established in you.
"You are praised as Rāma; thus the world is established. || 5 ||
In this ocean of existence, crowded with the waves of the tree of suffering, and terrifyingly devoid of the support of forbearance,
a person does not sink if they possess the raft of mindfulness of you.
"O Rāma, you were remembered thus in the forest of asceticism."
O Hari, when the Vedas have been lost,
you always assume the form of a fish for yourself,
at the end of the age, delighting all the quarters of the sky.
O All-pervading Lord, you are likewise Agni, the bearer of many forms.
O Mādhava, you have always assumed that tortoise form during the churning of the waters in age after age;
O Janārdana, there is nowhere else any being superior to you, who are yourself the supreme source of all that exists.
O Great-Souled One, you have pervaded this entire universe; you know all your own quarters and all directions.
How then are you the primordial and supreme abode?
And having abandoned all other refuge, I go for protection to [you]. || 9 ||
In the beginning, you alone existed; from you then arose the earth, water, fire, wind, space, as well as mind, intellect, the qualities of consciousness, and everything produced from them.
By you this entire universe is pervaded;
you are considered by me to be the eternal Puruṣa,
O Lord of the entire universe, whose form is the universe.
O thousand-armed one, victory to you, O God of gods!
Homage be to Rāma of great majesty. 11.
Thus praised, the best of gods was pleased and then manifested his form before King Supratīka,
and thereafter spoke to him.
And he said to Supratīka, "Choose a boon."
Having heard these words of his, the king, with great agitation, bowed to the God of gods and said:
"O Lord of Gods, grant this to me."
When your supreme form remains in dissolution, || 13 ||
When this was said, the excellent king in an instant attained dissolution into the form of the Slayer of Asuras;
remaining as one with Him, he became liberated.
That lord of the earth [performed] with many ritual sections.
Śrī Varāha said:
Thus has this Purāṇa been narrated by me to you—a portion of that which was originally composed by Svāyambhuva.
It is not possible for anyone here, even with many thousands of mouths, to speak of its entirety.

O blessed lady, this Purāṇa has been recounted by me to you only in brief and from memory; it contains descriptions of the creation measured by the waters of the ocean, as well as various priceless accounts of events that occurred here and there.
"It was spoken by the Self-Existent One, by Brahmā, and even by Nārāyaṇa; how could there be another?
We have declared to you that it is impossible for us."
Because it consists of that very form, this [scripture] is primary by virtue of its being remembered. || 17 ||
The number of grains of sand in the ocean and of dust particles on the earth may be known;
but there is no reckoning for the creations of the Supreme Lord as he sports. 18.
O lady of pure smiles, this portion of Nārāyaṇa has been described by me; this is the account regarding the Kṛta age. What else do you wish to hear? (19)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 12.
Dharaṇī said: Having seen this great wonder, the sage Gauramukha and those born of jewels [asked]: "What indeed is the excellent fruit obtained from the Guru? (1)
Who was that illustrious sage Gauramukha, so supremely righteous?
What deed did that bull among sages perform upon seeing Hari?
Śrī Varāha said: Having witnessed the deed performed by the Blessed One in the twinkling of an eye, the sage,
desiring to propitiate that very deity, departed for the forest.
The sacred ford named Prabhāsa, belonging to Soma, is extremely difficult to attain.
There, the god who is the destroyer of the Daityas is proclaimed by those who contemplate sacred sites;
he propitiated Hari, who is known by the name Daityasūdana.
While he was propitiating the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa,
the great yogi, the eminent sage Mārkaṇḍeya, arrived.
Seeing him arrived from afar, that sage, filled with supreme joy, honored him with devotion by offering water for his feet and the arghya oblation.
Then the sage asked him, who was seated upon a Kusha-grass mat that was aphrodisiac in nature:
"Instruct me, O tiger among sages; what shall I do, O observer of great vows? (7)
Thus addressed, that lord of brahmins, Mārkaṇḍeya of great asceticism,
then spoke with gentle words to the sage Gauramukha.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
This indeed is the great task—that there should be association with the virtuous.
But as for that matter which is accompanied by doubt, ask about that, O great sage.
Gauramukha said:
These who are called "Fathers" (pitaraḥ) by those who proclaim the Vedas—
are they common to all social classes (varṇas), or are they distinct for each?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Nārāyaṇa is the primordial teacher of all the gods;
from him Brahmā was born, and he too created seven sages.
"Offer sacrifice to me," thus was he addressed by that Parameṣṭhin;
then they first sacrificed the self by means of the self—so says the Śruti.
To those who were indeed born of Brahmā and whose actions were characterized by great transformative power, he uttered a curse:
"Since this great transgression has been committed, you shall all undoubtedly become fallen from knowledge. (13)
Having been thus cursed by Brahmā, those sons born of himself immediately procreated sons who would continue their lineages and then departed for the third heaven.
Then, after those expounders of the Veda had departed for the third heaven,
their sons quickly gratified them by means of the offering of funeral rites (śrāddha).
And all those inhabitants of celestial mansions, the seven mind-born sons of Brahmā,
remained there beholding that offering of the funeral cake as it was prescribed by the mantras.
Gauramukha said:
O Brahmin, who are those ancestors of yours and for how long do they remain? From what source do the hosts of ancestors arise, and how are they established in that world? (17)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Certain excellent ones who increase the soma of the gods are active;
those seven, Marīci and the others, are remembered as the Pitṛs in heaven. (18)
Four indeed possess form, while three others are formless;
I shall proclaim their creation of the worlds, so listen to that. || 19 ||
Learn from me in detail their power and great supernatural faculties (mahardhi). There are three other supreme hosts among them who bear the form of Dharma;
I shall proclaim their names and their worlds—listen to that.
The worlds named Saṃtānaka, where those radiant ones dwell—
those formless hosts of ancestors— are indeed the sons of Prajāpati.
Those who were the best among the progeny of Virāja are remembered as the Vairājas.
For they are the fathers of the gods; indeed, they worship those deities here in this world.
Having fallen from these worlds and reached the eternal worlds, they are indeed born again as exponents of the Veda at the end of hundreds of yugas. (23)
Having regained that memory, they once more perfected the unsurpassed yoga;
contemplating the pure course of yoga from which a return [to worldly existence] is difficult to attain.
These are the ancestors at the Śrāddha ceremony who increase the yoga of yogins;
they were first nourished by those devoted to yoga through the power of yoga.
Therefore, O best of yogins, offerings should be given to the yogins;
this indeed is the first, unsurpassed creation of the Soma-drinkers.
These best of the twice-born exist as one body;
though they dwell in the heavenly realm, they are the officiating priests for those residing in the world of mortals.
The sons of Brahmā, such as Marīci and others, were their priests, who had attained greatness.
Sanaka and the others passed away into the world of those known as Kalpavāsikas; from them came the Vairājas, who remained established in austerity;
and from them came the Satyalokas, who are liberated—such is this lineage of the Pitṛs.
The Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, belonging to Mārīci, are known as the Vairājas and the Barhiṣads; the Sukāleyas are the Pitṛs of the Prajāpati Vasiṣṭha.
They too are to be worshipped by the three castes, but not by a Śūdra, who is excluded.
A Śūdra, permitted by the three [higher] castes, may worship all the ancestors;
however, he does not have separate ancestors of his own Śūdra lineage.
O Brahmin, is it not seen among the wise that there are those who are liberated yet possess consciousness?
This is evident from the perspective of specialized scriptures and from the teachings of the Purāṇas. (31)
Thus, having understood the scripture through the praises of the sages,
Brahmā himself then obtained the memory of his sons born from his own creation;
and by that very knowledge, they too attained supreme liberation.

Kaśyapa and the others are to be known as belonging to the Vasus and the rest; likewise, the Gandharvas and others are certainly to be understood without distinction among the castes, beginning with the Vasus. (33)
O great sage, this ancestral creation has been described to you by way of summary;
indeed, its end is not seen even in ten million years.

I shall declare the times for the śrāddha; listen to them, O best of the twice-born. [The proper occasion arises] when material suitable for a śrāddha has arrived, or when a distinguished brahmin has come. (35)
One should perform the śrāddha ceremony after ascertaining that it falls on a vyatīpāta yoga, or during the solstices (ayana),
or when the equinoxes (viṣuva) have arrived, or during an eclipse of the moon or the sun;
O best of Brahmins, [it should be done] at all such times when the sun passes through the zodiacal signs.
One should perform voluntary śrāddhas during afflictions caused by constellations and planets, upon seeing evil dreams, and likewise at the arrival of the new harvest.
When the new moon coincides with the asterisms Ārdrā, Viśākhā, or Svātī,
the host of ancestors attains satisfaction for eight years through the performance of Śrāddha rites.
When the new moon occurs under the asterism Puṣya, Raudra (Ārdrā), or Punarvasu, the ancestors, being duly honored, attain satisfaction for twelve years. || 39 ||

On the day of Vāsava (Pūrvā-phālgunī), Ajaikapād (Pūrvā-bhādrapadā), and the constellation of the Pitṛs (Maghā), as well as on the new moon day under the constellation of Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj)— this [opportunity] is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
O best of the twice-born, when the new moon occurs during those nine asterisms,
then śrāddhas should be offered by those desiring inexhaustible fruit;
even with a thousand million [offerings], there is no end to the merit.
Furthermore, O ancestors, you proclaim to us this secret and meritorious time for the śrāddha ceremony:
namely, the third day of the month of Vaiśākha.
This is the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
On the thirteenth and fifteenth days of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, and on the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha,
during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
Likewise, [this applies] also during the Aṣṭakās and the two solstices. || 43 ||
A self-restrained man should also offer water mixed with sesame seeds here to the ancestors;
by him, a Śrāddha has been performed for a thousand years.
The ancestors declare this to be a secret.

If the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha should ever coincide with the Vāruṇa asterism (Śatabhiṣaj), that is the supreme time for the ancestors; yet, O twice-born one, it is not attained by those of meager merit.
O best of Brahmins, if the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā should indeed occur at that time,
water and food offered to the ancestors will always provide them with satisfaction.
For ten thousand years by those humans born in that family. || 46 ||
If the Pūrva-bhādrapadās occur at that very time,
then by the Śrāddha which is performed for the ancestors on that day, they attain supreme satisfaction.
The ancestors sleep for an entire Yuga.
The hosts of sages declare that the fortnight which they proclaim as the time for the śrāddha brings satisfaction to the ancestors. (47)
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā, Sarayū, Vipāśā, Sarasvatī, Naimiṣa, or Gomatī,
one should then perform worship with devotion.
Having performed what is harmful to his ancestors, he destroys them. || 48 ||

And the ancestors sing this: "When, having finally attained satisfaction from the waters of Māgha, shall we reach full contentment at the end of the dark fortnight of Māgha through the auspicious waters of sacred fords offered by our sons and others? (49)

When the mind and wealth of men are pure, the time is auspicious, the ritual procedure is prescribed, the recipient is as described, and there is supreme devotion, these grant to men their heart's desires. (50)
Likewise, there are verses sung by the ancestors here; listen to them, O best of beings. Having heard them, that which is destined to happen will indeed come to pass for you, O wise-souled one.
Blessed indeed would be the wise man born in our family who, without being stingy with his wealth, shall offer the funeral cakes. (52)
"Whatever wealth there may be—jewels, garments, the Mahāyāna, and all enjoyments and possessions—he will give it to the brahmins on our behalf. (53)
Or, at this time, a man whose wealth is limited to that alone, with a mind bowed in devotion, shall feed the foremost of Brahmins according to his ability with food. (54)
One who is incapable of giving food shall, according to his ability, give wild vegetables to the foremost of the twice-born, or even a small sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Even there, being devoid of the necessary means, O twice-born one, he will bow down and give to some eminent brahmin the sesame seeds situated at the very tips of his fingertips.
Bowing with devotion, he will offer a handful of water mixed with seven or eight sesame seeds, even while intending it for us.
"Having obtained it from anywhere at all, or even from cows for their daily fodder, he will give it to us with devotion when [the cow's milk] is lacking, thereby pleasing us. (58)
In the absence of all else, having gone to the forest, displaying his armpits, he shall recite this aloud to the Sun and the other world-protectors: || 59 ||

I have no wealth, no riches, nor anything else worthy of a śrāddha offering; I bow to my ancestors. May my ancestors be satisfied by my devotion as I stretch out these two arms upon the path of the wind.
This purpose regarding existence and non-existence was sung by the ancestors;
O twice-born one, he who performs [the rite] in this manner has truly performed the śrāddha.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 13.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O brahmin-sage, this was previously told to me by the wise son of Brahmā, the younger brother of Sanaka; now listen to [the account of] the brahmins.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who knows the Trimadhu, one who knows the Trisuparṇa, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas, a knower of the Veda, a Śrotriya, a yogin, and likewise one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman; || 2 ||
An officiating priest, a sister’s son, a daughter’s son, as well as a father-in-law, a son-in-law, a maternal uncle, and a Brahmin devoted to austerity; || 3 ||
One should employ at the śrāddha ceremony a disciple devoted to the five fires, as well as a relative, and one devoted to his mother and father. || 4 ||
A betrayer of friends, one with deformed nails, a twice-born man with black teeth, a defiler of virgins, one who has abandoned the sacred fire and the Vedas, and a seller of Soma; || 5 ||
Likewise, one who is cursed, a thief, a slanderer, a village priest, a teacher for hire, and one who has been taught by a teacher for hire; || 6 ||
The husband of a woman who previously had another husband, one who abandons his mother or father,
one who supports the offspring of a *vṛṣalī*, the husband of a *vṛṣalī*,
and likewise a *devalaka*— these do not deserve an invitation to a *śrāddha*. (7)
On the first day, the wise man should perform the invitation of the most eminent Brahmins;
having invited the twice-born, he should feed them and the ascetics once they have arrived at his home.
Having washed the feet and so forth of the twice-born who have come to his house, he should feed them;
then, with pure hands, he should seat them on their seats after they have sipped water (ācamana).
One should employ an even number for the ancestors and an odd number for the gods; or one may assign a single seat to each of the gods and a single seat to each of the ancestors.

Likewise, one endowed with devotion should perform the śrāddha for the maternal grandfather accompanied by the Vaiśvadeva rite; or else, one may perform the Vaiśvadeva rite as part of the ritual procedure for those attached to worldly life.
One should feed the Brahmins representing the gods facing east, and those representing the paternal and maternal ancestors facing north.
"O twice-born one, some say that the performance of the śrāddha for those two should be separate;
other great sages declare it should be performed together with a single cooking. (13)
Having offered kuśa grass for a seat and having worshipped according to the rite of the arghya offering,
the wise man should perform the invocation of the deities with their permission.
One who knows the ritual procedure should offer the *arghya* to the gods with barley-water;
having offered fragrant incense and lamps to them according to the rules,
one should prepare everything for the ancestors with the *apasavya* method.
Then, having obtained permission and having offered darbha grass cut in two,
the wise man should perform the invocation of the ancestors preceded by mantras.
With water mixed with sesame seeds and wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), the wise man should present the arghya and other offerings.
If at that time a guest— a twice-born traveler seeking food— arrives there,
he should, with the permission of the Brahmins, honor him according to his desire.
Yogins, who benefit human beings through various forms, wander this earth with their true nature remaining unrecognized. (18)
Therefore, a wise man should honor a guest who has arrived at the time of a śrāddha;
for a guest who is not honored by the best of the twice-born destroys the fruit of the śrāddha rite. (19)
O bull among men, having been permitted by those twice-born ones, he should then offer the side dishes and the food— excluding anything salty— into the fire three times.
"‘Svāhā to Agni Kavyavāhana’—this is the first oblation;
immediately after that, one should offer it to Soma Pitṛmat. (21)
And let another third oblation be offered to Vaivasvata;
then, one should pour out the very small remainder of the offering into the bowls of the Brahmins.
Then, having served very delicious food that is highly desired and well-prepared, one should say these non-harsh words: "Please enjoy it as you wish. (23)
Those who eat should do so with focused minds, in silence, with pleasant countenances, and at ease;
they should be free from anger and haste, and the giver should also offer the food with devotion. (24)
O best of the twice-born, having performed the recitation of mantras that destroy demons and the strewing of sesame seeds upon the ground, those very ancestors should be meditated upon.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather, their forms nourished by this oblation, attain satisfaction today. (26)
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather, residing today within the bodies of Brahmins, attain satisfaction. (27)
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through these rice-balls offered by me upon the earth. (28)
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through this devotion which has been uttered by me. (29)
May his maternal grandfather attain satisfaction,
as well as his father and his other ancestors;
may the Viśvedevas likewise attain the highest state.
And may the Yātudhānas meet their destruction. || 30 ||
Lord Hari, the master of sacrifice, the enjoyer of all *havya* and *kavya* offerings, the immutable Self and Supreme Lord, is present here;
by His presence, may all *rakṣasas* and all *asuras* immediately depart. (31)
When these Brahmins are satisfied, one should scatter food upon the surface of the earth;
one should give them water once each for the purpose of sipping (ācamana).
Permitted by them once they were well-satisfied, he then, being composed, took up all the food and water on the ground and gathered it into the funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
In the same manner, one should offer water and a handful of water using the *pitṛtīrtha*;
likewise, one should present the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) for the maternal grandfathers using that very same *tīrtha*.
Upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing southward, these should be honored with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
One should first offer the rice-ball (piṇḍa) for one's father near the remains of the meal;
another for the grandfather, and likewise yet another for that [grandfather’s] father.
At the root of the *darbha* grass, one should gratify the ancestors who feed on ointments by rubbing them with ointment;
likewise, at the *piṇḍa* for the maternal grandfather, one should do so with offerings of perfumes, garlands, and the like.
Having performed the worship, O lord of the twice-born, the wise man,
with devotion and a focused mind, should first offer water for sipping (ācamana) to the ancestors.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability, accompanied by the blessing "May there be a good svadhā.
Having given the dakṣiṇā to them, one should cause those representing the Vaiśvadevas to recite:
"May those who are the Viśvedevas be pleased by this. (38)
When those Brahmins have said "So be it," one should likewise request the blessings;
thereafter, O high-minded one, one should dismiss the gods first and the ancestors afterwards.
The same sequence is prescribed for the maternal grandfathers along with the gods;
likewise, one should perform the feeding according to one's capacity, as well as the giving of gifts and the dismissal of the twice-born before the washing of their feet. (40)
Having honored those who are knowledgeable regarding the paternal and maternal lineages, he should dismiss them with words of affection after they have been requested [to leave]. Then,
permitted to depart, he should follow them as far as the door.
Then he should perform the daily rite known as Vaiśvadeva, and thereafter,
having honored [the deities], he should eat together with his servants, kinsmen, and himself.
In this manner, a wise man should perform the śrāddha for his paternal ancestors as well as for his maternal grandfathers;
nourished by these śrāddhas, the ancestors shall grant all desires. (43)
Three things are purifying at a funeral feast (śrāddha): a daughter's son, a kutapa blanket, and sesame seeds;
likewise, the gift of silver and the sight [of these items]. 44.
O best of Brahmins, for one performing a śrāddha, anger, traveling on a road, and haste must be avoided;
this triad applies to the eater as well—of this there is no doubt. (45)
O twice-born one, for those men who perform the śrāddha ceremony, the Viśvedevas, the ancestors, as well as the maternal grandfathers, and the entire lineage are nourished. (46)
The host of ancestors has Soma as its support, and the moon is the support of yoga;
therefore, O best of Brahmins, a śrāddha performed in conjunction with yoga is highly praised.
O twice-born one, if a yogi stands before even a thousand brahmins,
he delivers all those who eat as well as the patron of the sacrifice.
O best of the twice-born, this was told to me by Sanatkumāra in a former kalpa,
and likewise by Vāyu and by Śambhu to the gods.
O twice-born one, it will likewise occur through the son of Śakti among the sages, and then through the one known as Maitreya, in due succession, up until what has been told to you by me.
This is the general ancestral rite (paitṛkī kriyā) found in all the Purāṇas;
having understood this section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) in its proper sequence, one shall be liberated from bondage.
Relying upon this, the sages of firm vows have now attained Nirvana through Gauramukha; you too should likewise become supreme.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, I have narrated this out of devotion to you who asked.
For one who, having sacrificed to the ancestors, meditates upon Hari—what could be greater than that? It is certain that there is no ancestral ritual (pitrya-tantra) superior to that.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 14.
Dharaṇī said:
O Lord, having thus heard the rules for the Śrāddha from the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, what did Gauramukha do thereafter, O All-pervading One? (1)
Śrī Varāha said:
Having then heard this system of the ancestors, O Earth, the great sage was made to remember his hundred births by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya.
Dharaṇī said:
"O Blessed One, who was this Gauramukha? Who is he remembered to have been in another birth? And how did he remember [his past]? Having remembered it, what did that most excellent being do? (3)
The illustrious Varāha said: In another birth of Brahmā, Bhṛgu was himself present in person;
and this great sage Mārkaṇḍeya is born from his lineage.
"That which was previously stated by Brahmā—that 'you shall attain a happy rebirth'—was prompted by your sons; it was for that reason that you were enlightened by Mārkaṇḍeya. (5)
He remembered all his births; and having remembered what was done [in each], listen, O lady of excellent hips, as I relate it to you in brief.
Having thus worshipped the ancestors for twelve years according to the prescribed rules for ancestral rites,
that sage thereafter commenced the hymn of praise to Hari.
At that sacred ford named Prabhāsa, renowned throughout the three worlds,
Gauramukha stood to offer praise to the God who is the destroyer of the Daityas.
Gauramukha said: I shall praise Mahendra, the destroyer of the pride of enemies, Śiva,
Nārāyaṇa, and the established foundation for those who know Brahman.
The primordial, ancient Hari, who dwells with the sun, moon, and the pair of Aśvins, and who eternally slays the Daityas.

He who, in the past, at the time of the destruction of the Vedas, assumed the form of a fish—possessing the body of a great mountain, with the brilliance of his tail's flickering flames terrifying the enemies of the gods; || 10 ||

Likewise, he who in ancient times assumed the form of a tortoise and supported the king of mountains used as a churning rod for the ocean—may that ancient Puruṣa, the slayer of Daityas and lord of gods, protect me out of his desire for my welfare. 11.
The Great Boar, that high-souled one known as the limb of sacrifice, who constantly entered from the surface of the earth into the realm below, is worshipped by the gods and the Siddhas.
May that ancient destroyer of the Daityas protect me. || 12 ||
And he eternally assumes the form of Nṛsiṃha in age after age, most fierce and terrifying to the foremost of yogins,
with a formidable mouth and a luster like the tip of gold.
May he whose intention is like a jewel, the destroyer of the asuras, protect us. || 13 ||
For the sake of destroying Bali’s sacrifice, that Great-Souled One,
whose true nature is a body of yoga, again assumed the guise of concealment,
characterized by a wooden staff and a deerskin.
May he who stepped upon the earth with his foot protect [us]. || 14 ||
Having conquered the earth twenty-one times,
the fierce [Rāma] gave it to Kaśyapa;
he, the son of Jamadagni, was the protector of his lineage.
May Hiraṇyagarbha, the slayer of the asuras, protect us. || 15 ||
May He, the destroyer of demons, protect us— He who manifested His primordial fourfold body, characterized by a likeness to Hiraṇyagarbha, through various distinct forms such as Rāma and others.
To grant fearlessness to the gods who were terrified by the pride of the demons Cāṇūra and Kaṃsa,

the Lord became Vāsudeva in age after age; in every kalpa he manifests in wondrous forms, and in age after age that Great Soul, assuming manifold bodies, appears under the name Kalki to establish the stability of the social orders.
The eternal, ancient one, composed of Brahman,
whose form neither gods, siddhas, nor daityas perceive— having abandoned the path of discursive knowledge.
May He who assumes many moving forms, such as that of a fish and others, protect us. 18.
Homage, homage to you, O Supreme Person;
again and yet again, homage, homage to you! Homage to you from the front and from behind.
Lead me to the state of liberation; salutations to you! || 19 ||
As that great seer of purified soul was thus offering salutations,
the God himself, bearing the discus and the mace, appeared before his very eyes.

Upon seeing him, his consciousness rose up from his own body, free from all waves; and having attained him, that divine self entered into dissolution within that eternal Brahman, which is known as the state beyond rebirth.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 15.
Dharaṇī said:
Then the king of the gods, Śatakratu, was cursed by Durvāsas:
"You shall dwell among mortals through the son of Supratīka. (1)
"O fool, you have been cast down from heaven!"—having been addressed thus, O supporter of the earth, Indra, accompanied by all the gods, approached the mortal world. || 2 ||
And what did that Blessed One, the Supreme Lord and highest among the knowers of yoga, do after that invincible one had been struck down?
O Lord, what did Svarge and Vidyutsuvidyūc do then?
Please, out of your grace, explain this doubt of mine. || 4 ||
Śrī Varāha said: O Earth,
the king of the gods, Śatakratu, was defeated by Durjaya in the land of Bhārata,
specifically in Vārāṇasī to the east.
It stands established, having taken recourse [to it], together with the gods, yakṣas, and great serpents.
Then, O beautiful one, Vidyut and Suvidyut, having resorted to yoga,
took recourse to a long-lasting fever of heat through the application of the activity of wind.
By means of their yogic power (yogamāyā), they both acted as if protecting the entire world.
Having heard that Durjaya was dead, they then brought their fourfold army and set out against the gods while stationed within the ocean.
Then those two Daityas, having arrived with a great army,
took refuge on Mount Himavat and remained there.
Even the gods, having assembled a great army and donned their armor, deliberated calmly, desiring to attain the position of Indra.
Thereupon, the sage Aṅgiras, the preceptor of the gods, said:
"In the meantime, you must indeed perform the first Gomedha sacrifice."
"Sacrifices must be performed with all the ritual offerings, O immortals, for there is but one goal.
This instruction has been given by me; let it be carried out immediately."
Thus addressed, the gods then provided cattle and livestock for them,
and released Saramā to guard them and ensure their safety.
And those cows, protected by Devaśunī on that mountain,
then went to where those asuras were grazing.

And those cows, seeing them, said to Śukra, their priest: "O Brahmin, these divine cows intended for sacrifice are being driven away by Saramā while she protects them; they have been deprived of their gods. Tell us, what shall be done now? (14)
Thus addressed, Śukra then replied to the Asuras:
"O Asuras, let these cows be taken away quickly; do not delay! (15)
When they had spoken thus, the Daityas then carried off those cows at their will;
once they were stolen, Saramā remained intent on searching for their tracks.
She saw the cows being led away by the sons of Diti on the mountain;
the bitch too was seen by the Daityas, having especially perceived their path.
Having seen her, they addressed these words to her with gentleness first, preceded by conciliation:
"O auspicious Saramā, having milked the milk from these cows... (18)
Saying, "Drink thus," those leaders of the Daityas quickly gave it to her; having given her the milk to drink, they [departed]. (19)
"Do not report these cows to the king of the gods," they said;
having spoken thus, the Daityas then released that bitch in the forest. (20)
Released by them, she went quickly toward the gods, trembling; and Saramā paid homage to Devendra, the best of the gods.
And the Marut gods were appointed by Devendra for her:
"O mighty ones, go in secret for the sake of protecting Devaśunī."
Having been addressed thus by him in that subtle form, they departed quickly;
having arrived at the mountain, they also paid homage to the Lord of the Gods.
The king of the gods asked her, "Where were the cows, O Saramā?
Thus addressed, Saramā replied, "I do not know."
Then Indra, filled with rage, said this to the Maruts: "Where are the cows prepared for the sacrifice? And how is it that there is a female dog? (25)
Thus addressed by the Lord of the Gods on the mountain, the Maruts,
remaining unperturbed, related that deed performed by Saramā.
Then Indra, the lord of gods and subduer of Pāka, overcome by great wrath, rose up and struck the female dog with his foot. || 27 ||
"O foolish woman, you have drunk the milk, and those cows have been carried off by the Asuras!
Having spoken thus, O Earth, he struck Saramā with his foot.
By the blow of Indra’s foot, milk flowed from her mouth;
with that flowing milk, wherever that bitch became cows,
there the Lord of the Gods went at that time along with his army upon the earth.
Having gone there, the Lord of the Gods beheld those cows brought by the Daityas.
Those Daityas who were exceedingly powerful and were guarding them were instantly slain by his armies; they abandoned the cows and fled in their own forms.
Then Surendra was surrounded by his subjects, who were filled with supreme joy;
and having obtained them, Mahendra was endowed with the highest delight.
That lord performed thousands of various sacrifices;
by those sacrifices being performed, the strength of Indra increased.
Indra, his strength increased, spoke to the divine army:
"Let the gods quickly arm themselves for the task of slaying the Daityas."
Thus addressed, the gods then immediately donned their armor;
accompanied by Indra, the gods went forth for the destruction of the asuras.
Having gone there, they quickly fought and conquered the army of the Asuras;
and the Asuras, defeated by the gods, those who remained after the slaughter,
being terrified and deprived of their senses, plunged into the waters of the ocean on that mountain.
O Earth, the Lord of the Gods, that sovereign deity, having ascended to the third heaven together with the world-protectors,
enjoyed it as before.
The man who constantly hears this supreme narrative of Saramā obtains the fruit of the Gomedha sacrifice. || 37 ||
And that king who, having been deprived of his kingdom, listens to this with a concentrated mind, that man regains his own kingdom, just as the lord of the gods regained heaven. || 38 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 16.
Dharaṇī said: "O Lord, those bulls among men who were born from that jewel at that time—
surely a boon was granted to them by the Blessed One in the Tretā Yuga."
There will surely be kings; how did their origin come about? What deeds did they perform? Tell me their individual names.
Śrī Varāha said:
O beautiful one, O upholder of beings, listen to the origin of that high-minded king named Suprabhamaṇija. || 3 ||
In the beginning, in the Kṛta age of old, there was a mighty-armed king known as Śrutakīrti, the most powerful in the three worlds. (4)
On earth, Suprabha, the son of Maṇija, attained the status of his son;
he was the mighty Śrutakīrti, known by the name Prajāpāla.
One day, he set out for a forest infested with beasts of prey;
there he beheld the great and auspicious hermitage circle of a sage.
In that place lived a sage named Mahātapa, most righteous, who performed austerities without food while chanting the eternal Brahman.
Then that illustrious king, the protector of his subjects and a man of great asceticism, set his mind upon entering and did indeed enter.
In that excellent hermitage, there were vine-arbors,
radiant as the moon and sun, frequented by the powerful paths of wild forest trees and the earth-born creepers.
The bees of noble lineage do not weary their knowledge. || 9 ||
Even the celestial damsels, with their outstretched fingers and nails as tender as the interior of a deep-red lotus,
left the ground far behind to follow the lofty footprints of Vṛtra’s enemy.
In some places nearby, various birds and intoxicated bees, exceedingly joyful, dwelt together;
there were branches of diverse proportions, beautifully flowered and joined in perfect symmetry, resounding with their loud songs.

It was frequented by birds dwelling in bowers of Kadamba, Nīpa, Arjuna, Śīla, and Śāla trees, warbling with sweet voices; it was like the unwavering resolve of a noble person engaged in their duties, remaining unperturbed by those who stand firm in their positions.

Then, by the twice-born householders on all sides, who had kindled their sacrificial fires and raised the smoke of the oblations, that [unrighteousness] was torn asunder—just as a female elephant of unrighteousness is rent apart by lions with sharp fangs and excellent, thick manes. || 13 ||
Thus, that king entered the excellent hermitage, observing various means;
and when he had entered, he of intense splendor—
A great ascetic, the foremost among the doers of merit,
he was seen like the sun of infinite rays upon a seat of kusha grass— the preeminent among the knowers of Brahman. (14)
Having seen this, that victorious king forgot his thoughts regarding the deer due to the sage’s discourse,
and he set his mind upon righteousness.
Having approached that unsurpassed sage, the king— || 15 ||
Seeing that king, the protector of subjects, who was free from sin, the sage performed the rites of hospitality for a guest,
beginning with the offering of a seat and words of welcome.
Then, having taken his seat and bowed to the bull among sages, the king, O Earth, asked this most difficult question. (17)
O Blessed One, whose vows are praised, tell me what must be done by men who are submerged in the suffering of saṃsāra and desire to cross over it, as I bow before you.

Mahātapa said: For men sinking in the ocean of worldly existence, a firm and most stable boat must be constructed through worship, charity, fire-offerings, various sacrifices, and meditations performed together.

O King, now make the ship of the Lord of the Three Worlds with great ropes such as the vital breaths (prāṇa) and others, which are fastened by the bolts of the gods' warriors who grant liberation. 19.
O lord of men, he who bows with devotion to Nārāyaṇa, the lord of gods and the remover of hell,
becomes free from sorrow and attains the supreme state beyond grief.
He attains that imperishable abode of Viṣṇu.
The King said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, tell me in truth how the eternal Viṣṇu is worshipped by men desiring liberation. (21)
Mahātapa said:
Listen, O King of great wisdom, how Viṣṇu is propitiated;
for Hari, the Lord of all yogis, is pleased with men as well as with women. (22)
"All the gods, along with the ancestors and those beginning with Brahmā who dwell within the cosmic egg,
have arisen from the presence of Viṣṇu"— this is the Vedic revelation.
Agni, as well as the Aśvins, Gaurī, the elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa), the serpent (Śeṣa), Kārttikeya, likewise Āditya, and the Mothers together with Durgā. || 24 ||
The Lord of Wealth (Dhanapati), Viṣṇu, Yama, Rudra, as well as the Moon and the Pitṛs—these were born primarily from the Lord of the Universe. || 25 ||
All beings indeed arose from the body of Hiraṇyagarbha;
thereafter, they each separately bore pride on every side.
"I am worthy," "I am the one to be sacrificed for"—such was their great clamor heard in the assembly of the gods, resembling the roar of a turbulent ocean. (27)
O King, as they were thus disputing, the Fire-god arose and said to me, "Sacrifice to me," speaking thus: "Meditate upon me. (28)
"Surely this body, belonging to Prajāpati, would meet its destruction if separated from me, for I am the Great Self. (29)
Having spoken thus, the fire emerged after casting off its body;
yet even after it had departed, that body did not decay.
Then the two Aśvins, the best of those worthy of sacrifice, appearing in embodied form as the prāṇa and apāna breaths residing within the body, said: "We two are the foremost. (31)
Having spoken thus, they both abandoned their bodies and departed for some other place; having brought about their destruction as well, the Kṣetrin remained in that city.
Then the voice spoke: "Goddess Gaurī, preeminence resides in me.
Having spoken thus, that auspicious goddess emerged from the sacred field (kṣetra) to the outside.
Even without her, that field remained deficient in speech;
then Gaṇapati, known as Ākāśa, spoke these words at that time.
"Without me, no body whatsoever shall remain for long;
at the end of time [it shall perish]," having spoken thus, he too departed from his body. (35)
Even though it has become separate, this body has not perished;
likewise, even without the principle called space, it does not fall apart.
But seeing that the field was established as being devoid of cavities, all those bodily elements indeed spoke these words: || 37 ||
"Once we have said, 'The maintenance of a body distinct from us does not occur,' all those embodied beings abandoned their bodies. (38)
Even a field abandoned by them is protected by the Puruṣa;
seeing him, Skanda spoke, and he is proclaimed as Ahaṅkāra (the Ego). || 39 ||
"Even the manifestation of the body is not possible without me";
having spoken thus, he departed from the body and remained separate. (40)
Because that field remained as if empty even though it was not actually empty, the Sun-god became angry upon seeing it; he is celebrated as Āditya.
"How can this field be desired even for a moment without me?
Having spoken thus, he departed; yet that body did not decay.
Then the host known as the Mothers, led by Kāma, arose and said:
"There is no existence of a body separate from me.
Having spoken thus, he departed, yet that body did not perish.
Then Māyā spoke out of anger and was proclaimed as Durgā;
having said, "There is no prosperity for him without me," she vanished once again.
Then the quarters of the sky rose up and spoke these great words:
"There is no doubt that our task shall not be accomplished without us.
Having arrived from the four directions, they then departed in an instant.
Then Dhanapati said, "O Vayu, since my body has perished, where can there be its rebirth? Having spoken thus, he too vanished into the crown of his head.
Then Viṣṇu said to the mind, "This body cannot endure to remain even for a moment without me," and having spoken thus, he vanished once more.
Then Dharma said: "I have protected all this;
now that [the time] has arrived, how will this come to pass? (48)
Having spoken thus, Dharma departed; that body did not decay.
Then Mahādeva, the unmanifest leader of beings, spoke: (49)
"May my body not become subject to decay; it shall be known as 'the Great' (Mahat). Having spoken thus, Śambhu departed, and that body did not perish.
Seeing him, the ancestors said:
"As long as we have departed, this body will surely perish.
Having spoken thus, they abandoned the body and vanished.
Fire is both the prāṇa and the apāna breaths; space and all the elements;
likewise, the field (kṣetra), the ego (ahaṃkāra), the sun, desire and the rest, the quarters, Vāyu, Viṣṇu, Dharma, Śambhu, and the objects of the senses are [all] by me. || 52 ||
But that field, once abandoned by them, remained exactly as it was,
being protected by Soma, the personified moon.
When Soma was thus established within the sixteen-fold imperishable [syllable],
I arose and wandered through that field endowed with qualities, just as before.
But having seen the body in its former state, protected by the Omniscient One,
all those field-deities fell into a state of embarrassment.
O best of kings, having thus praised that god, the Supreme Lord, they all then desired to go to their own abodes.
You are Agni, you are likewise Prāṇa, and you are Apāna Sarasvatī;
you are Ākāśa, you are the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and you are the constituent elements of the body.
O Lord, you are the ego; you are the Sun-god and the host of Aṣṭaka;
you are Māyā, the Earth, and Durgā; you are the quarters of space and the Lord of the Maruts.

You are Viṣṇu, you are likewise Dharma, you are Jiṣṇu, and you are Parājita; by virtue of your essential nature as the meaning of the Imperishable (Akṣara), you are designated as the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara). || 59 ||
"If we depart, how will this come to pass?
Thus, our very bodies must be abandoned right here. (50)
Therefore, O Lord, you must protect that which has come to such a state;
O Lord of Creatures, having created it yourself, we must not suffer the destruction of our station. (61)
Thus praised, the god then attained supreme satisfaction with them and said to them:
"You have been created by me for the sake of sport."
Since my purpose has been accomplished, what need have I for you?
Nevertheless, I shall now grant each of you two forms.
"Remain in the world of the gods in an incorporeal form for the sake of the duties of living beings,
but at the end of time, enter quickly into dissolution."
Furthermore, these physical forms should never think, "I am to be made. Thus, I now give names to you and to these images. (65)
Agni shall indeed be named Vaiśvānara, the Aśvins shall be Prāṇa and Apāna,
and likewise Gaurī shall be the daughter of the Himālaya mountain.
This group, beginning with Earth, shall become Gajavaktra (the Elephant-faced one).
These elements of the body shall indeed become the various beings;
likewise, the ego (ahaṃkāra) shall become Skanda Kārttikeya. || 67 ||
This Bhānu, in the form of Āditya, shall be both the embodied and the unembodied eyes;
furthermore, this group beginning with Kāma shall take the form of the Mothers.
This body is an illusion; this difficult path will come to an end through its cause.
There will be ten maidens, and these are the ten directions belonging to Varuṇa.
This Vāyu shall become Dhaneśa at the end of the cause;
this Manas shall undoubtedly become Viṣṇu by name. (70)
Dharma shall also undoubtedly be named Yama;
and the Lord Mahādeva shall become the principle of Mahat.
And the objects of the senses shall become the ancestors, there is no doubt;
O immortals, this Soma himself shall always be Yāmitra.
Thus has the Person of the Vedānta, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, been described; then the God, remaining in his own place, became silent along with all the deities.
Thus has been described to you, O King, that Lord Janārdana, who is to be known through the Vedas and possesses such power; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 17.
Prajāpāla said:
O great sage, how did the birth of Agni occur, or that of the two Aśvins? And likewise, how did the births of Gaurī, Gaṇapati, the Nāgas, and Guha come about?
Of the Sun, the Moon, and the Mothers, or likewise of Durgā and the Directions;
or of Kubera, Viṣṇu, Dharma, or Parameṣṭhin. || 2 ||
O Sage, how did these deities of the body come to possess physical forms— those of Śambhu, the ancestors, and likewise the Moon?
Furthermore, O Sage, what is their food, what is their designation,
and what is the lunar day (tithi) on which they are worshipped so that these [goddesses] bestow health upon men?
O Sage, you ought to tell me this, along with its secret significance.
Mahātapas said: The Self, whose nature is Nārāyaṇa, is to be realized through yoga;
it is omniscient, and as it sports, there arises within itself a desire for enjoyment.
When the great elements were agitated, this wondrous sound arose.
Filled with displeasure, he resolved upon that transformation;
as he was undergoing that transformation, a great fire then arose, surrounded by millions of flames, roaring and consisting of the nature of burning.
He too, being exceedingly radiant, resolved upon transformation.
From that fire undergoing transformation, there shone forth an extremely fierce wind;
and from that state of transformation, space (ākāśa) came into being.
That sky was characterized by sound, and that wind was full of power;
and that fire, joined with water, was then mutually conjoined.
The water was dried up by the splendor [of the sun], while the fiercely moving wind and the oppressed sky instantly made way for it.
Thus, all that solidity became condensed into a single mass;
this very earth, O illustrious one, grew larger than them.
Due to the fourfold hardness of yoga and from the increase of each successive quality, earth is to be known as having five qualities; they too are established within this [earth]. (11)
And as he was becoming solidified, he became the cosmic egg;
within it was the god Nārāyaṇa, possessing four forms and four arms.
Desiring to create various offspring in the form of Prajāpati, the Grandfather of the worlds could not achieve his creation through mere reflection. || 13 ||
Then, a very great and most terrible anger arose within him;
from that anger, a thousand-rayed fire, consisting of burning flames, rose up.
O King, desiring to burn him, he was then addressed by Brahmā, "Carry the offerings to the gods (havya) and the offerings to the ancestors (kavya)"; thus he became known as Havyavāhana.
Hungry, he approached Brahmā and said, "What shall I do? Please instruct me.
Then Brahmā replied, "You shall obtain satisfaction in three ways."
Since you first attain satisfaction when sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) have been given, and then lead the gods to their share of those fees, you therefore became the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. || 17 ||
O Vibhāvasu, whatever has been offered everywhere throughout the three worlds, carry that for the sake of the gods; therefore, you are the bearer of the oblation (Havyavāhana).
The body is said to be the "house," and since you are now its master, therefore, O all-pervading Lord, become the Gārhapatya fire. (19)
"O Lord, because you, when invoked, lead all men to the supreme state, your name shall indeed be Vaiśvānara; so shall your word come to pass. (20)
"Draviṇa" is said to mean strength, and since wealth is also "draviṇa," you alone bestow that; therefore, you became known as Draviṇodas (the Giver of Wealth). || 21 ||
"O Lord, because you shall always drink the subtle essence of the body,
therefore, my child, your name shall be Tanūnapāt."
"O Lord, since you indeed know all that has been born and all that is yet unborn, let your name therefore be Jātavedas."
"Men are [called] *nārāḥ* in general, and the twice-born (*dvijātayaḥ*) in particular;
since they shall praise you, therefore become *Nārāśaṃsa*."
Aga shall eternally be invisible, soundless, and of the nature of certainty;
because you are Aga and because you are all-pervading, you shall therefore become Agni.
The root *dhmā* signifies filling and sound; that which is celebrated by the name *idhmā* shall become fuel (*idhma*) because it is that by which the filled [fire] comes forth. || 26 ||
"O son, these names of yours are worthy of sacrifice in the great ritual;
men sacrificing to you with their desires will undoubtedly satisfy you. (27)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 18.
Mahātapas said:
"The majesty and greatness of Viṣṇu has been recounted to you incidentally.
O King, listen now to the majesty of the lunar days (tithis) as it is being told by me."

Thus transformed, the great Mahānagni, born from the wrath of Brahmā, spoke to the god Brahmā: "O Lord, let a lunar day (tithi) be granted to me, on which I may attain renown throughout the entire world. || 2 ||
Brahmā said: O best of beings, O Pāvaka, you were first born from the gods, the yakṣas, and the gandharvas on the first lunar day (pratipadā).
"From your foot, other deities will emerge at every step;
therefore, this lunar day shall be known by your name. (4)
On that lunar day, those who offer oblations with sacrificial food (haviṣya) according to the Prājāpatya rite to the [divine] forms,
their ancestors and all the deities shall be pleased.
The four kinds of beings— humans, animals, asuras,
and all the gods along with the gandharvas— shall be gratified when you are satisfied.
And listen to the great fruit of him who, devoted to you, observes a fast on the first day of the lunar fortnight, or subsists on milk alone.
For thirty-six cycles of four yugas, he is honored in the heavenly world;
such a man is born endowed with splendor, beauty, and wealth.
"In this life he was a king, and after death he is glorified in heaven.
Then that fire became silent and went to take refuge with Brahmadatta.
The person who, having risen early in the morning, listens to this constantly, is liberated from sins by the birth of Agni; there is no doubt about this. || 10 ||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 19.
Prajāpāla said:
O Brahmin, thus was the origin of the high-souled Agni produced;
how did the two gods, the Aśvins, come to be Prāṇa and Apāna? (1)
Marīci was the son of Brahmā; Brahmā himself existed in fourteen forms, and among them, Marīci attained preeminence.
His son was the sage named Kaśyapa, possessed of great splendor;
he himself became a glorious Prajāpati and the father of the gods.
O Lord, he indeed had twelve sons who were Ādityas;
because they were all the offspring of Aditi, they are celebrated as the Ādityas.
Among them, the one of great splendor, Mārttaṇḍa, renowned throughout the world,
is proclaimed as the twelfth, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa.
Those months of yours are the Ādityas, while you yourself, O Hari, are the year;
thus these twelve Ādityas, with Mārtaṇḍa as their preeminent leader.
Tvaṣṭṛ gave him a daughter named Saṃjñā, who possessed great luster;
from her two offspring were born: Yama and likewise Yamunā.
Unable to endure his splendor, Aśvinī became as swift as thought;
leaving her own shadow there, she departed for the Northern Kurus.
The Sun, the illuminator of the world, united with her who was of similar form and caste;
from her also two were born: Śani and Tapatī.
When the Blessed One, the best of men, treated his sons unequally,
he spoke to Saṃjñā with eyes bloodshot with anger:
"O beautiful lady, you must not show partiality toward your own offspring."
When she, having been addressed thus, shone with incomparable splendor,
Yama, deeply distressed, spoke to his father.
"O father, this woman cannot be our mother; she is always like an enemy, behaving like a co-wife, though she is devoted only to her own children. (12)
Having heard these words of Yama, that shadow, overcome with rage, cursed him:
"You shall become the king of the pretas before long. (13)
Having heard this, Mārtaṇḍa, desiring the welfare of his son, then said:
"O son, you shall be situated between dharma and sin; you shall become a guardian of the world (Lokapāla) and you shall shine in heaven."
Mārttaṇḍa, provoked by anger toward Chāyā, cursed Śani:
"O son, because of your mother's fault, you shall have a cruel gaze. (15)
Having spoken thus, Bhanu rose up with the desire to behold Yoga;
