then he, along with his horses, beheld her in the northern Kuru region.
Then, having assumed the form of a horse, he went there to the Northern Kurus and,
by means of the path of Prajāpati, united himself with his own self.
Upon that daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, who had the form of a mare, Mārtaṇḍa cast his seed of intense brilliance;
it fell blazing and split into two parts.
There, Prāṇa and Apāna, having previously been subdued within the womb by the Self, became embodied once again through the granting of a boon. (19)
Those two best of men were born from Tvaṣṭṛ’s wife in the form of a mare;
therefore, those two gods are celebrated as the Aśvins, the sons of the Sun.
Prajāpati himself is the Light (Bhānu), and the power (Śakti) of Tvaṣṭṛ is both supreme and non-supreme;
as before, she resides within his body, having taken form though being formless.
Then those two gods, the Aśvins, approached Mārtaṇḍa and said to him: "O Svaruci, what should now be done by us? (22)
Mārttaṇḍa said:
"O sons, worship the Lord Prajāpati, the bestower of boons, with devotion;
he, Nārāyaṇa, will surely grant you a boon."
Thus were the two Aśvins first addressed by the high-souled Mārtaṇḍa;
they performed a most difficult penance with intense fervor,
remaining composed while reciting the hymn consisting of the *Brahmapāra*.
After a long time, Brahmā, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, was pleased with them through supreme affection and granted this boon to the two of them.
Prajāpāla said:
"O Brahman, O great sage, by your grace I desire to hear the hymn to Brahmā of unmanifest birth as uttered by the two Aśvins. (26)
Mahātapa said:
Listen, O King, to how this hymn was composed for the Aśvins by Brahmā, and hear,
O sinless one, what kind of fruit those two obtained from that hymn.

Oṃ, salutations to you who are actionless, free from conceptual proliferation, without support, independent, without object of reliance, devoid of qualities, without light, without substratum, invincible, and formless;
O Brahman, Great Brahman, beloved of the Brahmins, Puruṣa, Supreme Puruṣottama!
O God, supreme among the great gods, Sthāṇu, the establisher of all that stands; O Bhūta, great Bhūta, lord of Bhūtas; Yakṣa, great Yakṣa, lord of Yakṣas;
Guhya, lord of the great Guhyakas; Saumya, great Saumya, lord of the Saumyas.
O Bird, Lord of Great Birds; O Daitya, Lord of Great Daityas;
O Rudra, Lord of Great Rudras; O Viṣṇu, Lord of Great Viṣṇus;
O Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa, salutations to Prajāpati!
Thus praised then by those two Aśvins, that Prajāpati was gratified with supreme affection and spoke these words.
"Choose quickly a boon, most difficult even for the gods to obtain, by which, through that granting of a boon, I may dwell happily in heaven while wandering. (29)
The Aśvins said: "O God Prajāpati, grant us a share in the sacrifice, as well as the status of Soma-drinkers among the gods and eternal equality. (30)
Brahmā said: "Incomparable beauty and luster, the status of a physician among all things,
and the sovereignty over the Soma in the worlds— all this shall be yours."
Because all of this was given by Brahmā to the Aśvins in ancient times on the second lunar day, that day is the most excellent among all lunar days.
A man who desires beauty should offer flowers for one year; being constantly pure, that man shall possess a beautiful form,
and whatever qualities are proclaimed for the Aśvins shall also belong to him.
The man who constantly hears this supreme account of the birth of the Aśvins becomes liberated from all sins and is blessed with sons. (34)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 20.
Mahātapa said:
In the past, the divine Lord Prajāpati, whose nature is righteousness, desiring to create various kinds of progeny, reflected deeply when he could not find them.
Then, from his anger, that powerful Rudra was born;
because of that weeping of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), his state as Rudra came into being. || 3 ||
Brahmā gave him an auspicious maiden born from his own form as a wife;
her father, the goddess Bhāratī herself, gave her the name Gaurī.
To Rudra of immeasurable body, Brahmā himself, the Lord of Creatures, [offered her];
having obtained that woman of beautiful limbs, he was filled with supreme joy.
At the times of creation, Brahmā addressed him with the words, "O Rudra, create progeny," repeatedly urging him;
yet the mighty one, saying "I am incapable," submerged himself in the water. (6)
"Devoid of ascetic power, one who merely intends to perform penance cannot create progeny.
Thinking thus, the majestic Rudra then immersed himself in the water. (7)
When the Lord of Gods had submerged in that [water], Brahmā again took that most beautiful maiden Gaurī into his own body.
Desiring again to create, the Blessed One produced seven mind-born sons; and beginning with Dakṣa among them, living beings increased properly.
Therein were all the gods, including Vāsava, the sons of Dākṣāyaṇī—
the eight Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and likewise the Maruts.
Then that fair-hipped Gaurī was given by Brahmā to Dakṣa as his daughter—
she who had previously been wedded to the high-souled Rudra.
And that goddess, the daughter of Dakṣa, O best of kings, was born again.
Then Dakṣa, his soul delighted, seeing his own grandsons who had brought about his prosperity,
began the sacrifice for the gratification of Prajāpati.
There, all the sons of Brahmā, as well as Marīci and the others,
established themselves each in their own path and performed the duties of officiating priests.
Brahmā himself became Marīci, while others likewise became different [sages];
Atri remained engaged in sacrificial rites, and Aṅgiras became the Āgnīdhra priest.
Pulastya became the Hotṛ priest, and Pulaha became the Udgātṛ;
at that sacrifice, Kratu, the great ascetic, was the Prastotṛ.
The wise Pratihartṛ shone at that excellent sacrifice;
Vasiṣṭha was the Subrahmaṇya priest, while Sanaka and others were the members of the assembly.
There, Brahmā himself was the one to be sacrificed for (the patron), and he, being the object of sacrifice, was worshipped.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Aṅgiras, and others—the grandsons of Dakṣa—are to be worshipped;
for they are the manifest ancestors, and when they are pleased, the entire world is pleased.
There, the gods who seek their shares are the Ādityas, the Vasus, as well as the Viśvedevas, the Pitṛs, the Gandharvas and others, and the hosts of Maruts. (18)
As soon as they had each taken their respective portions of the sacrificial offerings that were presented as oblations,
at that very moment Brahmā again rose up from the water.
That Rudra who had previously arisen from anger and was submerged in the great waters then emerged from that water, radiant like a thousand suns.
The god, who consists of all knowledge, who embodies all deities, and who is stainless,
shone through his ascetic power as the direct beholder of the entire world.
At that time, O best of men, there arose the creation of five divine beings who dwelt upon the earth and were of the four castes. (22)
At that time, the manifestation of the Raudra creation occurred instantly;
now, O best of kings, listen to the account of the Rudra creation.
Having performed great austerities in the water for ten thousand years,
when Rudra awoke,
he beheld the earth with its forests, abounding in crops, delightful, and teeming with humans and cattle.

And then he heard the voices of the officiating priests in the abode of Dakṣa, as well as those of the ascetics in the hermitage, loudly proclaiming, "Thus it is proclaimed by those established in yoga. (25)
Then, having heard this, the all-knowing Supreme Lord of great splendor became exceedingly enraged and spoke these words.
Formerly, however, I was created by the Poet (Kavi) as the all-pervading one; then he spoke these words: "Create living beings. (27)
"By whom now has this description of the creation and so forth been composed?
Having spoken thus, the Supreme Lord roared intensely out of anger.
As he roared, flames then issued forth from his ears;
there were spirits, vetālas, ucchuṣmas, pretas, and pūtanās.
The Kūṣmāṇḍas and Yātudhānas, all with blazing faces,
rose up there by the millions, equipped with various weapons.
Seeing those hosts of spirits with various weapons in their hands,
he created an exceedingly beautiful chariot consisting of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
In that [chariot], there were the Ṛgveda and the others as its horses; the three principles (triguṇas) were its triple-pole;
the threefold worship was its triple-bolt; the three daily ablutions were its axle of dharma; and the sound of the wind was its rattle. || 32 ||
The two banners are day and night, while the two poles are merit and demerit;
the chariot is all the sciences, and Brahmā himself is the charioteer. (33)
The Gāyatrī is his bow, and the syllable Oṃ is its string;
the seven musical notes are the arrows of that God of gods, O observer of noble vows. (34)
Having thus assembled his retinue, the powerful Rudra, the god of gods, went toward Dakṣa’s sacrifice out of anger. || 35 ||
As that god was departing, he led Ambarāṅgiras away;
at that time, the collection of mantras of the officiating priests was lost upon the arrival of Rudra.
Seeing this reversal, all the officiating priests then said: "O gods, prepare yourselves; a great danger has come upon you. (37)
"O Brahmin, some powerful asura created by Brahmā is approaching this sacrifice for the sake of a share of the sacrificial offering—a thing most difficult to obtain. (38)
Thus addressed, the gods then spoke to their maternal grandfather:
"O Father Dakṣa, tell us what our task is here; speak what you wish to say. (39)
Dakṣa said:
"Let the weapons be taken up quickly; let battle be waged here.
When this was spoken by the gods, who were bearing various kinds of arms, [the conflict ensued].
A great battle was waged together with the followers of Rudra.
There, the Vetālas, Bhūtas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Grahas, and Pūtanās, bearing various weapons, fought with the guardians of the world. || 41 ||
The gods, driving away the fierce spirits toward the abode of Yama,
hurled terrible arrows, swords, and battle-axes.
Even the fierce elemental beings, with torches, bones, and arrows,
rushed out of anger at Rudra in the battle and forcefully attacked the gods in the fray.
Then, in that most fierce battle of terrifying form,
Rudra pierced Bhaga’s eyes with a single arrow in the fray.
Then, seeing Bhaga with his eye destroyed by the fall of Rudra’s arrow,
the radiant Pūṣan fought Rudra out of anger.
Seeing Pūṣan discharging nets of arrows in that great battle, Rudra, the slayer of enemy heroes, tore out his teeth.
Then, having seen those teeth of Pūṣan struck down by Rudra,
the eight Vasus fled in all directions, while the eleven Rudras fled swiftly.
Seeing them suddenly broken and fleeing in all directions, the powerful Viṣṇu, the younger brother of the Sun, then spoke these words to his own army: || 48 ||
"Where have you gone, abandoning manliness, pride, and even magnanimity? Why do you not quickly remember your resolve, your lineage, and your prosperity? (49)
Endowed with the qualities of the Supreme Lord, yet formerly trembling out of fear,
the Lotus-born One himself prostrates on the earth in vain.
Having spoken thus, Janārdana— Hari, whose hands hold the conch, discus, and mace, and who is clad in yellow garments— then mounted Garuḍa.
Then a hair-raising battle took place between Hari and Hara.
With vigor, Rudra pierced Hari with the Pāśupata weapon,
and the wrathful Hari pierced Rudra with the Nārāyaṇa weapon.
When both the Nārāyaṇa and Pāśupata weapons were discharged into the sky,
they fought fiercely for a divine thousand years, each desiring to slay the other.
Thus, their battle then lasted for a divine millennium.
Among them, one had a mass of matted hair bound upon his head with a crown;
another was blowing a conch shell, and yet another held a beautiful drum.
One there has a sword in his hand, and another likewise holds a staff;
one has limbs radiant with the Kaustubha gem, and another is adorned with sacred ashes.
One [hand] brandishes a mace and the second a staff;
one shines with bones as neck-ornaments, while the other has jewels; one wears yellow garments there, and the second has a girdle of serpents.
Thus, seeing those two rivals, both of whom were of the nature of Rudra and Nārāyaṇa,
each excelling the other, the Grandfather (Brahmā) then [intervened].
He said, "Let these two weapons be pacified by their own inherent nature; you two, being of excellent vows. Thus addressed by Brahmā, they both attained a state of tranquility.
Likewise, Brahmā spoke these words to Viṣṇu and Hara:
"Both you gods, Hari and Hara, shall attain renown in the world. (59)
And this sacrifice, though now shattered, shall reach completion;
through the lineage of Dakṣa, this world shall attain renown.
Having spoken thus to Hari and Hara, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, then said this to the worlds: "Let a portion for Rudra be given to him."
"The portion of Rudra is the eldest portion"—this is the Vedic revelation.
O Supreme Lord, let the gods offer praise to Rudra for us.
"Quickly offer praise with these names and songs to the God who took Bhaga’s eyes and destroyed Pūṣan’s teeth,
so that he, with a gracious soul, may grant you boons. (63)
Thus addressed, those gods, having paid homage to the Self-born One, performed a hymn of praise to the high-souled Śambhu with supreme devotion.
The gods said: "Salutations to the one with uneven eyes; salutations to you, the three-eyed one. Salutations to the thousand-eyed one; salutations to you, the wielder of the trident. (65)
Salutations to the one who holds a skull-topped staff in his hand; salutations to the one who bears a staff in his hand.
O Lord, you possess a splendor equal to millions of suns and the flames of the sacrificial fire.
"O Lord, due to our deluded understanding, we have now brought about this state of non-perception; O Master, O Lord, may this which has been done by us be forgiven. (67)
Obeisance to Śambhu, the three-eyed one who removes suffering,
who holds a trident in his hand and has a deformed countenance;
O Lord of all gods, you whose nature is pure.
Be gracious, O Rudra, O Acyuta, O you who are the essence of all beings!
O destroyer of Pūṣan’s teeth, O you of terrifying form, O you who caused the neck of the lord of serpents, Pralamba, to quiver;
O you of vast body, O Acyuta, O Blue-throated One!
Be gracious, O Lord of the Universe, O You whose form is the universe! 69.
O Lord of Gods, O Blue-throated One, you whose skillful deed is the bursting of Bhaga’s eyes— accept the principal portion of the sacrifice; be gracious!
Protect us, O you who are endowed with all virtues! || 70 ||
O God, destroyer of Tripura, whose body is adorned with white unguents and who bears a skull,
protect us in all dangers.
O Lord of Umā, [your birth] was from the stalk of a lotus. || 71 ||
O Lord of the Gods, O Infinite One with the excellent face of the Vedas, we behold within your body the creations and all else,
together with the Vedas, their auxiliary limbs, the sciences, and the Pada and Krama recensions.
All [beings] are hidden within you, O God of gods.
O Bhava, Śarva, Mahādeva, Pinākin, Rudra, Hara! We all bow before you; O Lord of the Universe, O Supreme Lord, protect us. 73.
Thus praised by the gods at that time, Maheśvara, the god of gods,
was pleased and spoke these words to all the deities.
Rudra said:
"Let there be eyes for Bhaga, and likewise teeth for Pūṣan;
let the sacrifice of Dakṣa become free from flaw, O sons of Aditi."
"O gods, I shall likewise remove your state of being as animals."
The state of being like beasts that arose among you gods by the sight of me has been instantly removed by me; you shall regain your status as lords. (76)
And I am the primordial, eternal Lord of all sciences;
indeed, in the form of a husband, I abide in the midst of the creatures.
Therefore, my name shall be Paśupati in the world;
for those who worship me, let there be the Pāśupata initiation.
When Rudra had spoken thus, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, addressed these words to Rudra with affection and preceded by a smile: || 79 ||
"O Lord Pāśupati, you will certainly attain fame in the world;
and this god shall also become renowned in the world by your name.
You shall be worshipped by all, including the gods and others. (80)
Having spoken thus, the wise Brahmā then said to Dakṣa:
"Give Gaurī to Rudra, for she was previously offered to him."
Having spoken thus, Dakṣa then gave that maiden Gaurī, who was most beautiful, to the great Rudra in the presence of Brahmā.
Rudra accepted that most beautiful woman according to the prescribed rites,
acting with great respect out of a desire to do what was pleasing to Dakṣa.
Once Dakṣāyaṇī had been taken as his bride, the Grandfather bestowed Kailāsa, the abode of Rudra, in the presence of the gods.
Rudra also departed for Mount Kailāsa along with the spirits (bhūtas),
and the gods likewise went to their respective places filled with joy;
Brahmā too, accompanied by Dakṣa, went to the city of Prajāpati.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 21.
Mahātapas said:
While that supreme lord Rudra was dwelling there,
Gaurī became enraged, recollecting the enmity toward her father.
He reflected: "An offense was committed against Dakṣa by him in the past, since the sacrifice was destroyed; therefore, I shall assume another body. (2)
"Having propitiated him through ascetic penance, I shall go to his house;
how else could I approach my father Dakṣa, whose kinsmen have been destroyed? (3)
Having thus reflected, the beautiful Sundarī, the daughter of the Lord of Beings,
went to the great mountain Himavat to practice asceticism.
There, after wasting away her body over a long period of time,
she was consumed by the fire of her own body and thereby became the daughter of the Mountain.
Known by the names Umā and Mahatī Kṛṣṇā,
she obtained a beautiful form in the abode of Himavat.
Again she performed severe penance, remembering the three-eyed God;
having declared, "He alone shall be my husband," she remained steadfast in her ascetic practice.
While she was performing that severe penance on the great mountain Himavat,
after a long time, the God was propitiated by her through her asceticism.
Maheśvara, having become an old brahmin with all his limbs weakened and stumbling at every step, came to her hermitage.
Having approached her with great difficulty, that best of the twice-born said:
"O auspicious lady, I am hungry; give me food, for I am a brahmin. (10)
Thus addressed, the auspicious maiden Umā, daughter of the mountain, then said to the brahmin:
"O Brahmin, I shall give you food such as fruits;
perform your bath quickly, O Brahmin, and eat the food as you please. (11)
Thus addressed, the brahmin then went to the great river Gaṅgā at his side, seeking to bathe, and descended into it to perform his ablutions.
While that Rudra, in the form of a brahmin, was performing his ablutions,
he transformed himself into a terrifying and fearsome crocodile made of illusion; then, by that wicked Madgu, the brahmin was seized.
Then, seeing himself held by the powerful crocodile,
he showed himself as someone else who was aged and spoke these words.
"O maiden, an act of sacrilege has occurred; run and bring me away from this wrath!
You ought to save me before I fall into a state of transformation. (15)
Having been addressed thus, Pārvatī then reflected:
"How may I, purified by asceticism, touch this Brahmin with the feeling toward a father that I have for the Lord of Mountains, and with the feeling toward a husband that I have for Śaṅkara? (16)
"If I do not rescue him while he is held by the crocodile in the water, then the sin of killing a Brahmin will be mine; of this there is no doubt. (17)
In the case of any other transgression, it is possible to remove the dharma;
however, the murder of a Brahmin is not like this, for having been spoken of in such a way, she departed in haste.
Having gone quickly, the timid woman seized the twice-born man with her hand and dragged him from within the water, just then as Hara himself, the Lord of Beings, appeared.
That very Lord Rudra, whom she had propitiated before beginning her ascetic penance,
now took his place in her hand.
Seeing him, the goddess was ashamed; remembering his previous abandonment, the fair-browed one, deeply abashed, did not utter any reply.
Seeing Gaurī thus become silent, Rudra, as if smiling,
took me by the hand and said, "O blessed lady, how can you abandon me here?"
O blessed lady, if you should take my hand in marriage in vain, then I shall say that [this act] was for the sake of food at the daughter of Brahmā. (23)
"This cannot be a joke," said the Goddess Parāparā;
then, feeling bashful, she spoke these words preceded by a smile. (24)
O God of gods, Lord of the three worlds, this endeavor is for your sake;
you, the divine Maheśvara, were propitiated as my husband in a previous birth.

"Now, Your Lordship shall be my husband and no other; however, my father, the lord of mountains, is my master. Having obtained his permission according to the prescribed rite, you shall then take my hand in marriage."
Having spoken thus to her father, the beautiful goddess then joined her palms in reverence and addressed Himavat.
Therefore, Rudra, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, was my husband in another birth; now, through penance, he alone has been meditated upon as the one who provides my refuge.
Having become the Lord of the Universe, Śaṅkara came to my penance grove as a brahmin and begged for food;
urged by me with the words "Go to bathe," he went to the Ganges. || 29 ||
There, Śaṅkara, in the form of an old brahmin, was quickly seized by Makara; he then uttered a cry of "Abrahmaṇyam! (an outrage against the brahmins).
"O dear one, out of fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin, I then held him in my hand;
as soon as he was held, Śaṅkara revealed his own body. (31)
Then the god spoke to me as I approached for the taking of his hand:
"O Goddess, O lady rich in asceticism, do not hesitate at all."
Having been addressed thus by that high-souled Śaṅkara, and having obtained permission from the Lord of Gods, I have come to question you;
now let whatever action is appropriate be performed quickly. (33)
Having heard those words, the king of mountains was then filled with joy;
at that time, he spoke to his blessed daughter of beautiful countenance.
"O daughter, I am blessed in this world, for Rudra himself, Hara, shall become my son-in-law. O Goddess, through you I have become possessed of offspring;
indeed, O daughter, I have been placed by you upon the very heads of all the gods."
"Wait for but a moment until my return.
Having spoken thus, the king went to the presence of Brahmā, the lord of the mountains.
Then, having seen the Great-Souled One, the grandfather of all the gods,
the king of mountains bowed down and spoke to Brahmā.
"O God, this daughter of mine—her I give to Rudra. Permitted by you, O God, I shall do that; please instruct me. (38)
Then Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, with a joyful mind, said to the gods: "Go and bestow that auspicious maiden upon Rudra. (39)
Thus addressed, the king of mountains quickly returned to his own abode and promptly summoned the gods, the ṛṣis, and the hosts of Siddhas.
Having likewise gone to Tumburu, Nārada, Hāhā, and Hūhū, as well as to the Kinnaras, Asuras, and Rākṣasas, he [spoke].
Mountains, rivers, crags, trees, and likewise medicinal herbs,
as well as mountains and the stones from the confluence, arrived indeed in embodied form to witness the marriage of the daughter of Himavat with Śaṅkara.
There, the earth became the sacrificial altar; the seven oceans were the water-jars;
the sun was the lamp, as was the moon; and the rivers carried the water. (43)
Having thus prepared the materials for the wedding, the lord of the foremost mountains sent Mount Mandara to the presence of Rudra.
Then, having been addressed by Mandara, Śaṅkara arrived swiftly;
the Supreme Lord took the hand of Soma according to the prescribed rite.
At that festival, Parvata and Nārada sang,
the Siddhas danced, and the auspicious lords of the forest scattered many flowers.
The celestial damsels danced loudly and with great intensity. || 46 ||
During that marriage ceremony, amidst the flow of water,
the four-faced one, who is devoted to the world yet established in his own self,
said to the maiden: "Become [famous], O daughter, in the world."
"A woman belongs to her husband and to other men as well.
Having spoken thus to Umā along with Rudra,
the Grandfather returned to his own city.
The lord of mountains, having honored his son-in-law,
sent away the powerful Soma;
and having worshipped all the gods, various Daityas, and sages with diverse offerings, he dismissed them.
Then he dismissed the leaders of the mountains with gifts of ornaments, excellent garments, and food.
Free from sorrow, stainless, and purified,
the high-souled Himavat, king of mountains, gave Umā of the beautiful countenance to the best of gods.
It shone like the sacrifice in the world of Brahmā.
Thus has this lineage of yours been told, O best of kings—a lineage which neither gods nor asuras know;
and by me, the self-born, the marriage of Gaurī has also been well-proclaimed through three births, beginning with Dakṣa.
Śrī Varāha said: Thus, for that reason, she who is known by the name Gaurī assumed a physical form,
just as it was described when the protector of subjects questioned me.
Formerly, by a great seer whose self was purified through asceticism.
This origin of Gaurī has indeed been told by the supreme Ṛṣi, and how her marriage took place—all that has been narrated to you. (52)
All this was indeed accomplished by Gaurī through her third lunar day (Tṛtīyā).
On that third lunar day, a man should avoid salt;
and a woman who fasts on it attains good fortune.
Whatever woman may be unfortunate, or whatever man may be exceedingly unfortunate—
having heard this, one should avoid salt on the third lunar day.
One obtains all desires, good fortune, and abundance of wealth;
one always finds health in this world, as well as beauty and nourishment. (55)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 22.
Prajāpāla said:
O best of men, how did the birth of Gaṇapati occur, and how did he become embodied?
Cut through this doubt of mine, which remains fixed with painful persistence.
Mahātapa said:
"In former times, all the hosts of gods and the sages whose wealth is austerity undertook their tasks in this manner, and they succeeded; of this there is no doubt."
Just as rites performed by those who follow the true path are accomplished despite obstacles,
so too are they accomplished without obstacle by all those who act rightly.
Then the gods, together with the ancestors, reflected with vigor; they all conferred for the purpose of creating obstacles to improper deeds.
Then, while those inhabitants of heaven were deliberating, the thought occurred to them to go toward the high-minded Rudra.
Having approached their preceptor Rudra, who dwells on Kailāsa,
they all spoke with humility, preceded by prostrations.
The gods said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, wielder of the trident, three-eyed one!
You ought to create someone for the purpose of obstructing those who are not distinguished [by merit].
Thus addressed by the gods, Bhava, filled with supreme joy,
then gazed upon Umā with an unblinking eye.
While that high-souled one was looking at me in the presence of the gods,
a thought arose in him as to why [the forms] were being seen in the sky.
"The form of the earth exists, and likewise the form of the waters;
this form of fire and of the wind is indeed seen. But how is it that space has none? Thinking thus, the god laughed.

Having seen Umā, who is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), that which was seen in the sky by Śambhu, and that which was previously spoken by Brahmā regarding the body of embodied beings—[all this was revealed]. (11)
And furthermore, that smile which was given by that supreme deity [Śiva]—
this [was caused] by these four purposes regarding the four elements, beginning with earth.
Embodied and exceedingly radiant,
with a blazing face and great splendor, the youth illuminated the quarters of the sky as he laughed;
endowed with the qualities of the Supreme Lord, he was like another Rudra in person.
As soon as he was born, that great-souled one, through his loveliness, radiance, form, and beauty, utterly infatuated the women of the gods.
Having seen that supreme form of the high-souled youth,
the beautiful Umā gazed upon him with unblinking eyes.

Seeing him, the God became enraged; perceiving that feminine nature to be so fickle, yet [seeing] the beautiful form of the youth which was enchanting to the eyes, the Supreme Lord then cursed him for his suspicion regarding a woman. (16)
"O youth, you shall have the face of an elephant and likewise a protruding belly;
furthermore, you will certainly have serpents as your sacred thread.
Thus did the god, filled with intense anger, curse him. (17)
With fifty million hairs on his body, the three-eyed Lord stood up, shaking his frame; filled with wrath, he held a trident dripping with water from the sweat of his pores. || 18 ||
In whatever manner that god, with the trident in his hand, shook his primordial body,
in that same manner the hairs on his limbs became like water, and others likewise fell down upon the earth.

Then the various Vināyakas, elephant-faced and resembling the dark tamāla tree or black collyrium, rose up on high with diverse weapons in their hands; at that, the gods became agitated in their minds.
"What is this? they wondered, for a single being of wondrous deeds performs a great and peerless task;
this desired work of the gods has been accomplished.
Now, one might ask: from where could that [space] be encompassed? || 21 ||
While the gods were thus reflecting, the earth became agitated by the Vināyakas;
then the peerless Four-faced One, having ascended his celestial chariot in the sky, spoke these words: || 22 ||
Blessed are you, O gods, for you have been graced by the Supreme Lord, the leader of the gods, the three-eyed one of wondrous form.
And [salutation] to those who bow down to the enemies of the gods who create obstacles. || 23 ||
Having spoken thus, the Great-Grandfather said to the god who held the trident in his hand:
"O Lord, let him who was born from your mouth become the master of the Vināyakas, and let these [others] be his followers."
Likewise, by your own choice, may you move within this space; let there be movement of the body within these four,
for this space is established in many ways.
By you alone has the most excellent one been made; no other [has done so]. || 25 ||
"Be you the master with the image-weapon in hand; grant these weapons and boons.
Having spoken thus, when the Grandfather had been obtained [as his boon],...
And Trilocana spoke to his own self.
Vināyaka, the creator of obstacles, elephant-faced, named Gaṇeśa, and the son of Bhava—
may all these become your servants.
The Vināyakas have cruel gazes and are fierce;
their bodies are enlarged by the consumption of dried corpses and other offerings, as they bestow success in all undertakings. || 27 ||
And you, O noble one, receive worship at the forefront among the gods, in sacrifices, and in other matters; otherwise, it would not be so.
Otherwise, you will destroy the accomplishment of your purpose. || 28 ||
Having spoken thus, his body was likewise sprinkled with water contained in golden jars by the Supreme Lord together with the gods.
O Indra among kings, he shone among the Vināyakas. || 29 ||
Seeing that leader of the Gaṇas being consecrated, all the gods, remaining composed, offered praise in the presence of the trident-weapon.
The gods said:
Salutations to you, O elephant-faced one; salutations to you, O leader of the Gaṇas.
O Vināyaka, let there be salutations to you; salutations to you of fierce prowess.
Homage be to you, the creator of obstacles; homage to you, girdled with serpents!
Homage to you, who have issued from the mouth of Rudra and who rest upon a protruding belly! 32.
"By the salutations of all the gods, grant us freedom from obstacles at all times.
Thus praised by the gods, the high-souled leader of the Gaṇas was then consecrated and attained the status of being the offspring of Rudra and Soma.
O King, because this [attainment] was accomplished by the leader of the Gaṇas on the fourth lunar day, therefore it is the greatest of all lunar days. || 34 ||
O King, whoever eats sesame seeds on this day and worships Gaṇapati with devotion, he is quickly gratified; of this there is no doubt. (35)
O King, for whoever recites this hymn and whoever always listens to it, no obstacles shall arise, nor shall any sin accrue in any way whatsoever. (36)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 23.
Dharaṇī said: O Lord of Gods, O Upholder of the Earth, how did the mighty Nāgas become embodied through the touch of your limbs? What was the cause of that? (1)
Śrī Varāha said:
Having heard of the birth of Gaṇapati, the king, the protector of his subjects,
spoke with gentle words to that sage of rigid vows.
Prajāpāla said:
"O Blessed One, how did the subjects of Tārkṣya come to assume physical forms? How did the serpents become crooked? You ought to explain this to me. (3)
Mahātapas said: While Brahmā was creating the world, Marīci was meditated upon by him first with his mind as the cause of procreation; his son was Kaśyapa.
His wife was the daughter of Dakṣa, named Kadrū, who possessed a pure smile;
upon her, Mārīca begot sons of great strength.
Ananta, Vāsuki, and the exceedingly powerful Kambala;
Karkoṭaka, O king of kings, and another serpent, Padma.
Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, Kulika, and Aparājita—these are proclaimed as the principal descendants of Kaśyapa. || 7 ||

Indeed, by their procreation, this world has been filled with those who are crooked, performers of base deeds, and fierce with the virulent poison rising from their sharp fangs; upon seeing men, they would surely reduce them to ashes in an instant by biting them. (8)
O lord of men, just as the touch of sound affects human beings,
a most terrible destruction would arise day after day.
Seeing the destruction of themselves on all sides, all the subjects went for refuge to the Supreme Lord, the ultimate protector.
O lord of the earth, with reference to this very matter,
all the subjects in former times spoke to Viṣṇu, the lotus-born, the ancient one known as Brahmā.
The gods said:
O Lord of the lords of gods, O Supreme Lord, source of the worlds!
Protect us, the great-souled serpents with sharp fangs. 12.
O gods, whatever beings—whether serpents or those in the form of human cattle—should behold [him] with their gaze day after day, all that would be reduced to ashes. (13)
"O God, this creation made by you is being led away by serpents;
having understood this wicked conduct, O high-minded one, do what must be done. (14)
Brahmā said:
"I shall provide protection for you, of this there is no doubt. Go to your own abodes so that the subjects may not be filled with fear. (15)
Having spoken thus to the subjects by that Brahmā of unmanifest form,
they returned with supreme joy, having bowed down to the Self-born One.
When the subjects had arrived,
he first summoned those serpents headed by Vāsuki and, being extremely enraged, then cursed them.
Brahmā said: Since you shall constantly bring about the destruction of human beings born from me,
in another birth, due to a most terrible curse from your mother.
"Indeed, a terrible and extreme destruction will surely occur during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara."
Thus addressed, those best of serpents, trembling, fell at the feet of Brahmā and then spoke these words.
The Nāgas said:
"O Blessed One, our crooked nature was created by you; as well as our excessive venom, our cruelty, and our eyes being weapons—all these were made for us by you."
"O Lord, you have accomplished this; now, O Acyuta, bring peace."
Brahmā said:
"If indeed you have been created by me with such crooked intentions, then why, being free from all suffering, do you constantly devour human beings?"
The Nāgas said:
"O Lord of Gods, establish boundaries and separate dwellings for humans as well as for us, and let there be distinct conventions for each."
Having heard the words of the Nāgas, the god spoke these words.
"O Nāgas, I establish an agreement for you with human beings;
therefore, all of you listen to my instruction with one-pointed minds. (23)
Pātāla, Vitala, and the third called Harmya—
there you shall go to dwell in that ever-delightful house which has been granted to you.
There, enjoying various kinds of pleasures by my command, you shall remain again and again until the end of the seventh night. (25)
Then, at the beginning of the Vaivasvata [Manvantara], you shall become the descendants of Kaśyapa;
you shall be the heirs of all the gods and of the wise Suparṇa.
Then your entire offspring shall be consumed by fire;
this fault will not be yours at all, there is no doubt.
Those who are indeed cruel, gluttonous, and ill-behaved—their end shall come; this shall not be otherwise.
Eat when the time has arrived, and likewise bite a man when he has committed an offense against you. (28)

Those men who move about having bound themselves with mantras, medicines, and circles of Garuḍa, or having seen them—yea, you must behave with fear toward them; nothing else should be thought of, otherwise your destruction will follow. (29)
When this was spoken by Brahmā, all those serpents went to the place called the surface of the earth,
where they remained, enjoying every kind of pleasure.
They remained in the netherworld (rasātala) as if in sport. || 30 ||
Having thus received both the curse and the grace from the Four-faced One,
they remained in their abode in Pātāla with joyful hearts.
All this occurred for those great-souled ones on the fifth lunar day;
therefore, this auspicious tithi is blessed and removes all sins. (32)
He who is self-restrained in this regard and avoids sour things shall bathe the nāgas with milk; they will become his friends. (33)
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 24.
Prajāpāla said:
O best of the twice-born, how was Kārttikeya born from the ego (ahaṃkāra)?
O great sage, dispel this doubt of mine as I ask you. (1)
Mahātapa said:
From that Puruṣa who is remembered as the highest of all principles, the Unmanifest (avyakta) was produced; and that [Unmanifest] consists of three kinds of principles.
Between the Puruṣa and the Unmanifest, the state of "Greatness" (mahattva) arose;
that which was proclaimed as the Great One is called Ahaṃkāra. (3)
The Puruṣa is said to be Viṣṇu, or is remembered by the name Śiva;
the Unmanifest, however, is the goddess Umā, or Śrī, with eyes like lotuses.
From that union arose the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and he is Guha, the commander-in-chief;
O high-minded King, listen as I describe his origin.
The first was the god Nārāyaṇa; from him Brahmā came into being.
From that Self-born One (Svayaṃbhū) arose others, such as Marīci and the rest, who were born from the Sun.
Beginning with them, the gods, Daityas, Gandharvas, humans, birds,
animals, and all beings— this is proclaimed as the creation.
When the creation had been expanded, the gods and the daityas, possessed of great strength,
entered into a state of mutual rivalry and fought, desiring victory over one another.
The Daityas have powerful leaders who are fierce in battle:
formerly Hiraṇyakaśipu, the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa,
Vipracitti, Vicitti, Bhīmākṣa, and Krauñca.
These exceedingly powerful heroes constantly conquer the army of the gods day after day in great battle with their white arrows.
Seeing their defeat, Bṛhaspati said to the gods: "O Suras, your army is depleted, being without a leader. (11)
A single Indra is not able to protect the divine army;
therefore, seek out some commander without delay.
Having been addressed thus, the gods then went to the Grandfather of the Worlds and spoke these words with agitation: "Grant us a commander-in-chief. (13)
Then the four-faced one pondered, "What should be done by me for these?
Brahmā then reflected upon Rudra within his mind.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, the Ṛṣis, the Siddhas, and the Cāraṇas, placing Brahmā at their head, went to Mount Kailāsa. || 15 ||
There, having beheld Mahādeva, Śiva, Paśupati,
the all-pervading Lord, Śakra and the other inhabitants of the triple heaven praised him with various hymns.
The gods said:
"Seeking refuge, we all bow down to Maheśvara, the three-eyed creator of all beings."
O Lord of Umā, Lord of the Universe, Lord of the Maruts, Lord of the World, O Śaṅkara, protect us yourself! || 17 ||

O Lord who holds the trident in hand, O Supreme Person, O Infallible One, whose stainless light from the moon at the tip of Your mass of matted hair illuminates the entire three worlds—protect the three worlds from the Daitya within their very midst! 18.
You are the primordial god, the Supreme Person, Hari, Bhava, Maheśa, the destroyer of Tripura, the all-pervading Lord;
the slayer of Bhaga’s eyes, the enemy of the Daityas, the ancient one, whose banner bears the bull—protect me, O best among the supreme gods! 19.
O Lord of the daughter of the mountain, O beloved of the mountain’s beloved,
O Master, worshipped by the entire world of immortals;
O Gaṇeśa, Lord of beings, Śiva, imperishable and immutable.
Protect us, O Acyuta, O destroyer of the foremost Daityas!
You are established within the elements beginning with earth; you exist specifically as the nature of sound in space,
in two ways in air, and in three ways in fire and water.
O you who possess five qualities upon the fourfold earth, protect us! || 21 ||
You are the very nature of fire in the tree as well as in the stone; likewise,
O Blessed Maheśvara, you are the very nature of light even within the waters.
Protect us, who are oppressed by the hosts of Daityas; O Hara, deliver us!
O Three-eyed One, when this world did not yet exist,
where were the Moon, the Sun, and the Lord of Wealth?
At that time, you alone existed, O one with the opposing eyes.
It remains free from contradiction by valid means of cognition and the like. || 23 ||
O garlanded with skulls, crowned with the crescent moon, dweller in the cremation ground, covered in white ashes,
whose body is entwined by the lord of serpents, O dispeller of Death!
Protect us with your skillful wisdom, O Lord of the Gods.

You are the Supreme Person; this daughter of the Mountain is your power (Śakti), O Blessed One, whose form is present in all your limbs. Thus, the three worlds are held in your hand in the form of the trident.
The three sacrificial fires abide within the three eyes. || 25 ||
In the form of your matted locks reside all the oceans, the principal mountain ranges, and all the rivers;
the moon is your supreme wisdom— thus you abide.
O Lord, people of wrong views do not perceive this. || 26 ||
You are Nārāyaṇa, the source of the worlds, and likewise you are Bhava; you are indeed the four-faced Brahmā.
You exist in three forms according to the distinctions of the qualities such as Sattva, according to the distinctions of the fires, and according to the distinctions of the Yugas.
O Lord, these leaders of the gods, seeking your state of being, speak thus to please you; therefore, O Bhava,
adorned with prosperity, [grant us your favor].
Protect us, O Lord of All; O Rudra, salutations unto you! || 28 ||
Mahātapa said: Thus praised then by the gods, the god Rudra, the Lord of Creatures, spoke to the gods without agitation: "What is the task? Speak, do not delay. (29)
The gods said:
"O Lord of Gods, grant us a commander for the sake of slaying the Daityas;
this alone would be for the benefit of the gods, with Brahmā at their head. (30)
Rudra said:
"O gods, I give you a commander-in-chief; be free from your feverish anxiety.
There shall be one in the future, as recorded in the Purāṇas, regarding whom you need not worry about yoga and such matters. (31)
Having spoken thus and dismissed the gods, Hara,
the scorcher of foes, agitated the Śakti residing within his own body for the sake of his son.
As he was agitating that power, Kumāra appeared, possessing a luster equal to fire and the sun, bearing his innate power which is characterized solely by wisdom.
O Indra among kings, his origin is established as manifold;
indeed, he has been the commander of the celestial army throughout many Manvantaras.

O Lord, that deity who resides within the body and is celebrated as the ego (ahaṃkāra), he himself, by virtue of his specific function, O All-pervading One, becomes the commander-in-chief of the army.
When he was born, Brahmā himself, accompanied by all the gods,
then worshipped Śiva, the Lord of Devas and Paśupati.
Strengthened by that boon from all the gods, the ṛṣis, and the siddhas, he, the commander-in-chief,
spoke to the deities.
For the sake of a friend, play must indeed be performed. || 37 ||
Having heard his words, the high-souled Mahādeva spoke these words:
"I shall give you a cock as a plaything."
Likewise, let Śākha and Viśākha be your followers;
O Kumāra, you who are the leader of the Bhūtas and Grahas, become the commander of the army, O Lord of the Gods. || 38 ||
Having spoken thus, O King, the god and all the gods then praised Skanda, the commander-in-chief, with pleasing words.
The gods said: "O Lord, son of Maheśvara, general of the divine army, six-faced Skanda, Lord of the Universe, whose banner is the cock, O son of Agni! Be [our protector]. (40)
O Shaker of the Earth, Lord of Kumāra, Skanda, follower of the Bālagrahas!
O Conqueror of Enemies, Destroyer of Krauñca, Son of the Kṛttikās, born of the Mothers! 41.
O best of the lords of the bhūta-grahas, son of Pāvaka, of pleasing appearance, son of the lord of the great elements, three-eyed one, homage be to you! 42.
Thus praised by the gods at that time, the delighter of the Bhava lineage increased;
he became like twelve suns in appearance, a wondrous sight to behold.
O King, his splendor even scorched the three worlds.
Prajāpāla said:
How did they address that divine preceptor as the son of Kṛttikā?
And how was he the son of Agni, or how was he the delighter of his mothers? || 44 ||
Mahātapa said: "O Lord, regarding that origin which was described by me in the first Manvantara,
the Master was praised in this very same way by the gods who perceive the unseen."
Kṛttikā, Pāvaka, and likewise Girijā—these were the mothers of Guha at his second birth, and they were the causes of his manifestation. (46)
Thus has this been declared to you, O best of kings, as you asked:
the secret nectar of self-knowledge and the origin of the ego.
Skanda himself is Mahādeva, the destroyer of all sins;
the Grandfather (Brahmā) assigned the sixth lunar day for his consecration.
He who, with a restrained mind, should spend this [fortnight] subsisting on fruits alone—even one without a son shall obtain sons, and even one without wealth shall obtain wealth;
whatever a person desires in his mind, that he obtains. (49)
And that person who recites this hymn of Kārttikeya, in his home there shall be the welfare and health of children. (50)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 25.
Prajāpāla said:
O twice-born one, how does the light of the body assume form?
Cut through this doubt of mine as I bow before you, O best of the twice-born. (1)
Mahātapa said: That Self, which is the singular, eternal power of knowledge,
when it desired a second [being], then blazed while remaining established within its own self.
The radiant one who is called Sūrya and the other great-souled ones, their splendors having merged with one another, illuminate the three worlds. (3)
In him, O Lord, all the gods, all the Siddhas, and all the hosts together with the great seers were born as Sūtas; therefore, while becoming the Sun, he was praised.
From that energy which had quickly become liquefied, a body was produced;
thereafter, he is celebrated as Ravi by the exponents of the Vedas as a distinct entity.
Because he rose in the sky illuminating all the worlds, he is called Bhāskara; and because of his excellence, he is called Prabhākara.
Because he causes the day, he is called "divā" (day) and "divākara" (maker of the day);
therefore, Āditya is said to be the beginning of the entire world.
From his splendor, the twelve Ādityas were separately produced;
he alone is always awakened as the primary source of them all.
Having seen the Supreme Lord pervading the world,
the gods who were situated within him emerged and sang his praise.
The gods said:
You are the ancient source of the universe,
consuming the worlds with your very pure destruction.
O Protector, having arisen, proceed toward tranquility;
do not consume the worlds of the gods, O witness of karma!
O radiant Sun, you who are engaged in the Yajur-veda, your scorching splendor extends everywhere;
your sharp discus is like that of a god.
They call it that which is named Time, the destroyer of darkness. || 11 ||
The Sun is the primordial deity,
the soul of all that is moving and unmoving;
he is the power of the Grandfather (Brahmā), as well as Varuṇa and Yama.
The perfected ones speak of both the past and the future.
Dispel the darkness, O you who are worshipped by the world of gods; depart for peace, so say the ancestors.
You are the one to be known through the Vedāntas, O God, in the sacrifices.
"You are invoked; you are Viṣṇu by your very might!
Thus praised with devotion by them, O Lord of the Gods, O Śambhu, protect us by your very might! 13.
Thus addressed by the gods, he then assumed a gentle form;
possessing great luster, he quickly attained visibility before the deities.
All this burning of the gods was formerly quelled by the Sun on the seventh day; indeed, he assumed a physical form upon the earth.
The person who worships her with devotion should likewise worship the Sun;
she bestows upon him the desired fruit through Bhāskara.
This ancient narrative of Sūrya has been told to you, O King; it took place during the first Manvantara. Now, listen to the account of the Mothers.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 26.
Mahātapa said: Formerly there was on earth a great Daitya named Andhaka, who was powerful;
arrogant due to a boon from Brahmā, he brought the gods under his control. || 1 ||
Because of him, O gods, all those who possessed self-control were driven away from Mount Meru;
afflicted by the fear of Andhaka, they went to Brahmā for refuge.
Then Brahmā spoke to those best of gods who had arrived:
"O gods, what is the purpose of your coming? Tell me, why do you sit here?"
The gods said: "O Lord of the World, O Four-faced One, O Grandfather, we gods have all been tormented by Andhaka; protect us all! Salutations be unto you! (4)
Brahmā said:
"O best of gods, I am truly not able to protect you from Andhaka;
let us go for refuge to Bhava, Śarva, Mahādeva."
But, O best of gods, a boon was previously granted by me to him: "You shall indeed be invulnerable; no weapon shall touch your body. (6)
For this very powerful one, there is but a single slayer, Rudra, the scorcher of foes;
let us all go there to that Lord whose abode is Kailāsa.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā departed along with the gods into the presence of Bhava.
Upon seeing him, Rudra performed the customary rites such as rising from his seat,
and the Lord of Gods addressed Brahmā, the Sovereign of the World.
Śambhu said: "O all you deities, what is the task for which you have come into my presence?
Whatever it may be, I shall perform it quickly; indeed, my command must be carried out with haste."
The gods said:
"O Lord, protect us from the powerful Andhaka, whose mind is wicked."
Just as all the gods were thus praising the Supreme Lord,
Andhaka arrived at that very spot with a vast army.
Desiring to slay you in battle with his fourfold army, he, together with his forces,
sought to abduct your wife, the daughter of the mountain.
Seeing him suddenly approaching, striking down even the god Śakra,
the gods quickly donned their armor and became the followers of Rudra.
Rudra, the Supreme Lord, having meditated upon Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and Dhanañjaya, made them his bracelet, his waist-string, and his girdle.
And the lord of the Daityas named Nīla, having become an elephant,
quickly approached Bhava with a form as towering as Indra’s elephant.
That Daitya was recognized by Nandin and pointed out to Vīrabhadra;
Vīrabhadra, too, having swiftly struck him with the form of a lion, [attacked him].

Having quickly torn open the hide of that elephant, which was as dark as collyrium, he offered it to Rudra; he too made it his very garment. From that time forward, Rudra also became one who wears an elephant-hide cloak.
Having donned an elephant hide and blazing with ornaments of serpents,
he took up his formidable three-pointed trident and, accompanied by his hosts, pursued Andhaka.
Then, when the great battle between the gods and the dānavas had commenced,
Indra and the other guardians of the world, as well as Skanda the commander-in-chief and all the other hosts of gods, fought in that conflict.
Having seen that battle, Nārada went toward Nārāyaṇa and described the great battle on Kailāsa with the Dānavas.
Having heard that, Janārdana, mounted upon Garuḍa and taking up his discus,
arrived at that very place and fought with the Dānavas.
Having returned from there, all those gods, who had been restored by Hari in the battle, became dejected in countenance and intent on flight.
When the gods there had been defeated, Rudra himself went toward Andhaka;
there, a great battle took place between them that caused the hair to stand on end.
There, the god also struck the Daitya violently with his trident.
From the blood that fell upon the earth from him as he was thus struck,
indeed, countless other Andhakas were born in great numbers.
Having witnessed that great marvel, Rudra, the Supreme Lord, seized Andhaka on the tip of his trident in the battle and danced.
All the other Andhakas as well, and those others who had arisen there, were slain by the supreme Nārāyaṇa with his discus. 26.
From him, who was repeatedly impaled upon the trident, streams of blood rose up incessantly like a shower of frost;
then Rudra became filled with wrath.
From his mouth, due to that great anger, a flame issued forth;
she who bore that form is the goddess whom they know as Yogeśvarī.
Another [form] assuming her own essential nature was likewise created by Viṣṇu,
as well as by Brahmā, Kārtikeya, Indra, Yama,
the divine Varāha, and Viṣṇu the Supreme Lord.
And he fashioned for that goddess a form for the rescue from Pātāla, O King of kings; thus, O Indra among kings, these [forms] proceeded from Māheśvarī. (30)
That which was declared by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) regarding the determination of those causes—the emergence of the deities from the body—has now been proclaimed by me. 31.
Lust, anger, greed, pride, and delusion as the fifth;
envy is said to be the sixth, and likewise malice the seventh;
envy (or fault-finding) is to be known as the eighth—these are the eight mothers. (32)
Know that desire is Yogeśvarī, and likewise anger is Māheśvarī;
greed is declared to be Vaiṣṇavī, and intoxication is indeed Brahmāṇī. (33)
Delusion is known as Svayambhū, Kaumārī is envy born of Indra,
the goddess who bears the staff of Yama is slander itself,
and jealousy is called Varāhā; these are thus proclaimed.
This group beginning with desire has been described as residing within the body;
how it assumes form, that has been recounted by me to you. (35)
When his blood had been thoroughly dried up by these deities,
the demonic illusion (āsuri-māyā) was destroyed, and that Andhaka became a perfected one (siddha).
Thus, this entire nectar of the knowledge of the Self has been recounted to you by me.
O King, those Mothers provide protection in every way day after day for that person who constantly hears this auspicious account of their origin. (37)
O Supreme Person, he who recites this account of the births of the Mothers is blessed forever in this world and goes to the realm of Śiva. (38)
And among them, the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) was granted by Brahmā as the most excellent.
A man who always worships these [goddesses] with devotion, subsisting solely on bilva leaves, will find that they, being thoroughly pleased, bestow upon him security and health. (39)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 27.
Prajāpāla said:
How did the auspicious Durgā Kātyāyanī arise through Māyā? Established in the primordial field (Ādikṣetra), how did she, who is subtle, manifest as a distinct form? || 1 ||
Mahātapa said:
O King, in former times there was a powerful king named Sindhudvīpa;
O great monarch, he was an incarnation of Varuṇa and remained in the forest devoted to ascetic penance.
"May a son be born to me for the destruction of Śakra," thus resolved, that lord of men,
firm in his vows, remained there and with great austerity caused his own body to wither away.
Prajāpāla said:
O best of the twice-born, how could Śakra have done him harm, such that he, desiring his destruction, remained established in a vow for his son? (4)
Mahātapa said:
In another birth, he was the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, the best among the upholders of strength;
though invulnerable to all weapons, he was destroyed by the foam of the waters.
Struck by the foam of the waters, he attained dissolution therein;
then, born again from the lineage of Brahmā, he was known by the name Sindhudvīpa.
Remembering his enmity with Śakra, he performed supreme and intense penance.
Then, after a long time, the auspicious river Vetravatī assumed a beautiful human form adorned with ornaments and came to the place where the king was performing supreme penance.
Seeing her endowed with such beauty, that king, his mind filled with rage, said:
"Who are you, O fair-hipped one? Tell me the truth, O beautiful woman. (8)
The river said: "I am the wife of the high-souled Varuṇa, the lord of waters; known by the name Vetravatī, I have come here desiring you."
"One should abandon a woman who desires another man and is being unfaithful;
that man is to be known as a sinner and incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Knowing this, O Great King, accept me while I am devoted to you. (10)
Thus addressed by her, the king enjoyed her with longing;
immediately, a son was born to him, possessing a splendor equal to twelve suns.
Born in the womb of Vetravatī, he became known by the name Vaitrāsura;
powerful and exceedingly radiant, he became the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa.
In due course, he became a youth, powerful and of firm prowess; endowed with great yogic power, he conquered this earth.
After [conquering] the earth consisting of seven islands, he subsequently ascended Mount Meru.
There, he first conquered Indra, then Agni, and after that Yama;
then Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Dhanada, and finally Īśvara.
Indra, being defeated, went to Agni; Agni, being defeated, went to Yama;
Yama, approaching Nirṛti, [and] Nirṛti went to Varuṇa. || 15 ||
Accompanied by Indra and the others, Varuṇa followed Vāyu;
Vāyu, in turn, approached the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) together with all of Indra and the rest.
O Lord, Dhanada also went to his friend Īśa accompanied by the gods; that Dānava too, arrogant in his strength, took up a mace and rushed toward the world of Śiva. || 17 ||
Śiva, considering him invincible, went secretly to the city of Brahmā,
which is honored by gods, siddhas, and others who perform meritorious deeds.

There, Brahmā, the creator of the world, having entered the auspicious water born from the feet of Viṣṇu and restrained his movement through the sky, performed silent recitation (japa) within that pure water. [The mantra] is the Gāyatrī, which is the Māyā of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). Thereupon, the gods cried out in distress.
"Save us all, O Prajāpati! Save even the gods and the best of sages who have fallen into fear of the Asura! Thus they urged him, crying out, "Save us! Save us! (20)
Thus addressed, Brahmā then beheld the gods who had arrived and reflected: "This is the pervasive world-māyā of the Lord;
neither asuras nor suras exist here—what kind of māyā is this considered to be? (21)
As he was thinking thus, there appeared before him a maiden born of no womb (ayonija),
wearing white garments, her face radiant with a garland and a crown,
endowed with eight arms and raising divine weapons.
Holding a discus, a conch, a mace, a noose, a sword, a bell, as well as a bow,
and other weapons, she stood outside the water with her quiver fastened.
The Great Goddess, possessing the speed of a lion-vehicle, emerged;
though she was but one, she stood in many forms and fought all the asuras.
Having fought with divine weapons for a thousand celestial years,
the exceedingly powerful Vaitrāsura was slain in battle by the Goddess when his time had come;
then, a great tumultuous shout of joy arose among the divine army.
When the terrible Vaitrāsura was slain, all the inhabitants of heaven then bowed down;
"Victory! Fight! they cried, while the Lord himself sang this hymn of praise.
Maheśvara said: Be victorious, O Goddess Gāyatrī! O Great Illusion, O You of Great Radiance! O Great Goddess, O Highly Fortunate One, O You of Great Being, O You of Great Festival! (27)
O Goddess Maheśvarī, whose limbs are anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine garlands,
O Mother of the Vedas, salutations to you who abide in the three syllables.

O Goddess born from the lotus-throne, who dwells in the three worlds, who abides in the three principles, who resides in the three fires, O wielder of the trident; O three-eyed one, with a formidable countenance, with terrifying eyes, and most fearsome— salutations be to you, O Sarasvatī!
Salutations to you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, O Great Illusion, O fountain of nectar;
O omnipresent one, O Mistress of all beings, O Svāhā, O Svadhā, O Mother!
O you who are complete, who possess a radiance like the full moon, whose limbs are luminous, and who arise from existence;
O Great Knowledge, O Great Object of Knowledge, O Destroyer of the great Daityas;
O Goddess born of great intellect, free from sorrow, wearer of matted locks! 31.
O highly fortunate one, you are policy, you are song, you are the cow, and you are the imperishable syllable;
you are intellect, you are prosperity, you are the syllable Om, and you are established in the ultimate reality.
O Goddess, who acts for the welfare of all beings, salutations to you, O Supreme Sovereign!
Thus was the Goddess praised by Bhava, the Supreme Lord;
and the Supreme Sovereign was also addressed with a loud "Victory! by the gods.
As long as the four-faced one remained there, so long did he emerge from within the water;
then he beheld the Goddess, her purpose accomplished.
Having seen her and considering the work of the gods accomplished, the Grandfather (Brahmā) then spoke these words, intending toward future events.
Brahmā said:
"Let this goddess of beautiful limbs go to the mountain born of snow;
having gone there, all you gods, rejoice without delay. (36)
And on the ninth day, this goddess should always be worshipped with meditative concentration;
she will become the bestower of boons upon all the worlds, of this there is no doubt.
And whatever man or woman shall eat only flour on the ninth day, their heart's desire will indeed be fulfilled.
And whoever shall recite this hymn, spoken by you, O Mahādeva, both in the evening and likewise in the morning, for him you, together with the Goddess, [shall grant your favor]. (39)
"O God, the giver of boons, rescue him even in all calamities.
Having spoken thus to Bhava, Brahmā then addressed the Goddess once more.
"O Goddess, you must perform a great task for us; there is another yet to come:
the destruction of the asura named Mahiṣa. (41)
Having spoken thus, O King, Brahmā and all the gods then departed as they had come, after having established the Goddess on the snowy mountain;
because she was established there with joy, she became known as Nandā.
Whoever hears this account of the Goddess’s birth, or whoever recites it themselves, shall be liberated from all sins and attain supreme nirvāṇa. || 43 ||
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 28.
Mahātapa said:
Listen attentively, O King, protector of subjects, to this story, concerning how the directions were produced from the ears, O lord of the earth. (1)
When the initial creation had arisen as Brahmā was engaged in creating, a great thought occurred to him: "Who will sustain these creatures created by me?"
As he was reflecting thus, ten daughters of great splendor appeared from his ears as an opportunity arose among his subjects here.
O King, at that time there were six daughters, namely Pūrvā, Dakṣiṇā, Pratīcī, Uttara, as well as Ūrdhvā and Adharā. || 4 ||
They had four other daughters who were exceedingly beautiful, endowed with lovely forms, highly fortunate, and possessed of great dignity.
Out of affection, they said to the god Prajāpati, who is free from blemish:
"O God of gods, O Prajāpati, grant us a place."
O you whose origin is unmanifest, grant us [a place] where we may all dwell happily together with our husbands, and where our lords are highly fortunate.
Brahmā said: "O fair-hipped ones, this universe extends for a hundred crores [of yojanas];
at its end, O auspicious ladies, dwell according to your will—do not delay."
"O sinless ones, having created husbands for you who are endowed with beauty, I now grant them to you;
go now to whichever region pleases each of you as you desire."
Having been addressed thus, they all then departed as they pleased;
Brahmā also quickly created the mighty guardians of the worlds.
Having created the world-protectors, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, called those maidens back again and had them perform marriage rites.
He gave one to Indra, another to Agni, and to Yama;
and to the god Nirṛti, and to the high-souled Varuṇa.
O observer of noble vows, having yourself presided over the upper [direction], [worship] Vāyu, Dhanada, and Īśāna; and [worship] Śeṣa, who is established below.
Having given this, Brahmā further granted the lunar day (tithi) of the quarters;
the Lord then gave the tenth day under the name of the husband, along with curd-rice as the meal.
From that time forward, those goddesses, beginning with Indrāṇī, were celebrated;
and the tenth lunar day became exceedingly dear to them.
O King, for that man who, being observant of excellent vows, subsists on curd during that [fortnight],
those [deities] effect the destruction of his sins day after day.
And whoever, with a restrained mind, hears this account of the birth of the Quarters, shall attain a firm station in the world of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 29.
Mahātapa said:
Listen now to another account of the origin of the Lord of Wealth, which destroys all sins—how Vāyu, residing within the body, became Dhanada. || 1 ||
Within that which was the primordial body, the wind became established;
for a specific purpose, it was ordained by the deity of the field (Kṣetrapati) to possess a physical form.
In that regard, O highly fortunate one, I shall now proclaim the origin of the embodied wind; listen to it as it is being told by me, O sinless one. (3)
From the mouth of Brahmā, who was desirous of creating, the wind issued forth,
raining down fierce gravel; Brahmā restrained it, saying,
"Become embodied and peaceful," and thereupon it became embodied.
Whatever wealth and whatever fruit belongs to all the gods, protect all of that; because of this, you shall be called the Lord of Wealth (Dhanapati).
The Lord Brahmā, being pleased, granted him the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī);
on that day, he who remains self-controlled and pure, eating food not cooked by fire, [attains his goal].
The divine Dhanada, being pleased with her, quickly bestows everything upon her.
This is the form of the Lord of Wealth, which destroys all sins.
The person who hears this with devotion, or even recites it, attains all desires and goes to the heavenly world. || 8 ||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 30.
Mahātapa said:
That which is indeed recited as the name "Manu" and his status as Manu is,
for a specific purpose, Viṣṇu himself in embodied form.
O King, O best of men, that Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is higher than the highest,
conceived a thought regarding creation.
This creation has been brought forth by me, and it must indeed be protected by me alone. However, it is not possible for one who is formless to perform the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) here;
therefore, I shall create a single form by which this world may be protected.
O King, as he was thus reflecting with a mind fixed on truth,
O Monarch, that which had been produced in a previous creation appeared before him in embodied form.
Then, when he had appeared before him, Lord Nārāyaṇa himself beheld the three worlds entering into his body.
Then the Blessed One remembered his ancient boon;
being pleased, he granted him another boon regarding speech and the other senses.
You are the omniscient, the creator of all, and the one honored by all the worlds;
because you pervade the three realms, become the eternal Viṣṇu. || 7 ||
"The task of the gods must always be performed, as well as that of Brahmā;
and may you possess omniscience, O Lord—of this there is no doubt. (8)
Having spoken thus, the god then returned to his natural state;
and now the Lord Viṣṇu also remembered his former intention.
Then, having reflected, the Blessed One of great austerity entered yogic sleep;
having established within that sleep all creatures born from the objects of the senses, the Lord,
meditating with his supreme form, then indeed fell asleep.
From the belly of him as he slept, a great lotus emerged,
upon which rested the earth with its seven continents, its oceans, and its forests.
The expansion of that form is the netherworld (pātāla) situated upon the stalk;
likewise, Mount Meru is at the pericarp, and within its center is the birth of Brahmā.
Having thus observed the supreme origin of that body,
the wind residing within it released itself, emitting wind in equal measure.
And bear this victory over ignorance in the form of a conch;
for the purpose of cutting through nescience, let there always be a sword in your hand.
O Acyuta, you must bear this terrible Wheel of Time;
O Keśava, bear the mace for the sake of slaying the elephant of unrighteousness.
May this Māleyā, the mother of all beings, always remain upon your neck;
and may these two, Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, abide here under the guise of the moon and the sun.
O hero, let the Wind-god be your movement, and Garuḍa has been proclaimed as such;
let the goddess Lakṣmī, who traverses the three worlds, be ever your refuge;
and let the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī) be yours, for it becomes capable of assuming any form at will. || 17 ||
Whoever, devoted to the Supreme, eats only ghee on the twelfth day, whether man or woman, shall especially become a dweller in heaven. (18)
This Viṣṇu has been described to you; he slays the gods and demons, protects their bodies, and creates other forms from himself. (19)
In age after age, this all-pervading Puruṣa is indeed present in the Vedānta;
one should never speak of him as a mere human being with an inferior intellect.
Whoever should hear this Vaiṣṇava account of creation, which destroys all sins, shall attain fame in this world and be glorified in the heavenly realm. (21)
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 31.
In the beginning, Brahmā was immutable, pure, and designated as both the higher and the lower;
desiring to create living beings, he first contemplated their protection.
As he was thus reflecting, a man with white earrings, adorned with white garlands and unguents, emerged from his right side.
Seeing him in the form of a bull with four feet, the Blessed One said:
"O virtuous one, protect these subjects; become the eldest of the world."
Thus addressed, that Lord remained established in his state: during the Kṛta Yuga he possessed four feet;
in the Tretā he was reduced to three; in the Dvāpara he had two;
and in the Kali age, the Lord protects his subjects with only one foot.

That all-pervading Lord exists in six divisions among the Brāhmaṇas, established in three ways among the Kṣatriyas, in two ways among the Vaiśyas, and in one way among the Śūdras; He is the self-effulgent Lord throughout all the netherworlds, the islands, and the regions.

It is proclaimed to have four feet consisting of substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), action (kriyā), and genus (jāti); and it is remembered by the wise as having three peaks: the Saṃhitā, the Pada, and the Krama.
Likewise, having the syllable Oṃ at the beginning and end, two heads, and seven arms, bound by three bonds, he is the foremost of the Brahmins and protects the world. 8.
That Dharma was previously oppressed by Soma of wondrous deeds,
who desired to seize Tārā, the wife of his brother, the son of Aṅgiras.
Terrified by that powerful one of cruel deeds,
the lord then entered a dense and formidable forest.
When he had departed, all the gods and the wives of the asuras,
deprived of their sense of dharma, wandered about seeking to seize his aerial chariots;
and the asuras likewise wandered through the dwellings of the gods.
O King, when such lawlessness arose and righteousness was destroyed,
the gods and asuras, provoked by the offense regarding Soma and for the sake of a woman, fought one another with various weapons in their hands, O illustrious one.
Seeing those gods fighting with the asuras and filled with wrath,
Nārada approached his father Brahmā and spoke to him joyfully.
Then the Grandfather of all the worlds, having mounted his swan-vehicle, stopped them and asked, "For whose sake is this battle being waged? (14)
Everyone praised Soma, but he, having learned that his own son had fled from the pressing and taken refuge in the dense forest, [was distressed].
Then Brahmā, accompanied by the gods and asuras, went there in haste;
and together with the gods, he beheld a bull-like form with four legs, shining like the moon, as it was wandering about. Having seen it, he spoke to the gods.
Brahmā said:
"This is my eldest son, the great sage known as Dharmasāvarṇi, who has been severely tormented by the Moon, who desired to seize his brother's wife. (17)
"Now, all you gods and asuras together must indeed satisfy him, so that there may be an equal standing for both gods and asuras. (18)
Then, having learned from the words of Brahmā that he resembled the full moon, they all joyfully offered praise to that god.
The gods said:
Homage be to you, who resemble the moon; homage to you, O Lord of the world!
Homage be to you, whose form is divine, the one who reveals the path to heaven!
Salutations again and again to the one who is the very nature of the path of action and who is omnipresent.
By you this earth is protected, and indeed the three worlds are protected by you alone; Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka—all are protected by you.
There is nothing in this world, whether stationary or moving, that exists apart from you;
indeed, deprived of you, the world would perish instantly.

You are the Self of all beings; for the virtuous, you are the very nature of purity (sattva); for those characterized by passion (rajas), you are passion itself; and for those characterized by darkness (tamas), you are indeed darkness.
O Lord, you have four feet, four horns, and three eyes;
you have seven hands and three bonds. O you who take the form of a bull, homage be to you! (24)
"O Lord, deprived of you, we have all fallen onto the wrong path;
therefore, grant that path to us who are deluded, for you are indeed our supreme refuge. (25)
Thus praised by the gods at that time, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) in the form of a bull,
being satisfied, looked upon them with a serene mind and tranquil eyes.
As soon as those gods were seen by him with his own eye of Dharma,
in an instant their delusion vanished and they were perfectly endowed with the True Dharma.
The Asuras did likewise; then Brahmā said to him:
"O Dharma, from this day forward, let the thirteenth lunar day be your holy festival (tithi)."
The man who, having fasted upon that [day], should fully worship you—that person, even after having accumulated a mass of sins, is liberated from them. (29)
"O Lord, since this forest has been pervaded by you for a long time through your dharma, it shall therefore be known by the name Dharmāraṇya, O Lord. (30)
O Lord, you are perceived by the worlds through the Kṛta and other ages as having four, three, two, or one foot;
likewise, in the land of action, you are like the sky.
Engaged in yoga, protect your own home; protect the universe. || 31 ||
O King, as soon as these words were spoken, the Great-Grandfather vanished from the sight of the gods and demons while they were looking on, and returned to his own abode.
The gods, together with their bulls, went forth, freed from sorrow.
Whoever causes this arising of the Dharma to be heard shall then satisfy the ancestors with milk-rice according to their capacity on the thirteenth day during a śrāddha ceremony.
But he who goes to heaven shall approach the gods. || 33 ||
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. || 32 ||
Śrī Varāha said:
"Now, O King, hear of another primordial manifestation of Rudra. Thus he spoke.
A great ascetic, skilled in dharma, a wielder of patience as his weapon, and a sage of fierce splendor, he acted out of affection. || 1 ||

The Lord of Creatures, possessed of fierce splendor, was born; having realized the supreme knowledge that is the nature of reality, he became agitated with intense wrath, desiring to bring about creation at a time when the world had reached its full expansion.
Therefore, as he performed penance, the ancient one of steadfast fame— whose progress had previously been obstructed by passion and darkness—
became a supreme, most excellent, boon-granting, and majestic lord.
The person is blackish-red with tawny eyes. || 3 ||
Wept when addressed by Brahmā, "Do not weep";
from that he became the ancient Rudra. Lead forth the creation of expanded form.
You are capable, O noble-souled one. || 4 ||
As soon as these words were spoken, Dakṣa plunged into the water; once submerged, he created [the world] for the sake of his own manifestation,
while the gods then spread themselves across the surface of the waters.
But those born of Brahmā were created by him through his mind.
When that sacrifice of the Grandfather had been fully extended by the Lord of the Gods,
Rudra— who formerly had been submerged in the water— [emerged].
Having emitted the universe, he desired to create the gods.
The sacrifice flowed away from the gods, Siddhas, and Yakṣas who had approached it, and he fell under the sway of anger;
