reflecting upon his blazing fury, he thought: "By whom has this world been created out of delusion, excluding me? (7)
When "Hā! Hā! was uttered, there arose masses of tiny piśācas, vetālas, bhūtas, and hosts of yogins, along with flames of fire.
When they had spread out the cloud-mass through the sky,
the earth, and all the directions and worlds,
then he, by means of his omniscience, performed [the rite].
The bow is twenty-four cubits in length. || 9 ||
In his rage, he strung the triple-twisted bow and took up the divine bowstring;
then he pierced the teeth of Pūṣan, the eyes of Bhaga, and the testicles of Kratu.
With his seed discharged, Kratu fled from the sacrificial enclosure while Vāyu held back the wind;
all the gods approached Paśupati and everyone bowed down in prostration before Bhava.
Having arrived there, the Grandfather (Brahmā),
being well-pleased with Bhava,
embraced the gods and gazed upon those deities of the gods who were filled with devotion.
O hero-armed one, bring consciousness within.
Rudra said:
"I was created by you in the beginning; why then do these [gods] not allot me a share?"
O God of gods, by that wrath of yours, these beings born of sacrifice have had their knowledge stolen and have become deformed.
Brahmā said: O gods and all you asuras, worship Śambhu with loud hymns of praise for the sake of attaining knowledge.
By which the Blessed Lord Rudra is pleased, and by which there may be satisfaction regarding omniscience itself. || 14 ||
Having been addressed thus by him, those gods offered praise to the Great-Souled One.
The gods said: "Salutations to the God beyond gods, the three-eyed Great Soul, whose eyes are red and tawny, and who wears a crown of matted locks. (16)
Salutation to Sthāṇu, who is possessed by spirits and vetālas, who has a great serpent as his sacred thread, whose face utters a terrifying loud laugh, and who wears matted hair. || 17 ||
Salutation to the destroyer of Pūṣan’s teeth; salutation to the slayer of Bhaga’s eyes;
salutation to the Lord of the Great Elements, who shall have the bull as his emblem. || 18 ||
To the one who will bring about the end of Tripura, likewise to the destroyer of Andhaka;
to the one whose excellent dwelling is Kailāsa, and who dwells in an elephant hide.
Salutations again and again to Bhairava, whose hair stands erect and who is formidable with his distorted features;
salutations to him who is terrifying with flames of fire and who bears the moon upon his crest.
To the Supreme Lord who had performed the vow of a Kāpālika in the future,
and likewise to the wielder of the sharp trident who brought about the destruction of the Dāruvana forest.
Salutations to the one who wears a serpent as a bracelet, whose throat is blue, and who holds a trident;
to the one with a fierce staff in hand, and whose mouth is the submarine fire.

Salutations to the one who is to be known through the Vedanta; salutations again and again to the embodiment of sacrifice. Salutations to the destroyer of Daksha’s sacrifice and to the one who causes fear to the world.
Salutations to you, the Lord of All, the Divine One, Śiva, Śambhu, and Bhava; to the one with matted hair, the Terrifying One, and Mahādeva. || 24 ||
Thus praised by the gods, the eternal Śambhu, the fierce-bowed God of gods, said: "Tell me what I should do. (25)
The gods said: "O Bhava, if you are pleased with us, O Lord, grant us the Vedas, the Shastras, and spiritual knowledge without delay; and grant us the sacrifice along with its secret mysteries. (26)
Mahādeva said:
"May you all become cattle together;
I shall be your lord, and from that you will attain liberation."
"So be it," the gods said to him; thereupon, he became Paśupati.
Brahmā, with a serene inner soul, said to Paśupati:
"O Lord of Gods, let the fourteenth lunar day be yours; of this there is no doubt. (28)
On that lunar day, those who worship you endowed with faith,
having fasted, should afterwards feed the twice-born with food made of wheat.
Being pleased with him, lead him to the unsurpassed state.
Thus addressed then by Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, Rudra gave his teeth to Bhaga, his eyes to Pūṣan, and even to Kratu;
and he bestowed complete knowledge upon all the gods as well.
Thus was the manifestation of Rudra produced from Brahmā in ancient times;
by this very process, he is called the Lord of the Gods.
And that person who, having risen early in the morning, should listen to this constantly, being liberated from all sins, shall attain the world of Rudra. || 32 ||
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 33.
Mahātapa said:
O King, listen as I relate to you the origin of the ancestors.
Formerly, the Lord of Creatures, Brahmā, desiring to create various offspring, [proceeded to do so]. (1)
Having directed all those subtle elements externally with a one-pointed mind,
he who desires a high rebirth meditates upon the Supreme Brahman.
Then, as that Supreme Lord had entered into union with his own self,
the subtle elements (tanmātras) emerged from his body, possessing the color, form, and luster of smoke.
Saying "Let us drink the Soma," those ascetics, desiring to ascend upwards and established in the firmament, spoke thus to the gods.
Seeing them suddenly standing sideways with their faces turned upward, Brahmā said:
"May you all be the ancestors (pitṛs) of all householders."
Those among them whose faces are turned upwards are designated as Nāndīmukhas;
they are to be constantly honored in Vṛddhi-śrāddha rites according to the injunctions of the Śruti.
Let those twice-born ones who maintain the sacred fire, having placed Agni at their head,
satisfy them with the obligatory, occasional, optional, and ancestral (pārvaṇa) rites.
Let the Kṣatriyas who are excluded from the outer [sacrificial circle] satisfy themselves;
and let the Vaiśyas always honor those here who drink the clarified butter.
Permitted by the Brāhmaṇas, the Śūdras, being excluded from the ritual procedures and mantras, should properly worship those very ancestors by means of their names alone.
And those men of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes who have not maintained the sacred fires,
let them always worship [the deity] before the domestic fire at their respective times.
Thus honored, may you grant our desired wishes:
long life, fame, wealth, sons, learning, noble birth, and memory.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā, the Grandfather, then established for them the path known as the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) for the ancestors.
He created beings in silence; then the ancestors spoke to him:
"O Blessed One, grant us a means of subsistence by which we may find happiness. (13)
Brahmā said:
"Let the new moon day be yours; on that day, being satiated by humans with water, kusha grass, and sesame seeds, you shall attain supreme satisfaction, and not otherwise. (14)
Likewise, having fasted on this day with devotion to the ancestors, sesame seeds should be given;
being highly pleased, they shall grant him a boon without delay. (15)
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 34.
Mahātapas said:
The mind-born son of Brahmā was Atri, a man of great asceticism. His son was Soma, who became the son-in-law of Dakṣa.
The twenty-seven maidens celebrated as the daughters of Dakṣa are highly esteemed as the wives of Soma; among them, Rohiṇī is the most excellent.
"We have heard that Soma delights only in her and no other," so said the others upon their arrival, recounting the partiality of Dakṣa toward Śaśin.
Dakṣa also came repeatedly and spoke to him, but he did not act accordingly;
Dakṣa then cursed him, saying, "Become invisible."
Thus cursed by Dakṣa, Soma then cast off his body.
Soma spoke to Dakṣa: "It shall be so for you;
having abandoned this eternal Brahman-body, you will be born many times. (5)
Having spoken thus, Soma went to his destruction due to Dakṣa’s curse;
when Soma had perished, so did the gods, humans, animals, and all plants.
Then all medicinal herbs, especially those of superior quality, became exhausted;
as the herbs reached an extreme state of depletion, O bulls among the gods, [the sages were distressed].
"The Moon resides in the roots of the plants," said the distressed ones;
a sharp anxiety arose within them, and they sought refuge in Viṣṇu. (8)
The Blessed One said to them all, "Tell me, what shall I do?
They replied, "O Lord, Soma has been cursed and ruined by Dakṣa."
Then the God said to them: "O gods, let the ocean-jar be churned;
let medicinal herbs be quickly cast in from all sides by those who are well-restrained."
Having spoken thus, Hari himself then meditated upon the gods, Rudra, and likewise Brahmā; he also meditated upon Vāsuki for the purpose of serving as his eyes.
All of them together churned the abode of Varuṇa there;
O lord of the earth, when that had been churned, Soma was born once again.
That supreme Person within this body who is indeed known as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
he alone is to be considered Soma, designated as the individual soul (jīva) among embodied beings;
by the will of the Supreme, he has assumed a separate, gentle form.
Both gods and men, as well as these sixteen deities, trees, and likewise medicinal herbs, all depend for their livelihood upon that very Lord.
Then Rudra bore that very [ocean] entirely upon his head;
the waters became identical with him, and he is remembered as the one whose form is the universe.
The Lord Brahmā, being pleased, granted him the lunar day of the full moon (Paurṇamāsī). O King, one should fast on that day and accomplish that purpose.
O King of kings, if one subsists on a diet of barley, it bestows upon him knowledge, splendor, nourishment, and exclusively wealth and grain. (17)
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. || 35 ||
Mahātapa said:
O King, I shall describe those kings known as the Maṇijas who appeared in the beginning of the Tretā ages, and where they were born, O monarch.
O King, you who were formerly named Suprabha in the Kṛta Yuga have now been born as the illustrious one known by the beautiful name Prajāpāla.
O King, the remaining ones will be of great strength during the Tretā Yuga;
he who is born from Maṇi and possesses blazing splendor is celebrated as Śaṃtanu.
Suraśmi will become the king Śaśakarṇa, who is possessed of great strength;
and Śubhadarśana will become the Pāñcāla lord of men. || 4 ||
In the lineage of Aṅga, there was indeed Suśānti, as well as Sundara and Aṅga;
Sunda, Mucukunda, Sudyumna, and Tura were also born.
Sumanas was the son of Somadatta, and Śubha became Saṃvaraṇa; Suśīla was Vasudāna, and Sukhada became Supati.
Śambhu became the general, known as the handsome Daśaratha;
Soma became King Janaka—these were the kings in the Tretā Yuga, O monarch.
O King, all those lords of the earth, having enjoyed this land and performed various sacrifices, will undoubtedly attain heaven.
Śrī Varāha said:
Having thus heard this supreme narrative, the nectar of the knowledge of Brahman, that lordly royal sage was delighted and went to the forest to perform austerities.
O Dhātrī, by means of adhyātma-yoga, that sage, having cast off this body,
became one with Brahman and attained dissolution in Hari.
And that powerful king went to Vṛndāvana for the sake of performing penance;
there, he then began to offer praise to Hari, who is named Govinda.
The King said:
I bow to the Lord, the embodiment of the worlds, the Lord of the Cowherds, the younger brother of Indra, the immeasurable one.
I bow to that best of gods, the upholder of the earth, who is uniquely skilled in traversing the wheel of saṃsāra. || 12 ||
In the ocean of existence, terrifying with hundreds of waves of suffering,
with old age as its whirlpool and black despair as its bottomless depths,
may that which alone brings me happiness endure until the very end.
Homage be to you, O immeasurable Lord of the Earth!
O Lord, you who are joined with disease and the like, and who again encounter men and planetary spirits—
salutations to you, the Great-Souled One, who delights in battle!
Janārdana, the Lord of Rays, the one of fierce arms.
You are the supreme among all knowers, O Lord of the Gods;
by you this entire universe is pervaded.
O Lord of the Cowherds, O one of great majesty, protect me!
O Lord whose hand holds the fierce discus, [I am] terrified of worldly existence.
O God, you are the supreme among the foremost of the gods; you are the true form of the Supreme Person, radiant as the moon;
O Acyuta, whose mouth is fire, you are of fierce nature.
O Lord of the Cowherds, protect me as I fall into worldly existence! || 16 ||

O Acyuta, O Lord of the Gods, since many traversals of the wheel of saṃsāra manifest for embodied beings who are deluded by Your māyā, who—remaining within the realm of dualities—can cross over that māyā? (17)

O Lord of the Cowherds, those wise ones who worship you—who are without lineage, without touch, without form, smell, name, or description, unborn, and most excellent—become partakers of liberation, freed from the bonds of worldly existence. 18.

I perpetually bow to Him who transcends sound, whose form is like space, who is formless, who possesses an auspicious nature for those beyond ritual action, and who is most excellent; He who holds the discus and lotus in His hands, and who is described in the Purāṇas through such figurative designations. 19.
Trivikrama, who traversed the three worlds;
the Lord of the Earth in his fourfold form pervading the universe;
Śambhu, the all-pervading Lord of beings, the Sovereign of the gods.
I bow to Viṣṇu, whose form is infinite.
O Lord, you alone create all things, both moving and unmoving, and you alone withdraw them;
O Lord, lead me, who desire liberation, swiftly.
That state into which the yogis have entered, from which they do not depart. || 21 ||
Be victorious, O Govinda of great majesty!
Be victorious, O Viṣṇu! Victory to you, O Padmanābha!
Be victorious, O Omniscient One! Victory to you, O Immeasurable One!
Be victorious, O Lord of the Universe, whose form is the universe! || 22 ||
Śrī Varāha said:
Having thus offered praise, the king then laid down his own body and attained dissolution within the eternal Supreme Soul, Govinda.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 36.
Dharaṇī said: "O Lord, O All-pervading One, how are you propitiated by devoted men or by women? Tell me all this, O Creator of beings. (1)
The illustrious Varāha said:
"O Goddess, I am to be accomplished through devotion (bhāva), not by wealth nor by recitations (japa).
Nevertheless, I shall describe to you the physical austerities for my devotees."
Listen to me as I describe the various vows that I shall bestow upon that man whose mind is fixed on Me through action, thought, and speech. || 3 ||
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from guile—
these, O Supporter of the Earth, are said to be the mental vows.
Whether it be eating once a day, eating only at night, fasting, or whatever else there may be, all that constitutes a physical vow for men, and not otherwise.
Silence, study, and the chanting of hymns for the praise of the deity,
as well as abstaining from slander— this is the supreme vocal vow.
In this regard, another thing is heard: in former times, in a previous kalpa, there was a rishi of fierce austerity named Āruṇi, the son of Brahmā.
That best of the twice-born went to a certain forest seeking to perform penance;
thereupon, he practiced austerities there, devoted to fasting.
That brahmin indeed lived on the delightful bank of the Devikā;
once, he went to the great river for the purpose of ritual ablution.
Having bathed there and performed his recitations, the Brahmin saw before him a hunter approaching,
holding a great bow in his hand, with fierce eyes and a terrifying appearance.
He came to kill that twice-born man, desiring to seize his bark garments;
seeing him, the Brahmin was agitated out of fear of the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa,
and meditating upon the god Nārāyaṇa, that twice-born man remained right there.
Seeing that Hari had entered within him, the hunter, as if terrified, cast aside his bow and arrow and then spoke these words: ||| 12 ||
The hunter said:
"O Brahmin, I had come here previously desiring to kill you;
now, through the sight of you, that intention has vanished from me entirely."
O Brahmin, thousands of Brahmins along with tens of thousands of women have been slain by me, and two householders have also been killed. (14)
At times, even in hell, there exists a mind that is more exalted [than this].
Now I desire to perform penance in your presence; you ought to show me favor by granting me instruction. (15)
Although addressed in this manner, that Brahmin did not offer a reply;
for the bull among Brahmins considered him to be a slayer of a Brahmin and a doer of evil deeds.
Even though unbidden, that hunter, desiring dharma, remained right there;
and that brahmin also, having bathed in the river, took refuge at the foot of a tree.
Then, after some time, it is said that a hungry tiger came to that river, intent on killing that peaceful brahmin.
Just as the tiger was about to seize the Brahmin who had gone into the water, he was struck by a hunter and instantly deprived of his life. || 19 ||
Then, indeed, a man rose from that tiger’s body;
and a brahmin, having heard that agitated sound while submerged within the water, loudly uttered the words, "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa! (20).
The tiger also heard the mantra while his life-breaths were still in his throat;
as soon as he heard it, he gave up his life and became a virtuous man.
He said: "O best of the twice-born, by your grace, freed from sin and free from affliction, I shall go to that place where the eternal Viṣṇu resides. (22)
Thus addressed, the brahmin said, "Who are you, O bull among men?
He replied, "O Indra among kings, in my previous birth I was a powerful monarch known as Dīrghabāhu, well-versed in all dharmas. (23)
"I know the Vedas, and I discern the auspicious and the inauspicious;
I have no concern for a Brāhmaṇa—what is the use of these so-called Brāhmaṇas? (24)
When he spoke thus, all the Brahmins, filled with anger, said: "O invincible one, you shall become a cruel tiger! (25)
But because of your insult to the brahmins, O you who are deluded by the time of death, your remembrance of truth will be brought about by Keśava. (26)
Thus was I addressed in the past by those Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas;
I have now fully experienced that very curse of Brahmā in its entirety.
Then all those brahmins, having prostrated before me, O great sage, spoke these words to me long ago for the sake of bestowing their favor: || 28 ||
"O lowest of men, whoever shall stand before you after your sixth-meal-time, he shall become your food for some time. (29)
But when, having received the blow of this arrow while your life-breaths have reached your throat,
you hear from the mouth of a twice-born man the words "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa," then your departure to heaven shall occur; of this there is no doubt.
O best of beings, even as I harbored hatred toward the Brahmins, I heard the name of Viṣṇu coming from the mouth of another, right before your very eyes.
Furthermore, he who, having honored the Brahmins, utters "Obeisance to Hari" with his own mouth, shall release his vital breath; freed from all taints, he becomes liberated.
Truth, truth, and again truth—raising his arm, he declares:
"The Brahmins are the moving gods; the Supreme Person is the immovable one. (33)
Having spoken thus, that king, freed from all taint, went to heaven;
the Brahmin, ever steadfast in yoga, then addressed the hunter.
The sage said:
"O son of noble vows, since I have been protected by you from the king of beasts who desired to seize me, I am pleased with you; choose a boon."
The hunter said:
"O twice-born one, this alone is the boon for me that you speak to me; beyond this, what shall I do with another boon? Instruct me. (36)
The sage said:
"O sinless son, formerly you, who were possessed of many sins and of terrible form, sought me out while desiring to perform penance. (37)
Now, your sins have been destroyed by the bathing in the Devikā, by the sight of me, and by the long-term hearing of the name of Viṣṇu;
you are now pure of body—of this there is no doubt. (38)
Now, O virtuous one, accept a single boon from me; if you so desire, perform penance for a long time in my presence.
The hunter said:
"How can that Lord Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, of whom you have spoken, be attained by mortals? This alone is my boon. (40)
The sage said:
"Whatever vow a man may perform directed toward that Acyuta, that person, endowed with devotion, attains the Supreme. (41)
Knowing this, my son, you should observe this vow:
"I shall not eat meat, nor shall I ever speak an untruth. (42)
"O best of hunters, this vow has been firmly prescribed for you by me;
remain there, engaged in such austerity, for as long as you desire. (43)
Śrī Varāha said:
Perceiving him thus filled with anxiety, the Brāhmaṇa became a bestower of boons;
then, realizing he was a seeker of liberation, the sage deceived him and departed.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 37.
Śrī Varāha said:
Having set out upon that auspicious and beautiful path, that best of hunters performed austerities without food, remembering his guru in his mind.
When the time for alms arrived, he ate withered leaves;
once, overcome by hunger, he took refuge at the foot of a tree. (2)
Being hungry, he desired to eat a leaf from a nearby tree;
as he was doing this, an incorporeal voice spoke from the sky: || 3 ||
"Do not eat the cart; it is too high!"—when he had spoken thus, the bird abandoned that and seized another tree branch that had fallen.
That too would be thus forbidden, and likewise another as well;
thinking his entire burden to be thus, the hunter did not eat anything at all.
Without food, he performed austerities, mindful of his guru and free from sloth;
then, after a long time had passed, that best of sages arrived.
Durvāsas, whose self was purified by holy vows, beheld a certain hunter blazing with the splendor arising from his ascetic penance, like a sacrificial oblation.
Then that hunter, having bowed his head to the great sage, said:
"O Blessed One, I have achieved my life's purpose through the sight of you."
"Now the time for my ancestral offering has arrived; please take note of this," said the hunter to him.
"O great sage, by eating only these withered leaves, I shall indeed gratify you. Thus spoke the hunter. (9)
Durvāsas, wishing to test his austerity, spoke these words aloud to him, who was pure, possessed of a pure disposition, and had conquered his senses: ||| 10 ||
"Let well-prepared food consisting of barley, wheat, and rice be given to me, for I have come here afflicted by hunger and have arrived specifically for your sake. (11)
When this was said, that hunter fell into deep reflection;
lost in thought, he wondered, "Where will my livelihood come from? (12)
As he was thus reflecting, an auspicious golden vessel, endowed with supernatural power, fell from the sky; he took it up with his hand. (13)
Taking that [fruit], he spoke with trepidation to the sage named Durvāsas:
"O Brahmin, please remain right here while I go out for alms; O best among the knowers of Brahman, let this favor be granted. (14)
Having spoken thus, that best of hunters then went out for alms,
not very far from the city which was filled with wealth and women.
As he proceeded there, other most beautiful women emerged from the trees with golden vessels in their hands;
having quickly given him various kinds of food, they filled his bowl.
And he, considering himself to have attained the ultimate goal, returned once more to his hermitage; there he beheld that seer, the best among those who recite prayers.
Having seen him and set that alms-food down in a clean place, the best of hunters, with a clear mind, bowed to that ṛṣi and spoke these words: || 18 ||
"O Blessed One, O bull among sages, let the washing of my feet be performed; if I am worthy of your favor, you should do so. (19)
Thus addressed, that sage, desiring to know the power of his asceticism, said:
"I am unable to go to the river, nor do I have a water vessel."
"O Great-minded Hunter, how shall I quickly wash your feet?
Having heard this from the sage, the hunter became lost in thought:
"What shall I do? And how indeed will there be food for him? (21)
Having reflected thus in his mind and remembered his preceptor, the wise and discerning one went for refuge to that river, the Devikā.
The hunter said:
"I am a hunter, I am a doer of evil deeds, I am a slayer of Brahmins, O best of rivers!
Nevertheless, O Goddess, being remembered by me, protect me who have come to you for refuge. (23)
O auspicious one, I know neither the deity, nor the mantra, nor likewise the ritual worship;
having meditated upon the feet of the Guru as supreme, I behold them constantly.
O Goddess, best among rivers, have compassion for me who am in such a state;
quickly bring water near for the purpose of washing the sage. (25)
Having spoken thus, the hunter then went to Devikā, the destroyer of sins,
from where Durvāsas, firm in his vows, was staying.
Washing his feet herself, that best of rivers, the goddess Hrādinī,
approached the vicinity of the hunter’s hermitage.
Seeing that great marvel, Durvasā was filled with wonder;
having washed his hands and feet, the wise one, being highly pleased and endowed with faith, ate at its conclusion and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
To that hunter, who was reduced to a mere skeleton and weakened by hunger, he said:
"May the study of all the Vedas along with their compendiums, the Brahma-vidyā, and the Purāṇas become manifest to you. (29)
Thus Durvāsas granted him a boon and gave him a name:
"You shall become the foremost sage named Satyatapas. (30)
Having been granted this boon, the hunter said to that best of sages:
"O Brahmin, how can I, having become a hunter, teach the Vedas? (31)
The sage said:
"O best of beings, today your former body has departed from you who are fasting;
there is no doubt that your body consisting of asceticism has become separate."

Know that your former consciousness has gone to destruction, and that you are now pure and imperishable; you are the Pure Body (Śuddhakāya), and your other body is likewise. By means of that, O Sage, the Vedas along with the Śāstras will manifest to you.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 38.
Satyatapas said:
O Blessed One, regarding that which has been proclaimed as "two bodies," tell me their distinction; who indeed are they, O best among the knowers of Brahman?
Durvāsas said:
"Two or three bodies are not to be spoken of; rather, it is the opposite:
the locus of experience for living beings consists of three bodies."
The former state, called unrighteousness, is devoid of thorough knowledge;
the latter, however, which possesses vows, should be known as being exceedingly righteous. (3)
That which is the third [body], beyond the senses, for the purpose of experiencing merit and demerit, is declared by the wise knowers of Brahman to have three divisions:
namely, the threefold division consisting of torment, the experience of merit, and enjoyment. (4)
That state which indeed previously belonged to you as you were slaying living beings—that body known as sin is what is called by the name "evil. (5)
Now, as you practice auspicious conduct, austerity, and straightforwardness—
these other forms of dharma— your body has become established [in such a way] that you are undoubtedly capable of knowing the Vedas and Purāṇas.
When the eightfold group revolves, the man is then proclaimed to be in three states;
having passed through the eight divisions and reached the triple state, he is always auspicious, stable, and possessed of self-determination within his own soul.
When one further abandons five, then five, and even five more,
that person then attains the eternal Brahman through the single path.
Satyatapas said:
"O Blessed One, if consciousness does not arise within the body,
then by what means is the Supreme Brahman perceived?"
Durvāsas said:
The ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) has knowledge as its root, and knowledge likewise has ritual action and the like;
there is no difference between these two, O sage, just as there is none between stone and clay.

The ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) is proclaimed to have four divisions among the Brāhmaṇas and the other [castes]. Among them, three constantly perform the rites prescribed in the Vedas, while one performs service to the three; this is the activity ordained by the Veda.
Abiding in these dharmas, the worship of Brahman is pleasing to him;
for one who delights in the declarations of the Vedas, liberation will surely come to pass.
Satyatapas said:
"O great sage, regarding this supreme Brahman which has been described by you, even the high-souled practitioners of yoga do not know its true form. (13)

How can that Brahman be known, which is nameless, without lineage, formless, devoid of physical form, and free from all designations? Tell me its name, established according to the path of the Vedas. (14)
Durvāsas said:
That which is recited among the Vedavyāsas as the Supreme Brahman—that is the lotus-eyed Lord himself, the supreme Nārāyaṇa. 15.
O best of beings, by performing various sacrifices and by giving gifts,
that supreme god Nārāyaṇa himself, Hari, is attained.
Satyatapas said:
"O Blessed One, a sacrifice is indeed achieved only with great wealth by those performers of merit who employ officiating priests well-versed in the Vedas."
By attaining him, the Blessed Lord Hari is obtained as the very essence of suffering.

O Brahmin, without wealth it is impossible to give charity; even when wealth exists, one whose mind is attached to family has no inclination for it. O Brahmin, how can there be liberation for such a person? Lord Hari is difficult to attain by any means whatsoever.
Tell me in general what may be practiced by all castes, by which the eternal God may be attained with little effort. (19)
Durvāsas said:
I shall tell you the supreme secret, a mystery fashioned by the gods,
concerning that which was done formerly by Dharaṇī as she was sinking into the netherworld (rasātala).
The earthly nature of the earth was not exceeded by that in water;
but when that water was consumed by fire, the earth descended to the subterranean realm.
That auspicious goddess Bhūtadhāriṇī, who dwells in the subterranean realm (rasātala),
propitiated the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme,
through fasts, vows, and various kinds of observances.
After a long time, the eternal Lord whose banner is Garuḍa became pleased with her; he raised her up and established these two [images] in their place.
Satyatapas said:
O great sage, who was this person who performed the fast upon the earth?
And what were those vows? You ought to tell me this.
Durvāsas said: When, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the tenth day, the wise one, with self-restrained mind, having performed the worship of the deity and the fire-ritual according to the rules— (25)
Wearing clean garments and with a serene mind, having eaten well-prepared sacrificial food,
he should walk five steps and then perform purification of his feet once again.
Having prepared a tooth-stick made from a milk-tree, measuring exactly eight finger-breadths, one should consume it and then carefully perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having touched all the doors and meditated for a long time upon Janārdana—
him who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace in his hands, who wears a diadem and yellow garments.
Having meditated upon the god with a serene countenance, endowed with all the auspicious marks,
who is Janārdana in the form of the Sun, one should again take water in the hand.
Having meditated, a person should offer the arghya with water from his own hand;
at that time, O great sage, he should utter these words.
"O lotus-eyed one, having remained without food on the eleventh day, I shall eat on the following day; O Acyuta, be my refuge. (31)
Having spoken thus, he should then, during the night in the presence of the God of gods, sleep there according to the prescribed rule while muttering the mantra "Nārāyaṇāya. || 32 ||
Then, at the clear dawn, having gone to a river that flows to the ocean,
or another [body of water], or a pond, or even to his own home, he, with self-restraint, [should perform his rites].
Having brought pure clay, a person [should apply it] with this mantra:
"O Goddess, you are always the support and the nourishment of all beings;
by that truth, O lady of excellent vows, release me from my sin. (34)
"O Lord, the sacred fords within the interior of the cosmic egg have been touched by your hands;
therefore, having touched this earth, may I obtain that which was spoken of by you. (35)
"O Varuṇa, all fluids are eternally and ever-present within you;
therefore, having flooded this clay, purify it for me without delay. (36)
Having thus purified the clay and likewise the water, one should apply them to oneself;
having done this three times, one should indeed draw a diagram in the water with the remaining clay.

Then, having bathed there properly according to the rites for a universal monarch (cakravartin) and having performed his necessary duties, the man should proceed once again to the temple of the deity.
There, having propitiated the great yogin, the Lord Nārāyaṇa,
[he worshipped him] with "Obeisance to Keśava" for the feet, and to Dāmodara for the waist.
The pair of thighs to Nṛsiṃha; the chest to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa;
the throat to the Lord of the Kaustubha; and likewise the breast to the Lord of Śrī.
"To Trailokyavijaya" [he offers] the two arms; "to the Self of All," the head;
"to the Holder of the Chariot-Wheel," the discus; and "to Śaṅkara," the lotus.
With the mantra "To the Profound One" [he offers] a mace, and with "To the Embodiment of Peace," a lotus;
having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Furthermore, the wise man should place four jars before him, filled with water, adorned with garlands, and smeared with white sandalwood paste. (43)
With their necks adorned with mango sprouts, they were draped in white garments and covered with copper vessels filled with sesame seeds and gold.
The four oceans are proclaimed to be the jars;
in their midst, one should place an auspicious pedestal enveloped in cloth.
In that regard, [the vessel] may be made of gold, silver, copper, or likewise of wood;
in the absence of all these vessels, a vessel made of Palāśa wood is prescribed.
Having filled that vessel with water,
one should then place therein the Lord Janārdana in the form of a golden fish,
accompanied by the Vedas and Vedāṅgas and adorned with the Śruti and Smṛti.
There, having honored [the deity] according to the prescribed rite with various kinds of foods, fruits, flowers, perfumes, incense, and garments, it was made beautiful. 48.

"O Lord Keśava, just as the Vedas situated in the netherworld were recovered by you in the form of a fish, so may you rescue me. Having spoken thus in his presence, one should perform a vigil there. (49)
At dawn, when it is clear and bright, one should cause four jars to be given to four Brahmins according to the extent of one's wealth.
One should first give [the vessel] to a Bahvṛca, and likewise the southern one to a Chandoga;
one should give the excellent western jar to one belonging to a Yajurvedic school;
and the northern one may be given according to one's desire—this indeed is the prescribed rule.
May the Ṛgveda be pleased in the east, the Sāmaveda in the south, the Yajurveda in the west, and the Atharvaveda in the north. (52)
With this sequence of ritual application, one should cause [the recipient] to recite, "May [the Lord] be pleased";
and one should present a golden image of the Fish-form to the preceptor.
Having worshipped according to the rules and in due order with perfumes, incense, garments, and other offerings,
whoever bestows this mantra along with its secret [teachings],
having indeed granted him the ritual procedure, shall receive a fruit a hundred million times greater.
That lowest of men who, having approached a teacher, behaves toward him with hostility out of delusion, shall be cooked in hell for ten million births.
He who imparts the ritual injunction is called a "teacher" by the wise. (55)
Having thus given according to the prescribed rite and having worshipped Viṣṇu on the twelfth day,
one should provide a meal for the Brahmins according to one's capacity, accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
One should have jars prepared covered with copper vessels containing water and sesame seeds;
therein, [the gift] placed in a vessel of pure water is for a Brāhmaṇa who has a family.
The highly fortunate man should give the gift to the deity and then feed the Brahmins with abundant *paramānna* (milk-rice); thereafter,
the man himself should eat together with his children, remaining silent and with his senses restrained.
O best among the wise, listen now to the foremost fruit of merit belonging to that man who performs the Dharaṇī-vow according to this rite.
O observer of excellent vows, if I were to possess thousands of mouths, and O observer of great vows, if my lifespan were equal to that of Brahmā; (60)
At that time, it might be appropriate to describe the fruit of this dharma;
nevertheless, O Brahmin, I shall speak of it in brief—listen to that.
Ten times seven, ten times two, eight, and four;
four hundred thousand and forty thousand—this, when unified, constitutes a cycle of four yugas (caturyuga).
O Sage, seventy-one such yugas constitute a manvantara;
a day of Brahmā consists of fourteen such [manvantaras], and his night is held to be of equal duration.
In this way, thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve of those months are known as a year; a hundred of those years is the lifespan of Brahmā—of this there is no doubt.
Whoever observes this Dvādaśī even once according to this rite attains the world of Brahmā and remains there for that very duration. || 65 ||
Then, at the dissolution of Brahmā, he remains absorbed in that state for a long time;
then, upon re-creation, he becomes the deity Vairāja of great asceticism.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, even those committed in this world,
whether unintentionally or intentionally, perish at that very moment.
In this world, whether one is poor or a king who has fallen from his kingdom, by fasting according to the prescribed rite, he will certainly be reborn as a king. (68)
Even a woman who is barren shall become auspicious by this rite;
having fasted, she shall have a son who is supremely righteous.
The man who has committed an act of approaching one who should not be approached is liberated from that sin by resorting to this ritual procedure. (70)
By fasting once with devotion on this day, one may obtain the purification of the Vedas, even if the performance of Vedic rites has been neglected for many years. (71)
What is the use of saying more in this matter? O Great Sage, there is nothing that cannot be attained, nor is there any sin that does not perish. (72)
O Brahmin, by this rite she herself indeed fasted;
O dear one, there is no need for further deliberation regarding her sinking into the earth. (73)
This ritual procedure must not be given to one who is uninitiated, nor to an atheist, nor should it ever be disclosed to one who hates the gods or the Brahmins.
It should be bestowed upon one devoted to the guru; it instantly destroys all sin.
In this very life, for one who has fasted according to the prescribed rite, there arise good fortune, wealth, grain, and excellent women in various forms. (75)
Whoever should cause this supreme ritual manual of the Dvādaśī to be heard with devotion, or who hears it themselves, is liberated from all sins whatsoever. (76)
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. || 39 ||
Durvāsas said:
Likewise, in the month of Pauṣa, the nectar was churned by the gods;
there, the Lord Janārdana himself became the Tortoise. || 1 ||
This lunar day is declared to belong to Hari in his tortoise form:
it is the pure twelfth day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight in the month of Puṣya.
Having first made a formal resolve regarding that [observance], and having performed the rites such as bathing and so forth as before,
one should worship Janārdana on the night of the eleventh day (Ekādaśī),
O best of sages, worshipping Janārdana, the God of gods, with separate mantras.
Having first worshipped the feet with "Oṃ,
to Kūrma," and the waist of Hari with "Nārāyaṇa," one should worship the belly with "to Saṃkarṣaṇa," the chest with "Viśoka," and likewise the throat with "Bhavāya."
With "Subāhava," [he touched] the two arms; with "Namo Viśālāya Rathāṅgasāra," the head. || 4 ||

Having worshipped the deity with his own name-mantra using fragrant flowers, various offerings, and diverse fruits, and having placed the water-pot before him, he should adorn it with garlands and a white neck-thread.
Having fashioned that god made of gold from his own power, with Ratnagarbha as before,
and having fashioned Mandara in the form of a tortoise, he placed it there.
Having placed it in a copper vessel filled with ghee and set it upon a full water-pot,
one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa on the following day in this very manner.
On the following day, having fed the Brahmins with sacrificial fees according to one's ability, one should gratify the God of gods,
Nārāyaṇa, in his form as the Tortoise. Afterwards—
In that manner, he himself should eat together with his circle of servants. || 7 ||
O Brahmin, when this is done, all sin is destroyed; one should not entertain any doubt in this matter.
Having abandoned the wheel of saṃsāra, one becomes pure.
He attains the ancient realm of Hari;
his sins quickly go to destruction, and he becomes illustrious and established in the dharma of truth.
The sins accumulated over many previous births are destroyed by a person's devotion;
however, the aforementioned fruit shall indeed come to pass.
Nārāyaṇa, however, immediately attains satisfaction. || 9 ||
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 40.
Durvāsas said:
O most righteous sage, listen now to the account of the first Dvādaśī of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, dedicated to the Boar (Varāha), the upholder of the earth. || 1 ||
Having performed the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) and the ceremonial bath according to the previously mentioned procedure,
and having worshipped the Lord on the eleventh lunar day, the wise man [should proceed].
Having worshipped Acyuta with incense, food offerings, and fragrances,
a person should thereafter place a water-filled pitcher before him.
One should worship the feet with "Oṃ Vārāhāya," the hips with "Mādhavāya," the belly with "Kṣetrajñāya," and the chest of Hari with "Viśvarūpa."
One should worship the throat with "To the Omniscient One," the head with "To the Lord of Creatures," the two arms with "To Pradyumna," and the Sudarśana [discus] with "To the Divine Weapon.
The conch shell is worshipped with "To Him Born of Nectar. This is the procedure for the worship of the deity.
Having thus worshipped, the wise man should place into that jar a vessel made of gold, silver, or copper, according to his means and capacity.
Having established it filled with all types of seeds, the wise and discerning man should have a golden Varāha fashioned there according to his means.
Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, who had assumed the form of a boar, [was seen] having lifted up the earth— with its mountains, forests, and trees— by the tip of his tusk.
Upon a vessel containing all seeds, resting atop a jar filled with jewels,
one should place the supreme deity Hari, fashioned from gold.
O Sage, one should place a copper vessel covered with a pair of white cloths and worship it with perfumes, flowers, and various auspicious food offerings.
Having fashioned a mandala of flowers, the wise man should perform a vigil there; he should recite and contemplate the manifestations of Hari at that place.
Thus, at the end of this disciplined observance, when the sun has risen in the morning,
one who is pure, having bathed and worshipped Hari, should offer it to a Brāhmaṇa.
O brahmin-sage, one should especially cause this to be given to one who is learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, of virtuous conduct, wise, and a devotee of Viṣṇu. || 13 ||
Listen to me regarding the fruit that indeed accrues from giving that divine Hari in the form of a boar, together with a water-pot, to a Brāhmaṇa. || 14 ||
In this very life, one gains good fortune, prosperity, beauty, and contentment;
the poor instantly becomes wealthy, and the childless obtains a son. Misfortune perishes immediately, and Lakṣmī enters [the house] in an instant. || 15 ||
Behold the good fortune in this life and in the next world; in this regard, listen to an ancient historical narrative from the past.
In this world there was a king renowned as Vīradhanvan;
once that scorcher of foes went to the forest for the sake of hunting deer. (17)
While hunting herds of deer there, situated in the midst of the forest of sages, that king unintentionally killed Brahmins who were in the form of deer. || 18 ||
O Brahmin, fifty brothers there, the sons of Saṃvarta, who were devoted to the study of the Vedas, remained in the form of deer. (19)
Satyatapas said:
"O Brahmin, relying upon what cause did they assume the form of deer? This is my curiosity; be gracious to me who am prostrate before you. (20)
Durvāsas said: Once, O best of beings, having gone to the forest, they saw young fawns who had just been born and were deprived of their mothers.
For they each seized one [of the heads], and those [heads] remained upon their shoulders after they had died.
Then, all of them, being distressed, went into the presence of their father and spoke these words: "O Sage, except for the killing of the deer... (22)
The sons of the sages said:
"O Sage, as soon as they were born, five deer were killed by us. Since this was done unintentionally, please prescribe an expiation for us. (23)
Saṃvarta said:
"My father was indeed a perpetrator of violence, and I am even more so;
thus, you, my little sons, have become doers of sinful deeds."
"Now, having donned deer skins and being restrained in your vows, wander for five years; thereafter you shall become pure. (25)
Thus addressed, those sons, wearing deer-skins as sacred threads,
entered the forest unperturbed, chanting the eternal Brahman.
Then, when a year had passed, King Vīradhanvan arrived at that place where they were wandering in the form of deer.

And they too, wearing deer-skins and sacred threads, were seated at the foot of a certain tree chanting prayers; having seen them, the king, thinking they were deer, pierced them all at once, and those exponents of the Veda died. || 28 ||
Seeing those Brahmins of rigid vows dead, the king, trembling with fear, went to the hermitage of Devarāta. There he asked: "O great sage, has the sin of killing a Brahmin come upon me? (29)
Having related how that slaughter had occurred, the lord of men,
his soul overwhelmed by intense grief, wept, being deeply afflicted with sorrow.
Then that seer Devarāta said to the best of kings as he was weeping:
"Do not fear, O King; I shall remove your sin. (31)
And just as the Earth was sinking into the netherworld called Sutala,
she was lifted up by Viṣṇu, the God of gods, who had assumed the form of a boar.
In the same way, O Indra among kings, that very god Janārdana himself will deliver you, who are overwhelmed by the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thus addressed, the king was delighted and spoke these words:
"In what manner does that Lord become gracious to me? And by what means, O best of beings, does everything inauspicious perish when he is pleased? (34)
Durvāsas said:
Thus addressed by him, the sage Devarāta explained this vow;
and he too, having performed it, enjoyed abundant pleasures.
At the time of his death, O best of sages, that king went to heaven, to the realm of Indra, by means of a shining golden celestial chariot.
Taking the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), Indra went forth to meet him.
But seeing Indra approaching, Viṣṇu’s servants said to him:
"The king of the gods must not be seen by you, for he is inferior to you in ascetic power."
Thus, by his splendor, all the world-protectors departed;
and they were rejected by those servants of Viṣṇu as being devoid of merit.
In this manner, O great sage, that king traveled as far as the end of Satyaloka.

In this world free from rebirth and devoid of burning destruction, even today that great king remains, being praised by the gods. When the Lord of Sacrifice is thus pleased, what wonder is there that such a thing should come to pass? (39)
In this life, fortune, longevity, and the perfection of health—
each one, when worshipped according to the prescribed rite, bestows the highest nectar.
How much more so when the year is complete—he bestows his own station;
Nārāyaṇa, who possesses four forms, grants that which is most excellent, without a doubt. (41)
Just as Keśava, in the form of a fish, retrieved the Vedas,
and as the Lord, while the ocean of milk was being churned, supported Mount Mandara—
likewise, behold this second manifestation of Viṣṇu known as the Tortoise.
Just as Puruṣottama, assuming the form of a boar, upheld the earth from the netherworld (rasātala), behold likewise this third Vaiṣṇavī power.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 41.
Durvāsas said:
Likewise, in the month of Phālguna, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight,
the wise man, having fasted according to the prescribed rule, should worship Hari.
One should worship the feet with "To Narasiṃha," the thighs with "To Govinda," the waist with "To Viśvabhuja," and the chest with "To Aniruddha."

One should worship the throat with "To Śitikaṇṭha," the head with "To Piṅgakeśa," the discus with "To Asuradhvaṃsana," and likewise the conch with "To Toyātman," honoring them all with perfumes, flowers, and fruits.
Taking a water-pot before him, provided with a pair of white garments,
he should place upon it a golden image of Nṛsiṃha in a copper vessel;
having fashioned it from gold according to his means, or even from wood or bamboo.
Having placed it in a jar containing jewels and having worshipped it,
a person should present it on the twelfth lunar day to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas.
O great sage, I shall now fully relate that fruit which was obtained in the past by the king named Vatsa when he had performed this act.
In the region of Kimpuruṣa, there was a most righteous king;
he was renowned as Bhārata, and Vatsa was his son.
Defeated by his enemies in battle, stripped of his treasury, and deprived of his elephants and horses,
he went to the forest with his wife and dwelt in the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
Then, as time passed, he was asked by the great seer Vasiṣṭha, "What is your purpose? Why do you dwell in this great hermitage? (9)
The king said:
"O Blessed One, my treasury has been seized and my kingdom especially taken away;
with my resolve destroyed by my enemies, I have come to you for refuge."
You ought to show favor by granting me instruction.
Thus addressed, Vasiṣṭha then replied to him regarding this Dvādaśī, O Sage;
and he, in turn, performed everything according to the prescribed rite.
At the conclusion of his vow, the Lord Nārasiṃha was pleased with him and bestowed upon him a supreme discus that brings about the destruction of enemies.
By means of that weapon, that best of kings conquered his own kingdom;
established in his realm, the lord performed a thousand horse-sacrifices,
and in the end, O virtuous one, he attained the station known as the world of Viṣṇu.
O Sage, this auspicious Dvādaśī, which removes sins, has been described to you with great care; having heard it, do as you desire. (14)
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 42.
Durvāsas said:
O sage, in this very manner, having made a formal resolve on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) in the month of Caitra,
one should fast and thereafter worship Janārdana, the God of gods.
One should worship the feet with "To Vāmana," and the waist with "To Viṣṇu";
the belly and chest with "To Vāsudeva," and the entire body with "To Saṃpūrṇakāya."

Having worshipped the throat with "Salutation to the Creator of the Universe," and the head with "Salutation to Him whose form is the Sky," one should worship the arms with "Salutation to the Conqueror of the Universe," and the conch and discus with their own names.
Having worshipped the eternal God of gods according to this rite,
one should place the northern pitcher together with its pair in front, just as before.
The wise man, having placed a golden Vāmana in the previously mentioned vessel,
[should fashion him] short according to his means, wearing a white sacred thread.
One should place the water-pot at the side, as well as the small umbrella and the sandals;
and having set down the rosary, one should especially provide a seat.
At dawn, he should cause this, equipped with these utensils, to be given to a twice-born man, while uttering: "May Viṣṇu, who has assumed a dwarf form, be pleased."
Combined with the name of the month, this rite for the manifestation [of the deity] is proclaimed as the rule for every instance, concluding with the words, "May [He/She] be pleased."
It is heard that in ancient times there was a king, Haryaśva, the lord of the earth;
being childless, he performed austerities, desiring a son rich in ascetic merit.
O best of sages, while he was performing that very rite for the sake of a son,
Hari first arrived, having assumed the form of a brahmin.
"O King, O Lord, what have you resolved to achieve through this austerity? he asked.
The Brahmin replied to him, "It is for the sake of a son. Thus he spoke.
"O King, perform this very procedure," he said;
having spoken thus to the king, the Lord vanished in an instant. (12)
The king also quickly made him a master of mantras for the sake of that twice-born man;
likewise, he bestowed them upon the wise Jyotir-Gārgya, who was poor.
"O Blessed One, just as he himself became the son of Aditi who was previously childless, by that truth may a most excellent son also be born to me. (14)
O Sage, when it was given according to this rite, he had a son known as Kuvalāśva, a mighty universal emperor (cakravartin).
One without a son obtains a son; one without wealth obtains wealth;
one who has lost his kingdom regains his kingdom; and having died, he shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
Having praised [it] there for a very long time, one who has returned here to the mortal world shall become a wise universal monarch (cakravartin), just like Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 43.
Durvāsas said:

In the month of Vaiśākha, a man, having likewise made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the prescribed rule and having performed the ritual bath and other rites in that same manner, should then proceed to the temple of the deity. || 1 ||
There, having propitiated Hari with devotion by means of these mantras, the wise one [should worship]:
the feet for Jāmadagnya, the belly for Sarvadhārin,
the waist for Madhusūdana, and the chest for Śrīvatsadhārin.
He should offer his two arms to Kṣatrāntaka, his throat to Maṇikaṇṭha;
he should offer his conch and discus by their own names, and his head to Brahmāṇḍadhārin.
Having thus worshipped, the wise man should place a jar before it as previously described,
covered in the same manner and wrapped with a pair of cloths.
One should establish Hari in that vessel made of bamboo;
it is renowned by the name Jāmadagnya and is the destroyer of afflictions.
One should fashion an axe in the right hand of that deity;
having worshipped him with all types of perfumes and various auspicious flowers.
Then, a devoted man should keep a vigil before it;
at dawn, when the sun is bright, he should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
Listen to me regarding the fruit that belongs to one who is thus endowed with these observances.
In former times, there was a highly fortunate king named Vīrasena, possessed of great strength; being childless, he performed intense penance with great majesty.
While the great sage Yājñavalkya was performing that formidable penance, the great yogi arrived; having seen him not very far away, [he approached].
Then, seeing that rishi of supreme luster approaching,
the king stood up and greeted him with his palms joined in reverence.
Honored by him, the sage said: "For what purpose is this austerity being performed?
O King, you who know the dharma, tell me: what is the matter you wish to speak of? (11)
The king said:
"O illustrious one, I am childless; I have no lineage of sons.
Therefore, O twice-born one, having undertaken austerity, my own body is being emaciated."
Yājñavalkya said:
"Enough of this austerity involving such great hardship, O King;
your son shall be born with little effort, of this there is no doubt. (13)
The king said:
"O twice-born one, how indeed may I have a son with little effort?
O venerable one, being pleased, please tell this to me who am prostrate before you. (14)
Durvāsas said:
Thus addressed by that illustrious king,
the sage explained this Dvādaśī occurring in the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha.
For that king, desiring a son especially, fasted according to the prescribed rite and obtained a son, Nala, who was supremely righteous;
he who even today is celebrated in the world as the best of men, Puṇyaśloka.
Indeed, this is the incidental fruit for one who has gone [to that state], O Great Sage:
a virtuous son is born, endowed with wealth and learning, and possessing supreme luster. (17)
What is surprising about this life? Listen to me regarding the next world:
having dwelt for one kalpa in the world of Brahmā with hosts of apsarases, [he shall dwell there].
At the end of his play, upon creation again, he will certainly become a universal monarch;
he lives for thirty thousand years—of this there is no doubt. (19)
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 44.
Durvāsas said:
In the month of Jyeṣṭha as well, having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) in this very manner according to the prescribed rule,
a person should worship the Supreme God with various kinds of auspicious flowers.
One should first worship the feet with "Obeisance to Rāmābhirāma," the hips with "To Trivikrama," and the abdomen with "To the Sustainer of the Universe."

He should worship the chest with "To Saṃvatsara," the throat with "And to Saṃvarttaka," and the two arms— the one marked by the lotus and the other by the discus— with their respective names, "To the Wielder of All Weapons."
Having worshipped the thousand-headed head of that Great-Souled One,
and having thus worshipped according to the rule, one should place the pitcher as previously described.

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite two golden figures of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, covered with a pair of garments as before, they should be given to a Brāhmaṇa at dawn by a person who desires to achieve his heart's wish.
Formerly, King Daśaratha, being childless and intent on obtaining sons, questioned Vasiṣṭha, who was then highly honored by him.
That twice-born man explained this very procedure;
however, having perceived the king's secret intention, the king performed this [rite].
A powerful son named Rāma was born to him of his own accord;
O great sage, the imperishable Viṣṇu was thus pleased and manifested in four forms.
This which pertains to this world has been told; now hear that which pertains to the hereafter.
Remaining in heaven, they enjoy pleasures for as long as the number of Indras is ten times two squared;
when that time has passed, the mortal returns once more.
He would become a king who performs a hundred sacrifices;
the sins of that man perish, and he attains the stainless and eternal Nirvāṇa. || 9 ||
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 45.
Durvāsas said:
In the month of Āṣāḍha as well, having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) in this very manner according to the prescribed rite,
a man should worship the Supreme God many times with perfumes and flowers.
He should worship the feet with "To Vāsudeva," the hips with "And to Saṃkarṣaṇa," the belly with "To Pradyumna," and the chest with "To Aniruddha."
One should worship the two arms with "O Cakrapāṇi," the neck likewise with "O Bhūpati," the conch and discus with their own names, and the head with "O Puruṣa."
Having thus worshipped, the wise man should place a jar before it as previously described, covered with cloth; then, upon that [jar],
he should place the eternal Vāsudeva in his fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), made of gold.
Having worshipped that [image] in due order according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa who is a proponent of the Vedas and firm in his vows, as previously described.
Listen now to me regarding the merit of one who is thus endowed with these observances.
Vasudeva became the king, the increaser of the Yadu lineage;
Devakī was his wife, who observed identical vows.
That virtuous woman, devoted solely to the duty toward her husband, remained childless;
after a long time had passed, Nārada came to her home.
Having been worshipped with devotion by Vasudeva, he spoke these words:
"O Vasudeva, O sinless one, listen to my task for the sake of the gods.
Having heard this account, I have come quickly to your presence. (8)
O best of the Yadus, I saw the Earth in the assembly of the gods; having approached them, she spoke: "The gods are not capable of bearing this burden."
The Saubhas, Kaṃsa, Jarāsandha, and Naraka,
as well as the powerful Dānavas and gods of the Kurus, Pañcālas, and Bhojas,
are all together oppressing me; O best of gods, slay them!
Having been addressed thus by the Earth, those gods went to Nārāyaṇa;
and that Lord of Gods, through their mental power, appeared visibly before them in that very instant.
And the best of the gods himself said, "O gods, I shall accomplish this task myself by going among mortals like a human being; of this there is no doubt."
However, if a woman fasts together with her husband during the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha,
I shall enter her womb among human beings.
Having spoken thus, the god departed, and I myself have come here.
This has been taught especially for you who are childless:
by fasting, one obtains a son together with one's wife; of this there is no doubt.
And by observing this twelfth day, Vasudeva likewise attained it;
he obtained great prosperity, endowed with sons and grandsons. (15)
Having enjoyed the glory of sovereignty, he then attained the supreme goal.
This procedure has been described to you, O Sage, for the month of Āṣāḍha.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 46.
Durvāsas said: On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
one should worship the Supreme God with perfumes, flowers, and fragrant unguents.

One should worship the feet with "Salutation to Dāmodara," the waist with "Salutation to Hṛṣīkeśa," the belly with "Salutation to Sanātana," and the chest with "Salutation to the Bearer of the Śrīvatsa."
One should assign the two arms with "O Cakrapāṇi," the throat likewise with "O Hari," the head with "O Muñjakeśa," and the topknot with "O Bhadra."
Having thus worshipped and established the water-pot exactly as before,
one should place a pair of garments upon it and then set [the vessel] down.
Having worshipped that golden god of gods, named Dāmodara, according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order.
As before, one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
now hear from me the power of one who is thus endowed with these observances.
O Lord, this procedure for the month of Śrāvaṇa has been described to you;
now hear its power, which destroys all sins.
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, there was a king named Nṛga of great strength;
with his mind intent on the hunt, he wandered through a formidable forest.
Once, carried far by his horse, he entered a great forest teeming with tigers,
lions, and elephants, and infested by robbers and serpents.
There, the king, being alone, unyoked his horse beneath a tree;
then, having spread kusha grass himself, he lay down, overcome with sorrow. || 10 ||
At that very moment, fourteen thousand hunters arrived there from all sides at night to kill deer for the king. || 11 ||
There they saw King Nṛga, the most formidable, sleeping, adorned with gold and jewels, and endowed with supreme splendor.
Having gone quickly, those hunters reported it to their master;
he too, for the sake of the jewels and gold, prepared to kill the king. (13)
And for the sake of the horse, forest-dwelling swordsmen, having approached the sleeping king, proceeded to seize him. (14)
Then, from the body of the king, a certain woman arose, adorned with white ornaments, garlands, and sandalwood paste;
having risen, she took up the discus and struck down those barbarians. (15)
Having slain the Dasyus, that goddess quickly re-entered the body of the king; then the king, having awakened, saw that the Mlecchas had been killed and she had returned to her own form. (16)
Mounting his horse, he went once more to the hermitage of Vāmadeva.
There, with devotion, he questioned the sage: "Who is this woman? Who were those struck down by you?
O Sage, tell me of this matter; be gracious unto me. (17)
Vāmadeva said:
O King, in another birth you were of the Śūdra caste;
while serving a Brāhmaṇa there, you heard [the following].
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, however, || 18 ||
O King, because you fasted with devotion according to the prescribed rites,
it was on that very day of fasting, O sinless one, that you regained your kingdom.
In all calamities, that goddess protects you;
by her the cruel Mlecchas, filled with sin, were struck down,
and you too were protected, O King— she is indeed Śrāvaṇa-dvādaśī.
A single one protects against calamities, and a single one bestows sovereignty;
how much more so these twelve, since they did not yield even the station of Indra? (21)
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 47.
Durvāsas said:
Likewise, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
having made a formal resolve according to the rules, one should worship the supreme Lord.
Salutation be to Kalki for the feet; to Hṛṣīkeśa for the waist;
and likewise to the Destroyer of Mlecchas, the Embodiment of the Universe, for the belly.

One should worship the throat with "To the blue-throated one," the two arms with "To the sword-handed one," the hands with "To the four-armed one," and likewise the head with "To the universal-formed one."
Having worshipped in this manner, the wise man should place a water-pot before it as previously described; he should have an image of the god Kalkin made there out of gold.
Having covered it with a pair of white garments and adorned it with perfumes and flowers, one should present it at dawn to a Brahmin who is most learned in the scriptures;
hear now, O great sage, what the result shall be when this has been done. || 5 ||
Formerly, there was a very powerful king named Viśāla in the city of Kāśī;
having been deprived of his kingdom by his kinsmen, he entered Mount Gandhamādana.
O great king, having reached the beautiful Badarī in that valley,
that best of men— deprived of his kingdom and especially stripped of his splendor— remained there.
Once, the two ancient and most excellent sages, the divine Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who are saluted by all the gods, arrived there.
Seeing the king already present there, those two subduers of enemies beheld him meditating upon the supreme Brahman, the highest state known as Viṣṇu.
Those two, being pleased, said to that king whose impurities were exhausted: "O Indra among kings, choose a boon; we have come to you as givers of boons."
The king said: "I do not know who you two are; from whom shall I accept a boon? Since I am propitiating you both, I desire an auspicious boon from you. (11)
When they were thus addressed by the king, [he said]: "O Lord, whom do you seek to propitiate?
Or what boon do you choose? Tell me out of curiosity. (12)
Thus addressed, the king then said, "I shall propitiate Viṣṇu," and having spoken, he remained silent; thereupon, the two spoke again.
"O King, by the grace of that very god, a boon must be granted to us both; tell us what boon is in your heart. (14)
The king said:
"Grant me this boon: that I may possess the capability to worship the Lord of Sacrifice with various sacrifices accompanied by diverse sacrificial fees. (15)
Nara said:
"The Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, the illuminator of the world's path and the creator of the worlds,
shall perform austerities with me at Badarī."
This Lord was formerly a fish, then again he assumed the form of a tortoise; he became a boar, and thereafter he became a man-lion.
From him was born Vāmana, and then the mighty son of Jamadagni;
having again become the son of Daśaratha, he shone forth once more as Vāsudeva.
Having become a Buddha, O King, he indeed deluded the people; then,
having again slain his enemies— the Dasyus and Mlecchas— he,
this very Lord Hari, restored this earth to its natural state.
He is worshipped in the form of a fish by those desiring omniscience;
he is worshipped in the form of a tortoise for the sake of uplifting his own lineage.
Just as Hari is worshipped in the form of Varāha by one submerged in the ocean of existence,
so too is he worshipped by men in the form of Nṛsiṃha out of fear of sin.
A wise person should worship Vāmana for the destruction of delusion, the son of Agni (Kārttikeya) for the sake of wealth,
and the son of Daśaratha (Rāma) for the destruction of cruel enemies.
A wise man desiring sons should worship Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt.
One desiring beauty should worship Buddha, and for the destruction of enemies, one should worship Kalkin.
Having spoken thus to him, the sage said this very thing to that man:
"He too observed the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) and became a universal emperor (Cakravartin).
O Sage, by his very name, Badarī came to be known as Viśālā."
In this very life, having ruled as king, he went to the forest;
and having performed various sacrifices, he attained supreme nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 48.
Durvāsas said:
Likewise, in the month of Āśvayuja, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, one should make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and worship the eternal Lord Padmanābha. || 1 ||

One should worship the feet with "Salutation to Padmanābha," the waist to "Padmayoni," the abdomen to "Sarvadeva," and the chest to "Puṣkarākṣa"; likewise, one should worship the hand to "Avyaya" and the weapons as previously described.
Having worshipped the head for the sake of manifestation, one should place a water-pot in front as before;
therein, one should install the golden deity Padmanābha.
Having worshipped that very deity in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa when the night has turned to dawn.
O great sage, learn now what merit is gained when this is performed.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was a powerful king named Bhadrāśva;
after his name, the region became known by the name Bhadrāśva.
Once, O best of men, Agastya came to his house and said,
"I shall dwell in your home for seven nights."
Bowing his head to him, the king said, "Please stay.
His wife, named Kāntimatī, was exceedingly beautiful.
Her splendor became equal to that of the twelve Ādityas;
she had five hundred co-wives, O observer of vows.
O illustrious one, those auspicious women performed their daily tasks like slave-girls; terrified by Kāntimatī, they were distraught with fear.
Agastya, seeing her thus endowed with beauty and splendor and auspicious,
and seeing his wives performing their duties well out of fear of her,
the king gazed only at her joyful face.
Then, seeing the queen in such a state, supremely beautiful, Agastya, filled with joy, exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, O Lord of the World! (11)

On the second day as well, having seen the queen of great luster, Agastya spoke upon seeing her on that second day: "Alas, the world of moving and non-moving beings has been robbed! Alas, it has been robbed! (12)
On the third day, seeing her, he spoke again in this manner:
"Alas, these fools do not know Govinda, the Supreme Lord, who, being pleased, bestowed this very fruit upon the king on the first day. (13)
On the fourth day, raising his hands, he spoke again:
"Excellent, excellent, O Lord of the World! Women, Śūdras—excellent, excellent!
Twice-born Brahmins, excellent! Kings, excellent! Vaiśyas, excellent, again and again! (14)
"Excellent, Bhadrāśva! Excellent, O Agastya! Excellent, excellent to you!
Excellent, Prahlāda! Excellent, Dhruva of great vows!
Having spoken thus, Agastya danced exultantly in the presence of the king.
Seeing him in such a state, the best of kings, together with his wife, asked:
"O Brahmin, what is the cause of your joy that you are dancing in this manner? (16)
Agastya said:
"Alas, you are a foolish king; alas, these followers of yours are fools;
alas, the priests are fools, for they do not understand my intention. (17)
When this had been said, the king then spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"O Brahmin, we do not understand this question uttered by you. Tell us, O illustrious one, if you are inclined to show us favor. (18)
Agastya said:
"This queen, who was formerly a maidservant of a Vaiśya named Haridatta in the city of Vaidiśa, has you as her very husband."
A Śūdra, devoted to his service, became his very own artisan. || 19 ||
In the month of Āśvayuja, on the twelfth day, that Vaiśya,
remaining self-restrained, went in person to the temple of Viṣṇu and [worshipped] Hari with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
Having paid his respects, O high-minded one, he departed for his own home, leaving both of you as guardians to keep the lamps burning.
O best of men, when the Vaiśya had departed, the two of them remained there having lit lamps until the night was spent and dawn broke. || 22 ||
Then, in due time, both that husband and wife died;
by that merit, their birth occurred in the house of Priyavrata.
This wife of yours was formerly a maidservant of a Vaiśya;
she once extinguished the light of another lamp that had been lit in the house of Hari. (24)
Furthermore, O virtuous one, the merit of one who lights a lamp before Viṣṇu with his own wealth cannot be calculated;
it is for that reason that I have spoken these words to you, "O Hari, well done! (25).
Having practiced devotion to Hari for one year in the Kṛta age, a wise man attains the same result by practicing it for half a year in the Tretā age; of this there is no doubt.
By worshipping with devotion for three months during the Dvāpara age, one obtains the fruit;
but by uttering "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa" in the Kali age, one obtains that same fruit. By him the entire world has been conquered; I have declared that devotion alone is sufficient for Viṣṇu. 27.

O King, such is the fruit obtained by you through the excellence of a lamp offered for another at the presence of the Deity; this fruit has been described by me. Alas, the foolish do not know the fruit of the act of offering a lamp to Hari! (28)
Those twice-born ones and those kings who worship in this manner with various sacrifices out of devotion—they are remembered as virtuous men. || 29 ||
"O holy Agastya, I do not see anyone else on this earth besides him; therefore, O King, with great joy and in a state of agitation, I praised myself. (30)
That woman is blessed, and that Śūdra is considered even more blessed, for having performed service to her husband in his absence as if to Hari. || 31 ||
That woman is blessed, as is the Śūdra who is devoted to the service of the twice-born;
by his permission, devotion to Hari arises, and for that reason, the woman and the Śūdra are both virtuous.
Having adopted the disposition of an asura, Prahlāda knows no one other than Puruṣottama; for that reason, he is called a virtuous man.
"O virtuous one, O best of kings, having been born in the lineage of Prajāpati, he went to the forest while still a child;
having propitiated Viṣṇu, he attained that most beautiful station.
Therefore, O noble one, I have called him Dhruva. (34)
Having heard these words of the high-souled Agastya, that king,
who was a ruler of limited instruction, questioned the bull among sages.
And the highly fortunate Agastya, while traveling to Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika,
proceeded toward the abode of Bhadrāśva after Agastya had departed.
And when questioned by the king regarding that very twelfth day, Durvāsas, the best of sages, said:
"O you whose wealth is austerity, this very matter has already been told to you by me."
Having spoken these words again to the best of kings, Agastya said, "I am going to Puṣkara; I shall return to your home.
Having said this, the sage immediately vanished from sight.
The king also, having fasted on the twelfth day of Padmanābha according to that same rite, attained his supreme desire in this very birth.
Having fasted on the twelfth day together with his wife,
that excellent king obtained sons and grandsons in this very birth.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 49.
Durvāsas said:
Having gone to the holy site of Puṣkara, Agastya, the bull among sages,
quickly returned on the full moon day of Kārtika to the palace of Bhadrāśva.
Seeing that sage who had arrived, the most righteous king honored him with offerings of water for his hands and feet and other rites; once the sage had accepted a seat,
the king, filled with joy, spoke to that ṛṣi of rigid vows.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, O best of excellent sages, the procedure for the twelfth day in the month of Āśvayuja was previously described by you; that has been performed by me."
Now, tell me what merit there may be in the month of Kārttika.
Agastya said: Listen, O mighty-armed King, to the method by which one should observe the fast on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) in the month of Kārttika, and what fruit is obtained from it.
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should likewise perform the ritual bath;
one should worship the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, who is free from all blemish.
One should worship the head of Hari with "Obeisance to the Thousand-headed One" (namaḥ sahasraśirase);

the two arms with "To the Supreme Person" (puruṣāya); the throat with "To the One of Universal Form" (viśvarūpiṇe); the weapons with "To the Weapon of Knowledge" (jñānāstrāya); and likewise the chest with "To Śrīvatsa. (6)
