One should worship the belly of the God, who devours the world, as the divine form;
one should worship the waist as the thousand-footed, and the feet of the Lord.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods in the proper sequence, the wise one should worship every limb of Hari with the mantra: "Obeisance to Dāmodara."
Having thus worshipped according to the rite, one should place before him four jars filled with jewels and smeared with white sandalwood paste.
With their necks bound by garlands of flowers and draped in white garments,
they were placed upon copper vessels filled with sesame seeds and gold.
O best of kings, the four oceans should likewise be fashioned;
in their midst, according to the previously prescribed method, one should install Hari,
the Lord of Yogins, clad in yellow garments and practicing yogic sleep.
Having thus honored him as well, one should cause a vigil to be held there;
one should perform a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice and worship Hari, the Lord of Yogins.
Likewise, when a wheel with sixteen spokes has been fashioned by many kings,
having done this, one should cause it to be given to a Brāhmaṇa at dawn.
Four oceans should be given for four [images], and indeed one for the fifth;
however, being restrained and pure, one should cause the complete Yogīśvara to be given.
A gift given equally to one rich in the Vedas becomes twofold for one who knows them;
however, when given to a teacher of the Pañcarātras, it becomes a thousandfold.
But for one who provides this ritual procedure along with its secrets and mantras, what is given to him indeed becomes multiplied millions upon millions of times over.
If a teacher is available, the foolish person who would resort to and worship another attains a miserable state; moreover, what is given to him is fruitless.
One should first bestow [the gift] upon the teacher with diligence, and afterwards cause it to be given to another.
Whether ignorant or possessed of knowledge, the Guru alone is Janārdana;
whether established on the path or straying from the path, the Guru alone is the supreme goal.
But that lowest of men who, having approached a teacher, behaves toward him with hostility out of delusion, shall be cooked in hell for ten million births. || 19 ||
Having thus given according to the prescribed rite and having worshipped Viṣṇu on the twelfth day,
one should provide a meal for the Brahmins according to one's ability, accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
Indeed, having formerly performed this Dharaṇī-vrata,
Prajāpati likewise obtained progeny, liberation, and eternal Brahman.
In ancient times, the royal sage Yuvanāśva also obtained a son, Māndhātṛ, as well as the supreme, eternal Brahman, by means of this very rite.
And likewise, King Kṛtavīrya, the Haihaya lord of men,
obtained as his son Kārtavīrya and the supreme, eternal Brahman.
Śakuntalā also, having likewise performed penance, O great sage, obtained a son born of Śakuntalā, the son of Duṣyanta, who was a universal emperor (cakravartin). || 24 ||
Likewise, the ancient kings, the universal monarchs (cakravartins) mentioned in the Vedas, attained supreme sovereignty through this very procedure. || 25 ||
In ancient times, this vow was also performed by Dharaṇī when she had sunk into Pātāla;
therefore, it is known by her name as the supreme Dharaṇīvratam.
When this [earth] was completed, the goddess Dharā was lifted up by Hari, who had assumed the form of a boar and was now pleased; she remains even today, established like a ship upon the waters.
O Sage, this *Dharaṇī-vrata* has indeed been proclaimed to you by me.
That best of men who hears this with devotion and he who performs it shall be liberated from all sins and attain union with Viṣṇu (*sāyujya*). || 28 ||
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 50.
Śrī Varāha said:
Having heard the words of Durvāsas regarding the supreme vow of Dharaṇī,
Satyatapas immediately went to the excellent side of the Himavat mountain.
Where the river Puṣpabhadrā flows, where there is the Citraśilā rock, and where the Bhadravaṭa banyan tree stands—there his hermitage shone;
there, moreover, his great life-story will come to pass. || 2 ||
Dharaṇī said: "O Eternal One, throughout many thousands of kalpas, I have performed this vow and austerity; yet, O Lord, it has been forgotten by me. (3)
Now, O Supreme Lord, by your grace, my memory of the past has returned; I have become a rememberer of my former births and am free from sorrow. (4)
O Lord of Mountains, if indeed there is a great curiosity dwelling in your heart,
then tell me what Agastya did upon returning to the abode of Bhadrāśva, and what that king did as well.
Śrī Varāha said:
Having seen that the sage had returned, Bhadrāśva Śvetavāhana,
seeing him seated upon an excellent throne, performed a special act of worship.
O you who uphold everything, they asked the question known as the Dharma of Liberation.
Bhadrāśva said:
"O Blessed One, by what action is the cycle of worldly existence severed? Or, having done what, do they not grieve amidst the attainment of both the formed and the formless?"
Agastya said:
Listen, O King, with a concentrated mind, to this divine narrative concerning what is distant and what is near, arising from the distinction between the visible and the invisible. 8.
At that time, there was neither day nor night, neither the cardinal directions nor the intermediate directions,
neither heaven nor gods, neither day nor sun;
the king was known as Paśupati.
He protected many cattle.
While protecting them, he once, desiring to see the eastern ocean, went quickly to that great sea of infinite bounds.
On the bank is a forest where serpents dwell.
Eight wish-fulfilling trees, a river that carries all desires, and a fourth [object] moved upward there, as did others;
likewise, five principal persons and one [woman].
He bore a woman who was blazing with splendor. || 11 ||
That woman also, holding upon her own breast that broad [object] resembling a thousand suns,
beheld that king wandering about, his lower lip trembling threefold and displaying three colors.
They remained silent, as if they were dead; that king also entered that forest.
Once he had entered, all of them entered as well, and in an instant they became one in their fear.
Surrounded by those ill-behaved snakes as if by bandits, that king reflected:
"In what way will this come to pass?"
And how could these transmigrate and come into existence? || 14 ||
While the king was thus reflecting, a supreme man appeared, a man of three colors, wearing white, red, and likewise black—thus possessing three colors. (15)
He made a sign to me, saying, "Where else will you go?
As he was speaking thus, the great name [Mahādeva] arose for him.
He too covered the king and said, "Wake up!
When this was said, the woman then obstructed the king.
"Do not fear that which is woven of illusion; there is no other person [besides me], O King.
Then the Hero, the Lord of all lords, stood enveloping him.
Then five other men approached and sat down together around that best of kings; thereupon, the king became provoked.
When the king was besieged, all those bandits united;
taking up their weapons to plunder, they then hid from one another out of fear.
With them hidden away, the king’s palace shone with supreme splendor;
O King, even more than that, there came to be a full crore plus a fraction of other sinners as well.
In the house, there was earth, water, fire, and a pleasantly cool breeze; these five elements possessed nine qualities and were spacious and bright.
Only one of them remained, having been wrapped around and fastened for a very long time;
in this manner, O King, that cowherd quickly accomplished his task.

O King, seeing that agility and the form of the monarch in battle, a three-colored being spoke to that best of kings: tasya tallāghavaṃ dṛṣṭvā rūpaṃ ca nṛpater mṛdhe | trivarṇaḥ puruṣo rājann abravīd rājasattamam || 24 ||
"I am your son, O Great King; tell me, what shall I do for you?
Desiring to be your kinsman, we have reached this firm resolve. (25)
"O Lord, even though we have all been defeated, we remain thus, hidden within our bodies, O King. (26)
"When Maryyeka has attained the status of your son, there shall be a manifestation among all.
Having been addressed thus, the king then spoke again to that man: || 27 ||
"O best of beings, let him be my son who will act for others as well; I shall never be stained by human states or the pleasures of men. (28)
Having spoken thus to his son, the king then released him;
freed from them, he himself ceased [speaking] in their midst.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 51.
Agastya said: O King, that Trivarṇa, having been abandoned by the monarch and being independent, begot a son named Ahaṃnāman; that son begot Trivarṇaka. (1)
To him also was born a daughter whose nature was awakening;
she gave birth to a son named Manohva, who bestows spiritual knowledge.
His sons shall also be of all forms and enjoyers of the five pleasures;
their sons, respectively, shall have names beginning with the letter 'akṣa'.
These beings were formerly robbers, but having been brought under control by the king,
they all, as if bodiless, constructed a beautiful sanctuary.
His city has nine gates, a single pillar, and four crossroads;
it is filled with thousands of rivers and established for the performance of water-rites.
Then those nine entered that city together as one;
instantly, they became a personified king named Paśupāla.
Then, O great king, Paśupāla, residing in that city,
having uttered indicative words, remembered the Vedas in that city.
The king indeed performed all those eternal vows pertaining to the nature of the Self, as well as the observances and sacrifices prescribed therein.
Once, that king, being weary of promoting the ritualistic path (karmakāṇḍa),
remained in yogic sleep as the omniscient one and begot a son.
Having four faces, four arms, the four Vedas, and four paths—
from him onwards, animals and other beings remained under the sovereignty of the king.
In that ocean, in that forest, and likewise in grass and other such things, as well as in elephants and other such creatures, that king became equal [to all],
O high-minded one, having transcended the ritualistic portion of the Veda.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter in the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 52.
Bhadrāśva said:
O Brahmin, this story has been told by you regarding the subject of my question;
of whom did its manifestation arise, and by what deed was it brought about?
Agastya said:
This wondrous narrative has arrived, pertaining to the domain of all;
it is present in your body, in my body, and is common to all living beings.
He who desires birth from her seeks the supreme means for it himself—
he who, though born from a cowherd, is four-footed and four-faced.
He is the Guru, the narrator, and the one who sets that very discourse in motion;
his son is named Svara, and he is remembered as the seventh form.
O King, whatever means for the four [goals of life] was proclaimed by him,
they attained those through devotion to the four meanings of the Ṛg-veda verses.
Of these four, that which is the first is situated upon four peaks;
the second is the bull (vṛṣa); the third is said to be by that very path;
and the fourth is led by that [path]. Having worshipped it with devotion, one shall go to the world of the Son (Suta).
O King, they first heard the life-story of Saptamūrti;
his second [incarnation] was eternal and lived according to the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya).
Then, when the bull [the *sattva*] resides within the self, the maintenance of servants and so forth, the mounting of the bull, and dwelling in the forest are prescribed for the three [stages]. (8)
While another was saying "I am," she manifested as fourfold, onefold, and twofold;
from her, offspring born together with their distinctions were produced.
Having previously observed the eternal and non-eternal forms, the four-faced one thought: "O King, how shall I see my progenitor? (10)
Indeed, those virtues which belonged to my high-souled father are not now seen in any of his own offspring.
"The son of a father's son is one who bears the name of the grandfather; thus stands this Vedic tradition regarding one's own offspring, and not otherwise. (12)
"Somewhere my father must exist and must be seen by you.
Even though this was said, he became lost in thought, wondering, "What is to be done? (13)
As he was reflecting thus, his father’s weapon appeared before him;
with that weapon, he furiously churned Svara nearby.
As soon as it was churned, the four-faced one beheld its head, which was difficult to grasp and shaped like a coconut fruit.
And that [body], covered by ten layers of primordial matter (pradhāna), shone forth;
he cut it with his four-footed weapon like a sesame stalk.
When he had repeatedly cut it down at its very root, it did not appear to me to be truly destroyed;
saying "I am [still] here," that being likewise cut him down as well. (17)
When that was severed, he beheld another, shorter one upon her shoulder, who stood near her and spoke to them five as "I am Bhūtādi" (the source of beings). || 18 ||
Then, having likewise cut through even that, they beheld the fivefold emptiness;
making way for one another, they all spoke this in his presence: (19)
He too he severed with the weapon of non-attachment like a sesame stalk;
when that was cut, he saw another one even shorter by a tenth part.
Having cut that man with the weapon of his form, he beheld another;
likewise, he then made him short, white, and gentle.
When this was done, O best of kings, that lord again beheld his own body within the belly of Akāśa and his father there.
Seeing that [Self] within all living beings as equal, unmanifest, and subtle in form like a mote of dust, he experienced supreme joy and was freed from both pleasure and pain.
Such is this Person, named Svara, of great ascetic power;
his body is called Pravṛtti, and his great head is called Nivṛtti.
O best of kings, from this very narrative of his, O monarch, there arose a manifestation; indeed, this is the very same as the manifestation. (25)
This is the first history (itihāsa) concerning the entire world;
he who knows this in its true essence shall become directly intent upon his duties.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 53.
Bhadrāśva said:
"O twice-born one, who should be propitiated by one desiring the arising of higher knowledge? And how indeed is he propitiated? Tell me this, O twice-born one. (1)
Agastya said:
"Viṣṇu alone is the Lord to be constantly worshipped even by all the gods;
I shall declare the means for him by which he may become the granter of boons."
The secret of all the gods, the sages, and likewise of men is this:
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme deity; by bowing down to him, one does not suffer.
And it is heard, O King, that in ancient times the high-souled Nārada recounted this account,
which brings satisfaction, concerning Viṣṇu as well as the Apsarases.
In a former kalpa, Nārada went to Lake Mānasa for the purpose of bathing,
and there he beheld the entire host of apsarases.
Seeing him wearing a crown of matted hair, with nothing but bones and skin remaining, and carrying an umbrella, a staff, and a skull-bowl, those playful women—
Those excellent women questioned the son of Brahmā, who was endowed with ascetic power, as he desired to see the gods, asuras, and humans, and who was fond of quarreling.
The Apsarases said:
"O Blessed One, O son of Brahmā, O twice-born one, we desire a husband;
tell us how Nārāyaṇa may become our husband. (8)
Nārada said:
"A question preceded by a salutation is prescribed as auspicious in all circumstances;
yet that was not done by you out of pride and the arrogance of youth."
Nevertheless, because you have glorified the name of Viṣṇu, the God of gods,
and said, "May Hari thus become our husband," everything has been accomplished by the mere utterance of that name; of this there is no doubt.
Now I shall quickly describe the vow by which Hari himself attains the state of a granter of boons and bestows the status of a husband. || 11 ||
Nārada said: On that auspicious twelfth day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight in the spring, having fasted according to the prescribed rules, one should worship Hari during the night.
Having prepared a couch-covering adorned with various colorful designs,
one should place there an image of Hari made of silver, accompanied by Lakṣmī.
Then, above that, the wise man should have a pavilion constructed with flowers;
there he should arrange a vigil accompanied by dance, instrumental music, and song.
One should worship with "To Manobhava" the head, with "To Anaṅga" the hips,
with "To Kāma" the base of the arms, and with "To Suśāstra" the belly.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods with flowers—such as jasmine and *jāti*—on all sides, saying "To Manmatha" for the feet and "To Hari" for the rest; || 16 ||
Thereafter, O King, having taken four very beautiful stalks of sugarcane,
one should place them in the four directions of that deity while bowing down.
Having done this, at dawn one should indeed present it to a wise Brāhmaṇa who is proficient in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and possesses all his limbs in full.
Having likewise honored the Brahmins, one should complete this vow;
when it is performed in this manner, Viṣṇu will certainly become your husband.
"O beautiful ones, since you were asked yet did not pay me homage out of pride, this shall be the ripening of that insult for you. (20)
"In this very lake, the great sage Aṣṭāvakra will be present;
by mocking him, O beautiful ones, you shall receive a curse."
"By means of this vow, having obtained the Lord of Gods as your husband out of self-conceit, you shall suffer abduction by cowherds during a time of humiliation.
Furthermore, that God who was formerly the abductor of maidens shall become your husband. (22)
Agastya said:
Having spoken thus, the divine sage Nārada departed in an instant;
they too performed this vow, and Hari himself was pleased with them.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 54.
Agastya said:
Listen, O fortunate King, to the most excellent of vows, by which Viṣṇu is attained through auspiciousness alone; of this there is no doubt. (1)
Then, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should begin on the first day;
[observing] a single meal during the bright fortnight until the tenth lunar day.
Then, O King, having bathed at midday on the tenth day and having worshipped Viṣṇu,
one should perform the formal vow (saṃkalpa) with devotion as before for the twelfth day of the lunar fortnight.
Having stayed there for that same duration, one should cause barley to be given to a Brahmin;
at the time of giving, the oblation, and likewise during worship, Hari should be addressed as "Kṛṣṇa."
O best of kings, having thus observed the Cāturmāsya vow,
the wise and self-restrained man should again fast during the months beginning with Caitra and cause vessels of barley-meal, along with gold, to be given to the Brahmins.
In the same manner, one should cause śāli rice to be offered during the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa,
for as long as three months until the beginning of Kārttika arrives.
Having thus completed that [fast] as well, on the tenth day, the wise man, self-restrained and pure, should worship Hari with devotion, addressing Him by the name of the month.
O King, on the eleventh day, with his senses restrained, he should perform the ritual according to his ability and with devotion as previously described, using twelve [parts] of earth.
And one should place that [image], with its golden limbs and joined by the mountain ranges of the netherworld (pātāla),
before Hari according to the ritual procedure for the placement of the earth (bhūminyāsa).
Having worshipped it with the five jewels, the wise one should address it as "Priyadattā," [the image] being covered with a pair of white garments and provided with all the seeds.
One should keep a vigil there, and at dawn, O King, one should invite twice-born men in number up to twenty-four.
To each of them, one should cause to be given a cow and a bull,
as well as a pair of garments and a finger-ring.
O King, let the monarch cause each of these men to be granted a village, along with golden bracelets and earrings. 13.
One should cause all that to be given, including the middle one along with its pair; and likewise ornaments according to one's own capacity, even for a poor person according to his means.
Having fashioned a golden earth according to one's ability, as well as a pair of cows and a pair of garments, these should be given according to the extent of one's wealth and power. (15)
One should cause a cow to be made along with a pair of ornaments and all [other items] together with gold;
when this has been done, likewise on both the twelfth days of the dark and bright fortnights, || 16 ||
Having fashioned an image of the earth out of silver according to one's wealth and capacity, one should cause it to be given to the Brahmins, as well as a meal for them;
likewise, one should provide sandals, wooden shoes, and an umbrella according to one's ability. (17)
Having given these, one should speak thus: "May Kṛṣṇa Dāmodara, the god Hari who is the universal form, be forever pleased with me. (18)
The fruit that is obtained by performing both giving and feeding cannot be fully described even in a thousand years. (19)
Nevertheless, O sinless one, I shall describe to you briefly some of the fruits of this vow; hear now its auspicious ancient history.
In the first age, there was a king who was a proponent of Brahman and firm in his vows.
Desiring a son, he questioned Brahmā, the Supreme Lord;
Brahmā explained this vow to him, and he performed it accordingly.
At the conclusion of his vow, the Soul of the Universe himself became manifest before him;
pleased, he said: "O King, choose a boon, choose a boon from me."
The king said:
"O Lord of Gods, grant me a son who is proficient in the Vedic mantras,
a performer of sacrifices devoted to the act of sacrifice, endowed with fame, and long-lived."
Indeed, it possesses incalculable qualities; it is become Brahman and is stainless.
Having spoken thus, the king then spoke these words again:
"O Supreme Lord, grant me also at the end [of my life] an auspicious station, that place known as Munipada, reaching which one does not grieve. (24)
Having said to him, "So be it," the god vanished from sight;
and that king also had a son by name Vatsaprī.
Endowed with the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, a performer of sacrifices, and highly learned—his fame, O Great King, spread across the surface of the earth. (26)
Having obtained that powerful son Viṣṇudatta, the king also departed, intent on asceticism, having abandoned all pairs of opposites.
Then, O King, fasting and having conquered his senses, the monarch propitiated Hari on the beautiful Himavat mountain while offering hymns of praise.
Bhadrāśva said: O Brahmin, what kind of hymn of praise did that king offer? And what happened to him as he was praising Puruṣottama, the Divine One? (29)
Durvāsas said:
Taking refuge on the Himavat mountains, the king, with his mind fixed upon Him, offered praise to the god Viṣṇu, the all-powerful Lord. (30)
The king said:
[I bow to] the Perishable and the Imperishable, who reclines upon the ocean of milk,
who is the upholder of the earth, and the supreme state of all embodied beings.
I praise the Lord Janārdana, who is beyond the reach of the senses, who was placed before the Viśvabhujs and then cast aside.
You are the primordial god, whose nature is the ultimate reality, the all-pervading, ancient, and supreme person;
you are beyond the senses and the foremost among those who know the Vedas.
Protect me, O you who hold the conch, mace, and weapon in your hands! || 32 ||
O Lord of infinite form, this which has been performed by you for the sake of creation is celebrated among the gods and asuras,
O Lord Viṣṇu.
That would not be the conduct of one who has fallen into a trap. || 33 ||
In that very same way, O you of manifold forms, the state of being a tortoise and the state of being a deer were assumed by you;
yet, O Acyuta, because of your omniscience, your repeated births are proclaimed, though none of this truly exists.
O Nṛsiṃha, salutations! O Vāmana, O Jamadagni, O destroyer of the ten-faced one and his lineage, O Vāsudeva!
Salutations be to you, O Buddha, O Kalkin, O Lord of Birds!
O Śambhu, salutations to you, O destroyer of the enemies of the wise.
Homage be to Nārāyaṇa, O Padmanābha;
homage, homage to you, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)!
Homage to you, who are worshipped by the entire assembly of immortals!
Homage be to you, O foremost among all who possess complete knowledge!
Homage to you in the form of Nṛsiṃha with a terrifying face; homage to you, O Tortoise, equal to a vast mountain;
homage to you, O Fish, resembling the ocean.
I bow to you, O Ananta, who have assumed the form of a boar.
O Lord, this activity of yours was for the purpose of creation;
O All-pervading One, your true form does not reside in the primary [manifest] aspect. This meditation was revealed by me through ignorance.
Without these, you are not perceived, O Ancient One.

O Viṣṇu, you alone are the primordial sacrifice; you yourself are the constituent parts of the sacrifice, and you alone are the oblation. You are the sacrificial animal, the officiating priest, and the act of worship itself.
The hosts of gods and the sages worship you. || 39 ||
O Janārdana, O Lord, you are not divided within this world— whether stable or moving, from the gods down to the fire of time— which is supreme.
Grant me the perfection desired by my heart.
Salutations to you, O lotus-petal-eyed one; salutations to you, O Hare, both manifest and unmanifest!
I have come to you for refuge; deliver me from this cycle of worldly existence.
Thus praised at that time by that high-souled king standing beneath the vast mango tree, the Supreme Lord was gratified.
Then Hari himself, having assumed the form of a hunchback, arrived;
as soon as he had arrived, Sīpyāmra became a hunchback.
Seeing that great marvel, the king, who was firm in his vows,
became lost in thought, wondering how Viśāla could have become hunchbacked.
As he was reflecting, an idea occurred to him regarding that Brahmin:
"By his mere arrival, this has been accomplished; of this there is no doubt. (45)
"Therefore, he alone shall become the Blessed One, the Supreme Person.
Having spoken thus, the king paid homage to that brahmin.
O Blessed One, you are surely the Supreme Person come for our grace; O Hari, reveal your true form to me now!
Thus addressed, the Lord, who bears the conch, discus, and mace,
then appeared before him in a serene form and spoke these words.
Choose a boon, O Indra among kings, whatever dwells in your heart;
for when I am pleased, O monarch, these three worlds are but as a single sesame seed to me.
Thus addressed, the king, his eyes wide with joy, said,
"O Lord of Gods, grant me liberation," and said nothing more.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One spoke these words again:
"Since this broad mango tree has become crooked upon my arrival,
therefore this sacred site shall be known as Kubjakāmra."
Even those beginning with the animal realm and ending with Brahmins, if they cast off their own bodies here, five hundred celestial chariots shall belong to them,
and there shall be liberation for those yogins.
Having spoken thus to the king, Janārdana, the Lord, touched him with the tip of his conch;
as soon as he was touched, he attained supreme liberation.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should go for refuge to that God, by whom you shall not again fall into the path of sorrow. 54.
The man who, having risen early each morning, constantly hears this or recites the life-story of those two, shall become a bestower of liberation, dharma, and wealth. (55)
O Lord of Men, whoever shall perform this meritorious and auspicious vow, having enjoyed all prosperity here in this world, shall attain absorption into that [Brahman]. || 56 ||
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter in the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 55.
Agastya said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the unsurpassed Dhanya-vrata,
by which even one who is unfortunate becomes fortunate immediately.
On the first lunar day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one should observe the nocturnal fast (nakta) and worship Viṣṇu and Agni.
He should worship the feet with "To Vaiśvānara," the belly with "To Agni," the chest with "To Havis-bhuj," and the two arms with "To Draviṇoda."
Having thus worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, according to the prescribed ritual with the mantras "saṃvarttāya" for the head and "jvalanāya" for all [the limbs].
Having caused a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to be made right in front of him according to the prescribed rules, the wise one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) there with these mantras.
Then he should eat food mixed with barley meal combined with ghee,
and likewise during the dark fortnight, for as long as the Cāturmāsya period lasts.

During the months beginning with Caitra, the wise man should eat milk-rice (pāyasa) with ghee; during those beginning with Śrāvaṇa, he should eat barley meal (saktu). Then this [observance] is completed.
When the vow is completed, the wise man should have a golden image of Fire fashioned,
covered with a pair of red garments and adorned with red flowers and unguents.
Having likewise anointed the Brāhmaṇa and the God of gods with saffron—
[the Brāhmaṇa] who was complete in all his limbs and pleasing to behold— || 9 ||
Having worshipped according to the prescribed ritual with a pair of red garments, the wise man should subsequently cause that [gift] to be given to him with this mantra: ||| 10 ||
I am blessed; I am one whose actions are blessed; I am one whose efforts are blessed; I am possessed of blessings.
By means of this blessed vow performed, may I always be happy.
Having thus uttered this to that brahmin and having placed the treasure of the Great-Souled One [therein],
even one who is devoid of fortune immediately attains blessedness.
In this very life, good fortune, wealth, and abundant grain arise from the mere performance of this; of this there is no doubt. (13)
The fire indeed burns away the sin produced in his previous birth;
once that sin is burnt, he becomes one whose self is liberated in this very life.
The twice-born who constantly hears this, and he who recites it with devotion—both of them shall immediately become blessed in this world. (15)
And it is heard that this vow was formerly observed by the high-souled Dhanada,
while he was situated in a Śūdra womb during a previous kalpa.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter in the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 56.
Agastya said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the unsurpassed Kānti-vrata (vow of beauty), by performing which Soma in former times once again became possessed of splendor. || 1 ||
In ancient times, the Moon was seized by consumption due to the curse of Dakṣa;
it is said that by immediately performing this vow, he indeed became radiant once more.
But on the second day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, O Indra among kings, one should diligently observe the night-vow (nakta), worshipping Balarāma and Keśava.
One should worship the feet for Baladeva and the head for Keśava;
having thus worshipped this supreme form of Viṣṇu, the wise man [attains his goal].
On that day, the wise practitioner should cause the offering (argha) to be given with the mantra of Parameṣṭhin to that which is the nature of the other, known as Soma, consisting of two kalās.
Salutations be to the one whose form is nectar, the king of all medicinal herbs,
the sovereign of the world of sacrifice, Soma, the Supreme Self.
Having offered the arghya water to the Supreme Lord by this very path,
the man, together with a Brahmin, should eat barley-food with ghee at night.
During the four months beginning with Phālguna, one who is pure should feed [the deity] with milk-rice (pāyasa);
however, in Kārttika, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with śāli rice, and likewise with barley.
During the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, one should perform a fire-oblation of sesame seeds;
likewise, one should eat food mixed with sesame seeds—this is the prescribed sequence of ritual.
Then, when a full year has passed, one should worship a silver image of the Moon,
covered with a pair of white garments, adorned with white flowers and white unguents;
having likewise honored a Brahmin, one should then bestow it upon him.
O Nārāyaṇa, who possesses the form of the moon, salutations be unto you! By your grace, may I be radiant, all-knowing, and pleasing to behold in this world. 11.
It is said that by giving [this] with this mantra while remaining silent to a Brahmin,
as soon as it has been given, the man becomes radiant.
O King, this was also performed in ancient times by Soma, the son of Atri;
at the conclusion of his vow, Janārdana himself, being well-pleased,
quickly removed his consumption and granted him the digit known as Amṛta.
"That king Soma obtained that digit through austerity;
he attained the state of being Soma and shone as the lord of herbs. (14)
On that day, O King, the two Aśvins who partake of the Soma are celebrated;
they are renowned as Śeṣa and Viṣṇu, the primary pair, without a doubt. (15)
O best of kings, there is no deity whatsoever distinct from Viṣṇu;
the Supreme Lord is established everywhere under various names. (16)
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 57.
Agastya said:
After this, O great king, listen to the vow that brings about good fortune, by which auspiciousness quickly arises for both women and men. (1)
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
one who is pure and truthful should observe the vow of eating only at night.
Having worshipped Hari together with Śrī, or Rudra together with Umā—one should know that she who is Śrī is declared to be Girijā, and he who is Hari is the Three-eyed One (Trilocana). || 3 ||
Thus it is recited in all the Śāstras and Purāṇas;
whoever speaks otherwise than this, treating the Śāstra as something separate, [is mistaken].
O King, that which describes Rudra as the author of the scriptures for mortals,
or claims that Viṣṇu was created by Rudra, or that Śrī is Gaurī—
that should be known by the wise as the poetry of atheistic mortals.
O King of kings, having understood this and having worshipped Hari along with Lakṣmī with devotion, one should then worship that Supreme Lord with this mantra: || 6 ||
One should worship the feet with "O Gambhīra," the hips with "O Subhaga," the belly with "O Devadeva," the face with "O Trinetrā," the head with "O Vācaspati," and everywhere with "O Rudra."
Having thus worshipped Viṣṇu together with Lakṣmī, or Hara together with Gaurī, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order, the wise man [should proceed].

Then, O great king, one should have a fire-oblation performed before her with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, while reciting the mantra "Obeisance to the Lord of Good Fortune" (saubhāgyapataye).

Then, on the surface of the earth, one should eat wheat-food that is saltless, tasteless, and devoid of fat; this rule is prescribed even for the dark fortnight. On the second lunar day of the month beginning with Āṣāḍha, the breaking of the fast consists of eating there.
O King, after that, during the months beginning with Kārttika, he should eat barley; for three months, being self-controlled and pure, he should consume śyāmāka grain.
Then, O lord of men, on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha,
a wise man should have an image of Gaurī and Rudra fashioned together out of gold.
With a serene mind, one should also [worship] Hari along with Lakṣmī according to one's ability;
thereafter, one should give that [image] to a wise Brāhmaṇa who is a worthy recipient.

One should especially give to one who is destitute of food, even if he has mastered the Vedas, follows the path of the virtuous, or practices good conduct, particularly if his wealth is meager. || 14 ||
One should present [this gift], consisting of six vessels, to a Brāhmaṇa;
one vessel is filled with honey, and the second is filled with ghee.
The third is filled with sesame oil, the fourth is combined with jaggery,
the fifth is full of salts, and the sixth is combined with cow’s milk.
Having given these vessels, for seven future births, whether a woman or even a man, one shall be fortunate and handsome to behold. (17)
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 58.
Agastya said:
Now, O King, I shall tell you that which causes no obstacle; listen to me, by the proper performance of which no obstacle arises.

On the fourth lunar day of the month of Phālguna, this vow should indeed be undertaken. O King of Kings, one should eat only at night; the breaking of the fast is prescribed as an offering of sesame seeds and rice.
That very same offering should be cast into the fire, and it should likewise be given to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having indeed observed this vow for four months and likewise for five days,
one should have a golden elephant-faced [image] made and cause it to be given to a Brahmin.
Provided with five vessels of milk-rice as well as sesame seeds—
by performing this vow in such a manner, one is liberated from all obstacles.
In ancient times, when an obstacle arose for the horse-sacrifice,
Sagara completed that very sacrifice by performing this same rite.
In the past, when the god Rudra was destroying Tripura, he performed this very same act; therefore, Tripura was felled by him. When I drank up the ocean, I likewise performed this very same vow.
O scorcher of foes, other rulers of the earth as well performed this very same rite in former times— those seekers of austerity who had attained wisdom— in order to ensure freedom from obstacles.
On that day, he should likewise worship the one who is heroic, wise, elephant-faced, pot-bellied, and possessed of a single tusk. Furthermore, on that day:
One should perform the fire-oblation for the purpose of destroying obstacles. || 8 ||
By merely performing this, one is liberated from all obstacles;
through the grace of Vināyaka, a person becomes one who has accomplished his purpose.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 59.
Agastya said:
O King, listen to this vow of peace that I shall proclaim to you; by its performance, there shall always be peace for householders. (1)
O observer of noble vows, one should begin this for one year on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika, and should eat food free from sour substances.
Having worshipped the Lord Hari at night as he rests upon Śeṣa,
one should worship his feet with "To Ananta" and his waist with "To Vāsuki."
Having worshipped the belly for Takṣaka and the chest for Karkoṭaka,
one should worship the throat for Padma and the pair of arms for Mahāpadma.
One should worship the face for Śaṅkhapāla and the head for Kuṭilā;
having thus worshipped those belonging to Viṣṇu, one should worship them individually.
One should again perform a ceremonial bath with milk for those [ancestors] dedicated to Hari;
then, in their presence, the wise person should offer oblations of milk along with sesame seeds.
Thus, at the end of the year, one should provide a feast for Brahmins;
one should fashion a golden Naga and present it to a Brahmin.
O lord of men, for that king who thus performs this vow with devotion,
there shall be constant peace, and likewise no fear from the nāgas.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 60.
Agastya said:
O great king, listen now as I describe the Kāmavrata,
by which even those desires conceived in the mind are fully realized.
He who observes this vow for one year, eating only fruit on the sixth lunar day, and having taken his meal on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa; || 2 ||
On the sixth day, however, the wise one should perform the ritual completion (*pārayet*); O King, this is the first fruit.
Thereafter, he should eat pure boiled rice with effort, remaining restrained in speech. (3)
O Indra among kings, having remained for that single day on the seventh lunar day either with Brahmins or with fruits alone, O King, one should break the fast.
One should perform the fire-ritual while meditating on Keśava in the form of Guha;
having worshipped him by his name, one should observe this vow for one year.
Viṣṇu is to be worshipped by his own names as Ṣaḍvaktra, Kārttikeya, Guha, Senānī, Kṛttikāsuta, Kumāra, and Skanda. (6)
Upon the completion of this vow, one should provide a feast for Brahmins;
one should present a six-faced image made entirely of gold to a Brahmin.
"O divine youth, may all my desires be fulfilled;
by your grace, O Brahmin, please accept this with devotion without delay. (8)
By giving this pair to a Brāhmaṇa while reciting this mantra,
all desires indeed flourish in this very life.
One without a son obtains a son; one without wealth obtains wealth;
one who has lost his kingdom regains his kingdom—there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
O best of kings, this vow was formerly observed by Nala while he was living in the territory of Ṛtuparṇa, engaged in the practice of that ascetic observance.
Likewise, O best of kings, many other excellent monarchs who had been deprived of their kingdoms performed this ancient vow for the sake of attaining success.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 61.
Agastya said: Now, O great king, I shall describe another vow known as Ārogya,
which is supremely meritorious and the destroyer of all sins.
On the seventh day of that very month of Māgha, having fasted,
one should worship the god Bhāskara, the eternal form of Viṣṇu.
"O Āditya, Bhāskara, Ravi, Bhānu, Sūrya, Divākara, Prabhākara!"—having thus worshipped, the Sun is indeed fully honored. (3)
Having taken food on the sixth day, one should worship the Sun on the seventh;
and on the eighth day one should eat—this indeed is the sequence of the ritual procedure.
Whoever worships the Sun according to this rite for a full year shall obtain health, wealth, and grain in this life;
and in the hereafter, an auspicious state from which there is no return. || 5 ||
In former times, there was a sovereign king of great strength named Anaraṇya;
by him this deity was worshipped with this very vow, O King,
and being pleased with him, the god granted him the supreme boon of perfect health.
Bhadrāśva said:
Who was this sick king by whom health was attained? And how, O Brahmin, did the disease of the sovereign arise? (7)
Agastya said:
That king became a sovereign ruler of the whole earth, illustrious and handsome. Once, O best of kings, that most excellent of monarchs was possessed of great strength. (8)
He went to the divine Lake Mānasa, which was frequented by hosts of gods;
there he saw a vast white lotus situated in the middle of the lake.
And there he saw that most excellent person, the size of a thumb, clothed in red garments, two-armed, and of fierce splendor. (10)
Seeing it, he said to the charioteer: "Bring this lotus!
Bearing this upon my head in the presence of all the world, I shall become worthy of praise; therefore, fetch it without delay. (11)
Having been addressed thus by him,
O best of kings, the charioteer then entered and proceeded to take that lotus.
Then, as soon as it was touched, the syllable *huṃ* arose from the lotus;
by that sound, he was terrified, fell down, and died.
And at that very moment, by that sound, the king became afflicted with leprosy, his complexion vanished, and he was deprived of strength and vigor. || 14 ||
Then, having seen the Tathāgata and himself, that bull among men stood right there, afflicted with grief, wondering, "What is this? (15)
While he was thus reflecting, the wise Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā and a performer of great austerities, arrived; then he questioned that king.
O tiger among kings, how is the instruction for your body?
What must be done right now? Tell me, as I ask you. (17)
Having been addressed thus by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha,
the lordly king then related the entire account of Padma.
Having heard that, O King, the sage there then said: "Whether it was virtuous or unvirtuous, remain [in that state]; therefore, you have come to possess leprosy. (19)
Thus addressed, the king, trembling and with palms joined in reverence, then asked:
"O Brahmin, was I virtuous or was I wicked? O Sage, how did this leprosy come upon me? You ought to tell me this. (20)
Vasiṣṭha said:
This lotus, named Brahmodbhava, is renowned throughout the three worlds;
by merely beholding it, all the deities would be seen.
O King, this is seen somewhere during these six months.
But the man who enters the water as soon as this [tīrtha] is merely seen becomes liberated from all sins and is worthy of supreme nirvāṇa. || 22 ||
In the primordial state of Brahmā, his form was established within the waters;
by beholding this [form], one submerged in the water is liberated from saṃsāra. || 23 ||
O best of men, having seen this [sage] submerged in the water,
that charioteer entered again, O lord of men, desiring to seize him;
you, O evil-minded and sinful man, have therefore incurred leprosy.
"O Lord, because you saw this and then said 'Well done,' I was told by you that it was good;
yet, having fallen into delusion, I have been told that it was not good. (25)
For I am indeed the son of Brahmā, and I behold this Supreme Lord;
coming here day after day, you have seen him once again.
Even the gods say that this is the supreme golden lotus;
having seen the lotus of Brahmā in the Mānasa lake and Hari who has gone there,
we shall attain that Supreme Brahman, reaching which there is no rebirth.
And hear this other cause of leprosy, O King:
the Sun himself is stationed within this lotus-heart.
Having seen him as he truly is, this eternal Supreme Self is the reality;
I bear him upon my head as an ornament in the midst of the world.
While you were thus prattling, this evil was revealed by the god;
now, O high-minded one, propitiate him alone. (30)
Agastya said: Having spoken thus, Vasiṣṭha then proclaimed this very divine vow, known as Ārogya, which is the propitiation of the Sun.
That king also, filled with devotion, performed this vow;
he attained supreme perfection and became free from disease in an instant.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 62.
Agastya said:
Now, O great king, I shall describe another auspicious vow for obtaining a son; listen as I speak of it in brief.
O Lord of Men, that which occurs on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, performed with fasting, is indeed the vow for the attainment of a son.
Having made the formal resolve on the sixth day, one should worship Hari on the seventh day—
the Lord seated upon Devakī’s lap and surrounded by his mothers.
On the pure eighth day at dawn, one who is self-restrained should worship Hari;
having worshipped Govinda according to the prescribed rule and the previous ritual procedure.
Then one should perform a fire-oblation with barley, black sesame seeds, and curd mixed with ghee;
and one should devoutly feed the Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability, providing them with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then, one should first eat an excellent *bilva* fruit oneself;
afterwards, one may eat as desired, accompanied by fats and all kinds of savory juices.
By fasting every month according to this very procedure on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, even a man without sons shall obtain a son; of this there is no doubt.
It is heard that in ancient times there was a powerful king named Śūrasena;
being childless, he performed austerities on the excellent Himavat mountain.
As he was performing this, the god spoke to him regarding this vow;
the king also performed it and obtained a son.
Having obtained that highly fortunate Vasudeva, who had performed numerous sacrifices,
that royal sage also attained supreme liberation.
Thus, O King, the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī has been described to you by me;
at the end of the year, a pair of black cows should be given to a twice-born man.
This is what is called the "Vow for a Son," which I have proclaimed to you;
by performing this, a man is liberated from all sins whatsoever. (12)
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 63.
Agastya said:
Now I shall proclaim another unsurpassed vow of valor,
by which even a coward instantly attains great heroism.
In the month of Āśvayuja, one should fast on the pure ninth day;
having made the formal resolve on the seventh, one should remain without solid food on the eighth.
On the ninth day, O King, one should first devoutly partake of flour-based food;
one should feed the Brahmins with devotion and worship the Goddess—Durgā, the highly fortunate, the Great Māyā, and the one of great splendor. (3)
Having thus observed the fast according to the prescribed rule for as long as a year,
at the conclusion of the vow, the wise man should feed young maidens according to his ability.
Having adorned them with gold, garments, and other ornaments according to one's ability, one should afterwards ask for their forgiveness, saying: "May the Goddess be pleased with me."
When this is done, one whose kingdom has been lost shall regain his kingdom, without a doubt;
the unlearned shall obtain knowledge, and the fearful shall find valor.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 64.
Agastya said:
I shall now describe in brief another vow, the Sārvabhauma-vrata,
by the proper performance of which one quickly becomes a sovereign emperor.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
one who regularly eats only at night should always offer a pure oblation in the various directions.
Having worshiped the best of the twice-born with devotion using various flowers, the one of firm vows should offer a prayer to the quarters with this mantra:
"May you all grant success to me in birth after birth. (3)
Having spoken thus and having offered the bali-oblation to them with a pure mind,
he should then eat well-prepared curd-rice at night.
Whether performed first, last, or as desired, O King, for that man who practices this constantly for a year, victory over the quarters shall come to pass.
A wise man, beginning from the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, should diligently observe this vow according to the prescribed rules for one year on the eleventh lunar day;
this vow, beloved by the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), when performed, bestows riches.
He who remains without food on the eleventh day and eats on the twelfth day—
whether in the bright or the dark fortnight— that is indeed the great Vaiṣṇava vow.
O King, by performing such extremely formidable [observances], one destroys sins;
now, the Dharma-vrata is described as being observed by eating only at night on the thirteenth lunar day.
O King, beginning thus from the bright fortnight of Phālguna,
the wise man should especially undertake the Raudra vow on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
starting from the month of Māgha for a full year.
O King, it is thus declared that the vow of Indu consists of eating only at night on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight,
while the vow of the Pitṛs is observed on the new moon day.
O King, for one who performs the lunar-day vows (tithivrata) in this manner for fifteen years, what indeed could be said of the fruit according to the measure of those vows? || 11 ||
O Indra among kings, he has performed thousands of horse-sacrifices, hundreds of Rājasūyas,
as well as the rituals prescribed for the Kalpas.
A single vow, when performed, constantly destroys all sins;
moreover, O son of the best of men, he who performs all of this indeed becomes pure and free from passion, and attains all the worlds, O King.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 65.
Bhadrāśva said:
O knower of dharma, if you have known or indeed seen anything wonderful, tell that to me; my curiosity is great.
Agastya said:
This very Lord Janārdana is a source of wonder;
indeed, many various wonders of his have been witnessed.
O King, it is said that Nārada previously went to Śvetadvīpa;
there he beheld men of fierce splendor bearing conchs, discs, and lotuses.
"This is Viṣṇu, this is Viṣṇu, this eternal one is Viṣṇu"—upon seeing them, the thought occurred to him: "Which among these is the Lord Viṣṇu? (4)
As he was thinking thus, O Lord, his thought turned toward Kṛṣṇa:
"How may I propitiate the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace? (5)
"By whom I know that the supreme Lord among them is the divine Nārāyaṇa";
having reflected thus, he meditated upon that god, the Supreme Lord.
Then, for more than a thousand divine years, as that son of Brahmā meditated,
the Lord attained complete satisfaction.
And the Lord, having become manifest before him with a gracious soul, said:
"O son of Brahmā, O great sage, choose a boon; what shall I give to you?"
Nārada said:
O Lord of the World, you have been meditated upon by me for a thousand years;
if you are pleased with me, O Acyuta, tell me how that attainment of you may be achieved.
The God of gods said: "O Nārada, those twice-born ones who worship me by resorting to the Puruṣasūkta and by resorting to the primordial Saṃhitā, they shall attain me."
Even in the absence of the Vedic scriptures, those men who perceive me through the path proclaimed in the Pañcarātra will attain me.
A five-night [observance] is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
it shall not even reach the range of the ears of Śūdras and others.
Thus, O chief of Brahmins, have I related this ancient account from a former kalpa;
if anyone should take up the Pañcarātra consisting of thousands [of verses], [it shall be for his benefit].
And when my karma is exhausted, if anyone shall become devoted to me,
this Pañcarātra will dwell eternally in his heart.
O best of the twice-born, others will be completely enveloped by rajasic and tamasic dispositions, turning their backs on my command.

O Nārada, the three ages—Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara—shall come to me while I abide in goodness (sattva); but in the Kali age, those in whom passion and darkness (rajas and tamas) predominate shall approach me.
Moreover, I grant you another boon; listen now, O Nārada:
this scripture of mine known as the Pañcarātra, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain, you shall know in its entirety through my grace—of this there is no doubt. (17)
O twice-born one, I am to be attained through Veda, through the Pañcarātra, through devotion, and through sacrifice; not otherwise, my child, even in ten million times ten thousand years. (18)
Having spoken thus to Nārada, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, immediately vanished from sight; and Nārada also departed for heaven.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 66.
Bhadrāśva said: O Blessed One, in this world there are two distinct types of people, white and black, O Keśava;
who were the two women who became [the progenitors of] these two, and which of the two, the white or the black, is auspicious?
And who is that person, O Brahmin, who is one yet becomes sevenfold?
Who is he, O sage, who is twelvefold, auspicious, possessing two bodies and six heads? (2)
And why, O best of the twice-born, is this world so vast, O most excellent of brahmins, when the rising of the sun has been brought about by a husband and wife? (3)
Agastya said:
Those two women, the white and the black, are proclaimed to be sisters;
they are truth and untruth, the woman of two colors, declared to be Night.
O lord of men, that person who, having been born sevenfold, becomes one,
should be known as the ocean— existing as one yet established in a sevenfold manner.
O King, that Lord who exists in twelve ways as the double-bodied one with six heads should be known as the Year; two bodies are recorded as his two courses,
and the six seasons are his faces— this is remembered as the Year.
From that couple arose day and night, and from them, O best of kings, the sun and moon; thereafter, the world emerged from this God.
O best of kings, that Viṣṇu is to be known as the supreme deity;
for one who is devoid of Vedic rites does not behold the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter in the Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 67.
Bhadrāśva said:
O Sage, as for that supreme and inferior Lord Viṣṇu who is omnipresent—
how is that Supreme Lord to be understood in each of the four ages?
O Sage, what will be the conduct of the social classes in each successive age?
And how, O Sage, can the purity of Brahmins be maintained when they are mixed with the wives of others?
Agastya said:
"O best of men, in the Kṛta age the earth was enjoyed by the gods through Vedic rites;
likewise, O most excellent one, it was enjoyed by the Asuras and the gods during the Tretā age."
In the Dvāpara age, O best of kings, the qualities of sattva and rajas will predominate,
O high-minded one, as long as Dharmasuta shall remain king.
Then, O lord of men, darkness will prevail in the form of Kali; while that Kali age is current, the twice-born shall fall away from his own path.
O best of kings, kings, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of low birth will for the most part be devoid of truth and purity.
There, the twice-born will engage in sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached;
excluded from the path of the Vedas, they will speak untruths;
and they will perform marriages with women of the same lineage (sagotra) as well as those of unequal status.
For kings, being deceitful and possessed by greed for wealth, will harm the brahmins; even those of the lowest castes, devoted to trade, will assume the status of vaiśyas;
and those who are arrogant will become proud among the śūdra classes.
The Brahmins will become eaters of all things and devoid of purity;
bereft of truth and purity, they will declare that wine is a drinkable substance.
Then the world perishes, and the dharma of the social classes is destroyed. || 10 ||
Bhadrāśva said:

"Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or even a Śūdra, by what means is one purified after committing an act of approaching those who should not be approached? Or, tell me, who indeed is an 'agamya' (one forbidden to approach)?"
Agastya said: A Brāhmaṇa may have four wives; a Kṣatriya may have three wives; a Vaiśya may have two wives; and a Śūdra is traditionally held to have only one. || 12 ||
O lord of men, they say that a Brāhmaṇa woman is unapproachable for a Kṣatriya;
likewise, a Kṣatriya woman for a Vaiśya, and a Vaiśya woman for a Śūdra, O King.
Manu declared that a woman of higher caste is unapproachable for one of lower caste. (13)
O King, a mother, a maternal aunt, a mother-in-law, a brother’s wife, a daughter-in-law, a daughter, a friend’s wife, and one born of one's own lineage; || 14 ||
The king’s wife, his daughter, and other women who are foremost among those forbidden;

as well as other women such as washerwomen and the like—are proclaimed to be women not to be approached. Engaging in sexual intercourse with those who are forbidden to be approached results in sin. (15)
For approaching a womb other than one's own, it is sufficient for a Brāhmaṇa;
this alone is the purification for the remaining cases, which shall consist of a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). || 16 ||
For even over a long period of time, O bull among men, whatever sin has been accumulated by a Brāhmaṇa through association with those of mixed castes, [that too is destroyed]. (17)

By reciting the Gāyatrī ten times with the Praṇava while performing three hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one is liberated even from the sin of killing a Brahmin; how much more so from other remaining sins?
Alternatively, that bull among Brahmins who knows the supreme form is not tainted even by the commission of hundreds of sins, provided he is a student of the Vedas.
Remembering Viṣṇu, reciting the Veda, giving gifts, and worshipping Hari, a Brāhmaṇa remains truly pure; he can even deliver those who act contrary to his duty.
All this that I was asked by you, O King, has been related to you;
that which is told at length by Manu and others, O Ruler of the Earth, has been recounted by me to you in brief, O best of kings. (21)
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 68.
Bhadrāśva said:
O Blessed One, O best of the twice-born, you have lived for a long time; it behooves you, O most excellent one, to tell me what occurred within your body.
Agastya said:
"O King, this body of mine is filled with many wonders;
it shall endure for many kalpas and is purified by the knowledge of the Vedas."
O King, while wandering over the entire earth, I arrived at Ilāvṛta,
the great varṣa situated on the side of Mount Meru.
There I saw a beautiful lake, and on its bank a large hut. There I beheld an ascetic, weakened by fasting, whose body was reduced to mere skin and bone, and who wore garments of rags and bark.
Having seen him, O best of kings, I thought: "Who is this, O most excellent of monarchs?
O supreme among men, I must devise a means to win his confidence. (5)
As I was reflecting thus, that Great Sage said to me:
"Stay, stay, O Brahmin; let me offer you hospitality."
Having heard these words of his, I entered that hut;
there I beheld a brahmin who was as if blazing with splendor.
Seeing me standing upon the ground, the twice-born uttered the sound "hum.
From that "hum" sound, five maidens indeed burst forth, having pierced through the netherworld (pātāla).
One among them indeed took up a golden seat and set it forth;
another then offered me water held in her hand.
Another, having taken hold of my feet, began to wash them;
two others, taking up fans, stood on either side of me.
Then the one of great asceticism again uttered the sound "huṃ.
From that sound, O King, he took up a golden trough a yojana in width from within the interval and arrived; he made a leap into the lake.
Then, O King, seeing him, hundreds of auspicious maidens with golden jars in their hands approached; at that moment, the sage said to me: || 12 ||
"O Brahmin, all of this has indeed been prepared for your bath;
O best of beings, you ought to enter this wooden trough and bathe."
Then, O lord of men, at his word I entered that trough;
as soon as I did so, the trough sank into the lake.
O lord of men, thinking "I am submerged in water in a trough," I then emerged and beheld a world that was unprecedented.
It was a vast abode with pleasant courtyards and wide carriage-roads crowded with pure people,
frequented by ancient men who were knowers of the Self and established in the path of policy through the highest ethics.
Fierce with the iron bars of the course of saṃsāra,
standing at the bottom of the profound underworld, and primordial,
it is guarded by white men holding nooses and hooks in their hands.
It was endowed with various herds of elephants and horses. || 17 ||
The lakes were covered with various lotuses and water-lilies and teeming with diverse birds;
they seemed to sing aloud with the humming of bees resting upon the lotus petals, in many rhythmic melodies.
On their banks, there were peaks resembling Mount Kailāsa, strewn with many jewels and blue water-lilies.
These houses were inhabited by the virtuous and honored by the twice-born, the gods, and the learned brahmins.
On its banks are houses resembling the peaks of Kailāsa, filled with many jewel-lotuses, inhabited by fortunate ones, and attended upon by twice-born men, gods, and brahmins. (19)
The lotuses, bent down by swarms of bees, trembled incessantly under their heavy weight;
therein, a twice-born bird with a melodious voice uttered various mantras proclaimed in the Vedas.
There were many lakes with bodies adorned by garlands of white lotuses, possessing excellent garments and upper cloths, as well as birds; and likewise, there were twice-born Brahmins.
They recite the ancient ritual injunctions for the purpose of sacrifice.
Wandering among those lakes, I beheld numerous throngs of celestial nymphs,
as well as the daughters of the Vidyādharas.
And they arrived at that place for the purpose of bathing. || 22 ||
Then, O best of kings, while wandering about,
he once beheld another beautiful lake with excellent water;
however, one [lake] seen previously remained exactly as it was on its shore.
I see the hut just as I did before. || 23 ||
O King, as soon as I entered that hut and saw that ascetic standing in one corner,
I approached him and greeted him.
Smiling, he of incomparable power spoke.
The ascetic said:
"O Brahmin, O most excellent one, do you not recognize me, even though we have met before? It is because of this that you regard even this world as if you were a fool. (25)
"O best of the twice-born, this world which is not seen by the gods has been seen by me; for the sake of your pleasure, that world was shown to you by me."
Behold now, O Great Sage, the prosperity of my world:
rivers flowing with curds and milk, as well as lakes consisting of clarified butter. (27)

[He saw] houses with pillars made of gold, and within those houses, floors adorned with jewel-lotuses and possessing a luster like that of rubies; [floors] rich with the blossoms of the Pārijāta tree and frequented by Yakṣas and Kinnaras. (28)
O lord of men, having been addressed thus by that ascetic at that time,
my heart filled with wonder, I questioned him further.
O Blessed One, this world of yours is the most excellent among all worlds;
I have seen all the worlds inhabited by Brahmā, Śakra, and the others. (30)
"O one whose wealth is asceticism, this world appears to me as unprecedented, owing to its abundance of prosperity, sovereignty, and splendor, as well as its heaps of palaces and jewels. (31)
O Sage, I have beheld this most wonderful world of yours, with its lakes of pure water and especially with its aquatic flowers.
"How has the world come to be thus, and how have you yourself become established in this state? O bull among sages, tell me the cause of this, and who are you? (33)
O great sage, how is it that on the shore of a lake in the region of Ilāvṛta,
I beheld you, that lake, and that hut? O sage, in this world filled with golden palaces, what indeed is your place— a mere hut?
Thus addressed by me, O Indra among kings, that bull among sages spoke to me of what had occurred; listen to that. (35)
The ascetic said:
"I am the eternal Lord Nārāyaṇa, whose form is water; by me this entire universe, the three worlds with all things moving and unmoving, is pervaded. (36)
"That which is the form of that god Parameṣṭhin, even as water—that am I, Varuṇa; I am the supreme Nārāyaṇa himself. (37)
And in former times, you propitiated me for seven births;
therefore, even in the destruction of the three worlds, you alone have been singled out. (38)
Thus addressed by him at that time, with my eyes closed in sleep,
I fell upon the surface of the earth and rose up again instantly.
O King, as soon as I beheld that sage and that city,
I saw myself by my own self upon the summit of Mount Meru.
I beheld the seven oceans as well as the principal mountain ranges;
O King, I have seen the earth consisting of seven islands.
Even now, O observer of noble vows, I remain meditating upon that supreme world;
I have become intent on this thought: "When shall I attain that world? (42)
Thus, O King, I have told you this wonderful account of the Supreme Lord as it occurred within my body; what else do you wish to hear? (43)
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 69.
Bhadrāśva said:
O Blessed One, what has been done by you while observing that world—
whether it be a vow, austerity, or dharma— for the sake of attaining it, O Sage?
What wise person would desire the worlds without having propitiated Hari with devotion?
When Hari is propitiated, all the worlds are held within the palm of one's hand.
Having reflected thus, O Indra among kings, I propitiated the eternal Viṣṇu for a hundred years with sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Then, O prince, after a long time had passed,
while I was sacrificing to Janārdana, the Lord of Gods who is the embodiment of sacrifice,
all the deities together with Indra were summoned and arrived at once.
While the gods, together with Indra, remained each stationed in their own respective places,
the Blessed One whose banner is the bull arrived right there.
Mahādeva, Virūpākṣa, Tryambaka, and Nīlalohita—
that Supreme Lord also remained established in the Raudra state.
Seeing all those gods, sages, and great serpents who had arrived,
the blessed Sanatkumāra, born from the lotus, came forth.
Seated in a celestial chariot resembling the sun, which was the size of a mote of dust,
the great yogi remained there, knowing the past, the present, and the future.
Having approached Rudra, that great sage paid him homage with his head;
thus saluted by me, he stood near the wielder of the trident.
Having seen those gods standing there, as well as the sages beginning with Nārada, and Sanatkumāra and Rudra, this thought arose in my mind: || 10 ||
"O best of kings, who among these is the most excellent one to be worshipped with sacrifice?
By the gratification of whom would all these, including Rudra, become satisfied? (11)
O King, O sinless one, when they had thus stood there, I questioned Rudra:
"O best of gods, who among you is to be worshipped here for this purpose? (12)
When this was said, Rudra then spoke to me in the presence of the gods.
Rudra said:
"Let all the gods listen, as well as the stainless celestial sages (devarṣis) and the renowned brahminical sages (brahmarṣis); let everyone hear my words."
And you, O Agastya of great intellect, listen to my words as I speak them.
The God who is praised with sacrifices, from whom this entire world has arisen, and in whom the world together with the gods is always dissolved. (15)
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme deity, Janārdana whose nature is purity;
that blessed Supreme Lord manifested himself in three ways. (16)
Endowed with rajas and tamas, yet with rajas predominating over sattva,
the All-pervading Lord created Brahmā, whose seat is the lotus, from the lotus at his navel.
Endowed with rajas and tamas, that Lord also created me;
that which is sattva is the god Hari, and he who is Hari is the supreme state.
That which is the quality of passion (rajas) is Brahmā, born from the lotus;
he who is Brahmā is indeed the God, and he who is the God is the Four-faced One. That which is endowed with passion and darkness (tamas) is I myself; there is no doubt in this matter. (19)
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these three are said to be the qualities. By sattva a living being is liberated; sattva has Nārāyaṇa as its essence.
Through rajas conjoined with sattva, there arises creation characterized by a predominance of rajas;
and that conduct of the Grandfather (Brahmā) is recited in all the scriptures. (21)
Whatever action is outside the Vedas that is practiced by following a [non-Vedic] scripture is known as "fierce" (raudra); it is declared to be the lowest among men.
For that action which is deficient in passion (rajas) and is purely of the nature of darkness (tamas),
leads men to miserable states both in this world and in the next.
Through sattva a living being is liberated; sattva has Nārāyaṇa as its essence.
And the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa is conceived of as having the form of sacrifice.
In the Kṛta age, the pure Nārāyaṇa is worshipped in his subtle form;
in the Tretā age, he is worshipped in the form of sacrifice; and in the Dvāpara age, by means of the Pañcarātras.
In the Kali age, that Supreme Self, Janārdana, is worshipped by those of tamasic nature through my path in its many forms with a mind of hatred.
Therefore, there shall be no god other than him;
he who is Viṣṇu is himself Brahmā, and he who is Brahmā is indeed I myself. (27)
"O best of the twice-born, it is the settled conclusion regarding the Vedas that in this sacrifice within the three Vedas, one must be the sacrificer (yājya).
He who creates a division among our three [Vedas], O best of the twice-born, is a sinner of evil soul and shall attain a miserable state. (28)
And hear from me, O Agastya, as I speak this ancient account of how,
in the Kali age, human beings here do not practice devotion to Hari.
All those who dwell in the Bhūrloka, having previously worshipped Janārdana,
attain the Bhuvarloka; even while staying there, they propitiate Keśava and go to the heavenly realm (Svarga), and gradually they attain liberation (Mukti).
When the state of liberation was thus pervaded by all the worlds in that very manner,
the gods, who were partakers of liberation, then meditated with self-restraint upon Hari.
He too, being eternal and omnipresent, having manifested himself, said:
"O gods, best among all yogins, tell me, what is to be done?"
Having bowed down to that Lord of Gods, they spoke to the Supreme Lord:
"O God of gods, all people are established on the path to liberation;
how then shall creation proceed, and who will dwell in the hells? (33)
Thus addressed by the gods, Janārdana then said to them:
"Many men will approach me throughout the three ages."
In the final age, those who take refuge in me will become rare.
I shall quickly create this delusion which will bewilder the people. (35)
And you, O mighty-armed Rudra, compose treatises of delusion;
having shown them to involve little effort, demonstrate that their fruit is long-lasting. (36)
O Maheśvara, having displayed illusions, sorcery, and contradictory behaviors, quickly delude all people. (37)
Having spoken thus, that supreme deity then immediately concealed himself, and I was made manifest by him at that time.
Therefore, O best of beings, from that time forward, people will for the most part take delight in the scriptures composed by me. (39)
Those who perceive the path that follows the Vedas and the god Nārāyaṇa as one and the same become partakers of liberation.
O best of the twice-born, those men of sinful deeds who worship me as distinct from Viṣṇu and [as distinct] from Brahmā go to hell.
And for the sake of deluding those who have strayed from the path of the Veda,
this scripture has been presented by me under the designations of Naya and Siddhānta.
This bond is indeed the state of being a bound soul (paśu); when that [state] has fallen away, then the Pāśupata scripture arises, known by the name of Veda. || 43 ||
O Brahmin, I am the embodiment of the Veda; my true nature is not known by those who propound the meanings of other scriptures, except through the beginningless Veda.
O brahmin-sage, I am to be known through the Vedas, especially by the Brāhmaṇas. (44)
O Brahmin, for three ages I am Brahmā, and likewise Viṣṇu;
I am also the three qualities beginning with Sattva, the three Vedas, and the three fires. (45)
The three worlds, the three junctions of time, and likewise the three social classes—there are as many *savana*s; this universe is bound in a threefold manner.

O Brahmin-sage, he who thus knows that Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme, while Padmayoni Brahmā is the lower, and me as the lower still—knowing that in terms of qualities and primacy I am truly one, [he is not deluded]; for this is indeed delusion. (47)
Thus ends the seventieth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 70.
Agastya said: O King,
having been addressed thus by the wielder of the Pināka bow, the gods, the sages,
and I myself then bowed down before that deity.
O King, as soon as we had bowed our heads to the God and looked,
we beheld the lotus-seated Brahmā residing within the body of that very Rudra.
And we behold Nārāyaṇa within the heart, as subtle as a mote of light in a sunbeam, possessing the radiant luster of the blazing sun, emerging from the body of Bhava.
Seeing him, all my priests and sages were filled with wonder;
they raised shouts of "Victory! along with the sounds of the Sāman, Ṛg, and Yajus Vedas.
Having done so, they then said to the God: "O Supreme Lord, what is this?
For in this single form of yours, the three forms are perceived. (5)
Rudra said:
"O best of sages, whatever oblation is offered in this sacrifice intended for me,
all three of us shall receive a share of it."
O best of sages, no manifold state of being exists for us;
those with right vision perceive it thus, whereas others see it in many ways erroneously.
When Rudra had spoken thus, O King, all those sages questioned the god Śaṅkara regarding the purpose of the Māyā-śāstra.
The sages said:
"O Lord, for the sake of deluding the worlds, this scripture was composed by you separately;
tell us, O God, for what reason was it made by you? (9)
Rudra said:
In the land of Bhārata-varṣa there is a forest known as Daṇḍaka;
there, a twice-born man named Gautama was indeed performing intense and formidable austerity.
The Lord Brahmā, having attained complete satisfaction with him, spoke to that sage: "O you whose wealth is austerity, choose a boon."
Thus addressed at that time by Brahmā, the creator of the world, he immediately replied: "O Lotus-born One, give me a row of grains."
Thus addressed, the Grandfather granted him that very boon;
having obtained that boon, the brahmin established a great hermitage on Mount Śataśṛṅga.

O twice-born ones, at dawn, after the cooking was finished, that rice was harvested by the sage; likewise, at midday, it was cooked. That brahmin provided abundant hospitality for all guests to the brahmins.
Then, after some time, O best of the twice-born, there occurred a great twelve-year drought that caused one's hair to stand on end.
Seeing that drought, all those sages dwelling in the forest,
being tormented by hunger, then approached Gautama.
Then, seeing them arrived, Gautama bowed his head and said,
"O sons of the best of sages, please stay at my house."
Thus addressed by him, they remained there partaking of various kinds of food until that drought had come to an end.
When that drought had indeed ceased, those twice-born ones set their minds upon setting out for the purpose of a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Thereupon, reflecting thus, the supreme sage Mārīca spoke to that ascetic, the best of sages named Śāṇḍilya.
Mārīca said: "O Śāṇḍilya, I shall speak what is beneficial: your father is the sage Gautama;
without speaking with him, we shall not go to the penance grove to perform austerities."
When this was said, all those sages then laughed, saying:
"Has our own body been sold by us through the eating of this food?"
Having spoken thus, they spoke again regarding the approach to the one who possesses attributes;
having fashioned an illusory cow, they released it into his two dwellings.
Then, seeing that cow grazing in the field of śāla grass, the sage Gautama took water in his hand and said, "Go, O Rudra! Thereupon,
that illusory cow fell away along with the drops of water.
Then, seeing her slain and the sages likewise desiring to depart,
