the wise Gautama stood bowing and spoke to those sages.
"O Brahmins, tell me truly and without delay: for what purpose do you depart, leaving behind me who am ever devoted and especially humble? (26)
The sages said: "O Brahmin, O great sage, as long as this cow to be slaughtered remains within your body, we shall not eat food, even that which is yours."
Thus addressed, Gautama, the knower of dharma, then spoke to those sages:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, let an expiation for the killing of a cow be prescribed for me. (28)
"O Brahmin, this cow is like one who has fainted;
once bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, she will rise up again, without a doubt. (29)
"An expiation for one who has died would be required, but this was done for one who did not die; therefore, do not perform the vow nor harbor anger. Having said this, they departed.
Having departed by those paths, the wise Gautama went to the great mountain Himavat,
intending to worship me and to quickly perform great ascetic penance.
For one hundred and one years I was worshipped by him;
and being pleased, I said to him, "O observer of noble vows, choose a boon."
He said to me as I stood upon Jakaṭa: "Give the ascetic Gaṅgā to me;
let this holy river Bhāgīrathī go forth together with me."
When this was said, Śiva gave him a single lock of his matted hair;
taking it, he went to where that dead cow lay.
Drenched by that water, the cow rose up and departed; that beautiful woman became a great river with holy waters and pure pools.
Seeing that great marvel, the stainless Seven Sages arrived there in their celestial chariots through the sky, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! (36).
Excellent, Gautama! Who else among the virtuous is equal to you, who has thus caused the divine Jāhnavī to descend into Daṇḍaka? (37)
When he was addressed thus by them, Gautama then asked, "What is this? and Gautama looked for the reason why his cow had been killed. || 38 ||

Reflecting that all this had been produced through the illusory power (*māyā*) of the sages, he cursed them, saying: "Thus you shall become wearers of matted hair, ashes, and false vows; you shall be outside the Triple Veda (*trayī*) and excluded from Vedic rites. (39)
Having heard those cruel words of the great sage Gautama, the Seven Sages said, "O best of the twice-born, let it not be so at all times;
however, there is no doubt that your word shall not be in vain. (40)
Even if, in the Kali age, all those who are benefactors should indeed become doers of harm toward the best of the twice-born,
may they nevertheless be possessed of devotion in such a Kali age.
In the Kali age, the twice-born will always be consumed by the fire of your words;
they will be devoid of ritual action and excluded from Vedic rites. (42)
And her secondary name here shall be the river Godāvarī;
because a cow was given through the granting of a boon, she shall become the river Godāvarī.
O Brahmin, those people who, having reached this [place] in the Kali age, give gifts of land according to their capacity, rejoice together with the gods. || 44 ||
And when Jupiter is situated in Leo, he who goes there with a concentrated mind and bathes according to the prescribed rite likewise gratifies the ancestors.
Even if their ancestors have fallen into hell, they go to heaven;
for him whose ancestors reside in heaven, there is no doubt that they partake in liberation. 46.
"Having attained great renown, you shall go to eternal liberation. Having spoken thus, O best of beings, the sages then departed for Mount Kailāsa,
where I always dwell together with Umā.
And those sages said to me, "O Lord, in the Kali age all these best of the twice-born shall become your very forms, wearing matted hair and crowns;
by their own will they shall assume the guise of ghosts and bear false emblems."
For the sake of favoring them, let some scripture be bestowed, by which all those born of our lineage may live, even though oppressed by the Kali age. (49)
O best of the twice-born, having been thus entreated by them in former times,
I composed a Saṃhitā endowed with Vedic rites.
Then, having heard the account called Niḥśvāsa, the Bābhravyas and Śāṇḍilas merged into it; and the Baiḍālikas, having committed only a slight offense, departed.
"O twice-born ones, those men will indeed be deluded by me alone, even though I know the future;
for in the Kali age, men will compose scriptures out of greed and desire. (52)
For in the Niḥśvāsasaṃhitā, it is stated that its extent is exactly one hundred thousand [verses];
that indeed is the Pāśupata initiation, and here the Yoga is the Pāśupata.
Whatever else arises here apart from this Vedic path should be known as a minor action—fierce and devoid of purity. (54)
In the Kali age, those men who subsist upon Rudra will be like professional reciters (vaiḍālika);
seeking their own gain, men in the Kali age will compose their own scriptures.
They should be known as "dried-up Rudras" (ucchuṣma-rudra); I am not established within them.
In ancient times, when the work of the gods was at hand, I danced in my own form as Bhairava; such is this connection of those who perform cruel deeds.
Desiring to bring about the destruction of the Daityas, I let out a loud laugh.
Those drops of tears which formerly fell there from me shall become those countless, fierce [beings] upon the surface of the earth. (57)
Devoted to Ucchuṣma, fierce, and always fond of liquor and meat, those who were lustful for women and performers of evil deeds were born upon the surface of the earth.
Indeed, due to the curse of Gautama, there will be twice-born ones in their lineage;
among them, those who are of virtuous conduct shall be devoted to my teaching.
"Because of this doubt regarding both heaven and liberation, those who defile my lineage shall sink below like jackals. (60)
O twice-born ones, though previously consumed by the fire of Gautama, you shall nevertheless go to hell because of my word; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Rudra said:
Having been addressed thus by me, the sons of Brahmā departed as they had come;
Gautama, the scorcher of foes, also went quickly to his own home.
O Brahmins, this characteristic of dharma has been told to you by me;
he who acts contrary to this would be a devotee of heresy (pāṣaṇḍa).
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 71.
Śrī Varāha said: Having bowed down to Bhava, the ancient Rudra— the omniscient creator of all— Agastya, being self-restrained, questioned the Supreme Lord.
Agastya said:
You, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—this triad is remembered as the Triple Veda (Trayī).
In all the scriptures, everywhere, it is like a lamp, a fire, through its conjunctions with other lamps.
In which time is the Blessed One predominant, and in which [time] is Adhokṣaja? Or is it Brahmā? Tell me this, O three-eyed God. (3)
Rudra said:
Viṣṇu alone is the supreme Brahman; he is described here as having three divisions.
Those who are deluded do not understand this within the paths of the Vedic tenets.
In the sense of "entering" (viśapraveśane), the verbal root is *ṣṇu*, with the suffix *anu* following it;
thus [is derived] Viṣṇu, who is the eternal Supreme Self among all the gods. || 5 ||
O twice-born ones, this very Viṣṇu who is celebrated as tenfold and also as singlefold is the Sun, O illustrious one, endowed with the sovereignty of yoga.
That Supreme Lord always performs the works of the gods;
assuming a human state, he praises me age after age for the sake of setting the world on its path and for the accomplishment of the purposes of the gods.
And I am the bestower of boons upon him in every Dvāpara age, O twice-born one;
and I always praise him in Śvetadvīpa during the Kṛta age.
At the time of creation, I praise the four-faced one, and I myself become Time (Kāla).
In the Kṛta Yuga, Brahmā, along with the gods and asuras, always praises me;
and the gods, desiring worldly enjoyment, worship me in the form of the Liṅga.
Those seeking liberation worship with their minds that god who has a thousand heads;
he is the god Nārāyaṇa himself, the soul of the universe.
Those best of the twice-born who constantly perform the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña) please Brahmā; for the Veda is proclaimed to be Brahmā. || 11 ||
Nārāyaṇa, Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, Puruṣottama—
by these names the supreme, eternal Brahman is proclaimed.
And the wise declare that [Brahman] to be the yoga consisting of contemplation.
Whatever pacification of animals occurs at a sacrifice, and whatever act of oblation (homa) may take place, that is celebrated as "Om," and therein I am fully established. (13)
O Brahmin, for those engaged in the experience of karma, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—we three, including the mantras and so forth—are present; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (14)
"I am Viṣṇu, as well as the Vedas, Brahman, and even ritual actions;
a wise person should not consider these three as separate, for they are indeed one. (15)
O observer of noble vows, that sinful man who contemplates this otherwise through partiality goes to the terrible Raurava hell.
I, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas—O best of the twice-born, there is no distinction among all these in this [reality]. (17)
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 72.
Rudra said:
Listen, O best of the twice-born, to another [account] filled with wonder,
an unprecedented event that occurred while submerged in the water, O bull among sages.
"O twice-born one, in the past I was created by Brahmā and told, 'Create indeed the progeny. Being incapable of discernment, I remained submerged in the water. (2)
There, with a restrained mind, I remained for as long as a single moment, meditating upon the Supreme Lord, the Person the size of a thumb.
Then, from the water, eleven men rose up, possessing a radiance like the fire of universal destruction, scorching the water with their rays.
"Having been questioned by me, 'Who are you that, having emerged from the water, are heating this water with your splendor? And where will you go, O blessed ones? (5)
O best of the twice-born, though addressed by me in this manner, those most excellent beings said nothing at all;
indeed, those men departed in silence.
Then, following them, there appeared a most magnificent Great Being;
he was like a dark cloud and had eyes resembling lotuses.
I asked him: "Who are you, and who are these men who have come here? O bull among men, tell me, what is the purpose for which you are here? (8)
The Puruṣa said:
"Those men of radiant splendor who have gone before are indeed the Ādityas; they proceed swiftly, for you have been meditated upon by Brahmā."
Brahmā indeed creates the creation; for the sake of that creation, these men go forth to protect it, O God—of this there is no doubt. (10)
Śambhu said:
"O Blessed One, O best among great beings, how do you know that everything is by the name 'Bhava'? Tell me all that, for I am the Supreme."
Thus addressed by Rudra, that man replied:
"I am the eternal god Nārāyaṇa, who reclines upon the waters."
"May you indeed possess divine vision; behold me with effort.
When he was thus addressed by him, I then looked at him.
I beheld him indeed as being only the size of a thumb, with a brilliance like that of the blazing sun; and in his navel, there was a lotus.
There I beheld Brahmā and myself emerging from his lap;
having thus seen that Great-Souled One, I was filled with joy, O tiger among the twice-born, and my mind was inclined to praise him. (15)
O observer of noble vows, when his image had been produced,
that Soul of the Universe was praised by me with this hymn of praise, while my past deeds were remembered through my ascetic penance.
Rudra said: "Homage be to the infinite one, whose consciousness is pure, who possesses both form and formlessness, and who has a thousand arms."
To the creator of preeminent thousand-rayed splendor, whose body is vast and whose actions are pure. || 17 ||
To Śambhu, the remover of all the world's afflictions,
whose brilliance surpasses a thousand suns and the wind,
who upholds all branches of knowledge, and who wields the discus.
O sinless one, you who are eternally praised by all the gods.
O beginningless God, O infallible one, O you who have Śeṣa as your crest-jewel, O Lord, O All-pervading One, O Lord of beings, O Maheśvara!
O Lord of the winds, O Lord of all, O Lord of the universe!
O Lord of the earth, O Lord of the world, perpetual homage to you! || 19 ||
O Lord of the waters, Nārāyaṇa, benefactor of the universe, Lord of the earth, Sovereign of the universe, whose eyes are the universe!
O Moon, Sun, Acyuta, Hero, you whose form pervades the universe and is inconceivable, you who are the immortal and imperishable form! || 20 ||
O Nārāyaṇa, whose orb is opposed by the flames of the blazing fire, protect me from all sides! Salutations to you, the immortal and imperishable one who removes the suffering of the gods.
Protect me, who have come to you for refuge, forever, O Acyuta!
O All-pervading Lord, I behold Your many faces, and within them, situated in their midst, the Ancient One—
Brahmā, the Lord and progenitor of the worlds.
Homage be to you, O Grandfather! || 22 ||

O Supreme God among gods, through the many revolutions of the wheel of saṃsāra, you are worshipped in some places by those on the true path whose beings are purified by knowledge; what more can I say to you? (23)
He who knows you, O Lord, as beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), is the knower among all the knowers;
the qualities [of nature] cannot forcibly divide those [who have realized you].
For he who possesses a vast form indeed has a most subtle nature. || 24 ||
You are speechless, devoid of ego, and free from the senses; through the non-existence of karma, you are free from all action.
For although you possess the world of saṃsāra, you are not like those who are bound by it.
Furthermore, how are you to be known as the best of gods? || 25 ||

O God, your incomparable supreme form, both with and without form, is attained by those of pure disposition who worship you while effecting the cessation of saṃsāra; therefore, you are understood to be four-armed.
Yet even the gods and others do not know that wondrous cause of your body;
therefore, let those such as the Lotus-seated Brahmā worship your ancient form described as an incarnation.
The Great One, the lotus-born creator of the universe, does not know your form with absolute certainty;
however, having been purified by austerity, I know you—the ancient seer, the primordial source—through my penance.
"Padmāsana is my father, as is well known from the Purāṇas which have repeatedly declared it;
yet, O Lord, even one such as I am not awakened [to this truth], for those devoid of austerity do not know you. (29)

O Lord, you who are unknowable even to the foremost among beings such as Brahmā, these fools—devoid of the Vedas—desire awakening from their own endless delusions; yet wisdom does not reside in them, even though they possess noble reputations.
O Lord, by your grace, may those who know the Vedas attain the intellect of discernment through successive births;
for one who has obtained their gain from you, neither mere human status nor the state of gods and gandharvas shall be auspicious.
You are the form of Viṣṇu; you are both extremely subtle and gross. You are the fulfillment of all that is to be accomplished.
O Lord, you are gross, you are extremely subtle, and you are easily attained.
Through outward conduct toward you, they fall into hell. || 32 ||

Or rather, what is said when this [Self] remains—[a Self] which, possessing the nature of the pervasive, bears a uniform form through the principles (tattvas) consisting of ether, moon, fire, sun, earth, and wind, together with water, within its own essential nature? 33.
Thus, O Blessed One, accept this praise from me, your devotee, especially as it is offered by one such as I;
and as you have been invoked, bring forth the creation.
Grant me omniscience; salutations be unto Viṣṇu! || 34 ||
O Best of Gods, even if a man with a pure mind were to have four faces, or even ten million faces, he might then speak of your countless tens of thousands of virtues; therefore, be gracious! (35)

For one whose intellect is purified through union with samādhi and whose mind follows solely the state of Your being, You are ever present in the heart; homage to You, for there is no separate existence for the All-pervading One.
Thus, O Lord, having understood this all-pervading praise through the logic of the revolving wheel of saṃsāra, I have made it manifest.
O Acyuta, purify me who am afraid; grant me absolute oneness with you. || 37 ||
Śrī Varāha said:
Thus praised then by Rudra of immeasurable splendor, the Lord, being well-pleased, spoke these words with a voice as deep as a thundercloud. (38)
Viṣṇu said:
"Choose a boon; may it be well with you, O God of gods, Lord of Umā!
There is no difference between us, O God; we two are indeed one."
Rudra said:
"O Lord, I have been commanded by Brahmā, 'Create living beings.
In this regard, please grant me the threefold knowledge that brings about the manifestation of all creatures."
Viṣṇu said:
"You are omniscient, of this there is no doubt; you are the eternal mass of knowledge.
You shall always be the supreme object of worship for the gods. (41)
Thus addressed, the Lord of Umā spoke these words again with joy:
"O God, grant me another boon that is well-known among all living beings. (42)
"O Keśava, having become embodied, you yourself worship me;
carry me, O Lord of Gods, and accept a boon from me, so that I may become more worthy of worship than all the gods. (43)
Viṣṇu said:
"Having assumed human form for the sake of accomplishing the work of the gods, I shall worship you alone; and may you be the granter of boons to me."
"O God of gods, O Lord of Umā, as for what you have said—that 'you must carry me'—I shall carry you, the God, having become a cloud for a hundred years. (45)
Having spoken thus, Hari himself became a cloud and lifted Maheśvara out of that water, and he spoke these words: || 46 ||
O Lord, these eleven persons who were born of Prakṛti became Vairājas; they went to the earth and were designated as Ādityas.
O Śaṅkara, that twelfth portion of mine who has descended upon the earth under the name of Viṣṇu is propitiating you.
Having spoken thus, Nārāyaṇa created the Sun and likewise the Cloud from a portion of himself; we do not know where he has gone to his dissolution, along with the Sound.
Rudra said:
"In this way, this Lord Hari, the omnipresent creator of all beings, formerly became the granter of boons to me; therefore, I am superior even to the gods."
There is no god higher than Nārāyaṇa; he has not existed before, nor will there ever be another.
This is the secret of the Vedas and the Purāṇas, O best of beings;
I have proclaimed it all to you—how Viṣṇu is worshipped here.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 73.
Śrī Varāha said:
Once again, all those sages questioned that eternal one—
Rudra, the ancient Puruṣa, who is everlasting, fixed, and imperishable.
To Śambhu, who possesses all forms, who is unborn, who has three eyes, and who holds a trident in his hand. || 1 ||
The sages said:
"O Lord of the gods, you are superior to all the deities and to us as well;
therefore, we ask you this one question, which you ought to answer. (2)
O God of gods, Lord of Umā, please out of compassion tell us the dimensions and configuration of the earth, the extent of the mountains, the oceans, the rivers, and the expansion of the universe.
Rudra said: In all the Purāṇas, the world of the earth (bhūrloka) is proclaimed at length in the Vāyavya [Purāṇa], as well as those concerning Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others.
And now I shall briefly declare to you another form of forbearance;
listen to that, O best of beings, as I speak, you who are knowers of dharma. (5)

That Lord Nārāyaṇa—who is the form of the Supreme Self awakened by all knowledge, who is free from impurity, whose nature is inconceivable like an atom, who pervades all the worlds and the non-worlds, who wears yellow garments and has a broad chest, who supports the earth, and who, primarily by virtue of his qualities, is characterized as atomic, great, long, short, non-material, non-red, and so forth, being essentially of the nature of pure consciousness—created the waters in three ways, according to the predominance of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Having created that, the primordial Puruṣa, the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa—who consists of the entire universe, who consists of all things, who consists of the gods, who consists of sacrifice, and who consists of water—emerged from the lotus at the navel of him who was asleep in the yoga-slumber, appearing as the embodiment of water.

In that [egg], the Supreme Lord Brahmā, the storehouse of all Vedas and of inconceivable nature, became the Prajāpati. Having first produced Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra, and others who were endowed with the nature of knowledge, he subsequently created Svāyambhuva Manu, as well as Marīci and the others ending with Dakṣa. Starting from that Svāyambhuva Manu, who was created by the Blessed One, the vast expansion of the universe is described. That Manu had two sons, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda.

Priyavrata had ten sons: Āgnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Medha, Medhātithi, Dhruva, Jyotiṣmat, Dyutimat, Havya, Vapuṣmat, and Savana. Priyavrata established his seven sons as rulers over the seven continents; among them, he made Āgnīdhra the lord of Jambūdvīpa.

Medhātithi was the lord of Śākadvīpa; Jyotiṣmat in Kuśadvīpa; Dyutimat in Krauñcadvīpa; Vapuṣmat in Śālmalidvīpa; Havya, the lord of Gomedadvīpa; and Savana, the sovereign of Puṣkaradvīpa. Savana, the lord of Puṣkara, had two sons, Mahāvīta and Dhātaki. Their respective territories were established by name as Gomeda and Dhātakīkhaṇḍa, while Kumuda’s domain was known as Kaumuda.

The son of Vapuṣmān, the lord of Śālmaladvīpa, had three sons named Sakuśa, Vaidyuta, and Jīmūta. The country of Sakuśa was called Sakuśa, that of Vaidyuta was called Vaidyuta, and that of Jīmūta was called Jīmūta; these were the regions of Śālmaladvīpa. Furthermore, Dyutimān had seven sons: Kuśala, Manu, Goṣṭha, Uṣṇa, Pīvara, Andhakāraka, and Muni-dundubhi. After their names, the seven great regions on Krauñcadvīpa were likewise named.

Jyotiṣmat, the lord of Kuśadvīpa, also had seven sons, namely: Udbhida, Veṇumān, Rathopalambhana, Dhṛti, Prabhākara, and Kapila. The regions (varṣas) should be understood as having the same names as these [sons]. Medhātithi, the sovereign of Śāka[dvīpa], likewise had seven sons, namely: Śānta, Bhaya, Śiśira, Sukhodaya, Nanda, Śiva, Kṣemaka, and Dhruva. These are the seven sons, and the regions have the very same names as these.

Now, Āgnīdhra, the lord of Jambūdvīpa, also had nine sons. They were as follows: Nābhi, Kiṃpuruṣa, Harivarṣa, Ilāvṛta, Ramyaka, Hiraṇmaya, Kuru, Bhadrāśva, and Ketumāla. The regions (varṣas) bore these very names. From Nābhi [came] Hemavanta, Hemakūṭa, Kiṃpuruṣa, Naiṣadha, and Harivarṣa.

In the center of Meru is Ilāvṛta; to the north of Śṛṅgavān are Nīla, Ramyaka, Śveta, Hiraṇmaya, and Kuru; and to the south are Mālyavān, Bhadrāśva, Gandhamādana, and Ketumāla. Thus, in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, the arrangement of the worlds is established. In every Kalpa, in this very same way, the protection and regulation of the earth are carried out by seven sets of seven kings. This is the constant nature of a Kalpa. Now, I shall describe the creation from the navel [of the Lord].

Nābhi begot a son named Ṛṣabha upon Merudevī; Bharata was born as his eldest son. His father, Ṛṣabha, gave the southern region of the Himālayas to that Bharata, which became known as Bhārata-varṣa. Bharata’s son was named Sumati. Having given the kingdom to him, Bharata also departed for the forest. Sumati’s son was Tejas, whose son was named Satsu. His son was Indradyumna.

His son was Parameṣṭhin; his was Pratihartṛ; his was Nikhāta; Nikhāta’s was Unnetṛ; Unnetṛ’s son was Abhāva; his was Udgātṛ; his was Prastotṛ; and Prastotṛ’s was Vibhu. Vibhu’s son was Pṛthu; Pṛthu’s was Ananta; Ananta’s was Gaya; Gaya’s was Naya; his was Virāṭa; his was Mahāvīrya; from him came Sudhīmat; Dhīmat’s was Mahān; Mahān’s was Bhaumana; Bhaumana’s was Tvaṣṭṛ; Tvaṣṭṛ’s was Viraja; his was Rāja; Rāja’s was Śatajit.
To him were born a hundred sons, by whom these progeny were increased; by them this Bhārata-varṣa, consisting of seven islands, was marked.
Through the progeny of their lineage, this Bharata population was enjoyed;
indeed, by means of the sequence of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages, there were seventy-one cycles known as Yugas.
In connection with the world, this auspicious Manvantara of Svāyambhuva Manu has been described; now learn of his continents.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter in the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One.
Rudra said:
Hereafter, I shall describe Jambūdvīpa exactly as it is.
And also the enumeration of the oceans and the extent of the continents.
And as many years as there are, and whatever rivers are recorded therein, the dimensions of the great elements, and the separate courses of the moon and the sun. (2)
The thousands of divisions of the continents, contained within the seven [oceans], cannot be described here in their entirety by me, by which the world is pervaded. (3)
I shall describe the seven continents together with the moon, the sun, and the planets,
whose dimensions human beings declare by means of reasoning.
Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable should not be established by means of logic;
that which is beyond primordial natures is considered to be inconceivable.
I shall describe Jambūdvīpa as it truly is, consisting of nine regions; learn of its extent and its circumference in yojanas.
It extends for one hundred thousand yojanas all around,
filled with various inhabited lands and diverse, auspicious yojanas.
It was crowded with perfected beings (siddhas) and celestial musicians (cāraṇas), adorned with mountains increased by all kinds of minerals produced from networks of rock-essence (śilājatu),
and strewn everywhere with rivers originating from those mountains.
Jambūdvīpa is vast, glorious, and perfectly circular on all sides; it is the abode of all beings and is encompassed by nine auspicious regions.
It is surrounded on all sides by the salt ocean,
which is equal in extent to Jambūdvīpa itself on every side.
Stretching eastward from it are these six long mountain ranges,
which penetrate both the eastern and western oceans.
Himavān consists mostly of snow, as does Hemakūṭa, which abounds in gold; and the great mountain Niṣadha is pleasant and delightful everywhere.
It consists of four castes; it is golden, and Mount Meru is its membrane-like covering. It is circular in shape and proportion, square, and lofty.
Possessing various colors on its sides and endowed with the qualities of Prajāpati,
it was produced from the navel-circle of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
Because he was white in color in the east, he is therefore called *brahmaṇya*;
and because he was yellow in the south, he is thus regarded as belonging to the Vaiśya caste.
And because it resembles the wing of a bumblebee and is situated to the west,
the status of this Meru— whose name, meaning, and function have been explained— is said to be that of a Śūdra.
His northern side is perceived as red in color;
because of that, his status as a Kṣatriya is established—thus the colors have been proclaimed. || 17 ||
Their circular shape has been described according to their nature, color, and dimensions:
one is blue and made of lapis lazuli; another is white and bright, made of gold;
and the horned one is the color of a peacock's tail and made of refined gold.
These are the kings of mountains, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas;
the distance between them is said to be nine thousand [yojanas]. (19)
In the center, however, is the region named Ilāvṛta, which originates from Mahāmeru;
it extends for nine thousand yojanas in every direction.
Its center is Mahāmeru, like a smokeless fire;
the southern half of Meru is one vedi, and likewise the northern half is another.
Those regions that are six here are their mountain ranges;
the extent in yojanas of all those regions is thus prescribed.
The height of Jambūdvīpa is two thousand yojanas, and its width is said to be equal to that. (23)
The two mountains Nīla and Niṣadha are each one thousand two hundred yojanas in length; and those others which are inferior to them—
Śveta, Hemakūṭa, Himavat, and Śṛṅgavān— are likewise.
Niṣadha is proclaimed to be equal in measure to Jambūdvīpa;
Hemakūṭa is less than that by a twelfth part;
and Himavat is less than Hemakūṭa by a twentieth part. || 25 ||
The great mountain Hemakūṭa extends eighty-eight thousand [yojanas],
and the Himavat mountain extends eighty [thousand] from east to west.
Due to the circular shape of the continent, the decrease and increase of the regions and the mountains are proclaimed; as it is with these, so it is with those to the north.
In their midst are the inhabited regions and those very varṣas;
however, they are surrounded by mountains made rugged by waterfalls.
Continuous with various divisions of rivers and inaccessible to one another, beings of all kinds from diverse species dwell within them in every way. (29)
This is the region of Haimavata, where the lineage of Bhārata resides;
beyond it lies Hemakūṭa, where the supreme Kiṃpuruṣa dwells.
From Hemakūṭa to Niṣadha, that region is called Harivarṣa;
beyond Harivarṣa, on the side of Meru, lies Ilāvṛta.
Beyond Ilāvṛta is the well-known Nīla;
beyond Ramyaka is the famous Śveta, which is Hiraṇmaya;
and beyond Hiraṇmaya is what is remembered as Śṛṅgavat, belonging to the Kurus. (32)
Two years, the southern and the northern, are to be known as being situated in the shape of a bow;
indeed, there are four islands, and Ilāvṛta is square.
The southern half of the sacrificial altar (vedi) is known as that which lies to the east of Niṣadha; the northern half is indeed that which lies beyond Śṛṅgavat.
On the southern half of the Vedi are three Varṣas, and on the northern half are three;
between these two is to be known Ilāvṛta, where Meru stands.
To the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha,
there is a great mountain named Mālyavat, extending towards the north.
Its width and height are two thousand yojanas, and its length is proclaimed to be thirty-four thousand yojanas. (37)
To its west, the Gandhamādana mountain is to be known;
it is equal to Mālyavat in length, height, and breadth.
In the center of those two [oceans] is Mount Meru, a mountain of gold;
it is four-colored, golden, square, and lofty. (39)
All the unmanifest elements, beginning with water, have arisen from the Unmanifest;
from the Unmanifest came the earth-lotus, and Meru is its pericarp.
The great four-petaled [lotus] arose, manifest and endowed with five qualities;
from that, indeed, all extensive activities emerged. || 41 ||
The Supreme Person is attained by those men who have lived for many kalpas, who perform meritorious deeds, and who are self-realized and high-souled.
The great yogi, the great god, the object of meditation for the world, Janārdana;
he who has reached all worlds, the infinite, the pervasive, the immutable form. || 43 ||
His form is not composed of ordinary flesh, fat, and bone;
because of his state as a yogin and his lordship, the all-pervading one assumes a form consisting of pure being (sattva).
On account of that, the eternal lotus arose in the world;
such was the course of time at the beginning of the remainder of that kalpa.
Within that lotus was born the God of gods, the four-faced one, the Lord of the Lords of Creatures, the divine Īśāna, the sovereign of the universe. || 46 ||
Indeed, the emission of his seed is described in its entirety and in detail, according to the facts, through the process of the creation of progeny. || 47 ||
That water indeed became the body of Viṣṇu, adorned with jewels;
from it arose the earth, shaped like a lotus and possessing forests and trees.
O twice-born ones, listen as I describe in detail, according to their divisions and in due order, that expansion of this world-lotus as it has been proclaimed by the Siddhas.
There, four regions known as Mahāvarṣas are situated;
therein stands the mountain named Meru, which is of great power and mountain-like in form.
That [mountain] has various colors on its sides; it is said to be white in the east, yellow in the south, and the color of a bumblebee (dark blue) in the west.
The northern flank of that great-souled one is red in color;
Mount Meru, white and established within the royal lineage, shines there.
Resembling the rising sun and like a smokeless fire, it rose eighty-four thousand yojanas high. || 53 ||
Having entered sixteen [units] below, it is likewise sixteen in width;
and because it is situated like a shallow bowl (śarāva), it is thirty-two [units] wide at the top.
Its width is threefold, and its circumference is equal on all sides;
when measured by the standard of a circle, it is thus intended.
It is ninety thousand yojanas all around; furthermore, it is proclaimed that when measured as a square, its circumference is increased by six [thousand]. (56)
That mountain is greatly divine, endowed with celestial medicinal herbs;
it is entirely covered with auspicious mines consisting of gold.
There, all the hosts of gods, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas,
as well as the throngs of Apsarases, rejoice upon the king of mountains.
That Meru is surrounded by palaces created by the creators of beings;
it has four regions situated on its various sides. (59)
Bhadrāśva and Bhārata are in the west, as is Ketumāla;
and in the north are the Kurus, who are the refuge for those who have performed meritorious deeds.
The pericarp of that lotus is perfectly circular all around,
measuring thousands of yojanas in extent.
Its filament-networks are proclaimed to be nine and six;
their height is eighty-four, and they occupy the space within the openings.
Its filaments, measuring thirty thousand yojanas in extent,
are scattered all around it.
Its length is one hundred thousand [yojanas], its breadth is eighty-four, and its four leaves there are fourteen yojanas each. (64)

In that regard, listen with one-pointed attention to a brief description of that which I have called to you the "Karṇikā," variegated with hundreds of jewel-leaves and illuminated by various colors. (65)

It was a single, excellent mountain, circular in shape, possessing a thousand peaks and a thousand internal caves; it was made of gold, possessed a lovely reddish luster, and was covered with many clusters of leaves and hundreds of lotuses.
With pits inlaid with precious gems and altars variegated with jewels,
its pillars were adorned with gold and various gems, and its archways were embellished with jewels.
There is the delightful assembly hall of Brahmā, crowded with hosts of brahman-sages;
it is renowned throughout all the worlds by the name Manovratī.
There, the greatness of the god Īśāna— who possesses the splendor of a thousand suns and resides within a great celestial chariot— manifests eternally.
There, all the hosts of gods approached the four-faced Lord himself, who was worthy of worship, having honored him with offerings, veneration, and prostrations.
By those high-souled ones of beautiful mind, who remained on the path of virtuous conduct, celibacy was practiced at that time with resolute intentions.
Having sacrificed correctly and having partaken [of the offerings], they were devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods;
intent upon the householder's stage of life, they were humble and fond of guests.

These householders were established in white (pure) actions, dispassionate, and possessed of the nature of the cause; by means of restraints, observances, and gifts, their sins were thoroughly burnt away.
Their dwelling is the stainless, white world of Brahmā;
it is the supreme goal above all other states of existence,
and its extent is proclaimed to be fourteen thousand yojanas.
Then, on that beautiful mountain, which was dark yet lovely above, possessing the luster of the rising sun and variegated with jewels and minerals; (75)
In a palace with gateways of jewels, a dwelling filled with many gems,
on all sides of Mount Meru, it was perfectly circular in every direction.
The Cakrapāṭa, the best of mountains, extending thirty thousand yojanas, and Jārudhi, the lord of mountains—these are remembered as the northern [mountains]. || 77 ||
Learn now, in due order, the plateaus, the intermediate valleys, and the lakes situated to the north of these principal mountains. (78)
Extending ten yojanas in width and flowing out from the opening of the wheel,
that river flows upwards before descending and being established upon the earth.
As the moon moved through the city of Amarāvatī toward the Lord,
even the hosts of the light of the sun and moon were eclipsed by her.
The twice-born are pleased with all those best of the twice-born who perform the twilight rites at both sunrise and sunset, as well as with the eight excellent immovable mountains.
That auspicious one, who is honored by Rudra and Indra, is the revolving light of the stars.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 75.
Rudra said:
To the east of that very Meru, in a region of supreme splendor,
encircled by the Cakravāṭa range and resplendent with various minerals, (1).
There, the city of all the immortals rises up with its circular wall;
it is unassailable by the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas who are arrogant in their strength.
There, the excellent ramparts are made of Jāmbūnada gold, and the gateways are magnificent.
To the northeast of that [city], in a region of supreme splendor,
there is a place filled with people from all worlds and crowded with hundreds of celestial palaces (vimānas).
It was provided with great reservoirs, eternally joyful and auspicious, adorned with flowers of variegated hues and garlanded with flags and banners. || 4 ||
Adorned by gods, yakṣas, apsarases, and sages,
Amarāvatī, the city of Purandara, is beautiful, delightful, and prosperous.
In the center of that Amarāvatī is a dais of diamond and lapis lazuli;
there is indeed an assembly hall named Sudharmā, renowned throughout the three worlds for its virtues.
There dwells the glorious thousand-eyed lord of Śacī, the husband of Śrī,
surrounded by the Siddhas and all the divine beings.
And in that very place shall be the noble lineage of the high-souled Bhāskara;
there, the Lord of the Gods himself resides, saluted by all the deities.
And in the various directions surrounding it, there is the city named Tejovatī belonging to the high-souled Hutāśana, which is extensive and endowed with those respective qualities.
And the city of Vaivasvata, endowed with various virtues and beautiful, is known by the name Saṃyamanī; it is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Likewise, in the fourth quarter, there is the auspicious city named Kṛṣṇāvatī, belonging to the wise Virūpākṣa, the lord of the Nairṛtas.
In the fifth northern sector, there is the city known by the name Śuddhavatī,
belonging to the great-souled Varuṇa, the lord of the waters.
Likewise, in the northern sector of that city of the gods, there is a city of Vāyu named Gandhavatī, renowned as preeminent in all virtues. (13)
In its northern sector is the delightful city of the Lord of the Guhyakas,
named Mahodayā, which is auspicious and possesses pedestals of lapis lazuli.

Likewise, in the eighth inner enclosure belongs the city named Manoharā, belonging to the great-souled Īśāna; it is filled with various kinds of beings and with diverse forests abounding in flowers and auspicious grains, situated within hermitages. || 15 ||
This world of the gods is prayed for; it is celebrated as heaven. || 16 ||
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 76.
Rudra said:
That which is celebrated as the base of the pericarp and the center of Meru is recorded by calculation to be a thousand yojanas in measure. || 1 ||
Forty-eight thousand leagues by means of its circles;
that is known there as the base of Meru, the king of mountains. (2)
Among those many thousands of mountains, there is one of great height;
furthermore, its auspicious boundary mountains extend toward the eight directions.
Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa are the two mountains in the eastern direction;
these two extend from east to west and are situated within the ocean.
The wise call these the eight boundary mountains.
O best of the twice-born, that which has been described as Meru, the mountain of gold—listen as I speak of its supporting pillars (viṣkambhas). (5)
Furthermore, there are four great feet of Meru in the four directions,
by which the earth, consisting of seven continents, was firmly supported so that it did not waver.
Their extent is calculated at ten thousand yojanas;
they are fashioned horizontally and vertically, and are surrounded by slopes of yellow orpiment.
Adorned with realgar and caves, variegated with gold and jewels, they were radiant with many dwellings of perfected beings (siddhas) and pleasure grounds.
To its east is Mandara, and to its south is Gandhamādana;
Vipula stands on the western side, and Supārśva is situated in the north.
Upon their peaks stand four great trees,
frequented by gods, daityas, and apsarases, who abound in a multitude of virtues.
On the peak of Mount Mandara there is a tree named Kadamba;
with its long-extended branches and summit, the Kadamba is a sacred tree (caityapādapa).
It was adorned with flowers the size of large jars, possessing full-blown filaments,
fragrant with great scents, and delightful, which bloom in all seasons.
Surrounded in brief by the worlds that bring forth all beings,
he then filled the quarters with his fragrance, exceeding a thousandfold.
This tree named Bhadrāśva is the banner born upon the mountain of the Varṣa; it is a glorious, beautiful, and auspicious great tree,
where Hṛṣīkeśa himself is personally attended by hosts of Siddhas.
Then Hari, whose face was like that of a horse, reached the excellent peak of that auspicious Kadamba tree again and again. || 15 ||
And by him was that Varṣa beheld; it is called Bhadrāśva after his name, O leaders of all bipeds—of this there is no doubt. (16)
On the peak of the southern mountain, frequented by the gods,
stands a Jambū tree, adorned with great branches and bearing flowers and fruit instantly.
For upon the summit of that mountain fall fruits that are of immense size, sweet, soft, and like unto nectar.
From that most excellent of mountains flows the divine river named Jāmbūnadī, which carries a stream of fruit and flows with honey.
There, a gold named Jāmbūnada, brilliant as fire, arose—an incomparable ornament for the gods that destroys all evil. (20)
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
and guhyakas drank that honey-like nectar flowing from the jambu fruit.
She is the banner in the southern region, renowned throughout the worlds of Jambū;
after her name, it is called Jambūdvīpa by human beings.
To the south of the great-souled mountain Vipula,
there grew a very large tree called Śṛṅga, which was an aśvattha tree.
Of great height and massive trunk, it was an abode for the virtues of many beings,
adorned with beautiful, auspicious fruits of all seasons, each as large as a jar.
He is the banner of those who possess banners, served by gods and gandharvas;
he is renowned there as Ketumāla, celebrated by that name.
Listen now, O best of brahmins, to the etymological derivation of that name based on his deeds. (25)
When the churning of the Ocean of Milk had taken place, Indra placed a garland upon the shoulder of the Caityaka tree;
therefore, that region was known as Ketumāla.
Because it was marked by that [garland], the continent became famous as Ketumāla.
On the northern peak of Supārśva is a great tree named Vaṭa, a banyan with a massive trunk whose circumference is three yojanas. (27)
Adorned on all sides with various clusters of flower garlands and with branches hanging down, it was frequented by the Siddhas.
With fruits that are always like hanging jars and golden in color,
that tree indeed shines as the banner-tree of the Uttarakurus.
The younger brothers of Sanatkumāra were the mind-born sons of Brahmā;
seven highly fortunate ones among them became renowned there as the Kurus.
Therein, by the high-souled ones who possess steady knowledge free from passion,
the eternal world— though subject to destruction— is declared to be imperishable.
The region marked with the names of those seven high-souled ones is always renowned both in heaven and here on earth as Uttarakuru.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 77.
Rudra said:
"In that manner, I shall describe to you the four lords of mountains in their proper order—
delightful places to be traversed and resounded with the warbling of birds."
There were also many peaks belonging to various mountain ranges,
consisting of the playful sports of the gods together with divine women.
Resounding with the songs of kinnaras, they were rendered even more delightful by winds that were cool, gentle, and fragrant. || 3 ||
O sinless ones, hear their names as they shine forth in the four directions:
in the east is the one named Caitraratha, and in the south is Gandhamādana;
by their power, these possess excellent waters and are divided into nine sectors.
Likewise, having entered the forest groves, the deities, accompanied by thousands of celestial women,
sported in those regions filled with supreme joy.
There were delightful surroundings with the warbling of birds,
and bathing-places strewn with jewels containing waters of great merit.
They were large and resounded with many water-machines, while their hanging branches echoed with the cries of flocks of birds and swarms of bees.
And there were lakes adorned with lotuses, blue water-lilies,
and white lilies on those four mountains, which possessed manifold virtues.
Aruṇoda is to the east, Mānasa is remembered to the south,
Asitoda is to the west, and likewise Mahābhadra is to the north;
they are adorned with white and tawny water-lilies and kahlāra lotuses.
Listen as I describe in truth those mountains of the sunrise which are known by name as belonging to the east. (10)
Vikaṅka, Maṇiśṛṅga, Supātra, the great Upala, Mahānīla, Kumbha, Subindu, and likewise Madana. || 11 ||
Veṇunaddha, Sumedā, Niṣadha, and Devaparvata—
these are the excellent mountains, as well as other meritorious peaks.
To the east of Mandara are the Siddhas and mountains numbering ten thousand;
here, to the south of Lake Mānasa, are the great mountains.
Listen to those who have been mentioned by me according to their names:
Śaila, Triśiras, and Śiśira, the best of mountains. || 14 ||
Kapi, Śatamakṣa, Turaga, Sānumant, Tāmradṛś, Viṣa, and likewise the mountain Śvetodana; || 15 ||
Samūla, Sarala, and the Ratnaketu mountain; Ekamūla, Mahāśṛṅga, and Gajamūla-śāvaka as well. || 16 ||
Pañcaśaila, Kailāsa, and Himavat, the best of mountains;
listen as I describe those great northern mountains. || 17 ||
Kapila, Piṅgala, Bhadra, Sarasa, and Mahācala; Kumuda, Madhumān, Garjana, and likewise Markaṭa. || 18 ||
Kṛṣṇa, Pāṇḍava, and likewise Sahasraśiras; Pāriyātra, the lord of mountains, and Śṛṅgavān, the best of peaks—these are remembered as the glorious, excellent mountains in the west. (19)
O best of the twice-born, O Brahmins, listen as I describe those mountains situated to the north of Lake Mahābhadraka. (20)
The great mountain Haṃsakūṭa, the mountain Vṛṣahaṃsa, Kapiñjala the lord of mountains, and the peaked Indraśaila; || 21 ||
Nīla, Kanakaśṛṅga, the mountain Śataśṛṅga, Puṣkara, Meghaśaila, Viraja—the best of mountains—and Jāruci the lord of mountains; these are remembered as the northern [mountains]. || 22 ||
Now, learn of the plateaus, the inner valleys, and the lakes belonging to these principal mountains, in order, as they appear toward the north. (23)
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter in the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 78.
Rudra said:
Between that king of mountains, Sītānta, and Kumuda,
there is a valley frequented by various creatures and filled with birds.
There, three hundred yojanas in length and one hundred yojanas in width, is the delightful and beautiful lake Surocana, filled with delicious and pure water.
It was adorned with fragrant white lotuses (puṇḍarīka) measuring a droṇa in size,
and with great red lotuses (mahāpadma) possessing hundreds of petals.
That meritorious lake named Śrīsaras, presided over by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, and great serpents, is radiant here and in other worlds as well.
It was filled with clear waters and served as a refuge for all living beings;
and there, in the midst of that lotus forest, stood a single great lotus.
It is fashioned with ten million petals, possessing the luster of the rising sun;
it is eternally blossomed and sweet, appearing as an exceedingly perfect circle due to its constant movement.
Abounding with beautiful networks of filaments and resounding with the humming of intoxicated bees,
in its very center dwells the Blessed Goddess Śrī herself eternally; Lakṣmī, moreover, regards that abode as her own personified form— of this there is no doubt.
On the shore of that lake, frequented by perfected beings (siddhas),
there was a great and beautiful grove of bilva trees, always abounding in flowers and fruit.
It was one hundred yojanas wide and two hundred yojanas long,
filled on all sides with great trees whose peaks rose half a krośa high,
crowded with massive trunks and adorned with thousands of branches.
With fruits resembling the sun in number, both green and pale-white, tasting like nectar, as large as kettledrums, and fragrant; (10)
With trees being shattered and falling, it scattered the ground and the interior of the forest;
thus, by name, it became renowned throughout all the worlds as Śrīvana.
That auspicious place was filled on all eight directions by gods and others,
and was frequented by meritorious sages who subsist on bilva fruits;
there, Śrī is eternally established, attended by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas).
The interval between each individual lord of mountains and each mountain of jewels is one hundred yojanas in width and two hundred yojanas in length.
The stainless lotus grove, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
shines like a flower held by Lakṣmī, ever as if blazing with light.
And for half a krośa, that forest shines with its golden hue, covered by peaks and great trunks, and with the tips of its branches in full bloom. 15.
With a circumference of two cubits and a length and width of three cubits each,
they resembled powdered realgar and were adorned with pale-yellow filaments.
The entire forest shines, filled with enchanting blossoms that are fully opened and beautiful with fragrance, resounding with the humming of intoxicated bees.
That forest was frequented by Dānavas, Daityas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas,
Kinnaras, Apsarases, and those of great enjoyment.
There was the hermitage of the blessed Kaśyapa, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati),
crowded with hosts of perfected beings and holy men, and filled with various types of retreats.
Between Mount Mahānīla and Mount Kumbha, however, there is a river named Sukhā; on its bank is a great forest.
The beautiful and glorious Tālavana forest is fifty yojanas in length and thirty yojanas in circumference, with its trees rising half a krośa high.
They were possessed of great strength, great essence, stability, and immovability;
they were auspicious, resembling large collyrium in shape, rounded, and yielding great fruit.
Endowed with the qualities of refined fragrances and frequented by the Siddhas, it is said to be located right there, near the elephant Airāvata.
Between Airāvata and Rudra, on the Devaśaila mountain,
it is one thousand yojanas in length and one hundred yojanas in width.
For the entire ground was a single solid rock, devoid of trees and creepers,
and it was submerged on all sides by water reaching up to the height of a foot.
Thus, O best of Brahmins, these various inner valleys on the sides of Meru have been described to you in their proper order and according to tradition.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 79.
Rudra said:

Now, the mountain valleys situated in the southern direction, frequented by the Siddhas, shall be described. Between Śiśira and Pataṅga lies the White Land (Śuklabhūmi), where trees have been shed by the falling of the Muktā-latās.
Furthermore, the peak at Ikṣukṣepa is adorned with trees.
The delightful Udumbara forest was frequented by flocks of birds. || 1 ||
That forest shines, laden with fruits resembling great tortoises.
The eight classes of divine beings always frequent that forest. || 2 ||
Varāha Purāṇa || 3 ||

There flow rivers with clear, sweet, and abundant waters. There stands the hermitage of the venerable Prajāpati Kardama, crowded with various sages, and that forest extends for one hundred yojanas in circumference.

Likewise, between Mount Tāmra and Mount Pataṅga, there is a great lake extending for a hundred yojanas in width and twice that in length, adorned on all sides with dense, thousand-petaled lotuses and water-lilies resembling the rising sun. It is inhabited by many Siddhas and Gandharvas. In its center stands a great peak, one hundred yojanas long and thirty yojanas wide, adorned with various minerals and gems; upon it is a vast carriage-road with jeweled walls and archways.

In that [place] was a great city of the Vidyādharas. There dwelt a king of the Vidyādharas named Puloman, with a retinue of a hundred thousand. Furthermore, between Mount Śveta and the lord of mountains, Vikha-khācala, there was a lake.
On its eastern shore was a vast mango grove, filled on all sides with fruits as large as great jars, golden-hued and exceedingly fragrant.
Devas, Gandharvas, and others also dwell there.

Between the lord of mountains Sumūla and Vasudhāra, at a place thirty yojanas wide and fifty yojanas long, is the region named Bilvasthalī. There, fruits resembling coral fall, moistening the ground with their clay; and the Suguhyakas and others, subsisting on those Bilva fruits, frequent that region.

And likewise, between Vasudhārā and Ratnadhārā, there is a forest of fragrant *kiṃśuka* trees, thirty *yojanas* wide and one hundred *yojanas* long, which is in perpetual bloom; its fragrance perfumes a hundred *yojanas*.
There, it is inhabited by *siddhas* and provided with water.
And there is the great temple of the god Āditya.
Every month, the Blessed Sun, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), descends;
the gods and others pay homage to him, the progenitor of time.

Furthermore, between Mount Kailāsa and Pañcakūṭa lies a region extending a thousand *yojanas* in length and a hundred *yojanas* in width, as white as a swan, unassailable by small creatures, and like a staircase to heaven upon the circle of the earth.

Now, the mountain valleys situated in the western direction are described. Between the mountains Supārśva and Śikhin, there is a ground of stone extending for one hundred yojanas in every direction, which is eternally heated and difficult to touch.
In its center is a circle thirty yojanas wide, a place of fire. There, the Blessed One Saṃvartaka, the destroyer of the world, blazes at all times without fuel.

And between the two excellent mountains, Kumuda and Añjana, there is a grove of *ātuluṅga* trees extending for a hundred *yojanas*, inaccessible to all beings. That grove shines, being covered with fruits of yellow hue.
And between those two mountains, which are tawny and white, there is a lake-pond extending for many hundreds of *yojanas*, adorned with large *kumuda* lotuses resounding with the humming of bees.
And therein is the abode of the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord.

Likewise, between the two great mountains Śukla and Pāṇḍura, there is a single rocky region thirty *yojanas* wide and ninety *yojanas* long, devoid of trees. Therein lies a mud-free pond and a terrestrial lotus-pond (*sthalapadminī*) with trees, adorned by various kinds of lotuses.

In the center of that [region] stands a great banyan tree measuring five *yojanas*. In it dwells the Lord, the Moon-crested One, the Lord of Hairs, clothed in blue garments, being praised by Yakṣas and others.

Between Mount Sahasraśikhara and Mount Kumuda, there is a place fifty yojanas in length and twenty yojanas in width, with peaks as high as a thrown sugar-cane stalk, frequented by many birds and adorned with the fruits of various trees that exude sweet juices. Therein lies the great hermitage of Indra, fashioned according to divine design.

Likewise, between Śaṅkhakūṭa and Ṛṣabha, there is the delightful Puruṣasthalī, possessing many virtues and extending for many yojanas; it is filled with fragrant *kaṅkolaka* trees the size of *bilva* fruits. Therein dwell elephants and other beings, intoxicated by the scent of human bodies. Similarly, between Kapiñjala and Nāgaśaila, there is that plateau, two hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and one hundred yojanas in width, adorned with various forests, provided with groves of grapes and dates, endowed with many trees and creepers, and graced by numerous lakes.

And likewise, between Puṣkara and Mahāmegha, there is a great plateau sixty *yojanas* wide and one hundred *yojanas* long, as level as the palm of a hand and devoid of trees or creepers. On its sides are four great forests and lakes extending for many *yojanas*. There are plateaus and valleys measuring ten, five, seven, eight, thirty, and twenty *yojanas*. Among them are certain most formidable mountain recesses. Thus ends the eightieth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 80.
Rudra said:
Hereafter, the dwellings of the gods upon the mountains are described. There, on that mountain known as Śānta, is the pleasure-ground of Mahendra.
Therein lies the forest of Pārijātaka trees belonging to the King of the Gods.
On its eastern side is the mountain named Kuñjara;
upon it are eight cities of the Dānavas. Likewise, on Vajraka, the best of mountains, there are many cities of the Rākṣasas.
And they are known by the name Nīlakas; they can assume any form at will.
On Mahānīla as well, there are ancient cities belonging to the lords of mountains, where fifteen thousand Kinnaras are said to dwell.
Therein dwell kings such as Devadatta and Candra;
there are fifteen proud kinnaras,
and those golden cities that serve as entrances to the subterranean realms.

And on Candrodaya, the best of mountains, is the abode of the Nāgas; they enter into caves, and within those caves dwell the lords of the Dānavas, who are devoted to the domain of Vainateya. On Veṇumatī as well are three cities of the Vidyādharas, each thirty hundred yojanas in width and likewise in length.
Ulūkaromaśa, Mahāvetra, and others were kings of the Vidyādharas;
and upon each of the kings of mountains, Garuḍa himself is stationed.
On Kuñjara, the best of mountains, Paśupati is eternally established.
The bull-bannered Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, the best of yogins, the Lord who is the primordial Person, stands there surrounded by many thousands of millions of *gaṇas* and spirits.

On Vasudhāra is the abode of the Vasus, the possessors of flowers; and on the peaks of Vasudhāra and Ratnadhāra are the cities of the eight Vasus and the seven Ṛṣis in number. And on the supreme mountain Ekaśṛṅga is the station of Prajāpati, the four-faced Brahmā. And on Gajaparvata, the Blessed Goddess herself dwells, surrounded by the great elements.
And on Vasudhāra, the best of mountains, is the abode of sages, siddhas, and vidyādharas;
there are eighty-four other cities with great walls and gateways. And there dwell the gandharvas named Anekaparvata, who are skilled in combat.

And their sovereign is the god Rājarāja Ekapiṅgala. On the mountain Pañcakūṭa dwell the gods and rākṣasas; on Śataśṛṅga, the dānavas; and there are one hundred cities of the yakṣas. On the mountain Tāmrābha, there are one hundred cities of Takṣaka. On Mount Viśākha is the abode of Guha. And on the excellent mountain Śvetodaya is the palace of the great gandharvas.
On Harikūṭa dwells the god Hari; on Kumuda is the abode of the Kinnaras; on Añjana dwell the Mahoragas;

and on Sahasraśikhara is the residence of the Daityas of fierce deeds. On Mukuṭa, the best of mountains, which has a thousand peaks and is adorned with golden garlands, there are four sanctuaries. Thus, on these Meru mountains, there are the abodes of the gods.
The layout of the cities on Devakūṭa, the boundary mountain, is now described.
A region of one hundred yojanas in extent belonging to Garuḍa is situated above it;
alongside that very place are seven Gandharva cities, thirty yojanas wide and forty yojanas long.
And there are the Gandharvas named Āgneyas, who are exceedingly powerful;
and there is another city there, a circle thirty yojanas in extent, belonging to the Saiṃhikeyas.
And there, upon Devakūṭa, the deeds of the divine sages are seen.

And the city of the Kālakeyas is right there. Likewise, on the inner slope of that very mountain, to its south, is the city of the haughty Kāmarūpis, thirty *yojanas* in width and sixty-two *yojanas* in length, named Sunāman. And in the center of that Hemakūṭa is the banyan tree of Mahādeva. Now follows the description of Kailāsa: on the slope of Kailāsa, extending for a hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth, is the realm pervaded by the Bhuvanamālā; and in the middle of that is the assembly hall.
And there stands the celestial palace named Puṣkara;

it is the residence and abode of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada). There dwell the great treasures known as Padma, Mahāpadma, Makara, Kacchapa, Kumuda, Śaṅkha, Nīla, Nanda, and Mahānidhi. There also is the dwelling place of the world-protectors, beginning with Candra. And there flows the river named Mandākinī.
Likewise, there are rivers named Kanakamandā and Mandā;

there are also other rivers there. On its eastern side, there are ten cities of the Gandharvas, each eighty *yojanas* in length and thirty *yojanas* in width; and in them dwell kings such as Sakubāhu, Harikeśa, Citrasena, and others. Furthermore, on its western peak, there is a Yakṣa city measuring eighty *yojanas* in length and forty *yojanas* in width;
and in those [cities] dwell leaders such as Mahāmāli, Sunetra, Cakra, and others.
On its very southern side, within groves, caves, and mountain caverns, extending as far as the ocean, there are a hundred cities of the Kinnaras.
In those cities, there are a hundred kings, headed by Bhagadatta, along with Drumasugrīva and others.
And there, the marriage of Rudra together with Umā took place.

Gaurī performed austerities there, and Rudra remained in the form of a Kirāta. While stationed right there, Śaṅkara, accompanied by Soma, beheld Jambūdvīpa. There, the forest named Umāvana was resounded by the songs of many Kinnaras and Gandharvas, and was filled with Apsarases and numerous flowering creepers and vines;
it was there that the Blessed Maheśvara assumed his body half-female and half-male.
And there also was the arrow-forest of Kārttikeya.
Between Puṣpacitra and Krauñca, the consecration of Kārtikeya was performed; and on its eastern shore is the village named Kalāpa, the dwelling place of hosts of perfected sages (siddha-muni).
Furthermore, there are indeed many thousands of hermitages belonging to great seers such as Mārkaṇḍeya, Vasiṣṭha, Parāśara, Nala, Viśvāmitra, Uddālaka, and others.
Now, listen to the description of the portion of Niṣadha, the lord of mountains, to the west.
And upon its central peak is the abode of Viṣṇu, the sanctuary of Mahādeva.
On its northern shore is the great city known as Lambā, extending thirty yojanas, belonging to the Rākṣasas.
On its southern side is the city of Bilapraveśana.
To the west of the Divider (Prabhedaka) are the cities of the gods, dānavas, siddhas, and others.
Upon the summit of that mountain stands a great stone slab of Soma;
and on the day of the full moon, Soma himself descends upon it.
On its very northern side is the mountain named Trikūṭa;
there Brahmā sometimes resides, as does the abode of Fire, where the embodied Fire is worshipped by the gods. And on the excellent northern peak, known as Śṛṅga, are the abodes of the deities.
To the east is the abode of Nārāyaṇa; in the middle, that of Brahmā;

and to the west, that of Śaṅkara. There, as well, are certain cities belonging to the Yakṣas and others. On its northern shore, on the great mountain Jātudhāna, there is a lake named Nandajala with a circumference of thirty yojanas, where the Naga king named Nanda dwells, fierce with his hundred heads. These are to be known as the eight divine mountains. In that sequence, they possess the colors of gold, silver, jewels, lapis lazuli, emerald, and vermilion, and so forth.

And this earth is filled with hundreds of millions of countless [beings], among whom are the abodes of the Siddhas and Vidyādharas; and those [abodes] on the side of Mount Meru, forming a circular basin like a whorl of filaments, are celebrated as the "World of the Siddhas" (Siddhaloka).
This earth is situated in the shape of a lotus.
And this sequence is generally set forth in all the Purāṇas.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 81.
Rudra said:

Now listen to the descent of the rivers. There is that which is celebrated as the ocean of space (*ākāśasamudra*), known by the name Sāman; from it the river that travels through the sky has issued forth. It is incessantly agitated by Indra’s elephant. Its height is eighty-four thousand [yojanas]. It forms the Sudarśana region of Meru. Having cascaded down from the edges of the peaks of Meru, it becomes fourfold. Falling without support for sixty thousand *yojanas*, it proceeds in a clockwise direction and divides into four streams.

By the names Sītā, Cālakanandā, Cakṣus, and Bhadrā, she is called Gaṅgā because she flows across the earth, cleaving through many hundreds of thousands of mountains according to her course. Now, the Amaragaṇḍikā on the side of Gandhamādana is described: it is thirty-one thousand yojanas in length and four hundred yojanas in width. Therein lie all the Ketumāla regions. The men are dark-complexioned and possess great strength; the women are the color of blue lotuses and are beautiful to behold. And there are great *panasa* trees.

There dwells Īśvara, the son of Brahmā. There, at the well, men are free from old age and disease, and their lifespan is ten thousand years. On the eastern side of Mālyavat is the eastern ridge, Ekaśṛṅga, measuring one thousand yojanas in extent; there lie the regions known as Bhadrāśva, and the Bhadrasāla forest is situated there. The trees are black mango trees (*kālāmra*); the men are white with the complexion of lotuses, while the women have the hue of white water-lilies (*kumuda*); their lifespan is ten thousand years.

And there are five mountain ranges there, namely: Śailavarṇa, Mālākhya, Koraja, Triparṇa, and Nīla; the regions situated in that water derive their names from these very mountains. And those regions drink from these rivers.

They are as follows: the Sītā, the Suvāhinī, the Haṃsavatī, the Kāsā, the Mahācakrā, the Candravatī, the Kāverī, the Surasā, the Śākhāvatī, the Indravatī, the Aṅgāravāhinī, the Haritoyā, the Somāvartā, the Śatahradā, the Vanamālā, the Vasumatī, the Haṃsā, the Suparṇā, the Pañcagaṅgā, the Dhanuṣmatī, the Maṇivaprā, the Subrahmabhāgā, the Vilāsinī, the Kṛṣṇatoyā, the Puṇyodā, the Nāgavatī, the Śivā, the Śevālinī, the Maṇitaṭā, the Kṣīrodā, the Varuṇāvatī, the Viṣṇupadī, the Mahānadī, the Hiraṇyaskandhavāhā, the Surāvatī, and the Kāmodā.

And the Patākās—these are the great rivers. They are proclaimed to be equal to the Gaṅgā; they destroy sin from birth until the end of life. There are also crores of small rivers. Those who drink from these rivers have a lifespan of ten thousand years; they are devotees of Rudra and Umā.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter of the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 82.
Rudra said:

This natural disposition of the Bhadrāśvas has been proclaimed, and the Ketumālas have been described in detail. To the west of the Niṣadha mountain and the mountain of Indra, the principal mountain ranges, inhabited regions, and rivers are now being described. Thus, from these seven principal mountains—Viśākha, Kambala, Jayanta, Kṛṣṇa, Harita, Aśoka, and Vardhamāna—there is a progeny numbering in the tens of millions.

The districts inhabited by them should be understood as bearing those very names. For example: Sauragrāma, Attasāṃtapa, Kṛtasurāśravaṇa, Kambala, Māheya, Acala, Kūṭavāsa, Mūlatapa, Krauñca, Kṛṣṇāṅga, Maṇi, Paṅkaja, Cūḍa, Malasomīya, Samudrāntaka, Kuru, Kuñca, Suvarṇa, Taṭaka, Kuhaka, Śvetāṅga, Kṛṣṇapāṭavidaka, Kapilakarṇika, Mahiṣaka, Kubjaka, Raṇāṭa, Mahotkaṭa, Śukanāsa, Gajabhūmaka, Kurañjana, Manāhakiṃkisa, Pārṇabhaumaka, Coraka, and Dhūmajanman.

The people of these districts—Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Vāca, Sahāṅga, Madhureya, Śukra, Cakreya, Śravaṇa, Mattakāsika, Godāvara, Kulapañjā, Varjjaha, Modaśālaka, and Ekalavya—drink the waters of the rivers that rise from those mountains.

They are as follows: Plakṣā, Mahākadambā, Mānasī, Śyāmā, Sumedhā, Bahulā, Vivarṇā, Puṅkhā, Mālā, Darbhavatī, Bhadrānadī, Śukanadī, Pallavā, Bhīmā, Prabhañjanā, Kāmbā, Kuśāvatī, Dakṣā, Kāsavatī, Tuṅgā, Puṇyodā, Candrāvatī, Sumūlāvatī, Kakudminī, Viśālā, Karaṇṭakā, Pīvarī, Mahāmāyā, Mahiṣī, Mānuṣī, and Caṇḍā—these are the principal rivers; the remaining ones are minor rivers by the thousands. Thus ends the eighty-third chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 83.
Rudra said:
They describe, according to the proper method, all those who dwell upon the mountains of both the northern and the southern regions.
Listen to that, O Brahmins, as it is being proclaimed by me with a concentrated mind.
To the south of Śveta and to the north of Nīla, in the northwest region,
there is a land named Ramyaka; there human beings are born who are preeminent in intelligence, pure, and free from old age and foul odors.
There too, there is a very great tree known as the Rohita Nyagrodha; indeed,
by drinking the juice from its fruit, all the humans born there possess a lifespan of ten thousand years and are endowed with divine forms.
To the north of Śveta and to the south of Triśṛṅga is the region named Hiraṇmaya; there flows the river Hairaṇvatī,
and there dwell powerful Yakṣas who can assume any form at will.
By that [merit], one lives for eleven thousand years;
furthermore, another one hundred and fifteen years are lived.
In that region, small *lakuca* trees are situated;
indeed, by consuming their fruit, human beings live there.

Likewise, on Triśṛṅga, with its peaks successively composed of jewels, gold, and all kinds of gems, from its northern peak down to the edge of the southern ocean lies Uttarakuru. Garments and ornaments grow upon the very trees; there are milk-yielding trees and milk-based liquors. The ground is made of jewels and the sand is of gold. Therein dwell men who have fallen from heaven, possessing a lifespan of thirteen thousand years.

To the west of that very continent, after crossing four thousand yojanas, lies Candradvīpa, which is one thousand yojanas in circumference and situated beyond the world of the gods. In its center are two preeminent mountains named Candrakānta and Sūryakānta. Between them flows the great river named Candrāvatī, which is crowded with many trees, fruits, and various streams. This is the region of Kuruvārsa.

To its north, after crossing five thousand yojanas across the ocean adorned with garlands of waves, lies Sūryadvīpa, extending for a thousand yojanas in circumference. In its center stands a preeminent mountain, a hundred yojanas in width and rising to the same height. From it flows the river named Sūryāvartā. There resides the Sun; the inhabitants there have the Sun as their deity, possess his complexion, and have a lifespan of ten thousand years.

To the west of that island, after crossing the ocean for four thousand yojanas, there is an island ten thousand yojanas in circumference called Rudrākara. There is a throne of Bhadra (Bhadrāsana) adorned with many jewels, and there Vāyu dwells in embodied form. The inhabitants have the color of refined gold and a lifespan of five thousand years.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter in the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 84.
Rudra said:

This arrangement of the earth-lotus has been described. Now hear of Bhārata in its nine divisions, as follows: Indra, Kaseru, Tāmravarṇa, Gabhasti, Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gandharva, Vāruṇa, and Bhātara. Each is surrounded by an ocean and measures one thousand *yojanas*. And therein there are seven principal mountain ranges (*kulaparvata*), as follows: Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, and Ṛkṣaparvata.

The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra—these are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas). Others, such as Mandara, Śārada, Dardura, Kolāhala, Surama, Maināka, Vaidyuta, Vārandhama, Pāṇḍura, Tuṅgaprastha, Kṛṣṇagiri, Jayanta, Raivata, Ṛṣyamūka, Gomanta, Citrakūṭa, Śrīcakorakūṭa, Śailakṛtasthala, and so forth, are the minor mountains (kṣudraparvatas). The remaining ones are even smaller. Among them dwell Āryan and Mleccha populations, and they drink water from these rivers.

They are as follows: the Gaṅgā, Sindhu, Sarasvatī, Śatadru, Vitastā, Vipāśā, Candrabhāgā, Sarayū, Yamunā, Irāvatī, Devikā, Kuhū, Gomatī, Dhūtapāpā, Bāhudā, Dṛṣadvatī, Kauśikī, Niḥsvarā, Gaṇḍakī, Cakṣuṣmatī, and Lohitā—these are the rivers that have issued from the foot of the Himavat.

Vedasmṛti, Vedavatī, Sindhuparṇā, Sacandanā, Sadācārā, Rohipārā, Carmaṇvatī, Vidiśā, and Vedatrayī—these arise from the Pāriyātra mountains. Śoṇā, Jyotīrathā, Narmadā, Surasā, Mandākinī, Daśārṇā, Citrakūṭā, Tamasā, Pippalā, Karatoyā, Piśācikā, Citrotpalā, Viśālā, Vañjulā, Bālukā, Vāhinī, Śuktimatī, Virajā, Paṅkinī, Rirī, and Kuhū—these are born from the Ṛkṣa mountains.

The Maṇijālā, Śubhā, Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Śīghrodā, Veṣṇā, Pāśā, Vaitaraṇī, Vedī, Pālī, Kumudvatī, Toyā, Durgā, and Antyagirā—these arise from the foothills of the Vindhya. The Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇā, Veṇā, Vañjulā, Tuṅgabhadrā, Suprayogā, Vāhyā, and Kāverī—these arise from the foothills of the Sahya. The Śatamālā, Tāmraparṇī, Puṣpāvatī, and Utpalāvatī—these arise from the Malaya mountains.

The Tiryāmā, Ṛṣikulyā, Ikṣulā, Trividā, Lāṅgūlinī, Vaṃśavarā, Mahendratanayā, Ṛṣikā, Lūmatī, Mandagāminī, and Palāśinī—these are the rivers originating from the Śuktimat mountain. These are the principal rivers of the Kulaparvatas; the remaining ones are minor streams. This Jambūdvīpa measures one hundred thousand yojanas. Beyond this, learn of Śākadvīpa. With a circumference twice the extent of Jambūdvīpa, the salt-water ocean surrounds Jambūdvīpa entirely with double its size.

And there, the provinces are auspicious, and people die only after a long time; this land is free from famine, old age, and disease. Seven great mountain ranges remain there, and on both sides of it lie the salt ocean and the milk ocean. There, extending toward the east, is the lord of mountains named Udaya (Rising). To its west is the mountain named Jaladhara (Water-Bearer), which is also celebrated as Candra (the Moon). Indra takes water from that [mountain] and rains it down. Beyond that lies the mountain named Raivataka.

That very [region] is described as Nārada; and from that [region], Nāradaparvata arose. Beyond that is the mountain named Śyāma; and on that [mountain], the subjects attained a dark (śyāma) complexion. That very [region] is described as Dundubhi. On that [mountain], various kinds of subjects known as Siddhas are proclaimed to be sporting. Beyond that is the mountain named Rajata; that very [region] is called Śāka. Beyond that is Ambikeya, and he is called Vibhrāja. That very [region] is called Kesara, and from there the wind sets forth.

The regions are named after the mountains themselves; for example, Udaya, Sukumāra, Jaladhāraka, Kṣemaka, and Mahādruma are the principal ones, and they should also be mentioned by their second names. In the center of that [region] is a Śāka tree, and there are seven great rivers with two names each. Namely, these rivers are Sukumārī, Kumārī, Nandā, Veṇikā, Dhenu, Ikṣumatī, and Gabhasti.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 85.

Now hear about the third continent, Kuśadvīpa. Kuśadvīpa is surrounded by the Ocean of Milk, which is twice as wide as Śākadvīpa. There too, there are seven principal mountain ranges (*kulaparvata*), all of which have two names. They are as follows: it is called both Kumuda and Vidruma; Unnata and Hemaparvata are one and the same; Balāhaka and Dyutimān are one and the same; likewise, Droṇa and Puṣpavān are one and the same; and the mountain Kaṅka is the same as Kuśeśaya.

Likewise, the sixth mountain, named Mahiṣa, is called Hari; Agni dwells there. The seventh, however, is named Kakudmat, which is celebrated as Mandara. These are the mountains situated in Kuśadvīpa. From these, the division of regions (varṣabheda) occurs, each having two names. That which is Śveta is proclaimed as Udbhida for Kumuda; that which is Lohita becomes Veṇumaṇḍala for Unnata.

The cloud of Balāhaka is that very one called Rathākāra; the green [cloud] of Droṇa is that which becomes Balādhana. That of Kaṅka is named Kakudmat; that of Mānasamahiṣa is Vṛttimat, and that of Prabhākara is Kapila—these are the names by which they are reckoned. These are the regions (varṣas). There, the rivers have two names: she who is called Pratapā is also called Praveśā; the second is Śivā and she is also Yaśodā; the third is Pitrā and she is called Kṛṣṇā.

The fourth is named Hrādinī; she alone is called Candrā. The fifth is Vidyunmālā; she alone is Śuklā. The sixth is Varṇā; she alone is Vibhāvarī. The seventh is Mahatī; she alone is Dhṛti. These are the principal rivers; the remaining ones are small streams. Such is the configuration of Kuśadvīpa. It is said that Śākadvīpa is situated with double its extent. In its center stands a great cluster of Kuśa grass. And this Kuśadvīpa is surrounded by the Dadhimaṇḍoda ocean, which is twice the size of the Kṣīroda ocean.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 86.
Rudra said:

Next comes Krauñca, which is twice the size of Kuśadvīpa; it is surrounded by an ocean twice its own extent. In that [continent] there are seven principal mountains: the first is Krauñca, then Vidyullata, Raivata, Mānasa, Saiva-pāvaka, likewise Andhakāra, and Saivācchodaka. Devāvṛtta is called Surāpa. Beyond that is Deviṣṭha, which is Kāñcanaśṛṅga. Beyond Devananda is Govinda, also known as Dvivinda.

Beyond that is Puṇḍarīka; these seven mountains, consisting of jewels, are situated in Krauñca-dvīpa. All of them are equal in height to one another. Therein lie the regions: the region of Krauñca is known as Kuśala, and it is remembered as Mādhava; Vāmana’s region is Mano’nuga, and it is Saṃvartaka, then Uṣṇavān, Somaprakāśa, Pāvaka, Sudarśana, Andhakāra, Saṃmoha, and finally Munideśa, which is Prakāśa.
