Beyond that is Dundubhi, which is likewise called a calamity; there too, there are exactly seven rivers. || 1 ||
Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Sandhyā, Rātri, Manojavā, Khyāti, and Puṇḍarīkā are remembered as the seven [rivers].

Gaurī is indeed the Puṣpavahā; Kumudvatī is the Tāmravatī; Rodhasandhyā is the Sukhāvahā; Manojavā is the Kṣiprodā; Khyāti is the Gobahulā; and Puṇḍarīkā is the Citravegā. The remaining rivers are minor streams. Krauñcadvīpa is surrounded by the Ghṛtoda ocean, and the Ghṛtoda ocean is surrounded by Śālmala [dvīpa]. 2.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter in the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 87.
Rudra said:
"I shall describe the human beings in the three remaining continents;
now listen as I proclaim Śālmala, the fifth region."
Śālmala-dvīpa is considered to be twice the extent of Krauñca-dvīpa. || 1 ||

Surrounding the ocean of clarified butter (ghṛtasamudra), it stands established; its extent is double that [of the preceding], and there are seven principal mountains there, as many regions (varṣas), and as many rivers. And the mountains there are: Sumahān, Pīta, Śātakaumbha, Sārvaguṇasauvarṇa, Rohita, Sumanas, Kuśala, Jāmbūnada, and Vaidyuta—these are the boundary mountains (kulaparvatas) and the regions. Now, the sixth, Gomeda, is described.

Just as Śālmala is surrounded by the Suroda ocean, so too is the Suroda ocean surrounded by Gomeda, which is twice its size. And there, there are two principal mountain ranges: one is called Tāvasara, and the other is Kumuda. The ocean is the Ikṣurasa (sugarcane juice) ocean, and it is surrounded by Puṣkara, which is twice its size. In that region known as Puṣkara, there is a mountain named Mānasa. That continent is also divided into two parts of equal measure, and it is surrounded by the Svādūdaka (sweet water) ocean. Beyond that is the Kaṭāha (the shell). This is the measurement of the earth.

The measurement of the extent of the shell of the cosmic egg is such that no enumeration of these kinds of eggs exists. In every Kalpa, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, assuming the form of a boar, enters the depths of the subterranean realm (Rasātala) and, having lifted them up with a single tusk, establishes them in their place.
This path has been described to you regarding the length and breadth of the earth. May it be well with you; O twice-born ones, I shall go to my abode on Kailāsa.
The illustrious Varāha said:
Having spoken thus, Rudra departed, his form becoming invisible in an instant;
and all those gods and sages returned as they had come.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 88.
Dharaṇī said:
Some know Śiva as the Supreme Soul and the Meritorious One;
others know him as Hari, and some as Īśāna or the Four-faced One (Brahmā). || 1 ||
"O Lord, among these which deity is superior, and which is inferior? O All-pervading One, explain this to me; my curiosity is great. (2)
Śrī Varāha said: The supreme deity is Nārāyaṇa; from him the four-faced one was born.
From him, O Goddess, Rudra came into being, and he attained omniscience.
O fair-faced one, O lady of beautiful limbs, O sinless one, listen as I recount all her many various wonders. (4)
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, variegated with various minerals,
the three-eyed God who bears the trident dwells day after day.
One day, the god who wields the Pināka bow, honored by all beings, was present in great splendor, surrounded by his attendants and accompanied by Gaurī.
There, some groups with lion-faces roar like lions;
others have the faces of elephants, and likewise others have the faces of horses.
Others had the faces of porpoises, others had the faces of boars;

others were fierce with the faces of horses, or the faces of donkeys, or likewise the faces of goats; they had the faces of goats and fish, being cruel, infinite in number, and bearing weapons in their hands.
Some sang, danced, ran, and clapped their hands;
those of great strength laughed, shouted "kilakila," and roared.
Some leaders of the Gaṇas, seizing clods of earth, fought;
others, proud of their strength, fought with wrestling.
Thus was the Lord Maheśvara surrounded by thousands of Gaṇas.
While the best of gods himself remained sporting with the goddess,
Brahmā himself arrived in haste accompanied by the gods.
Then, seeing him arrived and having honored him according to the prescribed rites,
the supreme god Rudra spoke to the unborn Brahmā.
"O Brahmin, tell me quickly what is the purpose of your arrival;
and why have the gods come into my presence with such haste? (13)
Brahmā said: "There is a great Daitya named Andhaka; by him all the inhabitants of heaven have been afflicted, and having learned of my presence, they have come to me seeking refuge."
Then all these gods were told by me regarding Bhava:
"O Lord of Gods, let us go"; thereupon they assembled together. (15)
Having spoken thus, Brahmā himself looked toward the wielder of the Pināka bow and mentally remembered Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord. Then the god Nārāyaṇa stood positioned between the two.
Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, having come together as one,
gazed at one another with subtle vision, filled with joy.
Then, their threefold vision became unified as one;
from that vision, a maiden of divine form was born.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with dark, curly hair,
she has a beautiful nose, lovely forehead, a fine face, and is well-proportioned.
Whatever characteristics were defined by Tvaṣṭṛ for one whose tongue is Agni,
all of that is seen together in its entirety in a maiden.
Then, having seen that maiden, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara said: "Who are you, O auspicious one? Tell us; what is the wise purpose [for which you have come]? (21)
That maiden, who possessed three colors—black, white, and yellow—said:
"O best of beings, I have been born from the union of your glances.
Do you not know me, the fair-hipped one, your own power, the Supreme Goddess? (22)
Then Brahmā and the others, being pleased with her, granted her a boon:
"O Goddess Trikālā by name, protect the universe at all times. (23)
O sinless one, O highly fortunate lady, there will also be other names for you, arising from your qualities, which shall grant all accomplishments.
Moreover, O Goddess, there is another reason: you possess three colors, O fair-faced one.
O Goddess, quickly assume your own three forms through these three colors.
Thus addressed by the gods, she then assumed a threefold body—
white, red, and likewise black— and attained the state of the triple form (Trimūrti).
With that auspicious Brahman-form, she indeed creates progeny;
with a gentle appearance, O lady of beautiful hips, according to the ordinance of Brahma's creation.
She who is beautiful in her crimson hue, slender-waisted, and holds the conch and discus—that goddess is known as the portion (kalā) of Vaiṣṇavī;
she protects the entire universe and is celebrated as Viṣṇumāyā. || 28 ||
That goddess who, with her dark complexion, possesses a fierce form and holds a trident, and who is formidable with her fangs— that goddess indeed destroys the universe.
That goddess who is the creation of Brahmā, white-hued and radiant,
she— the highly fortunate maiden with eyes like the petals of a vast lotus—
having immediately taken leave of Brahmā, vanished right there.
That goddess, the giver of boons, vanished and went to the White Mountain to perform great and intense penance, desiring to attain omnipresence.
That maiden who was Vaiṣṇavī, having also taken leave of Keśava,
went to Mount Mandara to perform a most difficult penance.
That auspicious Kṛṣṇā, the large-eyed one, fierce and formidable with her fangs,
went to the excellent Nīla mountain to perform penance.
Then, after a long time, the Lord of Creatures began to create progeny; as he was creating, his strength increased.
When that mental progeny of his did not increase, he then reflected: "Why is it that my progeny does not grow in this manner? (35)
Then, O lady of excellent vows, Brahmā meditated with his heart through the practice of yoga; reflecting thus, the god perceived that maiden on the White Mountain (Śvetaparvata),
performing a very great penance, her sins consumed by that austerity.
Then Brahmā went to that place where the lotus-eyed lady was performing penance; having seen her, he spoke these words.
Brahmā said:
"O blessed lady, what austerity is being performed? It appears fitting for some purpose.
I am pleased with you, O large-eyed one; what boon shall I grant you? (38)
Sṛṣṭi said:
"O Blessed One, being situated in only one place, I am unable to remain [there] properly;
therefore, desiring omnipresence, I ask you for this boon. (39)
Thus addressed by the goddess Sṛṣṭi, Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, then said to that goddess: "You shall become omnipresent."
When she had been addressed thus by him, that lotus-eyed creation—
indeed, that lotus-eyed goddess— attained dissolution into his lap;
from that time forward, the creation of Brahmā began to flourish.
There were seven mind-born sons of Brahmā; others among them were rich in asceticism (tapodhana).
From them came yet others, and from them still more; thus the fourfold collection of beings—the creation of all things stationary and moving—is established everywhere.
Whatever consists of speech in the world, and whatever exists in the universe—whether stationary or moving—all that has been established by creation as past and future at all times. (43)
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter in the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 89.
Śrī Varāha said: Listen, O lady of excellent hips, to another great rite concerning that goddess who was designated as the triple power (triśakti) by Śiva, the supreme lord.
In that regard, emanation was previously described as being white in color and possessing its own essential form;
it is renowned as the "Single Syllable" (Ekākṣarā), auspicious and composed of all syllables.

In some places the Goddess is celebrated as Vāgīśā, and elsewhere she is Sarasvatī; she alone is the Goddess Vidyeśvarī, and she alone is in some places Amitākṣarā; she alone is Jñānavidhi in some places, and she alone is the Goddess Vibhāvarī.
O large-eyed one, O lady of beautiful countenance, those names which are auspicious and those which arise from knowledge— these are to be understood as belonging to her.
She who is Vaiṣṇavī, large-eyed, red-colored, and beautiful in form—
she is declared to be the other [form], Raudrī, who is both supreme and non-supreme.
All these three are accomplished for one who knows Rudra in truth;
O lady of excellent hips, this [Goddess], though one, is remembered as threefold according to her omnipresence.
O lady of excellent hips, this ancient creation has been described to you;
by it, this entire world, both moving and unmoving, is pervaded. (7)
The Grandfather (Brahmā) offered a hymn of praise to that Goddess which was equal to the creation he had first brought forth from his unmanifest birth.
Brahmā said: Be victorious, O Goddess who are born of Truth, O eternal one, O imperishable one! You who pervade all, O Mother of all beings, O Great Sovereign of all creatures! (9)
O you who possess all-knowledge, O lady of excellent limbs, you are the bestower of all accomplishments;
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, you are the source of success, wisdom, and progeny. 10.
You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, O Goddess; you are the source of origin, O fair-faced one. You are established as the syllable Om, O Goddess, and you alone are the source of the Vedas.
O lady of lovely countenance, you are the source of origin for the gods, the dānavas, the yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas, as well as for animals and plants.
O Sovereign of the Gods, you are Vidyā, the Mistress of Knowledge, the perfected one, and the universally renowned;
O lady of noble form, you are omniscient and the bestower of all spiritual accomplishments.
O Goddess who pervades all, whose doubts have vanished, who destroys all enemies, the sovereign of all vidyās— salutations to you, the bringer of auspiciousness!
O fair-faced one, O mistress of creatures, for him who approaches a woman who has bathed after her menses after praising you,
offspring will surely be born through your grace—
you who are Svarūpā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, and the deluder of all enemies. 15.
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 90.
Śrī Varāha said:
The goddess who has gone to Mount Mandara to perform penance is the Vaiṣṇavī,
the supreme Rājasa Śakti, who observes the vow of Kumārī.
She performed austerities alone in the beautiful city of Viśālā;
as she was practicing penance, after a long time, her mind became agitated.
From that agitation arose maidens with gentle eyes,
with dark, curly hair-ends, with lips like the *bimba* fruit and long eyes;
they were unrestrained by their hips and girdles, richly adorned with anklets, and possessed of great luster.
When the Goddess’s mind was thus agitated, hundreds of thousands and tens of millions of such women with various faces quickly rose up.
Having seen the maidens, that auspicious goddess, on that very mountain,
created by means of her ascetic power a city filled with hundreds of palaces.
With its broad streets adorned by golden palaces,
the houses possessed inner courtyards with jeweled staircases,
latticed windows made of gems, and nearby groves.
There are countless palaces and likewise maidens on that mountain;
O beautiful one, I shall describe the names of the principal maidens.
Vidyutprabhā, Candrakānti, Sūryakānti, and another, Gambhīrā, Cārukeśī, Sujātā, and Muñjakeśinī. (8)
Ghṛtācī, Urvaśī, and another, Śaśinī adorned with virtue;
Cārukanyā, Viśālākṣī, Dhanyā, and Pīnapayodharā. (9)
Candraprabhā, Girisutā, as well as Sūryaprabhā, Amṛtā, Svayaṃprabhā, Cārumukhī, Śivadūtī, and Vibhāvarī. (10)
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā—
these and hundreds of other maidens were in that supreme city.
All the auspicious female attendants of the Goddess bear nooses and goads;
surrounded by them, the auspicious Goddess is seated upon a lion-throne.
Fanned by women with white whisks, that graceful lady,
having undertaken the vow of lifelong maidenhood, prepared herself to perform austerities.
That highly fortunate woman, standing in the prime of youth with full and rounded breasts,
was adorned with garlands of campaka, aśoka, punnāga, and nāgakesara flowers.
The Goddess was worshipped on all her limbs, saluted by sages and gods,
and honored on every side by excellent women and maidens.
While the goddess, who enjoys all her limbs, remained engaged in penance,
Nārada, the son of Brahmā, arrived there.
Seeing that son of Brahmā, whose wealth was his asceticism, the goddess suddenly said this to Vidyutprabhā: "Let a seat be offered;
let water for the feet and water for sipping be given to him quickly. (17)
Thus addressed by the goddess, the auspicious maiden Vidyutprabhā then offered a seat, water for the feet, and the guest-offering to Nārada.
Then, seeing the sage Nārada seated and bowing down,
the Goddess, filled with great joy, spoke these words.
"Welcome, O best of sages! From which world have you come here? Tell me, what is your purpose, what is your business? Let there be no delay for you. (20)
Thus addressed by the goddess, Nārada, the knower of the worlds, then spoke:
"From the world of Brahmā to the world of Indra, from there to the world of Rudra, and then to the mountain."
"Therefore, O auspicious Goddess of the gods, I have come here to see you.
Having spoken thus, the illustrious sage gazed upon that goddess.
Having seen her for a moment, O Goddess of gods, Nārada was struck with wonder:
"Oh, what beauty! Oh, what radiance! Oh, what fortitude! Oh, what youth! (23)
"Ah, how free from desire the Goddess is!"— thus he fell into despondency regarding the gods,
gandharvas, siddhas, yakṣas, kinnaras, and rākṣasas.
"Such beauty as this is not seen anywhere among other women.
Thinking thus in his mind, Nārada was filled with wonder.
Having bowed to the boon-granting goddess, he leapt into the sky and,
filled with haste, went to the city ruled by the lord of the Daityas.
O Mistress of Beings, the Blessed One reached the city situated within the ocean by means of that [vehicle] called Mahiṣa,
and there he encountered the Asura in the form of a buffalo.
Having seen that great hero, who had obtained the boon and was the destroyer of the celestial armies,
the sage who wanders among the worlds was then honored by him with devotion.
With a joyful heart, Nārada described to him the unsurpassed beauty of the goddess exactly as it was, according to the facts, just as he had seen it in the city of the gods.
Nārada said:
O Lord of Asuras, listen with a concentrated mind to this one jewel among maidens,
by whom the three worlds, including all things moving and stationary, were obtained through a boon.
O Daitya, I have come from the world of Brahmā to Mount Mandara;
there I beheld the city of the Goddess, crowded with hundreds of maidens.
Among them, that maiden who was the foremost, a female ascetic observing vows,
was not seen as her equal among any of the gods, daityas, or yakṣas.
O Daitya, such was that auspicious woman; however, while wandering through the midst of the forest, I have never before seen her like that.
And all the gods, Gandharvas, sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas,
as well as other leaders of the Daityas, paid her homage.
Having seen that boon-granting goddess, I have come here quickly;
for no one can conquer her without first defeating the gods and the Gandharvas. (35)
Having spoken thus and remained for a moment, the wise Nārada took leave of him and departed by way of disappearance at that very instant, returning just as he had come.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 91.
Śrī Varāha said: When Nārada had departed, the Daitya, his mind filled with wonder after hearing that auspicious account spoken from the mouth of Nārada, began to reflect upon it. || 1 ||
Reflecting on that very matter, the best of the Daityas found no peace;
his great minister Alaṃśarman, who was possessed of great strength, brought [him there]. || 2 ||
He had eight ministers who were brave, wise in policy, and highly learned:
Praghasa, Vighasa, Śaṅkukarṇa, Vibhāvasu, Vidyunmālī, Sumālī, Parjanya, and Krūra. (3)
These excellent ministers of his have been proclaimed primarily;
they spoke to the seated lord of the Dānavas, "Let what must be done be performed."
Having heard those words of theirs, the mighty lord of the Dānavas,
having reached a firm resolve through Nārada for the sake of obtaining the maiden, spoke.
Mahiṣa said:
"The young girl was described to me by the great sage Nārada;
yet that beautiful woman cannot be obtained without first conquering the lord of the gods."
For this purpose, sirs, please deliberate and speak:
how may that young woman be obtained, and how may the gods be conquered?
Tell me all of that quickly. (7)
Thus addressed, they all then spoke straightforwardly;
having consulted together, they all said, "O Lord, we shall speak."
Thus addressed, Praghasa spoke to the lord of the Dānavas:
"O Daitya, that great virtuous woman whom Nārada described to you is the supreme goddess Śakti, the Vaiṣṇavī who sustains the worlds."
A king who desires to seize the wife of his guru, the wife of another king, or the women of his vassals, as well as those who should not be approached, perishes through such forbidden sexual conduct.
Thus addressed by Praghasa, Vighasa spoke these words:
"O King, what has been said by Praghasa regarding that goddess is correct."

Even if there is indeed a consensus and the matter has reached the mind as a memory, a maiden must always be chosen by those desiring victory; for the selection of a maiden can never be accomplished by one acting independently. (12)
"O best of ministers, if my words please you,
then let the ministers go and entreat that auspicious goddess."
"Let us first entreat that noble-souled one who is her kinsman with gentle words;
thereafter we shall proceed to the act of giving [the bride];
after that we shall employ dissension, and then punishment in due order. (14)
If she cannot be obtained by this gradual method, then we shall go forth armored and seize that auspicious lady by force. (15)
When Vighasa had spoken thus, all the remaining ministers,
praising his words, spoke auspiciously with voices full of joy.
"What you have said regarding that lovely-faced woman is excellent;
let that very thing be done quickly—let a messenger be dispatched there. (17)
He who is knowledgeable in all scriptures and principles, pure, and endowed with valor—having learned of that goddess from him by way of her complexion, form, and qualities; || 18 ||
Having understood that goddess through her prowess, heroism, audacity, strength, circle of kinsmen, completeness, position, and means— having thus known her, let the task then be undertaken. (19)
Then, O lady of beautiful hips, they immediately praised those words of the Daitya, saying "Excellent! Excellent!", and commended Vighasa, the best of ministers.
Having praised that messenger, they all proceeded to give instructions to the illustrious and auspicious Vidyutprabha, who was skilled in great illusions.
Having dismissed that messenger, Vighasa spoke these words:
"O Lord, let the lords of the Dānavas arm themselves with their fourfold army;
let victory over the celestial host be achieved."
When you, O Śakra, have arrived, that maiden— who was terrified by the prowess of the Asura king when the gods were defeated— will come under your control.
When all the world-protectors have been conquered, as well as the hosts of Maruts,
and when the Nāgas, Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and Gandharvas have been defeated on all sides,
you alone shall become Indra, along with the Rudras, Vasus, and Ādityas.
A hundred maidens of Indra, the wives of gods and gandharvas, come under your control; she too shall be brought entirely under your sway.
Thus addressed, the Daitya then spoke to his general,
Virūpākṣa, who was the color of a great cloud and possessed the luster of black collyrium.
"Let the army of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry be brought quickly, so that I may conquer in battle the gods along with the Gandharvas, who are otherwise difficult to defeat. (27)
When this was said, Virūpākṣa, the commander-in-chief, then quickly brought forth a vast,
infinite, and unconquerable army.
Each one of those dānavas there was equal to Vajrahasta in battle;
each one vied with the gods, desiring to conquer them by his own strength.
Among those who were the principal ones, there were nine crores of Arbudas;
the power of even one of them was as great as that of Artha.
Many thousands of those high-souled Daityas,
those skilled strikers, then held an assembly without agitation;
they set out on their march with the intent to destroy the army of the gods.
With diverse vehicles, various banners at their peaks, manifold weapons, and many forms of fierce appearance,
the Daityas, desiring to conquer the Suras, rose up on high.
They danced, their hands formidable as they grasped their weapons.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 92.
Śrī Varāha said:
Then the Daitya Mahiṣa, who could assume any form at will and possessed great strength,
mounted a rutting elephant and desired to go to Mount Meru.
Having reached Indra’s city, the lord of the Daityas rushed toward Śatakratu who was there with the gods; thereupon, the gods were filled with wrath.
Taking up their own weapons, especially their mounts,
and mounting them for battle, the Asuras rushed forward with great joy.
A tumultuous battle, hair-raising and terrible, broke out between those fierce warriors as they roared at one another.
There, Añjana, Nīlakukṣi, Meghavarṇa, Balāhaka,
Udarākṣa, Lalāṭākṣa, Subhīma, and Bhīmavikrama—
these eight Daityas, along with Svarbhānu, rushed against the Vasus in battle.
And likewise, there were twelve other Daityas corresponding in number;
now hear from me the names of the foremost among those excellent Daityas who became the Ādityas. (6)
Bhīma, Dhvaṅkṣa, Dhvastakarṇa, and likewise Śaṅkukarṇa;
Vajrakāya of great heroism, and likewise Vidyunmālī.
Raktākṣa, Bhīmadaṃṣṭra, and likewise Vidyujjihva;
Atikāya, Mahākāya, Dīrghabāhu, and Kṛtāntaka. || 8 ||
These twelve lords of the Daityas, having taken their own armies, rushed against the Ādityas in battle; likewise, other Dānavas also, being provoked,
calmly rushed against the Rudras in due order.
Kāla, Kṛtānta, Raktākṣa, Haraṇa, Mitrahā, Anila,
Yajñahā, Brahmahā, Goghna, Strīghna, and likewise Saṃvartaka.
Thus, these eleven lords of the Daityas,
intoxicated by battle and possessed of terrible prowess, rushed toward the Rudras in their respective order.
The remaining Daityas rushed against the remaining gods as was appropriate;
the Daitya Mahiṣa himself, however, charged at Indra with great speed.
And that powerful Daitya, arrogant due to the boon from Brahmā,
was such that he could not be slain in battle even by the wielder of the Pināka bow himself.
The Asuras and Yātudhānas were struck down severely by the Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, and Rudras; they were merely there to complete the number.
Even the armies of the gods were slain by the asuras in battle;
when this had occurred and the lord of the gods was thus broken, the deities fled in retreat.
Afflicted by various weapons— spears, pattisas, and mallets—
the gods, tormented by the asuras, went to the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 93.
Śrī Varāha said: Then the Daitya Vidyutprabha, having been thus dispatched as a messenger,
went into the presence of the Goddess and spoke to that woman of slender waist.
Having prostrated and become composed, he stood with humility in the assembly hall crowded with hundreds of maidens, and then spoke these words.
Vidyutprabhā said:
O Goddess, formerly in the first creation you were a sage born of Ka;
you became the powerful friend of Sarasvatī, known by the name Supārśva.
To him was born the highly effulgent and powerful Sindhudvīpa;
for he performed intense penance in the excellent city of Māhiṣmatī.
While he was performing severe penance without food, O beautiful lady,
the first daughter of Vipracitti— resembling the daughters of the gods,
renowned as Māhiṣmatī, and peerless on earth in beauty— [approached him]. || 5 ||

While wandering at her pleasure, surrounded by her friends, she arrived by chance at the valley of Mount Mandara; there she beheld the penance grove of the sage named Ambara, which was garlanded with various kinds of trees.

It was adorned with various bowers of creepers, as well as *vakula*, *lakuca*, *candana*, *spandana*, *śāla*, and *sarala* trees; indeed, it was beautified by the great-souled one with diverse forest groves.
Having seen that beautiful and auspicious hermitage, the daughter of the Asura,
the lovely Māhiṣmatī, the passionate woman, began to reflect.
Having personally terrified this ascetic in the hermitage,
I remain here playing with my friends, highly honored by them.
Having reflected thus,
O Sovereign of the Universe, that queen-consort became a buffalo together with her female companions, bearing sharp tips upon her horns.
To terrify that sage, the lovely-faced woman went with them;
but he, having recognized her through his eye of wisdom, became filled with wrath toward the demoness and cursed the fair-eyed one. (11)
"Since you, assuming the form of a buffalo, terrify me, therefore, O evildoer, become a buffalo for a hundred years! (12)
Thus addressed by her friends, she,
trembling, fell at his feet, pleading for him to put an end to the curse.
Having heard those words of hers, that sage, filled with compassion,
brought an end to her curse and spoke these words to her.
"O blessed lady, by giving birth to a son with this very same form, your curse shall come to an end; my word cannot be false. (15)
Having been addressed thus, she went to the excellent bank of the Narmadā,
where the great ascetic Sindhudvīpa was performing severe penance.
There, a daughter of the Daityas named Indumatī, who was exceedingly beautiful,
was seen by that sage bathing naked in the water.
That sage of great asceticism discharged his semen into a stone trough.
Seeing it in Māhiṣmatī—divine-scented and fragrant—he then said this to his female companions: "I shall drink this auspicious water."
Having spoken thus, she drank that semen produced by the sage;
she conceived from the seed of the sage and then gave birth to a virtuous son.
Her son was born wise, endowed with great strength and prowess,
known by the name Mahiṣa, who increased the lineage of Brahmā.
O Goddess, he, the crusher of the celestial armies, now seeks you as his bride.

"O sinless one, having conquered even the gods in battle and [conquered] the three worlds, that great asura, being well-pleased, will give everything to you, O Goddess. By offering yourself to him, O Goddess, perform a great service. (21)
Thus addressed by that messenger, the beautiful goddess then laughed heartily; she did not say anything at all.
While she was laughing, that messenger beheld the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, within her womb; he became utterly bewildered at that very moment.
Then the queen’s doorkeeper, named Jayā,
who was exceedingly radiant and slender-waisted, spoke the words that had been held in the queen's heart.
Jayā said:
"That which was indeed spoken by you regarding one who seeks a maiden—
if her vow of virginity is indeed lifelong— then [let it be so]."
Moreover, there are other maidens here who follow in the footsteps of the Goddess. || 25 ||
Not even one of them can be obtained, much less the auspicious goddess herself;
go quickly, O messenger, lest something else happen to you. (26)
Having been addressed thus, the messenger departed; meanwhile, the great sage Nārada, a man of immense austerity, arrived swiftly through the sky, dancing loudly.
Saying "By good fortune! By good fortune! as he spoke to that goddess of auspicious eyes, he, having been honored, sat down upon an excellent seat and then addressed her.
Having prostrated before the Goddess, the Sovereign of All, the one of great asceticism said:
"O Goddess, I have been sent into your presence by the gratified gods."
O Goddess, the immortals have been conquered by the Daitya named Mahiṣa;
O Goddess, that king of the Daityas has made an effort to seize you.
Having been thus addressed by the gods, O lady of excellent countenance, I inform you:
O Great Goddess, remain steadfast and strike down that Daitya.
Having spoken thus, Nārada immediately vanished and departed according to his own will;
and the goddess said to all those maidens, "Prepare yourselves! (32).
Then, by the command of the Goddess, all those highly fortunate maidens assumed terrible forms; bearing swords, shields, and bows,
they stood ready for the sake of battle in order to destroy the Daityas.
Then the entire Daitya army, quickly abandoning the host of gods,
rushed to where that great force of armed women belonging to the Goddess was stationed.
Then those proud maidens fought with the Dānavas;
in an instant, that fourfold army was struck down by them.
There, the heads of some were severed and fell; others had their chests torn open, and flesh-eaters drank their blood. (36)
Other leaders of the Daityas, having become headless trunks, danced;
thus, in an instant, all those evil-minded ones were destroyed.
Others all fled to where that Mahiṣāsura was.
Then the entire great army of the Daityas raised a cry of "Alas!
Alas! Seeing it thus thrown into confusion, Mahiṣa spoke these words:
"O General, why indeed has this army been broken before me? (38)
Then a Daitya named Yajñahanu, who had the form of an elephant, said: "This [sacrifice] has indeed been shattered on all sides by these young maidens. (39)
Then Mahiṣa, seizing his mace with speed, rushed toward those fair-eyed maidens; the impetuous one ran after them with great force.
Wherever that goddess, worshipped by gods and gandharvas, stood,
to that very place the asura advanced;
and seeing him approaching, she made herself twenty cubits tall.
A bow, a sword, as well as a spear, arrows, a trident, a mace, as well as an axe, a hand-drum, and likewise a large bell;
a śataghnī, a terrible mallet, a bhuśuṇḍī, and even a lance. || 42 ||
The mace, the discus, the bhindipāla, as well as the staff, the noose, the banner, and the lotus—these constitute the twenty [weapons]. || 43 ||
Having become a twenty-armed goddess, armored and mounted upon a lion,
she remembered Rudra, the Lord of Gods, the fierce cause of universal dissolution.
Then Rudra himself, whose banner bears the bull, arrived at that very place;
having been saluted by her, he was thus petitioned: "I shall conquer all the Daityas."
"O eternal God of gods, by your mere presence alone [this shall be accomplished]";
having spoken thus to all the asuras, the Supreme Goddess conquered them.
Having released that one buffalo and killed the rest, he pursued him;
meanwhile, the Goddess also saw him from there, and he too fled.
In one place the lord of the Daityas fought, and in another he fled; in one place again he engaged in battle, and in another he desisted once more. 48.
In this manner, O beautiful one, ten thousand divine years passed for him as he fought with her; meanwhile,
the entire universe wandered about with a terrified mind.
Then, after a long time, on the great mountain Śataśṛṅga,
that best of Daityas was struck down with a trident after being stepped upon by his feet.
He severed the head with his sword; and there, a man standing within emerged and, through the falling of the goddess’s weapon, departed for heaven.
Then all the hosts of gods, having seen Mahiṣa defeated,
together with Brahmā, offered praise to the Goddess with hearts full of satisfaction.
The gods said:
"Obeisance to you, O Goddess, highly fortunate one, profound, of fearsome appearance;
established in victory, perfected in the doctrine of stability, three-eyed, facing all directions! (53)
O Goddess who art knowledge and ignorance, victory and that which is to be conquered, O crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura;
O omnipresent one, O sovereign of all gods, O you of universal form, O Vaiṣṇavī! 54.
O Goddess who art free from sorrow, eternal, with eyes as beautiful as lotus petals, established in the vow of pure being, fierce in form, and radiant! 55.
O Goddess who bestows supernatural power and accomplishment; O Knowledge, O Unmanifest, O Immortal, O Auspicious One;
O Śāṅkarī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Brāhmī; O You who are saluted by all the gods! 56.
O you who hold a bell in your hand, whose weapon is the trident, the crusher of the great buffalo-demon;
O you of fierce form, the odd-eyed one, the great illusion, the streamer of nectar! 57.
O Goddess, you who are for the welfare of all beings, who consist of all beings, and who are eternal;
you are the mother of sciences, the Purāṇas, and the arts, and the sustainer of the world.

O auspicious one, you alone are the refuge for all the secrets of the gods and for all beings who have entered [the path], O Goddess—whether in knowledge or ignorance—for the sake of prosperity, O Mother!
O Virūpākṣī, likewise O Kṣānti, O you who are undisturbed within the agitated waters! 59.
Homage be to you, O Great Goddess; homage be to you, O Supreme Sovereign!
Homage to you, the eternal, imperishable, and immutable source of all the gods.
O Goddess, Supreme Sovereign, for those who take refuge in you, nothing inauspicious shall arise, even in the perils of battle. (61)
And whoever, O Goddess, being self-controlled, shall always recite this hymn when there is a terrible fear of tigers, or likewise a fear of thieves and kings; (62)
O Goddess, even that man who, though bound in fetters, shall remember you— he too shall be liberated from his bonds and dwell happily and at ease.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter in the glorious Varāha Purāṇa, the scripture of the Blessed One. 94.

Only the great Daitya Ruru remained in that great battle;

That terrible illusion, which deludes all the gods, increased;
and by it the gods were so bewildered that they immediately fell into a deep sleep.
And in the battle, the Goddess struck that Daitya with her trident.
O lady of auspicious eyes, when he was thus struck by her, both the shield and the head of that Daitya became completely separated from one another.

She who is the most terrible among all beings, the goddess who is the Supreme Sovereign,

For her attendants, goddesses numbering in the tens of millions,

Those who were not distracted by the Asuras, being hungry, spoke to that goddess:
